a11_0034345.text: Okay. We're pressing on with the procedure.

a11_0034345.speaker: McCandless
a11_0034345.text: And 11, Houston. We have a request for you. On the Service Module secondary propellant fuel pressurization valve: as a precautionary measure, we'd like you to momentarily cycle the four switches to the Close position and then release. As you know, we have no TM or talkback on these valve positions, and it's conceivable that one of them might also have been moved into a different position by the shock of separation. Over.

a11_0034345.speaker: Collins
a11_0034345.text: Okay. Good idea. That's being done.

a11_0034345.speaker: McCandless
a11_0034345.text: Houston. Roger. Out.

a11_0034345.speaker: McCandless
a11_0034345.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We're doing a non-propulsive vent on the booster at the present time. You may see some sort of a cloud coming out of it. And when you're ready, I have your evasive maneuver PAD.

a11_0034345.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0034345.text: Rog, And it's coming out.

a11_0034345.speaker: McCandless
a11_0034345.text: Roger. Out.

a11_0034345.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0034345.text: It's a haze. It's going by toward our minus-X direction, and several small particles are moving along with it. The actual velocity is fairly high - at least it appears to be high. And we've got an O 2 high [alarm] - flow high right now.

a11_0034345.speaker: McCandless
a11_0034345.text: Houston. Roger. Out.

a11_0034345.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0034345.text: And Houston, you might be interested that out my left-hand window right now, I can observe the entire continent of North America, Alaska, over the Pole, down to the Yucatan Peninsula, Cuba, northern part of South America, and then I run out of window.

a11_0034345.speaker: McCandless
a11_0034345.text: Roger, we copy.

a11_0034345.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0034345.text: That was Neil Armstrong with that report.

a11_0035712.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0035712.text: Hay, Houston, Apollo 11. All 12 latches are locked.

a11_0035712.speaker: McCandless
a11_0035712.text: Roger. 11, this is Houston. Understand 12 latches locked.

a11_0035712.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0035712.text: That was Buzz Aldrin reporting that all 12 of the latches in the docking mechanism had locked.

a11_0035712.speaker: McCandless
a11_0035712.text: 11, Houston. Whenever you're possessed of a free moment there, we've got this Evasive Maneuver PAD.

a11_0035712.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0035712.text: Go ahead, Houston. Apollo 11 is ready to copy.

a11_0035712.speaker: McCandless
a11_0035712.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Evasive Maneuver: SPS G&N; 63481, plus 0.95, minus 0.20; GETI 004:40:01.00; plus 0005.1, plus all balls, plus 0019.0; roll is your option; pitch, 213, 357; Noun 44 is NA; Delta-V T is 0019.7, 0:03, 0015.2. The rest of the PAD is NA. No ullage. LM weight, 33290. Readback. Over.

a11_0035712.speaker: McCandless
a11_0035712.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Standing by for your readback. Over. [No answer.]

a11_0035712.speaker: McCandless
a11_0035712.text: 11, Houston. Do you read? Over. [No answer.]

a11_0035712.speaker: McCandless
a11_0035712.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Do you read? Over.

a11_0035712.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0035712.text: All of a sudden there, we had a little click, and the signal strength began to start dropping off. Your transmissions were cut off very abruptly. How do you read now?

a11_0035712.speaker: McCandless
a11_0035712.text: Roger. Loud and clear. We had a handover to Madrid about the time I was - I guess halfway through the PAD. If you could give me the last value you read, I'll pick up there. Over.

a11_0035712.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0035712.text: Okay. Start with Delta-V Z . Over.

a11_0035712.speaker: McCandless
a11_0035712.text: Roger. Delta-V Z is plus 0019.0; roll, your option; pitch, 213, 357; and Noun 44 is NA. Delta-V T 0019.7, 0:03, 0015.2. The rest of the PAD is NA, and no ullage. LM weight 33290. Read back. Over.

a11_0035712.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0035712.text: Roger, Houston. Evasive Maneuver, SPS G&N; 63481, plus 0.95, minus 0.20; 004:40:01.00; plus 0005.1, plus all zeros, plus 0019.0; roll, crew option, 213, 357; NA; 0019.7, 0:03, 0015.2; no ullage; LM weight, 33290. Over.

a11_0035712.speaker: McCandless
a11_0035712.text: 11, this is Houston. Readback correct. Out.

a11_0041333.speaker: Collins
a11_0041333.text: We'd like to arm our logic switches.

a11_0041333.speaker: Collins
a11_0041333.text: Okay. Mark logic 1 and 2 armed. [Long pause.]

a11_0041333.speaker: McCandless
a11_0041333.text: Roger. We show the logic arm, and you're Go for Pyro arm.

a11_0041638.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0041638.text: Houston, we're ready for LM ejection.

a11_0041638.speaker: McCandless
a11_0041638.text: Roger. You're Go for LM ejection.

a11_0041638.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0041638.text: Houston, we are Sep[arat]ed. We have a Cryo Press light.

a11_0041638.speaker: McCandless
a11_0041638.text: Roger, 11. We recommend you turn the O 2 fans on manually and ensure that the O 2 heaters are in the Automatic position.

a11_0041638.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0041638.text: Roger. O 2 heaters are On, and we're going to cycle the O 2 fans now.

a11_0041638.speaker: McCandless
a11_0041638.text: Roger. O 2 heaters to Auto, or you can watch them in the On position, and O 2 fans manual On.

a11_0042816.speaker: McCandless
a11_0042816.text: Roger. In reference to your question on RCS usage; it looks like you are about 18, maybe 20 pounds below nominal at the present time. No problem at all. Over.

a11_0042816.speaker: Collins
a11_0042816.text: I wanted to be 18 or 20 pounds above nominal, babe.

a11_0043740.speaker: McCandless
a11_0043740.text: 11, Houston. Your systems are looking good. We're standing by for the burn.

a11_0043740.speaker: Collins
a11_0043740.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Could you confirm that pitch gimbal motor number 1 turned off? We just shut all four off, and we got a questionable indication on the ECS on pitch 1.

a11_0043740.speaker: McCandless
a11_0043740.text: Roger. Stand by a second. [Long pause.]

a11_0043740.speaker: Collins
a11_0043740.text: [Faint] Houston, did you copy our residuals?

a11_0043740.speaker: McCandless
a11_0043740.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Stand by, please.

a11_0043740.speaker: Collins
a11_0043740.text: Go ahead, Houston. You copy our residuals?

a11_0043740.speaker: McCandless
a11_0043740.text: Roger. We got 0.0 and 0.2, it looks like.

a11_0043740.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0043740.text: We had 0.1 while ago. It's - just went to 0.2.

a11_0043740.speaker: McCandless
a11_0043740.text: (Laughing) Okay.

a11_0043740.speaker: Collins
a11_0043740.text: That EMS Delta-V counter is minus 4.0.

a11_0043740.speaker: McCandless
a11_0043740.text: Minus 4.0. Roger.

a11_0043740.speaker: Collins
a11_0043740.text: And how about pitch gimbal 1? Can you confirm that Off?

a11_0043740.speaker: McCandless
a11_0043740.text: Can you stand by just a second on that? At the present time we cannot confirm it Off. We saw a current drop indicating that several gimbal motors had gone off. We'll be back with you in just a second on it. Over.

a11_0043740.speaker: Collins
a11_0043740.text: Okay. If necessary, we can recycle it.

a11_0043740.speaker: McCandless
a11_0043740.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. If you go ahead and cycle pitch gimbal motor number 1 On and then Off and give us a Mark, and we'll tell you what we see. Over.

a11_0043740.speaker: Collins
a11_0043740.text: Okay, fine. It's coming back on. Ready.

a11_0043740.speaker: Collins
a11_0043740.text: Mark.

a11_0043740.speaker: Collins
a11_0043740.text: And it's going back off. Ready.

a11_0043740.speaker: Collins
a11_0043740.text: Mark.

a11_0043740.speaker: Collins
a11_0043740.text: And that time we got an onboard indication, Houston. Thank you a lot.

a11_0043740.speaker: McCandless
a11_0043740.text: Roger. We confirm that it is Off.

a11_0043740.speaker: Collins
a11_0043740.text: Yeah. We do likewise.

a11_0044400.speaker: Collins
a11_0044400.text: And it's going back off. Ready.

a11_0044400.speaker: Collins
a11_0044400.text: And that time we got an onboard indication, Houston. Thank you a lot.

a11_0044400.speaker: McCandless
a11_0044400.text: Roger. We confirm that it is Off.

a11_0044400.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0044400.text: This is Apollo Control at 4 hours, 44 minutes. A news conference at Kennedy Space Center is about to begin. We will take down the live circuits and tape air to ground during this news conference, play it back after the conference. This is Mission Control, Houston.

a11_0044533.speaker: Collins
a11_0044533.text: Houston, Apollo 11. We're starting our maneuver to observe the S-IVB slingshot.

a11_0044533.speaker: McCandless
a11_0044533.text: Roger, 11. We've got an updated attitude for you on the slingshot observation.

a11_0044533.speaker: McCandless
a11_0044533.text: Roger. Roll 002.5, pitch 289.3, yaw 357.5, and there's also an update, minor correction, to your attitude for the P52. Over.

a11_0044533.speaker: Collins
a11_0044533.text: Roger. I have roll 2.5, pitch 289.3, and yaw 357.5. Over.

a11_0044533.speaker: McCandless
a11_0044533.text: Roger. And for your P52 and optics calibration, it'll be roll 346.5, pitch 345.0, yaw 007.8. Over.

a11_0044933.speaker: McCandless
a11_0044933.text: Roger. We're going to go ahead and enable the S-IVB for the slingshot maneuver. The LOX dump will start about 12 minutes from now. Over.

a11_0044933.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0044933.text: Okay, LOX dump about - I guess that'll make it about [GET 5 hours and] 01, huh?

a11_0044933.speaker: McCandless
a11_0044933.text: Right. I'll try to give you a little closer update as we approach it.

a11_0044933.speaker: McCandless
a11_0044933.text: And, 11, for you information, the magnitude of Midcourse Correction number 1, if we burn, looks like about 17 feet per second [5.2 m/s]. We're presently considering not burning it. This would make midcourse correction 2 tomorrow about 21.3 [fps, 6.5 m/s]. Over.

a11_0044933.speaker: McCandless
a11_0044933.text: Roger. You're looking good down here. [Long pause.]

a11_0045735.speaker: Collins
a11_0045735.text: Houston, Apollo 11. We're - We've completed our maneuver to observe the slingshot attitude, but we don't see anything - no Earth and no S-IVB.

a11_0045735.speaker: McCandless
a11_0045735.text: Roger. Stand by. In GET, I have a LOX dump start time for you. It's supposed to start at 5 plus 03 plus 07, and stop at 5 plus 04 plus 55. Ullage burn starts at 5 plus 37 plus 47, stops at 5 plus 42 plus 27. Over.

a11_0051258.speaker: McCandless
a11_0051258.text: Roger. If you'll give us Accept and stay in P00, we'll set your trunnion bias to zero. And, I have a plan for balancing your oxygen cryos. Over.

a11_0051258.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0051258.text: Houston, Apollo 11. We've got the, uh, what appears to be the S-IVB in sight, at, oh, I'd estimate a couple of miles away. It's at our number 5 window and the dump appears to be coming out of two radially opposite directions from the S-IVB.

a11_0051258.speaker: McCandless
a11_0051258.text: Roger. They're continuing with the non-propulsive vent from the liquid oxygen tank. It would be radially opposite, there. And Booster tells me it's the continuous vent system. They're also dumping a small amount of fuel at this time. We've got about 23½ minutes or so until the APS burn. Over.

a11_0051258.speaker: McCandless
a11_0051258.text: 11, Houston. We have a recommended configuration for your Cryo switches to even up the load between oxygen tanks 1 and 2. Over.

a11_0051258.speaker: McCandless
a11_0051258.text: Okay. You're coming in very weakly there. We're recommending O 2 tank 1 heater Off, O 2 tank 2 heater to Auto, O 2 tanks 1 and 2 fans both Off, H1 - H 2 tank 1 heaters to Auto, and H 2 tank 2 heaters to Off. Over.

a11_0051258.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0051258.text: Rog. We have that except the last one was H 2 fans to Off. Is that affirm? [Long pause.]

a11_0051258.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0051258.text: We have - the configuration we have now is, Hydrogen heaters: we got 1 Auto, 2 Off. Oxygen heaters; 1 Off, 2 Auto. And we have all the fans Off.

a11_0051258.speaker: McCandless
a11_0051258.text: This is Houston. Roger. We concur. Out. [Pause.]

a11_0051258.speaker: McCandless
a11_0051258.text: Eleven, this is Houston. We've completed the trunnion zero bias setting. You can retrieve the computer and go to Block.

a11_0052200.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0052200.text: Down in the Control Center you might want to join us in wishing Dr. George Mueller a happy birthday.

a11_0052200.speaker: McCandless
a11_0052200.text: Roger. We're standing by for your birthday greeting. [Pause.]

a11_0052818.speaker: McCandless
a11_0052818.text: Roger. At your convenience, we'd like to get a waste-water dump to 5 per cent remaining. After completion of this one, the next waste-water dump will be at about GET equal to 25 hours. Over.

a11_0052818.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0052818.text: This is Apollo Control at 5 hours, 31 minutes into the mission. Apollo 11's velocity now 12,637 feet per second [3,852 m/s]. Distance from Earth, 22,971 [nautical] miles [42,542 km]. The spacecraft weight, 96,573 pounds [43,805 kg].

a11_0053527.speaker: Collins
a11_0053527.text: Houston, Apollo 11. You copy our torquing angles?

a11_0053527.speaker: McCandless
a11_0053527.text: Roger. Leave them on there for another second, please.

a11_0053527.speaker: Collins
a11_0053527.text: Will do. [Long pause.]

a11_0053527.speaker: McCandless
a11_0053527.text: 11, this is Houston. We copy the angles, but stand by before you go ahead and use them. Over.

a11_0053527.speaker: Collins
a11_0053527.text: Standing by.

a11_0053527.speaker: McCandless
a11_0053527.text: 11, Houston. We request that you re-do P52, and if the angles come out the same magnitude, go ahead and incorporate them. Over.

a11_0053527.speaker: Collins
a11_0053527.text: Okay. We'll do it.

a11_0053527.speaker: McCandless
a11_0053527.text: They look a little large right now.

a11_0053527.speaker: Collins
a11_0053527.text: Yeah. Roll - roll looks a little large, especially, there.

a11_0053527.speaker: McCandless
a11_0053527.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_0053527.speaker: McCandless
a11_0053527.text: We're showing a waste-water quantity of about 13 percent on TM now, 11. Over.

a11_0053527.speaker: Collins
a11_0053527.text: Roger. It's off, now.

a11_0053527.speaker: McCandless
a11_0053527.text: Roger. We copy.

a11_0053527.speaker: Collins
a11_0053527.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Torquing angles essentially the same, and we're going to go ahead and torque them now.

a11_0053527.speaker: McCandless
a11_0053527.text: Roger. We concur.

a11_0053527.speaker: Collins
a11_0053527.text: Okay.

a11_0053527.speaker: McCandless
a11_0053527.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Could you give us a - an Auto optics check to a third star or a different star from the one you've been using?

a11_0053527.speaker: Collins
a11_0053527.text: Sure, be glad to. I can go back and do the whole thing and pick different stars.

a11_0053527.speaker: McCandless
a11_0053527.text: I don't think there any - any need to do that. We'd just like to confirm it with a different star, since that roll angle was a little larger than we expected.

a11_0053527.speaker: Collins
a11_0053527.text: Okay.

a11_0053527.speaker: McCandless
a11_0053527.text: Apollo 11, Houston. I have a TLI-plus-11-hour PAD when you're ready to copy.

a11_0053527.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0053527.text: Wait one. [Long pause.]

a11_0053527.speaker: Collins
a11_0053527.text: Old star number 30 looks like it's right dab smack in the middle of the sextant.

a11_0053527.speaker: McCandless
a11_0053527.text: Houston. Roger. Out.

a11_0053527.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0053527.text: Apollo 11, ready to copy.

a11_0053527.speaker: McCandless
a11_0053527.text: Roger, 11. This is a TLI plus 11 hour P37 format: 013:44, 4793, minus 165, 049:23. Read back. Over.

a11_0053527.speaker: McCandless
a11_0053527.text: This is Houston. Readback correct. Out.

a11_0055500.speaker: Collins
a11_0055500.text: Roger. Do you have any update for the roll, pitch and yaw angles on the top of page 37 in the Flight Plan, or are they still good?

a11_0055500.speaker: McCandless
a11_0055500.text: Yes, indeed. I'll give them to you in just a second here. [Long pause.]

a11_0060917.speaker: Duke
a11_0060917.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Be advised your friendly White Team has come on for its first shift. If we can be of service, don't hesitate to call.

a11_0060917.speaker: Collins
a11_0060917.text: Thank you very much. And we're about to take our marks, Charlie, on this P23 optics Cal. I've got it in the sextant now, and I'm about to split the image and Mark.

a11_0061600.speaker: Duke
a11_0061600.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We have scrubbed the Midcourse 1. Over.

a11_0061600.speaker: Duke
a11_0061600.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We see your middle gimbal angle getting pretty big. Over.

a11_0061600.speaker: Collins
a11_0061600.text: Well, it was, Charlie, but in going from one Auto Maneuver to another, we took over control and have gone around gimbal lock; and we're about to give control back to the DAP.

a11_0061600.speaker: Duke
a11_0061600.text: Roger, Mike. We see it increasing now.

a11_0061600.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0061600.text: Hey, maybe you better call Lew and tell him we might be a little bit late for dinner.

a11_0061600.speaker: Duke
a11_0061600.text: Okay. Sure will. We'd like for you to turn on - the fan on in O 2 tank number 2, Buzz. And, 11, did you - On your optics calibrations, did you proceed or recall the program? Over.

a11_0063100.speaker: Collins
a11_0063100.text: Houston, Apollo 11. [Pause.]

a11_0063100.speaker: Duke
a11_0063100.text: Go ahead, 11. Over.

a11_0063100.speaker: Collins
a11_0063100.text: Roger. You looking at our Delta-R/Delta-V? It looks like Delta-R is pretty large, there. We wanted to talk to you about it before we incorporate it.

a11_0063100.speaker: Duke
a11_0063100.text: Stand by, Mike. We don't have anything on our downlink here, I don't think, on the DSKY. Stand by.

a11_0063100.speaker: Collins
a11_0063100.text: Okay. Our Noun 49 is reading: register 1, plus 08793; register 2, all balls.

a11_0063100.speaker: Duke
a11_0063100.text: Copy.

a11_0063100.speaker: Duke
a11_0063100.text: 11, Houston. Guidance is looking at the Noun 40 - 49 stuff. We'll be back with you momentarily. Over.

a11_0063100.speaker: Collins
a11_0063100.text: Okay, Charlie. Thank you. We'll just hold right here in the program.

a11_0063100.speaker: Duke
a11_0063100.text: Roger. We got your downlink now. Over.

a11_0063100.speaker: Collins
a11_0063100.text: Okay. [Long Pause.]

a11_0063100.speaker: Duke
a11_0063100.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We'd like you to reject the Noun 49 stuff on the DSKY right now, Mike, and try it again. Over.

a11_0063100.speaker: Collins
a11_0063100.text: Okay. Will do.

a11_0063100.speaker: Collins
a11_0063100.text: Okay, Houston. Apollo 11. Here's another [Noun] 49 for you. Are you getting it on the downlink?

a11_0063100.speaker: Duke
a11_0063100.text: Roger. We see it. Stand by.

a11_0063100.speaker: Duke
a11_0063100.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We recommend you accept the Noun 49 display on the DSKY now. Over.

a11_0063100.speaker: Collins
a11_0063100.text: Okay. It looks like an awful big one. We noticed that you'd moved star number 2 to the tail end of the listing, and we should be marking first on star 40. Did that have anything to do with it?

a11_0063100.speaker: Duke
a11_0063100.text: Negative. We don't believe so, Apollo 11. We think that this is possibly due to some TLI dispersions, and it's probably satisfactory, so go ahead and accept this. It fits our criteria anyway that if you repeat the mark and you get an equivalent size error, to go ahead and accept it. And this is an equivalent size error. Over.

a11_0063100.speaker: Collins
a11_0063100.text: Okay. We'll do it.

a11_0063100.speaker: Duke
a11_0063100.text: And 11, Houston. Your state vector in the LM slots are - is good. Over.

a11_0063100.speaker: Collins
a11_0063100.text: Roger. Thank you.

a11_0063100.speaker: Collins
a11_0063100.text: Houston, Apollo 11. If you like this one, we'll accept it as well.

a11_0063100.speaker: Duke
a11_0063100.text: Stand by. [Long pause.]

a11_0063100.speaker: Duke
a11_0063100.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We recommend you accept the Noun 49. Over.

a11_0063100.speaker: Collins
a11_0063100.text: Okay, Charlie. Thank you. We'll do that now.

a11_0063100.speaker: Duke
a11_0063100.text: Thank you. [Long pause.]

a11_0063100.speaker: Collins
a11_0063100.text: And we're going to proceed on this one, too, Charlie.

a11_0063100.speaker: Duke
a11_0063100.text: Roger. Copy.

a11_0064835.speaker: Collins
a11_0064835.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Another Noun 49 for you.

a11_0064835.speaker: Duke
a11_0064835.text: Rog. We copy. Stand by. [Long pause.]

a11_0064835.speaker: Duke
a11_0064835.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We'd like you to recycle and do this one over again. Over.

a11_0065341.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0065341.text: Rog. Why don't you sing out when you think we've done enough battery charging on B.

a11_0065341.speaker: Duke
a11_0065341.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We'll be charging battery B up until the sleep period. We'll discontinue charging at that time. Also, at about 12:25 in the Flight Plan, we have battery A charge. That has been deleted. Over.

a11_0065341.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0065341.text: Rog. Understand. We'll charge until the sleep period on B and delete the battery A charge.

a11_0065341.speaker: Collins
a11_0065341.text: And, Houston, Apollo 11. These Auto optics maneuvers or P23s, Auto maneuvers, don't seem to be going to the substellar point. Can you come up with the roll, pitch, and yaw angle for the substellar point on this star? It's our second star.

a11_0065341.speaker: Duke
a11_0065341.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Your angles in the Flight Plan we feel are still good; 198.6, 130.7, 340.0. Just slightly off than those in the Flight Plan. Over.

a11_0072056.speaker: Collins
a11_0072056.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Star 40 has just disappeared now in the sextant. Could the trunnion angle 47 - something be a little high?

a11_0072056.speaker: Duke
a11_0072056.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We'd like you to press on to star 44. Over.

a11_0072056.speaker: Collins
a11_0072056.text: Yeah, Roger. How many marks have you recorded on star 40?

a11_0072100.speaker: Duke
a11_0072100.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We'd like you to press on to star 44. Over.

a11_0072100.speaker: Collins
a11_0072100.text: Yeah, Roger. How many marks have you recorded on star 40?

a11_0073300.speaker: Collins
a11_0073300.text: Houston, Apollo 11.

a11_0073300.speaker: Duke
a11_0073300.text: Go ahead. Over.

a11_0073300.speaker: Collins
a11_0073300.text: Roger. Forty-four is just not bright enough for this. There is a reddish glow filling the black area of the sextant, and the star is lost somewhere in there, and I cannot see it.

a11_0073300.speaker: Duke
a11_0073300.text: Roger. Stand by. We'll come up with another star. Over.

a11_0073300.speaker: Collins
a11_0073300.text: Yeah. I'd appreciate that. [Long pause.]

a11_0073300.speaker: Duke
a11_0073300.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We'd like you to go on to star 45. Over.

a11_0073300.speaker: Collins
a11_0073300.text: Okay.

a11_0073300.speaker: Duke
a11_0073300.text: And, Mike, we think these large Delta-Rs, Noun 49, you're getting is really meaningful since it's been way before TLI since we had a state vector update; and we think it's normal. Over.

a11_0073300.speaker: Collins
a11_0073300.text: Okay. Could be, Charlie. Some of the early markings: I might not have had precisely the substellar point. I think as time goes by they've been coming more accurate but old Enif here is just flat invisible.

a11_0073300.speaker: Duke
a11_0073300.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a11_0073300.speaker: Collins
a11_0073300.text: And, Houston, Apollo 11. Understand that the same three gimbal angles you gave me should be valid for star 45 as well. Is that affirmative?

a11_0073300.speaker: Duke
a11_0073300.text: I believe that's right. Stand by one. Over.

a11_0073300.speaker: Collins
a11_0073300.text: Okay.

a11_0073300.speaker: Duke
a11_0073300.text: That is negative. Stand by one.

a11_0073300.speaker: Collins
a11_0073300.text: Okay. Because there's quite a difference between the gimbal angles you have and the gimbal angles the program wants, but with inaccurate state vector, I'm inclined not to believe the program.

a11_0073300.speaker: Duke
a11_0073300.text: Stand by. [Long pause.]

a11_0073300.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0073300.text: Houston, Apollo 11. LMP is back on the line.

a11_0073300.speaker: Duke
a11_0073300.text: Roger. Copy.

a11_0073300.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0073300.text: Read you five-by.

a11_0073300.speaker: Duke
a11_0073300.text: Roger. The same, Buzz. And, 11, the angles for you are 197.8 for roll, 128.5 pitch, 340.0 yaw.

a11_0073300.speaker: Collins
a11_0073300.text: Okay. Just as a matter of comparison, P23 for this star would like to go to 235.66, 154.31, and 31365. Over.

a11_0073300.speaker: Duke
a11_0073300.text: Roger. We copy, 11. We understand that the program can give you almost an infinite combination of angles in P23, and it's not too unreasonable. If you'll stand by, we'll look at these that we see on the DSKY. Over.

a11_0073300.speaker: Collins
a11_0073300.text: Okay. Then in the meantime I'll just go ahead and maneuver to yours. 197.8, 128.5, and 340.0.

a11_0073300.speaker: Duke
a11_0073300.text: Rog.

a11_0074324.speaker: Collins
a11_0074324.text: Okay, Charlie. If the attitude you gave me on star number 45 - The reticle is off, I'd say, a good 30 degrees in roll, and the star is not in sight. Over.

a11_0074324.speaker: Collins
a11_0074324.text: I think something's wrong with those attitudes.

a11_0074324.speaker: Duke
a11_0074324.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. I wondered if you have Auto Optics selected. Over.

a11_0074324.speaker: Duke
a11_0074324.text: Roger. Looks like to us we need a Proceed, Mike, to get the sextant pointed at the star. Over.

a11_0074324.speaker: Duke
a11_0074324.text: 11, Houston. Those shaft and trunnion angles were exactly what we were computing on the ground. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0074324.speaker: Collins
a11_0074324.text: Okay. I'm going to trim up the attitude here and give it another try.

a11_0074324.speaker: Collins
a11_0074324.text: Okay. I have this star loud and clear now, Charlie, so I might as well do a bunch of marks on this one to get a good horizon count.

a11_0074324.speaker: Collins
a11_0074324.text: It still looks like I'm far from the substellar point, however. I'm off quite a bit in roll.

a11_0074324.speaker: Duke
a11_0074324.text: Roger. We'd like you to mark right where it is now, Mike, and we'd like two sets of marks on this. Over.

a11_0074324.speaker: Collins
a11_0074324.text: Okay. Fine. But the reticle is not parallel to the horizon. I have to move off quite a bit in order to get it parallel to the horizon. [Pause.]

a11_0074324.speaker: Duke
a11_0074324.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Our procedures guys are saying that the reticle does not have to be parallel. Over.

a11_0074324.speaker: Collins
a11_0074324.text: Well, then we're not at the substellar point, if we're not.

a11_0075139.speaker: Duke
a11_0075139.text: Roger. We see it, 11. Stand by. [Long pause.]

a11_0075139.speaker: Duke
a11_0075139.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We'd like you to accept this one and every mark thereafter. Over.

a11_0075139.speaker: Collins
a11_0075139.text: You need me to wait in the Noun 49 display for any length of time?

a11_0075139.speaker: Collins
a11_0075139.text: Okay, Charlie. I'd be glad to give you as many of these as you like.

a11_0075139.speaker: Duke
a11_0075139.text: Roger. We'd like six marks on star 45, Mike, and then we'll probably go back to star 2 again. Stand by. We'll have further word on that.

a11_0075139.speaker: Collins
a11_0075139.text: They seem to be getting smaller, Charlie? Are you sure you wouldn't like some more?

a11_0075139.speaker: Duke
a11_0075139.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We'd like you to do two more on star 45. Over.

a11_0075139.speaker: Collins
a11_0075139.text: Okay, Charlie. There's your two more marks. Where do you want to go from here?

a11_0075139.speaker: Duke
a11_0075139.text: Hello, Apollo 11, Houston. We'd like you to go back to star number 2 with an attitude as follows: roll, 195.2; pitch, 123.9; yaw, 340.0. Mike, that'll give you a trunnion angle of about 31.4. Over.

a11_0075139.speaker: Collins
a11_0075139.text: Okay. Understand star number 2 and roll, 195.2; pitch, 123.9; and yaw, 340.0. Over.

a11_0080207.speaker: Collins
a11_0080207.text: Okay, Charlie. I'm there, and I've got a trunnion angle of 30.5 degrees. Again, misaligned considerably in roll and I do believe that's important to getting good marks.

a11_0080207.speaker: Collins
a11_0080207.text: See, if I'm - my reticle's not parallel, then I'm not marking normal to the horizon and I'm not marking at the substellar point. I'm marking off somewhere else.

a11_0080207.speaker: Duke
a11_0080207.text: Apollo 11, Houston. The ground-computed values for your shaft and trunnion are just what you're getting on the DSKY there, Mike. The horizon looks cocked off to you - You look like you're off in roll because the angles that we gave you to maneuver to, to prevent the LM reflection from fouling up your optics, we feel like a - you should go ahead and mark on the star just as is. Over.

a11_0080207.speaker: Collins
a11_0080207.text: I'll bet you a cup of coffee on it.

a11_0080207.speaker: Collins
a11_0080207.text: Verb - or a Noun 49 for you, Charlie.

a11_0080207.speaker: Duke
a11_0080207.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We'd like to accept this one and give us two more and that will be enough. Over.

a11_0080800.speaker: Duke
a11_0080800.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We see your termination on P23. Thank you very much. Mike, we'll have a - We're trying to work up a story here for you; we'll be with you momentarily on an explanation of what's happening. Over.

a11_0080800.speaker: Collins
a11_0080800.text: Okay, Charlie. It just appears to me that you have to have the reticle tangent to the horizon at the point at which you mark or else you're not at the substellar point; you're off laterally, and therefore you're measuring a larger trunnion angle than you should.

a11_0080800.speaker: Duke
a11_0080800.text: Seems so to me. Our procedures people are working on this, and we'll be back with you momentarily. Over.

a11_0080800.speaker: Duke
a11_0080800.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We'd like you to go P00 and Accept. We'll have a PTC REFSMMAT for you momentarily. Over.

a11_0080800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0080800.text: The PTC REFSMMAT, which CapCom Charlie Duke just referred to, is the Passive Thermal Control attitude that the crew will place the spacecraft in. In this attitude the spacecraft will be rotated at a rate of about 3 revolutions per hour to maintain the proper temperature balance.

a11_0082444.speaker: Duke
a11_0082444.text: Hello Apollo 11, Houston. We'd like you to do a P52, option 1 preferred, and establish PTC as listed in the Flight Plan at 12 hours. We'd like you to commence that right now, Mike. And we have some stars recommended for you. For stars 26, 30, and 24, when you get to attitude 000. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0082444.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0082444.text: Okay, Charlie. He's off the wick right now. Understand you're ready for us to do a P52, option 1?

a11_0082444.speaker: Duke
a11_0082444.text: 11, it's a P52, option 1 preferred. Over.

a11_0082444.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0082444.text: Roger. And, let's see, that is Spica, Menkent, and what else?

a11_0082444.speaker: Duke
a11_0082444.text: Roger. Stars - Codes are stars 26, 30, and 24. Over.

a11_0083542.speaker: Duke
a11_0083542.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We notice your Program Alarm, Mike, was due to using these stars in the P23 attitude. If you'll go to 000, the stars we gave you will work. Over.

a11_0084129.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0084129.text: Wait till we finish the maneuver and we'll give you the DSKY.

a11_0085307.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0085307.text: Houston, Apollo 11. The DSKY is yours.

a11_0092240.speaker: Duke
a11_0092240.text: Roger, 11. Read you about four-by. How me? Over.

a11_0092240.speaker: Collins
a11_0092240.text: You're loud and clear, Charlie. We pitched down some to get a better comm attitude.

a11_0092240.speaker: Duke
a11_0092240.text: Roger. Did you copy our recommendation on proceeding with the P52, Mike? Over.

a11_0092240.speaker: Collins
a11_0092240.text: Negative. We didn't. I've got that in work. I'm starting on P52.

a11_0092240.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0092240.text: This is Apollo Control at 9 hours, 36 minutes into the flight of Apollo 11. The mission continuing to go smoothly at this point. The communications noise that we were experiencing previously cleared up after the crew was able to get the spacecraft in a good attitude for antenna lock-on and we had one brief conversation which we taped. We're presently communicating with the crew at this time. We'll pick up the tape and then continue to follow live conversation.

a11_0093556.speaker: Collins
a11_0093556.text: Roger. You copy our torquing angles? We're about to torque them.

a11_0093556.speaker: Collins
a11_0093556.text: Rog. The reason for the delay there, Charlie, is that - difficult to find two stars that are not occulted by the LM and also are not in the midst of a man-made star field up here, with dumps.

a11_0093556.speaker: Duke
a11_0093556.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. You can torque the Noun 93. Over.

a11_0093556.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0093556.text: That brings us up to date with the taped conversation that we had. We'll continue to stand by for any live communications with the spacecraft. Most of that conversation with Mike Collins involved the platform alignment that the crew is involved in at the present time, aligning the stable platform used by the guidance system as an attitude reference. Apollo 11 is presently 46,688 nautical miles [86,466 km] from Earth and the velocity is 8,750 feet per second [2,667 m/s].

a11_0093600.speaker: Collins
a11_0093600.text: Roger. You copy our torquing angles? We're about to torque them.

a11_0093600.speaker: Collins
a11_0093600.text: Rog. The reason for the delay there, Charlie, is that - difficult to find two stars that are not occulted by the LM and also are not in the midst of a man-made star field up here, with dumps.

a11_0093600.speaker: Duke
a11_0093600.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. You can torque the Noun 93. Over.

a11_0094034.speaker: Collins
a11_0094034.text: Okay, Houston. That completes the P52. We verified the third star with Antares, and Auto optics are pointing at it pretty closely. How do our platform drift angles look so far, Charlie?

a11_0094034.speaker: Duke
a11_0094034.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We didn't have a chance to get a good check for you. We're going to run a drift check from this alignment until the next one, approximately 12 hours, and we'll have something for you later. Over.

a11_0094034.speaker: Duke
a11_0094034.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We'd like you to establish your PTC. We recommend you select quads Alpha and Delta. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0094034.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0094034.text: Roger. Understand. Alpha and Delta quads [faintly] for PTC.

a11_0095253.speaker: Duke
a11_0095253.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Would you verify that the Attitude Set switch is in GDC? Over. [Pause.]

a11_0095253.speaker: Collins
a11_0095253.text: The Set switch. Stand by one, Charlie.

a11_0100329.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0100329.text: Hi, Houston, Apollo 11. How many miles out do you have us now?

a11_0100329.speaker: Duke
a11_0100329.text: We have you - Stand by, Buzz. Roughly about 50,000 [nautical miles, 93,000 km]. Stand by.

a11_0100329.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0100329.text: It's a beautiful sight.

a11_0100329.speaker: Collins
a11_0100329.text: Charlie, on the PTC, we're just waiting our 20 minutes here for all thruster activity to damp out. You might let us know how that's coming.

a11_0100329.speaker: Duke
a11_0100329.text: Roger. Will do. We have you about 48,000 [nautical] miles [89,000km] now?

a11_0100329.speaker: Collins
a11_0100329.text: Thank you.

a11_0100329.speaker: Collins
a11_0100329.text: Houston, Apollo 11. We still have our oxygen fan on for Tank 2. Is that what you want?

a11_0100329.speaker: Duke
a11_0100329.text: Stand by. [Pause.]

a11_0100329.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0100329.text: Hey, Charlie, I can see the snow on the - on the mountains out in California, and it looks like LA doesn't have much of a smog problem today.

a11_0100329.speaker: Duke
a11_0100329.text: Roger, Buzz. Copy. Looks like there's a good view out there then.

a11_0100329.speaker: Duke
a11_0100329.text: And, Apollo 11, Houston. We'd like you to keep the O 2 fan on. It will give you an ECS configuration prior to sleep. Over.

a11_0100329.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0100329.text: Okay. Fine. [Long pause.]

a11_0100329.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0100329.text: Charlie, with the monocular, I can discern a definite green cast to the San Fernando Valley.

a11_0100329.speaker: Duke
a11_0100329.text: Roger.

a11_0100329.speaker: Duke
a11_0100329.text: How's Baja California look, Buzz? [Pause.]

a11_0100329.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0100329.text: Well, it's got some clouds up and down it, and there's a pretty good circulation system a couple of hundred miles off the west coast of California.

a11_0100329.speaker: Duke
a11_0100329.text: Roger. 11, we'd like you to close the waste storage vent valve right now.

a11_0100329.speaker: Collins
a11_0100329.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a11_0100329.speaker: Collins
a11_0100329.text: Waste storage vent valves closed.

a11_0100329.speaker: Duke
a11_0100329.text: Copy. [Long pause.]

a11_0100329.speaker: Duke
a11_0100329.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We'd like - The rates are looking pretty good right now on the PTC, but we'd like you to continue holding. Over.

a11_0100329.speaker: Collins
a11_0100329.text: Okay. Fine.

a11_0102028.speaker: Duke
a11_0102028.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Your rates look really great, now. You can start your PTC.

a11_0102028.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0102028.text: Roger. If you'd like to delay PTC after - for 10 minutes or so, we can shoot you some TV of a seven-eighths Earth. That's - We'll leave that up to you.

a11_0102028.speaker: Duke
a11_0102028.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We'll have our answer for you on the TV in about one minute. Over.

a11_0102556.speaker: Duke
a11_0102556.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We're ready at Goldstone for the TV. It'll be recorded at Goldstone and then replayed back over here, Neil. Any time you want to turn her on, we're ready. Over.

a11_0102556.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0102556.text: Okay. It'll take us about 5 minutes to get rigged.

a11_0102556.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0102556.text: CapCom Charlie Duke advised the crew that we would be recording the television at Goldstone. We don't have an estimate at this time as to how long it will take to get a playback of that from Goldstone.

a11_0102556.speaker: Duke
a11_0102556.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Could you verify the reading on your O 2 flow indicator? Over. [Pause.]

a11_0102556.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0102556.text: We're showing 0.2. We just inadvertently touched the Rapid Repress button. That made a temporary glitch in the flow.

a11_0102556.speaker: Duke
a11_0102556.text: Roger. During that glitch there, did it go almost a peg high? Over.

a11_0102556.speaker: Duke
a11_0102556.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Could you tell us - tell us if the O 2 flow indicator was pegged to high prior to closing the waste storage vent valve? Over.

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. A while ago we tracked into the scan limits and disabled the Auto drive on the High Gain. We'd like you to position the antenna at pitch 30, yaw 270, go to Reacq; that will give us a narrow beamwidth. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0103059.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0103059.text: That yaw 270 and pitch 3 - What was the pitch?

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Pitch 30, Neil.

a11_0103059.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0103059.text: Okay. [Pause.] I think we've got you. [Pause.]

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Roger. We've got a good signal there. Thank you much. [Long pause.]

a11_0103059.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0103059.text: Okay, Houston. We are sending a picture of Earth down right now, so you can let us know if they're receiving at Goldstone.

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Roger, 11. Goldstone is receiving the TV. Stand by. We'll let you know on the quality. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Goldstone says that the TV looks great. Over.

a11_0103059.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0103059.text: [Faint] Roger. We're zooming in on Earth now.

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Did you copy? Over.

a11_0103059.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0103059.text: Roger. We copied, Charlie.

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Roger. Your transmissions the last couple of times have been about two-by. Over.

a11_0103059.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0103059.text: Okay. How do you read me now?

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Rog. You're five-by now.

a11_0103059.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0103059.text: Okay. We're zooming the lens on in, until it will just about fill the monitor.

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_0103059.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0103059.text: Okay. It's in full zoom, now.

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Copy, 11.

a11_0103059.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0103059.text: And how about the f-stop? Is 22 going to be adequate?

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Stand by. We'll get with the Goldstone TV guy. We don't have anything here at Houston. Stand by.

a11_0103059.speaker: Collins
a11_0103059.text: It looks good on the monitor, as far as the f-stop goes. Therefore, we just assumed it's okay at Goldstone. [Long pause.]

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Goldstone says it - TV looks really great, five-by; we don't - The AGC looks like it's working fine. The f:22 is good; we have no real white spots. They're real pleased with it. Over.

a11_0103059.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0103059.text: Okay. You just cut out, Charlie. We understand that it's looking great. We'll leave it the way it is and wait for you to come back on.

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Roger. How do you read me now? Over.

a11_0103059.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0103059.text: Five-by.

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Okay. My comments were - My comments were from Goldstone that they see no white spots as we saw in 10. Looks like the AGC's working real well. The f:22 looks good. Over.

a11_0103059.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0103059.text: Okay. Very good. Well, we shut out the Sun coming in from the other windows into the spacecraft, so it's looking through a - the Number 1 window on Earth, and any reflected light [fades out] so, it ought to be a pretty good picture.

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We'd like you to keep the TV on for about 10 minutes or so, so we can get come good comparison on the camera. You can do anything your heart desires on the TV: interior, exterior, pan in and out, anything you'd like. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: 11, Houston. Over. [No answer.]

a11_0103059.speaker: Collins
a11_0103059.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Over.

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Roger. Go ahead. Over.

a11_0103059.speaker: Collins
a11_0103059.text: Charlie, I'm sorry; you keep cutting out. We heard up to you can do anything, and then after that we didn't hear anything, and we knew that wasn't right anyhow because we can't. But what do you want us to do?

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Roger. We'll check this uplink on our voice. That transmission on the TV was - We'd like to get about 10 minutes worth of signal at Goldstone so we can look at the camera quality back here at Houston for about 10 minutes or so when they patch it back into us. What we were saying was that you can go interior or exterior on the camera. On the exterior shots, we'd like to look...

a11_0103059.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0103059.text: You cut out again.

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Stand by.

a11_0103059.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0103059.text: Start over with: We were saying. [Long pause.]

a11_0103059.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0103059.text: Okay, Houston. You suppose you could turn the Earth a little bit so we could get a little bit more than just water?

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Roger, 11. I don't think we got much control over that. Looks like you'll have to settle for the water. [Long pause.]

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: 11, Houston. We're going to change - thinking about changing our voice uplink to another site. If you'll stand by, we'll see if we can improve the quality. Over.

a11_0103059.speaker: Collins
a11_0103059.text: Okay, Charlie.

a11_0103059.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0103059.text: We'll stand by for your call.

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We'll try once more on this TV request. We'd like 10 minutes worth of TV. And we'd like a narrative, if you could give us one, on the exterior shots. You could al - we also suggest you might try the - an interior position. Over.

a11_0103059.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0103059.text: Roger. We're seeing the center of the Earth as viewed from the spacecraft in the eastern Pacific Ocean. We have not been able to visually pick up the Hawaiian Island chain, but we can clearly see the western coast of North America, the United States, the San Joaquin Valley, the High Sierras, Baja California, and Mexico down as far as Acapulco, and the Yucatan Peninsula; and you can see on through Central America to the northern coast of South America, Venezuela, and Colombia. I'm not sure you'll be able to see all that on your screens down there.

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Roger, Neil. We just wanted a narrative such that we can - When we get the playback, we can sort of correlate what we're seeing. Thank you very much. [Pause.]

a11_0103059.speaker: Collins
a11_0103059.text: I haven't seen anything but the DSKY so far.

a11_0103059.speaker: Duke
a11_0103059.text: Looks like they're hogging the windows.

a11_0103059.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0103059.text: You're right.

a11_0104658.speaker: Duke
a11_0104658.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. On your cryos, we'd like, at this time, for you to place all four cryo heaters to Auto and turn off all four cryo fans. Over.

a11_0104658.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0104658.text: Okay. All four cryo heaters are Auto. And all four cryo fans are off, all off.

a11_0104658.speaker: Duke
a11_0104658.text: Roger. That's going to be your sleep configuration.

a11_0104658.speaker: Duke
a11_0104658.text: And, Buzz, we'll be terminating the battery charge in about a half hour.

a11_0104658.speaker: Duke
a11_0104658.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. You can terminate the TV at your convenience. We've got enough tape, and you can start PTC at your convenience. The rates look super for starting up. Over.

a11_0105732.speaker: Duke
a11_0105732.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We have a Flight Plan update for you and some P37 block data, if you're ready to copy. Over.

a11_0105732.speaker: Collins
a11_0105732.text: Okay, Houston. PTC is started now; looks good to us, and we'll be ready to copy in a minute or two.

a11_0105732.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0105732.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Ready to copy the Flight Plan update and P37.

a11_0105732.speaker: Duke
a11_0105732.text: Roger. Stand by one, Buzz. [Long pause.]

a11_0105732.speaker: Duke
a11_0105732.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Coming at you with the P37 block data. Over.

a11_0105732.speaker: Duke
a11_0105732.text: Roger, 11. That was a good readback. That was the block data scheduled for 12 hours. We'd like to just say that on a Flight Plan update here, just to remind you of some things, and that you can do them at your convenience and then go to sleep early if you'd like. We don't have anything else planned, but we'd like to just remind you on the filter change, the O 2 fuel cell purge. And we'd like a LM/CM Delta-P and accomplish the pre-sleep checklist. [Pause.]

a11_0105732.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0105732.text: Okay. We've completed the filter change, and we'll get started on the fuel cell purge, and stand by for the LM/CM Delta-P.

a11_0105732.speaker: Duke
a11_0105732.text: Roger, 11. Would you hold off on the fuel cell purge? EECOM's saying we might not have to do that. Over.

a11_0105732.speaker: Duke
a11_0105732.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We just decided to delete the O 2 fuel cell purge. Over.

a11_0105732.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0105732.text: Roger. Delete the O 2 fuel cell purge.

a11_0110621.speaker: Duke
a11_0110621.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We've been noting some funnies on the O 2 flow indicator transducer. We've kind of got a suspicion it's the transducer. We - weexpected to see an O 2 flow pegged high with the waste stowage vent to Vent. It was not. We also noted some funny indications when you closed the waste stowage vent valve. We're going to continue to look at this through the night, and we'll be with you in the morning with an assessment of the problem. Also, we'd like to ask specifically, when you place the waste stowage vent valve to Vent, does the detent - correction - does the arrow line up

a11_0110621.speaker: Collins
a11_0110621.text: Stand by one, Charlie. We'll give you something on the detent.

a11_0110621.speaker: Collins
a11_0110621.text: Right now it's at Closed, and I'm lined up with Closed. Before I was at Vent; and best I can recall, it was quite accurately lined up with Vent. Would you like me to go to Vent again momentarily and see where it lines up?

a11_0110621.speaker: Duke
a11_0110621.text: That's negative. That question's answered. Thank you much.

a11_0110621.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0110621.text: This is Apollo Control. During that last transmission you heard CapCom Charlie Duke advise the crew that we are not seeing as high an O 2 , or oxygen flow, as we would have expected at this point. This would indicate that the enrichment of the cabin atmosphere, which was 60 percent oxygen, 40 percent nitrogen at launch and which is normally enriched with pure oxygen during the course of the flight, is not enriching as rapidly as we would expect. This could be a transducer problem - one of the devices that measures the O 2 flow rate - or possibly a partial obstruction of one of the vents. The p

a11_0110621.speaker: Duke
a11_0110621.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We have an S-band configuration for you. Over.

a11_0110621.speaker: Duke
a11_0110621.text: Roger, Buzz. We'd like you to place the S-band antenna Omni A switch to the Bravo position. S-band antenna Omni switch to the Omni position, the High Gain track to Manual, and the High Gain angles will be yaw 270, pitch minus 50. Over.

a11_0110621.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0110621.text: Roger. Understand. Omni to Baker and Omni, Manual. And the angles are yaw 270, pitch minus 50, and was that narrow or wide? Over. [Pause.]

a11_0110621.speaker: Duke
a11_0110621.text: Stand by. Roger. We'd like it in Wide, and you can set that configuration up now. Over.

a11_0110621.speaker: Duke
a11_0110621.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. You can terminate the battery Bravo charge, and we'd like a crew status report. We're about to tell you good night. Over.

a11_0111808.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0111808.text: Houston, Apollo 11. The battery charging is complete, and the crew status report is as follows: radiation; CDR, 11002; CMP, 10002; LMP, 09003; negative medication; fit as a fiddle, over.

a11_0111808.speaker: Duke
a11_0111808.text: Rog. Copy, 11. Thank you much. We'd like to ask one question. Have you tried the gas separator on the water? How is that working? Over.

a11_0111808.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0111808.text: Yes. Mike's got a couple of comments on that.

a11_0111808.speaker: Collins
a11_0111808.text: Yeah, it's working good so far, Charlie. We've got one installed on the water gun and the other one installed on the spigot down in the LEB, and we [break in recording] mention one problem with them is that they leak at the junction between the food bag and the water filter. However, with that exception, they seem to be working pretty good. We were getting some gas through initially, and I think that was just getting the system purged out to begin with; and the last tubeful we poured was almost free of bubbles. Over.

a11_0111808.speaker: Duke
a11_0111808.text: Roger. Sounds good. We'll check in on that problem with the SPAN guys and let you know in the morning. If you have to call us tonight, we'd like you to do it on Down Voice Backup. We're configuring the MSFN for that mode; and as far as we can see, you're cleared for some z's. Over.

a11_0111808.speaker: Collins
a11_0111808.text: Okay. Maybe we'll get around to lunch.

a11_0111808.speaker: Duke
a11_0111808.text: How about a peanut butter and jelly?

a11_0112900.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0112900.text: This is Apollo Control at 11 hours, 47 minutes into the flight of Apollo 11. At this time we are receiving the television data from Goldstone. The data is coming in. It will be processed here and converted, and we estimate that it will be available for playback in about 20 to 30 minutes and we will have a firm time on that as soon as possible. At the present time, Apollo 11 is 56,704 nautical miles [105,016 km] from Earth, and the velocity is 7,821 feet per second [2,384 m/s]. We've had no further conversations with the crew since we passed along a good night to them at 11 hours, 20 minutes; g

a11_0114700.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0114700.text: This is Apollo Control at 12 hours, 5 minutes. We expect to have the unscheduled television transmission, which came in to Goldstone, California, and was taped there and has been transmitted to Mission Control Center, ready and converted for replay in color at 8:45 pm Central Daylight Time. That would be about 7 minutes from now. The TV transmission runs for a total time of about 16 and a half minutes and is of an exterior shot out the window of the Earth. At the time of the transmission, Apollo 11 was some 50,980 nautical miles [94,415 km] from Earth. The transmission came into Goldstone at a

a11_0120500.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0120500.text: This is Apollo Control at 12 hours, 12 minutes. We expect to be ready to release the television transmission from the spacecraft which was received at Goldstone, California. That should be ready to go in a little less than a minute.

a11_0121200.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0121200.text: And we are starting to get lock-on from the tape replay and we expect that we will have a color picture shortly.

a11_0123634.speaker: Duke
a11_0123634.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. I hope you aren't, - we aren't disturbing you. We'd like to terminate the Noun 65 now. Over.

a11_0125200.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0125200.text: This is Apollo Control at 13 hours, 27 minutes into the flight of Apollo 11. The spacecraft now travelling at a speed of 7,279 feet per second [2,219 m/s] which would be about 4,963 miles an hour [7,986 km/h], and it's at a distance of 63,880 nautical miles [118,306 km] from Earth. Our Flight Surgeon reported a short while ago that Command Module Pilot Mike Collins appeared to be sleeping soundly at this time. Biomedical data on the other two crewmen indicates that they are still awake. We've had no further conversation with the spacecraft since our last report, and it appears that the crew wi

a11_0132700.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0132700.text: This is Apollo Control at 14 hours, 6 minutes into the flight of Apollo 11. The mission is progressing very smoothly. All spacecraft systems are functioning normally at this time, and the Flight Surgeon reports that all three crewmen appear to be sleeping. For Commander Neil Armstrong and Lunar Module Pilot Buzz Aldrin, they appeared to begin sleeping about 5 minutes ago. Command Module Pilot Mike Collins has been asleep for about an additional 30 minutes to an hour. At the present time, Apollo 11 is 66,554 nautical miles [123,258 km] from Earth and travelling at a speed of about seventy thous

a11_0140600.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0140600.text: This is Apollo Control; 14 hours, 25 minutes into the flight of Apollo 11. The spacecraft presently 67,819 nautical miles [125,601 km] from Earth, traveling at a speed of 7,012 feet per second [2,163 m/s]. Here in Mission Control, the shift change is in progress. Flight Director Glynn Lunney and his team of flight controllers coming on to replace Gene Kranz and his White Team. The Capsule Communicator on the upcoming shift will be Ron Evans, and we anticipate that the change-of-shift briefing for this shift will begin in about 10 or 15 minutes. At 14 hours, 26 minutes; this is Apollo Control,

a11_0152800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0152800.text: This is Apollo Control; 16 hours, 38 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 11 presently being tracked by the Honeysuckle Creek, Australia tracking station. Geographically, the spacecraft is practically directly over or out from the Philippine Islands. Now showing some 5 hours and 51 minutes remaining in the crew rest period. Crew still asleep at this time. Continuing to decelerate as the spacecraft gets out toward the changeover point between the Earth's sphere of influence and the Moon's sphere of influence. Velocity now showing 6,493 feet per second [1,979 m/s]. Apollo 11 now out 76,453 nautic

a11_0163800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0163800.text: This is Apollo Control; 17 hours, 33 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 11 now some 79,700 nautical miles [147,604 km] out from Earth at a velocity of 6,320 feet per second [1,926 m/s]. Telemetry display for the crew biomedical readings now shows all three men in a fairly deep sleep. The mean heart rates in the 40s for all three men. Command Module cabin pressure holding at 4.7 pounds per square inch [32.4 kPa]. Cabin temperature is 63 degrees [Fahrenheit, 17°C]. No measurements on the Lunar Module in terms of cabin pressure in as much as the Lunar Module has not been activated and will not b

a11_0173300.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0173300.text: This is Apollo Control; 18 hours, 38 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 11 now some 83,644 nautical miles [154,909 km] out from Earth, continuing to decelerate in velocity, now some 6,114 feet per second [1,864 m/s]. The reveille time for the crew of Apollo 11 in some 3 hours and 50 minutes. All systems still functioning normally aboard the spacecraft as the crew continues their nine-hour rest period. All measurements normal, as the flight controllers here watch the systems on telemetry and the displays here in the control center. At 18 hours, 39 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Co

a11_0183800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0183800.text: This is Apollo Control; 19 hours, 43 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Crew now has some 2 hours, 46 minutes remaining in the scheduled sleep period. Distance outbound from Earth now 87,409 nautical miles [161,882 km]. Apollo 11's continuing to decelerate in velocity, now traveling at 5,930 feet per second [1,807 m/s]. All going well in the Apollo 11 mission. Crew sleeping apparently in deep sleep. Systems still performing quite well. And at 19 hours, 43 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control.

a11_0194300.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0194300.text: This is Apollo Control; 20 hours, 38 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. One hour, 51 minutes remaining in the crew rest period at this time. Apollo 11 on a line projected outward from Earth as directly over the southern tip of the Indian sub-continent. Distance now 90,509 nautical miles [167,623 km]. Velocity continuing to decelerate, now 5,788 feet per second [1,764 m/s]. Crew is still asleep at this time. And at 20 hours, 39 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control.

a11_0203800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0203800.text: This is Apollo Control; 21 hours, 38 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 11 now being tracked by the tracking station at Madrid. Some 51 minutes remaining in the scheduled sleep period for the crew of Apollo 11. When the sleep period ends depends on the business of the day, whether the flight controllers here and the spacecraft communicator wake the crew up or whether they wake up on their own accord and call in to begin the second day of translunar coast. Upon awakening the Flight Plan calls for change of the carbon dioxide removing filters in the spacecraft cabin, a report on the differentia

a11_0213800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0213800.text: This is Apollo Control at 22 hours, 49 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Crew has been awake for some time according to the surgeon. Spacecraft communicator here in Mission Control with the Green Team, Bruce McCandless, is standing by to make a call to the crew. He's in the process of taking over from Ron Evans. Flight Director Cliff Charlesworth has asked that he make a call to the crew. We're standing by for this call momentarily.

a11_0224900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0224900.text: Apollo 11, Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

a11_0225155.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0225155.text: [Faint] Roger. Standing by for your updates. Over.

a11_0225155.speaker: McCandless
a11_0225155.text: Okay, 11. This is Houston. At time approximately 22:30 in the Flight Plan, in your post-sleep checklist, and in all other post-sleep checklists, we'd like you to delete the statement that says Auto RCS Jet Select, 16, to On, and what we're doing here is picking this up in the procedure for exiting PTC that's in your CSM checklist. And in the CSM checklist on page Foxtrot 9-8: if you want to turn to that, we'd like to change the order of the steps in that. Over.

a11_0225155.speaker: McCandless
a11_0225155.text: Okay. Right now it reads, "To exit G&N PTC". Then you've got a pen-and-ink change that says, "Auto RCS Select, 12, Main A and B". And you come down to the printed Step 1. We'd like to take and move the "Auto RCS Select, 12, Main A and B" down to be the second step, so the procedure would read, Step 1, "Manual Attitude 3, Accel Command"; Step 2 "Auto RCS Select, 12, Main A B." Step 3 would be, "Verify DAP Load", and so on. Over.

a11_0225155.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0225155.text: [Faint] Roger. I copy. Is that "Auto RCS Select, 12, Main A, Main B" to be the... [Fades out.]

a11_0225155.speaker: McCandless
a11_0225155.text: Roger. It should be the second step in that procedure. At time 22:40, or when you get to it, we'd like to commence a charge on Battery A. [Pause.] And at time 24:10, we have an updated attitude for your P52 and optics calibration. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0225155.speaker: McCandless
a11_0225155.text: Roger. P52 and optics calibration attitude: roll, 330.5; pitch, 086.3; yaw, 000.0. The nominal attitude that's pen-and-inked in for the P23 is still good. At time 25:30, approximately, after you complete P23, we're requesting a waste-water dump down to a nominal 25 percent. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0225155.speaker: McCandless
a11_0225155.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Did you copy the attitudes and the waste-water dump? Over.

a11_0225155.speaker: McCandless
a11_0225155.text: 11, this is Houston. We're not reading you at the present time. You're way down in the noise level. Stand by, please.

a11_0225904.speaker: McCandless
a11_0225904.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. How do you read? Over.

a11_0225904.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0225904.text: Roger, Houston. Apollo 11. Loud and clear. How me?

a11_0225904.speaker: McCandless
a11_0225904.text: Okay. Beautiful. Did you copy the attitudes for the P52 and the waste-water dump? Over.

a11_0225904.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0225904.text: Rog. Okay. We note the battery charge as soon as we get around to it, and the attitude for the P52 optics Cal: roll, 330.5; pitch, 086.3; and yaw, all zeros. The attitude for the P23 as in the Flight Plan is okay, and I copy your battery charge. Crew status report as follows. Sleep: CDR, 7; CMP, 7; LMP, 5.5. And we've completed the post-sleep checklist. Standing by for a consumable update. Over.

a11_0225904.speaker: McCandless
a11_0225904.text: Roger. We're requesting a waste-water dump at GET 25:30 down to a nominal 25 percent, and here we go with the consumables update. At GET of 22 hours, RCS total is minus 3.5 percent. Alpha, minus 3.5 percent; Bravo, minus 1.5 percent; Charlie, minus 5.0 percent; minus 4.0 percent; H 2 minus 2 pounds, O 2 minus 4 pounds. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0225904.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0225904.text: I copied those consumables, and I'll read you back our RCS quantities. We got 86 percent in Alpha, 87 in Bravo, 88 in Charlie, and 90 in Delta. Over.

a11_0225904.speaker: McCandless
a11_0225904.text: And did you copy the waste-water request?

a11_0225904.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0225904.text: Roger. Waste-water at - and we got the time on that, and it will be down to 25 percent.

a11_0230645.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0230645.text: Roger. We've started charging Battery A, and the voltage started off a lot higher than I expected. It was just a little bit shy of 40. It looks like it's dropping down some now, the battery charge voltage. Seemed to me yesterday when we were doing this on Battery C, it started out initially on a much lower battery charge voltage. Over.

a11_0230645.speaker: McCandless
a11_0230645.text: Roger. Stand by a second, and I'll get some reading on that.

a11_0230645.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0230645.text: On charging Battery A: now, it's at about 39.3 and, oh, about 1.5 amps. Looks like it's gradually increasing in the amps charge [garble].

a11_0230645.speaker: McCandless
a11_0230645.text: Roger. On our TM, we're showing you at 39.11, and your current's about what you report.

a11_0230645.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0230645.text: Okay. I guess you're happy, then. [Pause.[

a11_0230645.speaker: McCandless
a11_0230645.text: I think we're losing you in the noise again, 11. Stand by.

a11_0231033.speaker: McCandless
a11_0231033.text: Roger, 11. On your battery charging question, we feel that it's probably a difference between individual batteries; and it does seem to have gone away as sort of a start-up transient here. Other factors that might conceivably have an influence on it would be battery temperature, things of this sort. EECOM seems to feel that it's operating within the normal design limits. Over.

a11_0231033.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0231033.text: All right. Very good. Thank you.

a11_0231409.speaker: McCandless
a11_0231409.text: 11, this is Houston. If you're interested in the morning news, I've got a summary here from PAO. Over.

a11_0231409.speaker: McCandless
a11_0231409.text: Okay. From Jodrell Bank, England, via AP: Britain's big Jodrell Bank radio telescope stopped receiving signals from the Soviet Union's unmanned Moon shot at 5:49 EDT today. And a spokesman said that it appeared that the Luna 15 spaceship "had gone beyond the Moon". Another quote: "We don't think it has landed," said a spokesman for Sir Bernard Lovell, Director of the Observatory. Washington UPI: Vice President Spiro T. Agnew has called for putting a man on Mars by the year 2000, but Democratic leaders replied that priority must go to needs on Earth. Agnew, ranking government official at the Ap

a11_0231409.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0231409.text: Roger. Thank you, Bruce. Another thing on that number 2 item, we all [garble] before we left, and we hope we get a chance to see him another time. Over.

a11_0231409.speaker: McCandless
a11_0231409.text: Roger. And I understand he was down there and really enjoyed watching the launch. We all think it was pretty magnificent, and you all are doing a great job up there.

a11_0232200.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0232200.text: A flight dynamics officer reports that, in terms of distance, Apollo 11 will reach the half-way mark at 25 hours, 0 minutes, 53 seconds. At that time the spacecraft will be 104,350 [nautical] miles [193,256 km] from both the Earth and the Moon.

a11_0235703.speaker: McCandless
a11_0235703.text: Roger. Mike, we've got some comments on the performance of P23 for today if you've got a minute to talk.

a11_0235703.speaker: McCandless
a11_0235703.text: Okay. For today, we'd like you, on P23, to make a trunnion bias determination prior to P23 sightings, as called out in the procedures, and also one afterwards. Our intent here is to check out the possibility that some sort of thermal effect may be giving you errors in the angular read-out in the sextant. The bias that you get beforehand should be incorporated, that is a Proceed on Noun 87 after you get two consecutive measurements equal to within 0.003 degrees. And, of course, move the trunnion off a couple of degrees between the measurements. The Earth should be a lot smaller in your field of

a11_0235703.speaker: Collins
a11_0235703.text: Roger. Stand by one. We're going to stop PTC, and then we'll talk about this P23.

a11_0235703.speaker: Collins
a11_0235703.text: Okay. We're stopping PTC now and maneuvering to our P52 and optics cal attitude. In regard to the P23, what I was trying to tell you yesterday was about that. The M-line is not anywhere parallel to the horizon at the roll, pitch, and yaw which you gave me to go to for the substellar point, and I was trying to maneuver off to get it parallel to the horizon when you all said that was not necessary.

a11_0235703.speaker: McCandless
a11_0235703.text: Roger, 11. I guess in keeping the cups of coffee score, why you get that one. [Pause.]

a11_0235703.speaker: Collins
a11_0235703.text: Well - Okay - Well, this morning, let's just see how close it comes to being parallel to the M-line. Before we start marking the first time, it appeared that the computation of those three angles was somewhat off, and that I was wasting a lot of gas by going to those three angles and then having to make large attitude changes after that to get the M-line parallel, and in some cases it appeared to be just an accepted attitude required, and you all said that it wasn't needed. So I was marking in some cases with the M-line not parallel. I thought perhaps you had some processor for computing that

a11_0235703.speaker: McCandless
a11_0235703.text: Roger, 11. We don't have that capability. We do require that the M-line be parallel to the horizon in order to get a good mark. We feel that possibly the - the state vector information that you were using for your maneuver basis yesterday may have needed to be updated a little. And if you'll stand by a second, we'll give you an evaluation of what we feel you'll get today by the Auto maneuver.

a11_0241056.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0241056.text: Roger. I'm getting ready to do an O 2 fuel cell purge. Do you have any particulars on this? And I assume you want these one at a time, or can I triple up? Over.

a11_0241056.speaker: McCandless
a11_0241056.text: We'd like them one at a time, and stand by. I don't think we have any sequence. You can do them in any order you want.

a11_0241056.speaker: McCandless
a11_0241056.text: And we're watching you on TM down here.

a11_0241503.speaker: Collins
a11_0241503.text: Houston, Apollo 11. You want to look at these Noun 93s before I proceed on?

a11_0241503.speaker: McCandless
a11_0241503.text: Yes, please. Stand by a second.

a11_0241503.speaker: Collins
a11_0241503.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a11_0241503.speaker: McCandless
a11_0241503.text: 11, this is Houston. On our TM, here, we're only seeing values in two registers. Can you read us out the contents of Register 3, please?

a11_0241503.speaker: Collins
a11_0241503.text: Register 3: minus three balls 24.

a11_0241503.speaker: McCandless
a11_0241503.text: Roger. Minus three balls 24. And you can go ahead and Proceed.

a11_0241503.speaker: Collins
a11_0241503.text: Okay. Proceeding at this time. [Long pause.]

a11_0241503.speaker: McCandless
a11_0241503.text: 11, Houston. After you've completed P52, we'd like to uplink you a new state vector so we can start out clean on this P23. Over.

a11_0241503.speaker: Collins
a11_0241503.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a11_0241503.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0241503.text: Houston, are you observing the higher O 2 flow on Fuel Cell 3? [Pause.]

a11_0241503.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0241503.text: Houston, Apollo 11. It's triggered the Master Alarm three times, now. [Master alarm goes off in the background] There goes number four. It goes up to about 1.4, then oscillates back down to about 1.1. Over.

a11_0241503.speaker: McCandless
a11_0241503.text: Roger. We're showing 1.3 now on TM. Stand by a second. [Pause.]

a11_0241503.speaker: Collins
a11_0241503.text: And we're in P00, now, for a state vector.

a11_0241503.speaker: McCandless
a11_0241503.text: Roger. Give us Accept, please.

a11_0241503.speaker: Collins
a11_0241503.text: Roger that. [Long pause.]

a11_0241503.speaker: McCandless
a11_0241503.text: 11, Houston. On your O 2 flow, Fuel Cell 3: apparently it was flowing a little higher than the other two during purge, but the flow rate's acceptable. Over.

a11_0241503.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0241503.text: Roger, understand. It seems to be flowing a little bit more, and actually putting out more current than the other two, also. Over.

a11_0241503.speaker: McCandless
a11_0241503.text: Roger. We copy. [Long pause.]

a11_0241503.speaker: McCandless
a11_0241503.text: 11, this is Houston. We've completed the uplink; the computer is yours. You can go back to Block.

a11_0241503.speaker: Collins
a11_0241503.text: Okay. Thank you. [Long pause.]

a11_0241503.speaker: McCandless
a11_0241503.text: Go ahead, 11. [Long pause.]

a11_0241503.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0241503.text: Houston, 11. I don't believe we were calling you right then.

a11_0242200.speaker: McCandless
a11_0242200.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Go ahead.

a11_0242200.speaker: Collins
a11_0242200.text: Rog. I'm in a good attitude here to do - I have in the sextant this last P52 star [off-mike to crewmate] What number's [garble]? [to CapCom] star 37. Is that all right for the optics calibration to save some gas, or do you want to go over to star 40?

a11_0242200.speaker: McCandless
a11_0242200.text: Star 37 will be fine for the optics calibration. And we haven't noticed a Verb 66, yet, after our state vector uplink. Over.

a11_0242200.speaker: McCandless
a11_0242200.text: When you move on into P23, we recommend that you use the CMC-computed angles for your Auto maneuver and see how that works out. If it doesn't bring you up with the M-line parallel to the horizon to the substellar point, we'll see if we can get you some ground-computed angles. I guess the big thing here is to make sure that the M-line is parallel to substellar point so we can get a good angular measurement. Over.

a11_0242925.speaker: Collins
a11_0242925.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Marking on this star, I get a Noun 87 twice in a row of five balls, so that's sufficient for a Cal.

a11_0242925.speaker: Collins
a11_0242925.text: Okay. Now I want to go to P00, and I'm going to take your three angles and do a Verb 49 maneuver to your substellar point. Okay?

a11_0242925.speaker: McCandless
a11_0242925.text: Okay. We recommend that for the first star, if we gave you a new state vector, we'd like to try the CMC-computed angles for the Auto maneuver.

a11_0242925.speaker: McCandless
a11_0242925.text: And have you hit Proceed on this display to enter the zero?

a11_0242925.speaker: McCandless
a11_0242925.text: 11, Houston. Over the past 2 hours we have seen a slight continuing increase in partial pressure of CO 2 . Have you in fact changed the CO 2 canister yet this morning? We don't need to do it right now; we'd just like to confirm that our instrumentation is in good shape. Over.

a11_0242925.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0242925.text: No. We haven't changed any canisters this morning.

a11_0242925.speaker: McCandless
a11_0242925.text: Okay. Then you can plan on accomplishing that after P23 is over and you've got the LEB clear.

a11_0242925.speaker: Collins
a11_0242925.text: Houston, Apollo 11. We're in process of maneuvering to P23's desired attitude. It likes roll 8.37, pitch 61.33, and yaw 339.87. Over.

a11_0242925.speaker: McCandless
a11_0242925.text: Roger. We copy. And that's for star 01?

a11_0244107.speaker: Collins
a11_0244107.text: Houston, Apollo 11. On this star, the Auto maneuver works just fine. I'm right at the substellar point. Everything looks beautiful except there is no star in sight. It is just not visible.

a11_0244107.speaker: McCandless
a11_0244107.text: You're not getting any reflections or anything like that that would obscure your vision, are you?

a11_0244107.speaker: Collins
a11_0244107.text: Well, of course, the Earth is pretty bright, and the black sky, instead of being black, has sort of a rosy glow to it, and the star, unless it's a very bright one, is probably lost somewhere in that glow, but it is just not visible. I maneuvered the reticle considerably above the horizon to make sure that the star is not lost in the brightness below the horizon. However, even when I get the reticle considerably above the horizon so the star should be seen against the black background, it still is not visible.

a11_0244107.speaker: McCandless
a11_0244107.text: Roger. We copy. Standby a minute, please. [Long pause.]

a11_0244107.speaker: McCandless
a11_0244107.text: 11, this is Houston. Can you read us the shaft and trunnion angle off the counters?

a11_0244107.speaker: Collins
a11_0244107.text: Yeah, be glad to. Shaft, 331.2 and trunnion, 35.85.

a11_0244107.speaker: Collins
a11_0244107.text: It's really a fantastic sight through that sextant. A minute ago, during that Auto maneuver, the reticle swept across the Mediterranean. You could see all of North Africa, absolutely clear; all of Portugal, Spain, southern France; all of Italy, absolutely clear. Just a beautiful sight.

a11_0244107.speaker: McCandless
a11_0244107.text: Roger. We all envy you the view up there.

a11_0244107.speaker: McCandless
a11_0244107.text: Roger. On our ground computers we confirm the shaft and trunnion angle that you have as being pointed at the star. However, it looks as though that shaft and trunnion angle is also pointing into the structure of the LM, so that while you will be getting the Earth's horizon, the star LOS is obscured by the LM. We recommend an Auto maneuver to the attitudes in the - pen-and-inked into the Flight Plan. Roll 177.2, pitch 298.2 and yaw 330.0. Over.

a11_0250652.speaker: McCandless
a11_0250652.text: 11, this is Houston. While you're maneuvering there, could we get a LM/CM Delta-P reading from you? Over.

a11_0250652.speaker: Collins
a11_0250652.text: Rog. Just a tad under 1, Bruce, 0.95 [psi, 6.5 kPa].

a11_0250652.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0250652.text: This is Apollo Control. That reading was the difference in pressure between the Lunar Module cabin and the Command Module cabin.

a11_0251114.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0251114.text: This is Jim Lovell calling Apollo 11.

a11_0251114.speaker: Lovell
a11_0251114.text: I was a little worried. This is the backup Commander still standing by. You haven't given me the word yet. Are you Go?

a11_0251114.speaker: Armstrong
