a11_0251114.text: You've lost your chance to take this one, Jim.

a11_0251114.speaker: Collins
a11_0251114.text: Okay. Our maneuver is complete, and at this attitude the M-line is exactly 90 degrees out of phase. It is exactly pointed along the vector toward the center of the Earth instead of being parallel to the horizon.

a11_0251114.speaker: Collins
a11_0251114.text: I'm going to hold right here for your next suggestion.

a11_0251819.speaker: Collins
a11_0251819.text: Okay, Houston. It appears to be okay now. We've changed our attitude slightly, and I have a star and I'm maneuvering to get the M-line parallel.

a11_0251819.speaker: McCandless
a11_0251819.text: This is Houston. Roger. We copy.

a11_0251819.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0251819.text: Houston, Apollo 11. You - stand by one.

a11_0251819.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0251819.text: Distance is now 103,263 nautical miles [191,243 km]. Velocity 5,256 feet per second [1,602 m/s].

a11_0253608.speaker: Collins
a11_0253608.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Are you copying these Noun 49s. I've been going through them fairly swiftly?

a11_0253608.speaker: McCandless
a11_0253608.text: Yes. We certainly are. I see a - what a plus 0.1 and a plus 0.2 on nautical miles and feet per second. Over.

a11_0254345.speaker: McCandless
a11_0254345.text: Yes, Mike. We show you in Verb 59 right now. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0254345.speaker: Collins
a11_0254345.text: That's right. I - I haven't entered - I gave the - I gave it back to the computer for a second. I put the mode switch from Manual back to CMC while I fooled with the DSKY, and the computer drove the star off out of sight. So the delay here has been in going back to Manual and finding the star again, which I've finally done. And in just a second here, I'll go to Enter and get a 51 and mark on it. As I say, for some reason the computer drove the star off out of sight.

a11_0254814.speaker: McCandless
a11_0254814.text: Roger. We show you with a little less than an hour to the Midcourse Correction number 2 burn. We recommend that you terminate the P23 activities here and press on with a waste-water dump, which we need from you, and getting ready for the burn. Over.

a11_0254814.speaker: McCandless
a11_0254814.text: And I have your Midcourse Correction number 2 PAD here when you're ready to copy.

a11_0254814.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0254814.text: [Faint.] Roger, Houston. Apollo 11, ready to copy MCC-2.

a11_0254814.speaker: McCandless
a11_0254814.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Midcourse Correction number 2. SPS/G&N; 63059; plus 0.97, minus 0.20; GET ignition 026:44:57.92; plus 0011.8, minus 0000.3, plus 0017.7; roll, 277, 355, 015; Noun 44, Block is N/A; Delta-V T 0021.3, 00:3, 0016.8; sextant star 30, 208.2, 37.0. The rest of the PAD is N/A. GDC align, Vega and Deneb; roll align 007, 144, 068. No ullage. LM weight: 33302. For your information, your heads will be pointed roughly towards the Earth on this burn. Read back. Over.

a11_0254814.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0254814.text: Roger. Midcourse Correction number 2. SPS/G&N: 63059; plus 0.97, minus 0.20; 026:44:57.92; plus 0011.8, minus 0000.3, plus 0017.7; 277 - Are you still copying, Houston? Over.

a11_0254814.speaker: McCandless
a11_0254814.text: Roger. Still copying. Go ahead. [Long pause.] Apollo 11, this is - Apollo 11, this is Houston. I copied your transmission about roll, 277. And go ahead from roll, 277. Over.

a11_0254814.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0254814.text: Roger. 355, 015; N/A; 0021.3, 00:3, 0016.8; 30, 208.2, 37.0. Vega and Deneb; 007, 144, 068. No ullage. LM weight, 33302. Heads towards the Earth. Over.

a11_0254814.speaker: McCandless
a11_0254814.text: 11, this is Houston. Readback correct. Out.

a11_0254814.speaker: McCandless
a11_0254814.text: Roger. We'd like you to terminate Battery A charge at GET 26 hours and re-initiate Battery A charge after Midcourse Correction 2. Over.

a11_0255800.speaker: McCandless
a11_0255800.text: Roger. If you can give us Accept, we'll send you up a state vector and a target load for the maneuver.

a11_0255800.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0255800.text: Okay. Give us 1 minute to check the P23 damage.

a11_0260717.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0260717.text: Houston, Apollo 11.

a11_0260717.speaker: McCandless
a11_0260717.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

a11_0260717.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0260717.text: Roger. I wonder if you have a star that might be a little closer to the direction we're burning than the one you gave us.

a11_0260717.speaker: McCandless
a11_0260717.text: Roger. We're going to re-work the attitude in the sextant star for you in order to improve the High Gain Antenna coverage, and we'll have that for you in a few seconds.

a11_0260717.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0260717.text: Fine. We're already maneuvering to that attitude.

a11_0260717.speaker: McCandless
a11_0260717.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_0260717.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0260717.text: Maybe you can make it just a change in roll. Apollo 11. Over.

a11_0260717.speaker: McCandless
a11_0260717.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_0260717.speaker: McCandless
a11_0260717.text: 11, this is Houston. Over.

a11_0260717.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0260717.text: Go ahead.

a11_0260717.speaker: McCandless
a11_0260717.text: Roger. On your attitude for the burn: we'd like you to use roll 096, pitch 356, yaw 018, and that will give you a sextant star of 01, shaft 253.8, trunnion 24.2. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0260717.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0260717.text: [Garble] Apollo 11. Roll 096, 356, 018, star 01 [garble].

a11_0260717.speaker: McCandless
a11_0260717.text: 11, this is Houston. We are having difficulty reading you through the noise. Could you read back again, please? Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0260717.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0260717.text: Roger, Houston. Apollo 11. How do you read now?

a11_0260717.speaker: McCandless
a11_0260717.text: Roger. Very weakly in the noise, but I think I can copy. Go ahead.

a11_0260717.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0260717.text: Okay. Roll 096, 356, 018; star 01 [garble].

a11_0260717.speaker: McCandless
a11_0260717.text: Roger. I got all of that except trunnion. It's trunnion 242. Over.

a11_0260717.speaker: Collins
a11_0260717.text: Houston, Apollo 11. How do you read on Omni A?

a11_0260717.speaker: McCandless
a11_0260717.text: Roger. Loud and clear, 11.

a11_0260717.speaker: Collins
a11_0260717.text: Okay. We'll stay on Omni A for a while, then.

a11_0260717.speaker: McCandless
a11_0260717.text: Okay. I got all your readback except the value for trunnion, and if it's 242, confirm, please.

a11_0260717.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0260717.text: Roger. 242.

a11_0260717.speaker: McCandless
a11_0260717.text: Okay.

a11_0263829.speaker: Collins
a11_0263829.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Could you give us a couple of High Gain Antenna angles, please?

a11_0263829.speaker: Collins
a11_0263829.text: Houston, Apollo 11. How do you read on High Gain?

a11_0263829.speaker: McCandless
a11_0263829.text: Read you loud and clear on the High Gain down here, and everything's looking good from our standpoint for your burn. Over.

a11_0263829.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0263829.text: This is Apollo Control at 26 hours, 40 minutes. We're just under 4 minutes to the midcourse correction maneuver. Apollo 11's distance from the Earth is 109,245 nautical miles [202,322 km]. Its velocity is 5,033 feet per second [1,534 m/s]. Spacecraft weight; 96,361 pounds [43,709 kg].

a11_0264538.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0264538.text: Houston, burn completed. You copying our residuals?

a11_0264538.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0264538.text: And, Houston, looked like we saw about 87 or 88 psi [600 or 607 kPa] on chamber pressure that time. I'd like you to look at that on the ground.

a11_0264538.speaker: McCandless
a11_0264538.text: Roger, 11. We'll take a look at that and get back with you in a few minutes. [Long pause.]

a11_0264538.speaker: McCandless
a11_0264538.text: 11, Houston. On our real-time telemetry we saw 95 to 97 psi [655 to 669 kPa] on chamber pressure. We'll - We will look at the recordings down here, though, and get back with you again. Over.

a11_0264538.speaker: Collins
a11_0264538.text: No, we're not going to trim those residuals.

a11_0264538.speaker: McCandless
a11_0264538.text: 11, Houston. Could we get your Delta-V counter reading, please, from this burn?

a11_0264951.speaker: McCandless
a11_0264951.text: 11, Houston. Could we get your Delta-V counter reading, please, from this burn?

a11_0264951.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0264951.text: Houston, is there anything else you need on the burn status report? [Pause.]

a11_0265441.speaker: McCandless
a11_0265441.text: Roger. I just want to remind you, we haven't noticed on the TM the Verb 66 after the burn. And for your information, we played the recorded TV back last night, I believe, after you all turned in for your rest period, and the pictures came out quite well. Over.

a11_0265441.speaker: Collins
a11_0265441.text: Did you get any usable pictures out of MILA on that first pass?

a11_0265441.speaker: McCandless
a11_0265441.text: Not that we've seen. We had word on the voice loop that MILA reported that they had gotten a minute's worth of TV signal, and Goldstone reported that they had gotten about a minute's worth of modulation but that they weren't able to get anything off of it.

a11_0265441.speaker: McCandless
a11_0265441.text: Okay. Here's another input here, 11, that the MILA data was recognizable as a picture, but we don't have any evaluation as to the quality of the picture. Over.

a11_0265441.speaker: McCandless
a11_0265441.text: And for our information, we've been watching a pCO 2 again. Did you change a lithium hydroxide canister this morning? Over.

a11_0265441.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0265441.text: Yes. We did, and we've been seeing 1.7 percent in the spacecraft ever since.

a11_0265441.speaker: McCandless
a11_0265441.text: Roger. That agrees with our data.

a11_0265441.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0265441.text: Houston, Apollo 11. We're starting our maneuver to PTC attitude.

a11_0265441.speaker: McCandless
a11_0265441.text: Roger. From a propellant-balancing standpoint, we recommend that you use quads Alpha and Bravo to start the PTC maneuvers. Over.

a11_0265441.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0265441.text: This is Apollo Control at 27 hours. Apollo 11's distance now 110,198 nautical miles [204,087 km]. Velocity, 4,984 feet per second [1,519 m/s].

a11_0270614.speaker: McCandless
a11_0270614.text: Roger. For Cryo-balancing purposes, we'd like you to turn the heater in oxygen tank number 1, Off, at this time. Over.

a11_0270614.speaker: McCandless
a11_0270614.text: Everything else in the Cryo system remains the same.

a11_0270614.speaker: Collins
a11_0270614.text: Okay. We have O 2 heater Tank 1, Off.

a11_0270614.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0270614.text: This is Apollo Control at 27 hours, 7 minutes. The crew is now in the process...

a11_0270614.speaker: Collins
a11_0270614.text: How is EECOM today? Is he happy with all those good things?

a11_0270614.speaker: McCandless
a11_0270614.text: Oh, EECOM is happy, and after you get PTC set up, we've got a little procedure from EECOM here to check out the O 2 flow and the O 2 flow sensor in your cabin enrichment. Over.

a11_0270614.speaker: Collins
a11_0270614.text: It'll be a while, Bruce. We're just now arriving in PTC attitude, and we're going to our 20 minutes of monitoring thruster activity.

a11_0270614.speaker: McCandless
a11_0270614.text: Roger. We copy. He'll be here.

a11_0271303.speaker: Collins
a11_0271303.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Are you going to take control of the Omnis now and switch us between B and D?

a11_0271303.speaker: Lovell
a11_0271303.text: This is Houston. Stand by one. [Long pause.]

a11_0271303.speaker: Lovell
a11_0271303.text: 11, Houston.

a11_0271303.speaker: Collins
a11_0271303.text: Go ahead.

a11_0271303.speaker: Lovell
a11_0271303.text: Mike, how about selecting Bravo at this time, and I'll give you a Comm configuration here, shortly.

a11_0271303.speaker: Collins
a11_0271303.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a11_0271303.speaker: Collins
a11_0271303.text: That PTC sure worked well last night.

a11_0271303.speaker: Lovell
a11_0271303.text: Outstanding. [Long pause.]

a11_0271303.speaker: Lovell
a11_0271303.text: 11, Houston.

a11_0271303.speaker: Collins
a11_0271303.text: Go ahead.

a11_0271303.speaker: Lovell
a11_0271303.text: Okay. Roll for the Comm situation: have S-band antenna Omni A in Bravo, S-band antenna Omni to Omni, High Gain Track to Manual, and the pitch is minus 50 and yaw is 270. [Pause.]

a11_0271303.speaker: Collins
a11_0271303.text: You may have to repeat some of that there, James. We got a - We got a LM guy taking care of the High Gain right now.

a11_0271303.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0271303.text: Yes, and he's eyeballing the Earth.

a11_0271303.speaker: Collins
a11_0271303.text: He's got his head out the window.

a11_0271303.speaker: Lovell
a11_0271303.text: I understand, I had trouble on [Gemini] 12 with him, too.

a11_0271303.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0271303.text: Say again what you'd like.

a11_0271303.speaker: Lovell
a11_0271303.text: Okay, The S-band antenna Omni A switch to Bravo which you have now, and S-band antenna Omni to the Omni position, and the High Gain Track to the Manual position.

a11_0271303.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0271303.text: To Manual.

a11_0271303.speaker: Lovell
a11_0271303.text: And the pitch and yaw angles are minus 50 for pitch and yaw is 270.

a11_0271303.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0271303.text: Minus 50 and 270.

a11_0271303.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0271303.text: Hey, Jim, I'm looking through the monocular now, and I guess to coin an expression, the view is just out of this world. I can see all the islands in the Mediterranean. Some larger and smaller islands of Majorca, Sardinia and Corsica. A little haze over the upper Italian peninsula, some cumulus clouds out over Greece. The Sun is setting on the eastern Mediterranean now. The British Isles are definitely greener color than the brownish green that we have in the islands, in the peninsula of Spain. Over.

a11_0271303.speaker: Lovell
a11_0271303.text: Rog. Understand that the Northern Africa - Mediterranean area is fairly clear today, huh?

a11_0271303.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0271303.text: Right.

a11_0271303.speaker: Collins
a11_0271303.text: Yes. We see a bunch of roads with cars driving up and down, too.

a11_0271303.speaker: Lovell
a11_0271303.text: Do you find that the monocular is any good to you, Buzz?

a11_0271303.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0271303.text: Yeah, It'd be nice if it had another order of magnitude of power on it. Of course, it has a tendency to jiggle around a little bit, and you might want to have some sort of a bracket. I hate to use that word though. [Pause.]

a11_0271303.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0271303.text: Got an anticyclone going in the southern hemisphere southeast of Brazil, and some - Well, the diameter of it must be over 2,000 miles [3,000 km] across.

a11_0271303.speaker: Lovell
a11_0271303.text: How does the weather look up in the southern part of the western hemisphere, or up in the United States area?

a11_0271303.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0271303.text: Well, you all are just beginning to come over the LM now. I can see parts of Central America, and it looks to be fairly, fairly clear there. The islands in the Caribbean there, beginning to come in and rather a few streaming lines of clouds. Looks like there is a system up to the - well, off of Greenland that has some large cloud streamers extending back down to the southwest. The east coast of the US is just coming into view now, and it doesn't look too bad that I can see right now. We may have some pretty good shots later on this afternoon. Over.

a11_0271303.speaker: McCandless
a11_0271303.text: Roger. Thank you.

a11_0271303.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0271303.text: That was Buzz Aldrin giving the description of what he could see on the Earth. The backup Lunar Module Pilot Fred Haise is also in the Control Center at the present time.

a11_0271303.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0271303.text: Houston, Apollo 11.

a11_0271303.speaker: Lovell
a11_0271303.text: Go ahead, 11.

a11_0271303.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0271303.text: I've got a comment about the point on the Earth where the Sun's rays reflect back up toward us. In general, the color of the oceans is mostly uniform and it's bright and darker blue except for that region that's about one-eighth of an Earth's radius in diameter; and in this circular area, the blue of the water turns a grayish color, and I'm sure that's where the Sun's rays are being reflected back on up toward us. Over.

a11_0271303.speaker: Lovell
a11_0271303.text: Roger, Buzz. We noticed the same thing. It's very similar to looking at a light shining on something like a billiard ball or a bowling ball. You get this bright spot in the blue of the water, and that turns it to sort of a grayish color.

a11_0271303.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0271303.text: Yes. Is there a Navy term for that?

a11_0271303.speaker: Lovell
a11_0271303.text: [Laughing.] A lot of gray paint.

a11_0272527.speaker: Lovell
a11_0272527.text: 11 - 11, Houston.

a11_0272527.speaker: Collins
a11_0272527.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a11_0272527.speaker: Lovell
a11_0272527.text: Mike, are you satisfied with P23 now?

a11_0272527.speaker: Collins
a11_0272527.text: Yeah, I'm happy with the last updates we got, you know, in terms of what it did to our state vector. Still not altogether happy with the various procedures. If we could pick stars within the smaller range of trunnion angles so that you could allow P23 to pick its own maneuver and go to that substellar point and then have that star visible, that would - seems to me to be the simplest and best way to do it.

a11_0272527.speaker: Lovell
a11_0272527.text: How about the...

a11_0272527.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0272527.text: [Garble] correction on that last [garble].

a11_0272527.speaker: Lovell
a11_0272527.text: How about the horizon now? Is it pretty well defined for you and no longer hazy?

a11_0272527.speaker: Collins
a11_0272527.text: Yes. We're far enough out now that the - I think the horizon definition variation is lost in the noise. [Long pause.]

a11_0272527.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0272527.text: Hey, Jim.

a11_0272527.speaker: Lovell
a11_0272527.text: Go ahead, Buzz.

a11_0272527.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0272527.text: Look like - Looks like the best way to get a good, steady view through the monocular is to just steady it out and let it float right in front of your eye, and then you kind of float up next to it so that you're not touching it at all. It has a very slow drift, and you get a better, steadier view that way.

a11_0272527.speaker: Lovell
a11_0272527.text: Sounds good. [Long pause.]

a11_0272527.speaker: Lovell
a11_0272527.text: How does it feel to be airborne again, Buzz?

a11_0272527.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0272527.text: Well, I'll tell you, I've been having a ball floating around inside here, back and forth, up to one place and back to another. It's like being outside, except more comfortable.

a11_0272527.speaker: Lovell
a11_0272527.text: It's a lot bigger than our last vehicle.

a11_0272527.speaker: Collins
a11_0272527.text: [Garble] kept me busy, I'm...

a11_0272527.speaker: Collins
a11_0272527.text: Say again that last?

a11_0272527.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0272527.text: Yes. It sure is nice in here.

a11_0272527.speaker: Lovell
a11_0272527.text: I said it's a lot bigger than the last vehicle that Buzz and I were in.

a11_0272527.speaker: Collins
a11_0272527.text: Oh, yeah. It's been nice. I've been very busy so far. I'm looking forward to taking the afternoon off. I've been cooking, and sweeping, and almost sewing, and you know, the usual little housekeeping things.

a11_0272527.speaker: Lovell
a11_0272527.text: It was very convenient the way they put the food preparation system right next to the nav station.

a11_0272527.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0272527.text: Everything's right next to everything in this vehicle.

a11_0272527.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0272527.text: Not where the waste management's concerned.

a11_0272527.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0272527.text: Jim, it's been a little warm in the machine throughout yesterday, and last night during the PTC, it cooled off somewhat with the windows buttoned up, and we've seen suit temperatures of about, oh, the high 40s and cabin temperatures in the low 60s. But this seems to be still a little bit on the - a little bit on the warm side.

a11_0272527.speaker: Lovell
a11_0272527.text: I understand that it got a little warm during the day and cooled down a little bit when you put the shades up, but you're still a little bit warm. Do you have any moisture condensation or anything like that on the wall?

a11_0272527.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0272527.text: No, we haven't been able to detect any moisture any place in the spacecraft. It seems to be fine.

a11_0272527.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0272527.text: One of the hydrogen filters - the one that we've got on the hot water - seems to keep flowing when you remove one of the food bags from it. Its flow rate is quite small, right near the end of one ounce, and that contributes a little bit of moisture to the atmosphere.

a11_0272527.speaker: Collins
a11_0272527.text: Yeah, I think on that hydrogen thing, it's - I'm not sure, but I think it's a back-pressure problem. If the thing sees any back-pressure at all, like when the bag is attached, well the flow rate will slowly decrease to where it's almost zero, and you wait, and you wait, and you wait for that last ounce. You think you have it and you remove the bag, and then you very rapidly thereafter see maybe, oh, a glob the size of a dime or a quarter come out and just hang there. That appears to be true even though the opening into the bag is not restricted.

a11_0272527.speaker: Lovell
a11_0272527.text: Understand.

a11_0272527.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0272527.text: In general, I think they do quite a good job, especially on the guns, in removing a lot of the hydrogen bubbles.

a11_0272527.speaker: Lovell
a11_0272527.text: Have the water temperatures been good? Are you getting hot water?

a11_0272527.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0272527.text: Yeah. It seems reasonably warm.

a11_0272527.speaker: Collins
a11_0272527.text: We made three cups of coffee today. The last one - you know when all the plumbing was warmed up, the hydrogen gun and everything, was the warmest of the three. I don't know who had that one - Neil, did you have that one? How was your coffee? You didn't drink it till later, did you? But anyway, it's pretty good. It's not piping hot, but it sure beats stone-cold coffee. [Long pause.]

a11_0272527.speaker: Collins
a11_0272527.text: Jim, we've been sitting here a little over 20 minutes now. How does the thruster firing activity look? Are you ready to go on with this PTC?

a11_0272527.speaker: Lovell
a11_0272527.text: Rog. Stand by.

a11_0272527.speaker: Lovell
a11_0272527.text: We're all set to go, Mike.

a11_0272527.speaker: Collins
a11_0272527.text: Okay. I'll press on then.

a11_0273559.speaker: Collins
a11_0273559.text: Houston, Apollo 11. PTC has started and it looks good.

a11_0273559.speaker: McCandless
a11_0273559.text: 11, Roger. This is Houston. Roger. Out.

a11_0274600.speaker: McCandless
a11_0274600.text: Roger. If you're free for a couple of minutes, we have a procedure here that will let us verify the O 2 flow transducer and at the same time get some more of our cabin enrichment out of the way. Over.

a11_0274600.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0274600.text: [Faint.] Go ahead, Houston. We're ready to copy.

a11_0274600.speaker: McCandless
a11_0274600.text: Roger. The primary purpose of this is, as I mentioned, to let us check out your O 2 flow transducer. However, we still need about 2 hours' worth of cabin enrichment, so we'd like to keep the vent that we're going to set up going for this purpose. Okay. We want you to install the cabin vent quick disconnect which you'll find in compartment R-6, that is Romeo-6, on the urine connector on panel 251. When this is completed, verify that the waste stowage vent valve is closed, and then open or position the waste management overboard drain to the Dump position. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0274600.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0274600.text: Okay. Understand that. [Pause.] Install the cabin quick disconnect out of R-6 on the 251 urine connector and verify the waste dump valve is closed, and say again the last part.

a11_0274600.speaker: McCandless
a11_0274600.text: Roger. And then put the waste management overboard drain valve into the Dump position. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0274600.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0274600.text: Roger. Put the waste management overboard drain valve to the Dump position.

a11_0274600.speaker: McCandless
a11_0274600.text: Right. That's the one down on panel 251 also. And we'll watch your O 2 flow on telemetry down here.

a11_0274600.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0274600.text: Okay, Houston. That configuration is set up.

a11_0274600.speaker: McCandless
a11_0274600.text: 11, this is Houston. Say again, please.

a11_0274600.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0274600.text: You do have the O 2 flow transducer checkout setup accomplished.

a11_0274600.speaker: McCandless
a11_0274600.text: Okay. Understand you have opened the drain valve at this time.

a11_0274600.speaker: McCandless
a11_0274600.text: Roger. We're not getting telemetry data from you right due to low signal strength. There it comes back. I expect it'll probably take us anywhere from 15 minutes to half an hour to see an increase in O 2 flow due to the size of the cabin versus the small size of the drain. Over.

a11_0280716.speaker: Collins
a11_0280716.text: Rog. I've got the world in my window for a change and looking at it through the monocular, it's really something. I wish I could describe it properly, but the weather is very good. South America is coming around into view. I can see on the - what appears to me to be upper horizon, a point that must be just about Seattle, Washington, and then from there I can see all the way down to the southern tip - Tierra del Fuego and the southern tip of the continent.

a11_0280716.speaker: McCandless
a11_0280716.text: Roger. Sounds like you've got a beautiful view up there.

a11_0280716.speaker: Collins
a11_0280716.text: Absolutely fantastic. I hope the pictures come out; we're rotating around where it's going out of view again.

a11_0280716.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0280716.text: I'm waiting to pick it up in the sextant.

a11_0280716.speaker: McCandless
a11_0280716.text: Sounds like one of these rotating restaurants.

a11_0283609.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0283609.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Do you need some help keeping Omnis locked on us?

a11_0283609.speaker: McCandless
a11_0283609.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Negative. We had a command computer at the Madrid site go down. We had to switch over to Ascension temporarily. We're now back remoting through Madrid, and the computer is back, and we're ready to resume control of your Omnis and full communication. Over.

a11_0283609.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0283609.text: Okay. You've got it.

a11_0283609.speaker: McCandless
a11_0283609.text: Okay. One thing that we did miss in the drop-out in the noise here is your LM/CM Delta-P reading for about 28 hours GET. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0283609.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0283609.text: Okay. The LM/CM Delta-P is 0.98.

a11_0283609.speaker: McCandless
a11_0283609.text: Roger. 0.98, and what have you been reading for O 2 flow on your onboard gauge? Over.

a11_0283609.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0283609.text: Well, right now, after we put that gadget in, we've got it back to 0.35. Before that, we were reading off-scale low. I think ours is relatively correct, at least when time comes for the water accumulator to kick in at 10 seconds, it goes on up to about 0.75, 0.8, something like that.

a11_0283609.speaker: McCandless
a11_0283609.text: This is Houston. Roger. Out. [Long pause.]

a11_0283609.speaker: McCandless
a11_0283609.text: And, 11, this is Houston. A little more information based on our analysis of your last SPS burn: it looks like you got a good solid burn there. We show 94 psi chamber pressure and it looks like the SPS is definitely Go. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0283609.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0283609.text: Good to hear it.

a11_0283609.speaker: McCandless
a11_0283609.text: Roger. We thought you'd feel that way about it. [Pause.]

a11_0283609.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0283609.text: We're right in the middle of - well either [garble] salmon salad, or something like that. That's probably why we're not answering you right away.

a11_0283609.speaker: McCandless
a11_0283609.text: Okay. Well, we don't want...

a11_0283609.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0283609.text: My compliments to the chef, that salad salmon is outstanding.

a11_0283609.speaker: McCandless
a11_0283609.text: Roger. Understand that's the salad salmon. Over.

a11_0283609.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0283609.text: Something like that, salmon salad.

a11_0283609.speaker: McCandless
a11_0283609.text: There we go, the salmon salad, very good.

a11_0283609.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0283609.text: Okay. Bruce, we're coming up on the water accumulator activity, and it's going on up to 0.85, ah, oh, about 0.95 and it reached a peak there and then gradually dropped back on down to 0.6 now, 0.4, and it looks like it's pretty well - pretty well leveling off back down to 0.35. Over.

a11_0283609.speaker: McCandless
a11_0283609.text: Roger. We're copying that. [Long pause.]

a11_0283609.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0283609.text: At 28 hours, 40 minutes; we're showing Apollo 11's distance as 114,922 nautical miles [212,836 km] from Earth; velocity, 4,819 feet per second [1,469 m/s]. The crew is eating lunch at the present time, and it sounds like there's some music in the background that they are enjoying during their lunch period.

a11_0283609.speaker: McCandless
a11_0283609.text: 11, Houston.

a11_0283609.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0283609.text: Go ahead.

a11_0283609.speaker: McCandless
a11_0283609.text: Roger. On that O 2 flow transducer, down here on telemetry, our values are agreeing pretty well with what you read out onboard, and the EECOMs have been noticing this cycle, but it still looks like the indicated rate is lower than what we would expect. We're still working on the problem, and we'll let you have a more complete diagnosis on it in a little while.

a11_0283609.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0283609.text: Okay. It's a tight fix then.

a11_0283609.speaker: Collins
a11_0283609.text: We run a tight ship.

a11_0283609.speaker: McCandless
a11_0283609.text: Roger. Is that music I hear in the background?

a11_0283609.speaker: Collins
a11_0283609.text: Buzz is singing.

a11_0283609.speaker: McCandless
a11_0283609.text: Okay.

a11_0283609.speaker: Collins
a11_0283609.text: Pass me the sausage, man.

a11_0290000.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0290000.text: This is Apollo Control at 29 hours, 20 minutes. Apollo 11's distance from the Earth is now 116,747 nautical miles [216,215 km], velocity 4,758 feet per second [1,450 m/s]. One of the clocks in the control center is now displaying the time to landing, the landing time being based on the time in the Flight Plan. It shows we're 73 hours, 26 minutes, 30 seconds from the lunar landing.

a11_0293209.speaker: McCandless
a11_0293209.text: Roger, 11. We've been watching your activity on the DSKY there, and by selecting another major program with a Verb 37 Enter and all that, we show you collapsing the deadband in PTC and having driven the CMC rate from 0.3 degrees per second down to 0 degrees per second, although of course, with all the Auto RCS coils shut off, you're not firing any thrusters. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0293209.speaker: McCandless
a11_0293209.text: Well, you can just continue in your present configuration in PTC. However, if you go to turn any thrusters on, the CMC would then try to bring you into an attitude-hold position rather than continuing with the PTC. Over.

a11_0293209.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0293209.text: And, Houston, we're just looking at you out our window here. Looks like there's a circulation of cloud that's just moved east of Houston over the Gulf and Florida area. Did that have any rain in it this morning?

a11_0293209.speaker: McCandless
a11_0293209.text: Roger. Our report from outside says that it's raining out here, and it looks like you've got a pretty good eye for the weather there.

a11_0293209.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0293209.text: Yeah, well, it looks like it ought to clear up pretty soon from our viewpoint. The western edge of the weather isn't very far west of you.

a11_0295815.speaker: McCandless
a11_0295815.text: 11, this is Houston. As a result of our venting through the waste management drain, why, we've concluded that your O 2 flow rate sensor is, in fact, malfunctioning. I mentioned when we - you talked us through the cyclic water accumulator dump that even though it was moving, probably indicating a higher flow rate, it didn't seem to be indicating a flow rate that's high enough; and based on that and the flow that we're getting right now, we've concluded that the transducer is malfunctioning. We'd like to continue the O 2 flow for about another hour, shutting it off at about 31 hours GET, to get

a11_0295815.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0295815.text: Okay. Does it look to you like it just has a bias on it? [Long pause.]

a11_0295815.speaker: McCandless
a11_0295815.text: Roger, 11. It does seem to be a bias. Looks like it has a fairly high threshold before it starts indicating. EECOM seems to think, though, that for high flow rate purposes, it will still give you a relative indication during the mission. Over.

a11_0300000.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0300000.text: This is Apollo Control. We have a correction on those last distances and velocities. That distance and velocity is in reference to the Moon instead of the Earth. To the Moon - Apollo 11's distance from the Moon is 105,729 nautical miles [195,810 km] at the present time. Velocity in reference to the Moon, 4,230 feet per second [1,289 m/s].

a11_0301220.speaker: McCandless
a11_0301220.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. We'd like you to terminate charging on Battery A at GET 30 plus 15. Over.

a11_0301220.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0301220.text: Okay. 30 plus 15 for Battery A charge terminate.

a11_0301220.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0301220.text: This is Apollo Control. Apollo 11's distance from the Earth is 119,116 nautical miles [220,603 km]. Its Earth-referenced inertial velocity, 4,679 feet per second [1,426 m/s].

a11_0301534.speaker: McCandless
a11_0301534.text: Roger. If you're free for a minute, I've got some updates to the P37 PADs that we passed up to you yesterday afternoon, I guess. As a result of doing Midcourse Correction number 2, the Delta-V required in the TLI plus 35, 44, and 53 PADs have changed slightly. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0301534.speaker: McCandless
a11_0301534.text: Okay. TLI plus 35 PAD: the Delta-V T should be 7992 instead of 8016. TLI plus 44: it should be 6112 instead of 6141. And TLI plus 53: it should be 8172 instead of 8209. Read back. Over.

a11_0302928.speaker: McCandless
a11_0302928.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

a11_0302928.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0302928.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a11_0302928.speaker: McCandless
a11_0302928.text: 11, this is Houston. Goldstone reports they are receiving a TV picture coming down from you all. A little snowy, but a good TV picture. Over.

a11_0302928.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0302928.text: Roger. We're just testing the equipment up here.

a11_0302928.speaker: McCandless
a11_0302928.text: Roger.

a11_0302928.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0302928.text: Ask them if they can read the numbers.

a11_0302928.speaker: McCandless
a11_0302928.text: Okay. Stand by. [Long pause.]

a11_0302928.speaker: Network (CapCom)
a11_0302928.text: Goldstone, this is Houston CapCom. Over.

a11_0302928.speaker: Comm Tech
a11_0302928.text: Houston CapCom, Goldstone M&O. Go ahead.

a11_0302928.speaker: Network (CapCom)
a11_0302928.text: Roger. Stand by a minute, Goldstone.

a11_0302928.speaker: McCandless
a11_0302928.text: 11, this is Houston. What numbers are you referring to? Over.

a11_0302928.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0302928.text: Well, I guess if they can't see any numbers, why, it's kind of a lost cause.

a11_0302928.speaker: McCandless
a11_0302928.text: Negative. Stand by. We wanted to know...

a11_0302928.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0302928.text: [Garble.]

a11_0302928.speaker: McCandless
a11_0302928.text: We wanted to know what numbers, before we asked them.

a11_0302928.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0302928.text: Okay. I'm showing them the DSKY, and I'd like to know whether they can read what's showing on the DSKY, and also whether they can see P-R-O-G, V-E-R-B, and N-O-U-N. Over.

a11_0302928.speaker: McCandless
a11_0302928.text: Roger. Stand by a second.

a11_0302928.speaker: Network (CapCom)
a11_0302928.text: Goldstone M&O, Houston CapCom. Over.

a11_0302928.speaker: Comm Tech
a11_0302928.text: CapCom, Goldstone. Go ahead.

a11_0302928.speaker: Network (CapCom)
a11_0302928.text: Roger. Did you copy the spacecraft request?

a11_0302928.speaker: Comm Tech
a11_0302928.text: That's affirmative. I am reading the numbers on our monitor here.

a11_0302928.speaker: Network (CapCom)
a11_0302928.text: Okay, that's - standby. Roger. That's both the numbers on the DSKY itself, and the little words like Program and Verb, Noun, Computer Activity, things of this sort?

a11_0302928.speaker: Comm Tech
a11_0302928.text: Roger. I can read the numbers clearly. We can't distinguish what the words are, because it is a little snowy.

a11_0302928.speaker: Network (CapCom)
a11_0302928.text: Roger. Thank you.

a11_0302928.speaker: Comm Tech
a11_0302928.text: Okay. I read Verb, Noun, and Program.

a11_0302928.speaker: Network (CapCom)
a11_0302928.text: Roger. Do you see - Over in the left hand corner, there's a big square one that says Computer Activity, Comp Activity?

a11_0302928.speaker: Comm Tech
a11_0302928.text: Roger. I see a flash occasionally in that area.

a11_0302928.speaker: Network (CapCom)
a11_0302928.text: Right. That's the one.

a11_0302928.speaker: Comm Tech
a11_0302928.text: Okay. It looks like he's moved the camera at this time.

a11_0302928.speaker: Network (CapCom)
a11_0302928.text: Roger.

a11_0302928.speaker: McCandless
a11_0302928.text: 11, this is Houston. Goldstone M&O reports that they can read the numbers on the DSKY. They can also read Verb, Noun, Program, and see the Comp Activity light flashing. Over.

a11_0302928.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0302928.text: Very good. Thank you

a11_0302928.speaker: McCandless
a11_0302928.text: And they also report you appear to have panned the camera over to another location now.

a11_0302928.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0302928.text: Yeah, we're going to work on something else.

a11_0302928.speaker: McCandless
a11_0302928.text: Roger.

a11_0302928.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0302928.text: This is Apollo Control. We do not have lines called up between here and Goldstone at the present time, and so we cannot receive the pictures in Houston. Goldstone is recording. The lines will be up for the scheduled TV pass, approximately 6:30 this evening, Central Daylight Time.

a11_0302928.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0302928.text: This is Apollo Control. The tape from this unscheduled TV pass will probably be fed from Goldstone to Houston following the regularly scheduled TV transmission this evening.

a11_0305111.speaker: Collins
a11_0305111.text: Houston, Apollo 11.

a11_0305111.speaker: Duke
a11_0305111.text: Go ahead, 11.

a11_0305111.speaker: Collins
a11_0305111.text: Oh, Charlie. That you?

a11_0305111.speaker: Duke
a11_0305111.text: That's me. How are you there?

a11_0305111.speaker: Collins
a11_0305111.text: Oh, just fine. How's the old White Team today?

a11_0305111.speaker: Duke
a11_0305111.text: Ah, the old White Team's bright-eyed and bushy-tailed. We're ever alert down here.

a11_0305111.speaker: Collins
a11_0305111.text: Ever alert and vigilant. Hey, you got any medics down there watching heartrate? I'm trying to do some running in place down here, and I'm wondering just out of curiosity whether it brings my heart rate up.

a11_0305111.speaker: Duke
a11_0305111.text: Well, they will spring into action here momentarily. Stand by. [Long pause.]

a11_0305111.speaker: Duke
a11_0305111.text: Hello, 11. We see your heart beating.

a11_0305111.speaker: Collins
a11_0305111.text: Okay, Well - look at the CDR's and the CMP's and see if they go up any. We're all running in place up here. You wouldn't believe it.

a11_0305111.speaker: Duke
a11_0305111.text: I'd like to see that sight. Why don't you give us a TV picture of that one.

a11_0305111.speaker: Collins
a11_0305111.text: I think Buzz is trying.

a11_0305111.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0305111.text: You got it.

a11_0305111.speaker: Duke
a11_0305111.text: Okay. It's coming into Goldstone, Buzz. As Bruce said, we don't have it here in the center. [Long pause.]

a11_0305111.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0305111.text: I'm afraid this isn't going to help out the PTC very much.

a11_0305111.speaker: Collins
a11_0305111.text: Yeah. I don't know if it's a vibration or what it is, but it makes the pitch and yaw rate needles on FDAI number 1 jump up and down a little bit where we jump up, and down.

a11_0305111.speaker: Duke
a11_0305111.text: Rog. Rog. Goldstoners say they see you running there, Mike.

a11_0305111.speaker: Collins
a11_0305111.text: Okay.

a11_0305111.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0305111.text: Ask him what he's running from. [Long pause.]

a11_0305111.speaker: Duke
a11_0305111.text: 11, Houston. Mike, we see about a 96 heartbeat now.

a11_0305111.speaker: Collins
a11_0305111.text: Okay. Thank you. [Long pause.]

a11_0305111.speaker: Collins
a11_0305111.text: Well, that's about all that is reasonable, without getting hot and sweaty.

a11_0305111.speaker: Duke
a11_0305111.text: Rog. We copy.

a11_0305800.speaker: Collins
a11_0305800.text: Goldstone should be getting about the best picture of the Earth we can give them right now, Charlie.

a11_0305800.speaker: Duke
a11_0305800.text: Roger, Mike. Thank you much.

a11_0305800.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0305800.text: We've got a little distortion in the horizontal direction from banding on our monitor. I wonder if they're getting the same thing?

a11_0305800.speaker: Duke
a11_0305800.text: Stand by, Buzz. I'll let you know.

a11_0305800.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0305800.text: I guess it would be more described as a waviness. [Long pause.]

a11_0305800.speaker: Network (CapCom)
a11_0305800.text: Goldstone M&O, Houston CapCom.

a11_0305800.speaker: Comm Tech
a11_0305800.text: Goldstone M&O.

a11_0305800.speaker: Network (CapCom)
a11_0305800.text: Okay. The crew is complaining of some horizontal banding on their monitor. Do y'all see that on the picture?

a11_0305800.speaker: Comm Tech
a11_0305800.text: Stand by.

a11_0305800.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0305800.text: They wouldn't see anything now. We don't have anything in focus, Charlie.

a11_0305800.speaker: Duke
a11_0305800.text: Roger. He's checking on it. I'll see if they had it earlier. Stand by.

a11_0305800.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0305800.text: I guess when we're showing the DSKY or when we're showing the Earth might be the better time.

a11_0305800.speaker: Duke
a11_0305800.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a11_0305800.speaker: Comm Tech
a11_0305800.text: Houston CapCom, Goldstone.

a11_0305800.speaker: Network (CapCom)
a11_0305800.text: Go ahead.

a11_0305800.speaker: Comm Tech
a11_0305800.text: Okay. Our TV people confirm they see this horizontal band.

a11_0305800.speaker: Network (CapCom)
a11_0305800.text: Okay.

a11_0305800.speaker: Duke
a11_0305800.text: 11, Houston. The Goldstone TV people also see the banding when - at the same time y'all do. Over.

a11_0305800.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0305800.text: Okay. Would they call it a horizontal waviness, instead of banding, maybe?

a11_0305800.speaker: Duke
a11_0305800.text: I'm not talking to them directly. Stand by, Buzz, Let me see what they - how they describe it.

a11_0305800.speaker: Network (CapCom)
a11_0305800.text: Goldstone M&O, Houston CapCom. Could you put the TV guy on the loop, please?

a11_0305800.speaker: Comm Tech
a11_0305800.text: CapCom, Goldstone. Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_0305800.speaker: Comm Tech
a11_0305800.text: Houston CapCom, Goldstone M&O Net 1.

a11_0305800.speaker: Network (CapCom)
a11_0305800.text: Go.

a11_0305800.speaker: Comm Tech
a11_0305800.text: The TV people do not have access to Net 1 in that area. Suggest we use Net 2 for that purpose.

a11_0305800.speaker: Network (CapCom)
a11_0305800.text: Okay. Going to Net 2. [Long pause.]

a11_0305800.speaker: Duke
a11_0305800.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. The Goldstone TV guys say that they have some horizontal banding across the upper part of the picture and across the lower part. They would consider the lines just straight, no waviness to them at all. Over.

a11_0305800.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0305800.text: Roger. Understand. They do seem to distort vertical lines though.

a11_0305800.speaker: Duke
a11_0305800.text: Say again about the vertical lines, Buzz.

a11_0305800.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0305800.text: Rog. When there's a vertical line, these horizontal bands tend to put small waves in it.

a11_0305800.speaker: Duke
a11_0305800.text: Rog. I copy. He didn't mention that. Stand by, I'll check again. [Long pause.]

a11_0305800.speaker: Duke
a11_0305800.text: Hello, 11. Houston. The Goldstone TV said that when you get a sharp vertical line on the picture, when the horizontal banding goes across, it does appear to bend it slightly. The same as Apollo 10, they said. Looks okay to them. Over.

a11_0305800.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0305800.text: Okay. Understand. It's not our monitor. It must be the transmitter or the system.

a11_0305800.speaker: Duke
a11_0305800.text: Rog. I guess so, Buzz. We'll have them look into it, and see if they can suggest anything.

a11_0305800.speaker: Duke
a11_0305800.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We've lost our command interface with Goldstone. We'd like you to switch to Omni Delta. Over.

a11_0305800.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0305800.text: Roger. Going to Delta.

a11_0305800.speaker: Duke
a11_0305800.text: Rog.

a11_0305800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0305800.text: Apollo 11, at this time, is 121,158 nautical miles [224,385 km] from Earth, traveling at a speed of 4,613 feet per second [1,406 m/s]. We anticipate that the change-of-shift briefing will begin at about 4:00 pm Central Daylight Time.

a11_0305800.speaker: Duke
a11_0305800.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We'd like you to terminate the O 2 purge if you have not done so already, and the TV camera people say that the lines are inherent in the camera, Buzz; and it's something that we expected. Over.

a11_0305800.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0305800.text: Roger. Understand about the camera. Say again about the O 2 purge.

a11_0305800.speaker: Duke
a11_0305800.text: Roger. We can terminate the O 2 purge at this time. Over.

a11_0305800.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0305800.text: Oh, okay. Fine. Will do.

a11_0311318.speaker: Duke
a11_0311318.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Please select Omni Bravo on board. Over.

a11_0311318.speaker: Collins
a11_0311318.text: [Garbled, may be 'Take on the'] Bravo, Charlie.

a11_0311318.speaker: Collins
a11_0311318.text: How's everything going down there? You guys happy with the spacecraft systems?

a11_0311318.speaker: Duke
a11_0311318.text: Rog. Affirmative. Everything's looking really good to us. Over.

a11_0311318.speaker: Collins
a11_0311318.text: Charlie, how far out can you pick up TV off the Omni?

a11_0311318.speaker: Duke
a11_0311318.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We're just about to the limits where we can get any kind of picture at all on the Omnis on the TV. It - the picture, I guess, would be just almost zero at this point.

a11_0311318.speaker: Collins
a11_0311318.text: Okay. Well, for this TV program coming up in a couple of hours, you might give some thought to how you want us to stop PTC, if you do, for the best High Gain angle; and also it would be nice if you could stop us at such an attitude that we'd have the Earth out of one of our windows.

a11_0311848.speaker: Duke
a11_0311848.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We got a - some PIPA biases and gyro drift updates for you if you give us P00 and Accept. Over.

a11_0311848.speaker: Duke
a11_0311848.text: Okay. Thank you much. Our biggest drift on the gyros is 0.03 degrees per hour with - on the X-Gyro. On the PIPAs, the Y-PIPA's the biggest and it's 0.006 feet per second so we're just trying to tweak it up. The biggest we have is about one-sigma on both gyros and accelerometers.

a11_0311848.speaker: Duke
a11_0311848.text: The system really looks good to us.

a11_0311848.speaker: Collins
a11_0311848.text: Glad to hear it, Charlie. [Long pause.]

a11_0311848.speaker: Duke
a11_0311848.text: 11, Houston. You can go back to Block. We've got the load in.

a11_0312225.speaker: Collins
a11_0312225.text: Boy, you sure get a different perspective in this thing in zero g. Right now, Neil's got his feet on the forward hatch, and he can, with his arms, reach - all five windows. He can reach down into - the LEB where the overboard drain is. He can practically reach over in the cockpit.

a11_0312225.speaker: Duke
a11_0312225.text: Sounds like Plastic Man to me.

a11_0312225.speaker: Collins
a11_0312225.text: I'm hiding under the left-hand couch trying to stay out of his way.

a11_0312225.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0312225.text: Houston, Apollo 11. You got a cloud over the Houston area right now?

a11_0322458.speaker: Duke
a11_0322458.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We got a TV attitude for you and also an update to your CMC erasable load and your alternate contingency checklist, if you could break that out too. Over.

a11_0322458.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0322458.text: Roger. I'm not sure I caught all of that. Go ahead with what you have.

a11_0322458.speaker: Duke
a11_0322458.text: Roger, 11. If you'll break out your alternate and contingency checklist for the CSM, we got an update to some of the erasable loads on page F2-20. Over.

a11_0322458.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0322458.text: Okay. Be getting that out, and you can give us the attitude for TV.

a11_0322458.speaker: Duke
a11_0322458.text: Roger, 11. Your TV attitude will be roll 261, pitch 090, yaw 000. High gain angle: pitch plus 28, yaw 271. That puts the left-hand window pointed at the Earth. We recommend exiting PTC with your updated procedure in the checklist. Over.

a11_0322458.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0322458.text: Roger. We copy roll 21 - 261, pitch 090, yaw 000, High Gain pitch plus 28, yaw 271. And we'd like this with the procedure we have in the book. Over.

a11_0322458.speaker: Duke
a11_0322458.text: That's affirmative. [Long pause.]

a11_0322458.speaker: Collins
a11_0322458.text: Charlie, Apollo 11. I have a couple of questions on stopping the PTC. It seems to me the easiest way to stop it would be - we're essentially, of course, at 0 degrees yaw and close enough to 90 degrees pitch, so it's just a question of stopping at 260 roll, roughly, and - How about for a procedure going Manual Attitude, three, to Rate Command and then, seeing as how our deadband has already collapsed, I'll turn on the panel 8 RCS thrusters, at which time it should stop at whatever attitude it finds itself in. And if I do all of that as it comes up on 261 degrees roll, we should stop right there

a11_0322458.speaker: Duke
a11_0322458.text: Sounds pretty good. Stand by one.

a11_0322458.speaker: Collins
a11_0322458.text: Sounds like it might save a little gas.

a11_0322458.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0322458.text: Houston, Apollo 11. What page do you want in that revision? Over.

a11_0322458.speaker: Duke
a11_0322458.text: Roger, 11. If you'll turn to page F2-20. Over.

a11_0322458.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0322458.text: Okay, I have it. [Pause.]

a11_0322458.speaker: Duke
a11_0322458.text: Roger, 11. Under column A on page F2-20. [Pause.] Line 5, line 05, the new data is 01042; line 07, the new data is 00256. Skipping down to line 11, 00070; line 12 is 00042; line 13 is 77730. In column Bravo, lines 3, 4, and 5, which are blank, should be all zeros for line 3; line 4 is 20017; line 5, 20616. Over.

a11_0322458.speaker: Duke
a11_0322458.text: Roger. Good readback, Buzz. And stand by, Mike, on the 'coming-out-of-the-PTC' recommendation. Over.

a11_0322458.speaker: Collins
a11_0322458.text: Okay. Fine. [Long pause.]

a11_0322458.speaker: Duke
a11_0322458.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston, with a recommendation on exiting PTCM. Over.

a11_0322458.speaker: Collins
a11_0322458.text: Go ahead.

a11_0322458.speaker: Duke
a11_0322458.text: Roger, Mike. We'd like to see you go to Accel Command on the Manual Attitude switches. Then to turn on the Auto RCS Select switches, and then go Rate Command. That will prevent us from firing jets uncoupled. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0322458.speaker: Collins
a11_0322458.text: Okay. Fine. And I would guess, go Rate Command and roll first, and then followed by pitch and yaw.

a11_0322458.speaker: Duke
a11_0322458.text: Okay. That sounds good if - And when you get to the roll attitude desired, just go Rate Command at that time and it'll stop us right on.

a11_0322458.speaker: Collins
a11_0322458.text: Yeah. I agree, Charlie. That sounds right.

a11_0322458.speaker: Duke
a11_0322458.text: Rog.

a11_0323900.speaker: Duke
a11_0323900.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston with some more words on exiting PTC. Over.

a11_0323900.speaker: Duke
a11_0323900.text: Roger. Mike, when you were playing with the P37 a while ago and we collapsed the deadband back down, the DAP assumed that the deadband was centered around the new attitude that we happened to be at, at that time. Since then, we've drifted out a couple of degrees in both pitch and yaw from that attitude such that if we did the procedure as we called it up to you of going Accel Command, turning on all of the Auto RCS Select switches and then Rate Command, it would attempt to fly back to the pitch and yaw attitude that it had when the deadband collapsed. We can prevent that by - just immediately

a11_0323900.speaker: Collins
a11_0323900.text: Not going to let these LM guys play with my DSKY any more.

a11_0323900.speaker: Duke
a11_0323900.text: You sound like you'd better protect it. It looks like just about anything that you do with that DSKY is going to collapse that deadband back down.

a11_0323900.speaker: Collins
a11_0323900.text: Charlie, we just Stab[iliz]ed to 261 degrees roll, and it looks like whoever figured it out did a good job. It's right there, dab-smack in the middle of window Number 1.

a11_0324600.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0324600.text: Looks like Houston's still got a little cloud over it, Charlie.

a11_0324600.speaker: Duke
a11_0324600.text: We've got a constant overcast here in the room. We'll be right there. Stand by.

a11_0324600.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0324600.text: Of course, a little cloud from up here probably covers 8 or 10 states. [Long pause.]

a11_0324600.speaker: Duke
a11_0324600.text: 11, Houston. Some of our guys just came in from outside and said it's pretty clear over the Center here. It's cleared up completely. All the storms have moved on.

a11_0324917.speaker: Collins
a11_0324917.text: Oh, yeah, Charlie. I can see it through the sextant now, and I can see the coastline is clear. Those clouds are just inland a few miles.

a11_0324917.speaker: Duke
a11_0324917.text: Okay. We copy. [Long pause.]

a11_0324917.speaker: Collins
a11_0324917.text: Looks like the southeast part of the country is all socked in. [Pause.]

a11_0324917.speaker: Collins
a11_0324917.text: California looks nice. The San Joaquin Valley shows up as a real dark spot with a lighter brown on either side of it. You can't tell that it's green. It looks just sort of dark gray or maybe even real dark blue.

a11_0324917.speaker: Duke
a11_0324917.text: How does the Mojave look? Is it clear?

a11_0324917.speaker: Collins
a11_0324917.text: Ah, yeah. As usual.

a11_0324917.speaker: Duke
a11_0324917.text: Rog.

a11_0324917.speaker: Collins
a11_0324917.text: The - around - It looks like there are some clouds just to the west of the Sierras, northeast of Bakersfield a little bit; and crossing over into the Mojave from Bakersfield looks clear; and then as you get on further to the southeast of there, there's a few clouds.

a11_0324917.speaker: Duke
a11_0324917.text: Roger, 11. Can you pick out Edwards in the sextant? Over.

a11_0324917.speaker: Collins
a11_0324917.text: I can see a 104 taxiing out for take-off on the runway.

a11_0324917.speaker: Duke
a11_0324917.text: Hey, man. That's super.

a11_0324917.speaker: Collins
a11_0324917.text: Pretty safe bet there's almost always a 104 taxiing out for take-off. [Long pause.]

a11_0324917.speaker: Duke
a11_0324917.text: 11, Houston. Could you pick out anything around Edwards, a dry lake or anything? Over.

a11_0324917.speaker: Collins
a11_0324917.text: Negative, Charlie. I just - I don't have that resolution. But to give you some idea, I can - on the lower Texas coast, I can see - knowing what I'm looking for, I can see Padre Island. I can just barely make out the fact that there's a thin spit of land and then there's a little dark zone which is the Laguna Madre between it and the mainland.

a11_0324917.speaker: Duke
a11_0324917.text: Roger, 11. That's pretty significant. Thank you much, Mike.

a11_0324917.speaker: Collins
a11_0324917.text: Right.

a11_0324917.speaker: Collins
a11_0324917.text: How far out are we, Charlie?

a11_0324917.speaker: Duke
a11_0324917.text: Stand by. I'll give it to you exactly. Looks like around 130,000, but stand by.

a11_0324917.speaker: Collins
a11_0324917.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a11_0324917.speaker: Duke
a11_0324917.text: 11, Houston. The exact range is 125,200 [nautical] miles [231,870 km], and you're traveling 4,486 feet per second [1,367 m/s].

a11_0324917.speaker: Collins
a11_0324917.text: Pretty far and pretty slow. Just past halfway. [Long pause.]

a11_0324917.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0324917.text: Hey, Charlie, what's the latest on Luna 15?

a11_0324917.speaker: Duke
a11_0324917.text: Say again, Buzz? Over.

a11_0324917.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0324917.text: Roger. What's the latest on Luna 15?

a11_0324917.speaker: Duke
a11_0324917.text: Stand by. I'll get the straight story for you.

a11_0333400.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0333400.text: We have lost lock on the High Gain Antenna at this time. Apollo 11 is presently 127,991 nautical miles [237,039 km] from Earth, traveling at a speed of about 4,400 feet per second [about 1,340 m/s]. The regularly scheduled time for the television transmission is 6:47 pm Central Daylight Time, and we are anticipating that that transmission will occur as scheduled.

a11_0333744.speaker: Duke
a11_0333744.text: Roger. Latest on Luna 15 - TASS reported this morning that the spacecraft was placed in orbit close to the lunar surface, and everything seems to be functioning normally on the vehicle. Sir Bernard Lovell says the craft appears to be in an orbit of about 62 nautical miles [115 km]. Over.

a11_0333744.speaker: Duke
a11_0333744.text: And also, President Nixon has reported - or declared a day of participation on Monday for all federal employees to enable everybody to follow your activities on the surface. Many state and city governments and businesses throughout the country are also giving their employees the day off, so it looks like you're going to have a pretty large audience for the EVA.

a11_0333744.speaker: Collins
a11_0333744.text: Oh, that's very nice, Charlie. I'll tell Neil about it.

a11_0334100.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0334100.text: This is Apollo Control at 33 hours, 45 minutes and we do have a correction to the time given for the beginning of that TV nominally. The Flight Plan time is beginning at 34 hours, to 34 hours, 15 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. The previous conversion of that, that we gave you for Central Daylight Time was in error. It should be 6:32 pm Central Daylight Time beginning, assuming we start as the Flight Plan nominally has the transmission listed at 34 hours Ground Elapsed Time. At the present time, Apollo 11 is 128,431 nautical miles [237,854 km] from Earth and the velocity, continuing to drop off s

a11_0334757.speaker: Collins
a11_0334757.text: Houston, Apollo 11. We've stopped PTC. We're in the right position. We're setting up for TV.

a11_0335231.speaker: Duke
a11_0335231.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We have you stopped in the PTC; attitude looks good to us. Mike, I'd like to get a Comm check. The last couple of transmissions from the spacecraft has been garbled, from especially Buzz. Could you both give me a Comm check? Over.

a11_0335231.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0335231.text: Roger, Charlie. It's Buzz here. How do you read? 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; 5, 4, 3, 2, 1.

a11_0335231.speaker: Duke
a11_0335231.text: Roger. You're about four-by with a slight decrease/increase in volume, sort of a wavy volume to it. Over.

a11_0335231.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0335231.text: Okay. I moved my mike around. How about now? Is this any better?

a11_0335231.speaker: Duke
a11_0335231.text: Hey, that's beautiful right there. Thank you.

a11_0335231.speaker: Collins
a11_0335231.text: Okay, Charlie. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. How do you read me?

a11_0335231.speaker: Duke
a11_0335231.text: Roger. You're five-by. Is Neil on?

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We got the network all configured for the TV. You can start any time you want. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Okay, 11. We have a picture. We see the Earth right in the center of the screen. Over.

a11_0335700.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0335700.text: Roger, Houston. Apollo 11 calling in from about 130,000 [nautical] miles [241,000 km] out. And we'll zoom our camera in slowly and get the most magnification we can. Over.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger.

a11_0335700.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0335700.text: This view is coming to us from about 129,000 nautical miles [239,000 km].

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: 11, Houston. The definition is pretty good on our monitor here. The color's not too [garbled], at least on this set. Could you describe what you're looking at? Over.

a11_0335700.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0335700.text: Roger. You're seeing Earth, as we see it, out our left-hand window, just a little more than a half Earth. We're looking at the eastern Pacific Ocean, and the north half of the top half of the screen, we can see North America, Alaska, United States, Canada, Mexico, and Central America. South America becomes invisible just off beyond the terminator or inside the shadow. We can see the oceans with a definite blue cast, see white bands of major cloud formations across the Earth, and can see coastlines, pick out the western US, San Joaquin Valley, the Sierra mountain range, the peninsula of Baja Ca

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger, 11. It's a pretty good picture on clarity here. We're having - can you tell us - It appears to us that there are two distinct cloud formations trending east-west, one approximately about along the equator, and one around 30 or so south latitude. Could you tell us exactly where those cross the land masses? Over.

a11_0335700.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0335700.text: Well, yes. They cross just south of the lower part of Mexico, probably through Central America. That is the equatorial band which we assume to be the inter-tropical convergence zone. The other band, which is about 30 south correctly, seems to appear to join the equator at the far left, or just beyond the horizon on the left edge of Earth, or at least it looks like it's going to join it. We don't have an explanation for that banding.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger, Neil. Thank you. It also appears that just to the left of the terminator, up in the northern hemisphere, there's a cloud band trending - a gap in the cloud, trending northwest/southeast. It appears to us that that comes in about over the northern United States, or perhaps the central United States. Is that about correct? Over.

a11_0335700.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0335700.text: I can see on the monitor the thing you're talking about, but right now I can't get my eye to the window to pick out just where it crosses the shore line.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: You guys are doing a good job. It's a real steady picture, here. We're - Clarity is excellent. The color, it's - the clouds are - The whites are distinct. The rest if it looks like, to me anyway on the monitor I'm observing, is a fairly greenish blue is the way I'd describe it. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: It appears that the...

a11_0335700.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0335700.text: Well, we can't observe... [hears Duke] We can't observe much green from the spacecraft.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger. On this monitor, the landmasses appear to be just a darker grayish color rather than a brown.

a11_0335700.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0335700.text: Well, it's true that we do not have the depths of color at this range that we enjoyed at 50,000 miles out. However, the oceans still are a definite blue and the continents are generally brownish in cast, although it is true that they're tending more toward gray now than they were at the closer ranges.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger, 11. We've been - I've just been vectored to another monitor and sure enough, the browns are coming in a lot more distinctly on the Eidophor that we have up on our screen in the Control Center. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Okay, world, hold on to your hat. I'm going to turn you upside-down. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: 11, that's a pretty good roll, there. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Oh, that was pretty sloppy, Charlie. Let me try that one again. [Pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: You'll never beat out the Thunderbirds. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Apollo 11, Houston. That practice did you some good. It's looking - real smooth roll, there.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Oops! Spoke too soon. [Pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: I'm making myself sea sick doing it, Charlie. I'll just put you back right-side up where you belong.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: You don't get to do that every day. [Pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: 11, Houston. Could you describe, from your view, the polar cloud cap? It appears to us to extend down the western coast of North America. Would you estimate how far it extends down? Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0335700.text: Trying to fit everybody into the window.

a11_0335700.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0335700.text: It appears that the cloud cap comes down a little bit below the southern extremity of Alaska.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: We've - 11, we've lost our picture here, now. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Okay. Apollo 11, Houston. We've got the picture back now. [Pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0335700.text: Unfortunately, we only have one window that has a view of the Earth and it's filled up with the TV camera, so your view now is probably better than ours is.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger. We copy.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: 11, Houston. If you could comply, we'd like to see little smiling faces up there, if you could give us some interior views. I'm sure everybody would like to see you. Over.

a11_0335700.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0335700.text: Okay. We'll reconfigure the TV for that.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Apollo 11, Houston. It appears to us that we're seeing a view from outside plus a little of the inside. It appears you've taken the camera away from the left window now. Over.

a11_0335700.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0335700.text: That's correct. We're moving it back and reconfiguring for interior lighting.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: We can still see the Earth through the left window, and it appears that we can see a floodlight off to the left, either that or some Sun shafting through the hatch window.

a11_0335700.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0335700.text: It's a floodlight.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Rog.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Now we're coming in. Can't quite make out who that head is.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: That's big Mike Collins, there...

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: You got a little bit of... [hears Duke.] Yeah, hello there sports fans. You got a little bit of me, plus Neil is in the center couch, and Buzz is doing the camera work this time.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger. It's a little dark now, 11. Maybe a bigger f-stop might help.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Yeah, that's in work. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: It's getting a lot better now, 11. Mike, you're coming in five-by. I got a good...

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: I'd have put on a coat and tie if I'd known about this ahead of time.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Is that Buzz holding your cue cards for you? Over.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Cue cards have a 'no'. We have no intention of competing with the professionals, believe me. [Pause.] We are very comfortable up here, though. We do have a happy home. There's plenty of room for the three of us and I think we're all learning to find our favorite little corner to sit in. Zero g is very comfortable, but after a while you get to the point where you sort of get tired of rattling around and banging off the ceiling and the floor and the side, so you tend to find a little corner somewhere and put your knees up or something like that to wedge yourself in, and that seems more at home.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger. Looks like Neil is coming in five-by there, 11. Mike, see you in the background. The definition is really outstanding. The colors are good. It's a real good picture we're getting here of Commander Armstrong. We - Buzz, when you take the camera over towards the window where the Sun's shafting through, it tends to blank it out, though.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Yeah, Neil's standing on his head again. He's trying to make me nervous.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: He's disappearing up into the tunnel, of course, as he would going into the Lunar Module, only backwards.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger. We can see portions of the LEB now. The systems test meter panel in the lower part of the picture, or we did have it, anyway.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Okay. And then directly behind his head are our optical instruments, the sextant and the telescope that we use to take sightings with.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger, copy. And we see the DSKY flashing with a 6 51. In fact, we can read Registers 1 and 2 quite clearly.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: The old High Gain angles telling us which way the Earth is.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Copy. That's a beautiful picture. Clarity is outstanding. [Pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: We can also give you the time of day in our system of mission elapsed time. Elapsed time: 34 hours, 16 minutes and umpteen seconds. Can you see that clearly enough, Charlie?

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger, Apollo 11. We can see it counting up every - every second. We got 34:17:02 now. [Pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Okay. Back to the High-Gain angles.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Now we have amputated those. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: 11, Houston. It's a - We have a beautiful rainbow there now as you move the camera around. That looks like the star charts coming into view, now. Over.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Yeah. Those are Buzz's two star charts that he is using right now as sun shades over the right-hand window, window Number 5.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger. We see the Sun shining in through it behind him and blotting out the equatorial - correction, ecliptic plane, and the stars that you're using for the navigation.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: You're right. He doesn't really need the charts. He's got them memorized. They're just for show.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: We copy.

a11_0335700.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0335700.text: While we're pointing up in this direction, we see out our side windows the Sun going by and, of course, out one of our windows right now we've got the Earth. Right behind my window, of course, we have the Sun, because the Sun is illuminating the star charts that we see. This line represents the ecliptic plane and these lines, vertical lines, represent our reference system that the spacecraft is using at this time. As we approach the Moon, the Moon will gradually grow larger and larger in size and eventually it will be in eclipse. It will be eclipsing the Sun as we go behind it, as we approach

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger, 11. We've - Could you attempt a little bit better focus there, 11? Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: 11, Houston. That's a lot better on the star chart now. We can make out the ecliptic plane and the planets and the Sun and the Moon as it - as they have gone at various places throughout the ecliptic plane. Over.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Okay, Charlie. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0335700.text: If we can get some of the wires untangled here, we'll give you a demonstration of how easy push-ups are up here.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: 11, Roger. Good view of Buzz, there. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0335700.text: When it gets pretty hard doing it that way, why, we just roll over and do it the other way.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Rog. We copy. We couldn't figure out whether that was a chin-up or a push-up. Just take your choice, I guess. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Well, it looks like it's probably almost your dinner time down there, Earth. We'll show you our food cabinet here in a second.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: 11, Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: 11, Houston. We see a box full of goodies there. Over.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: We really have them, Charlie. We've got all kinds of good stuff. We've got coffee up here in the upper left and various breakfast items, bacon in little small bites, beverages like fruit drink. And over in the center part we have, oh, all kinds of things. Let me pull one out here and see what it is.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Rog.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Would you believe you're looking at chicken stew, here? All you have to do is - 3 ounces of hot water for 5 or 10 minutes. Now we get our hot water out of a little spigot up here with a filter on it that filters any gases that may be in the drinking water out, and we just stick the end of this little tube in the end of the spigot and pull the trigger three times for 3 ounces of hot water and then mush it up and slice the end off it and there you go, beautiful chicken stew.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Sounds delicious. [Pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Yeah. The food so far has been very good. We couldn't be happier with it.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Could I borrow that flashlight a second?

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: The surgeons are saying thank you, there, for that.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: And it is sort of down in a dark corner, so we have a flashlight here to help us see things; and if I can let go of it carefully, it'll just hold itself right where it is.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: As long as it's still, it will.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Apollo 11, Houston. That's a pretty good demonstration. You started off really stable there, Mike. It...

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Well, the problem is, no matter how carefully you let go, you bump it just a tiny little bit, set it in motion and once in motion there she goes. Try that again.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: It looks fairly stable now with slow rotation. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Well, so much for the food department. I'm going to close up the store down here.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger. We copy.

a11_0335700.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0335700.text: Charlie, we checked out the cable lengths, and we're thinking we might want to see if we can take the TV into the LM with us tomorrow for part of the time. Over.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger. Good show. We'd like to see it if it'll reach that far. Over.

a11_0335700.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0335700.text: We'll give it a try.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: And where I sleep is down underneath this couch.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Houston. Roger.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Slowly sinking into the sack there. [Pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: It's really comfortable. [Pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Forgot to give Buzz his flashlight back. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Could you give the folks a view of your patch if - on your CWGs? Over. [Pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Stand by one, Charlie; we'll try and give you a close-up.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: 11, Houston. We have the patch. Could you attempt to improve the focus slightly? Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: 11, Houston. The scan on the camera makes the - that's a little bit better now. The flashlight seems to flicker, due to the scan on the TV. We can't see the eagle. Now it's a little bit better. Over. Could you open the f-stop a little bit more? Over. [Pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: It's open all the way. We're going to have to move Buzz around little bit.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Okay, Apollo 11, Houston. The color is better now. It's coming in. We could attempt a little bit better focus on it. There we go; it focuses a lot better now. We see the eagle coming right in on the lunar surface. Over. That's very good now.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Apollo 11, Houston. That's very good now. We can see the Earth in the background, Apollo 11, and the eagle coming in.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
