a11_0335700.text: It's probably pretty hard to see the olive branch, isn't it?

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger. It is.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Well, that's what he has in his talons, is an olive branch.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Copy. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We're really impressed with the clarity and the detail that we have in the picture. The colors are - now, it's a really, an excellent picture now that I'm looking at it on our monitor, which is about 12 seconds before the networks can get it out due to the conversion that we have here on our TV converter. The - We're looking at the controls in the display - the main display console and we can see the DSKY up on the panel. Over.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: It would be nice if you could take a look at all the circuit breakers; make sure the right ones are in and the right ones are out.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger. Big Brother's watching.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: And we're glad of it. [Pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Boy, you guys have sure been doing a good job of watching us, Charlie. We appreciate it.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: The spacecraft's been beautiful, 11. We've really no complaints at all. Looks - Things are really great. [Pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Can you see this DSKY on the MDC?

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: That's affirmative. It appears that - can't quite tell what program went P00. We see you punching in a Verb 35, I think it is. Over.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Yeah. Might as well tell the EECOMs or tell the GNC and everybody to hold on to their hat and I'll push the Enter button.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Rog.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: We see a real display now. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: That's a good demonstration of how the crew has the interface with the computer, talking to the programs and all that we have in the computer.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Well, that's right, Charlie. Sometimes it tells us things and sometimes we tell it things and mostly it talks to us. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: 11, Houston. We just lost our pic - I see we're going back outside now. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: 11, Houston. You copy? Over.

a11_0335700.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0335700.text: Roger. We copy, And as we pan back out to the distance at which we see the Earth, well, it's Apollo 11 signing off.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Roger, Apollo 11. Thank you much for the show. It's a real good half hour. Appreciate it. Thank you very much. Out. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Okay. That's it, Charlie.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: 11, Houston. We appreciate the show. Thank you very much. Over.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Right.

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Would you key Error Reset on the DSKY, please? Over. [Pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Okay. We should be straightened out now, Charlie, and back in P00. [Long pause.]

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Houston, Apollo 11. How do we stand on this O 2 fuel cell purge? You want to go ahead and do that as scheduled in the Flight Plan?

a11_0335700.speaker: Duke
a11_0335700.text: Stand by, 11. Over.

a11_0335700.speaker: Collins
a11_0335700.text: Okay.

a11_0344142.speaker: Duke
a11_0344142.text: Roger, Buzz. The attitude that we're in right now is a convenient one to start PTC in. We'd be satisfied with this attitude. So we'd like you to disable quads Charlie and Delta; and we'll wait about 5 to 10 minutes, and then we'll establish the PTC. Over.

a11_0344142.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0344142.text: Roger. Disable Charlie and Delta, and we'll wait before starting PTC.

a11_0344600.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0344600.text: This is Apollo Control at 34 hours, 46 minutes. Apollo 11 is presently 131,000 nautical miles [242,612 km] from Earth, traveling at a speed of about 4,300 feet per second [about 1,300 m/s]. During the TV transmission, the crew advised that they may possibly be able to take the color television camera into the Lunar Module with them tomorrow at about 56 hours, 30 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. They reported that the cables had been checked and appear to be long enough to take them into the Lunar Module. During the next hour or so, the activity here in Mission Control will be revolving around gett

a11_0350109.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0350109.text: Houston. Would you say again what your request is?

a11_0350109.speaker: Duke
a11_0350109.text: Roger, 11. We'd like you to go back to Attitude Hold. Over.

a11_0350109.speaker: Duke
a11_0350109.text: 11, Houston. Looks like we're going to have to reinitialate [sic] - reinitialize this PTC.

a11_0350109.speaker: Collins
a11_0350109.text: Okay. Do you have any roll angle that you'd like to stop it in, Charlie? I haven't stopped it yet.

a11_0350109.speaker: Duke
a11_0350109.text: 11, Houston. It's your preference right now if you want to. Over.

a11_0350747.speaker: Duke
a11_0350747.text: Roger, 11. The problem on that initial starting up the PTC was we failed to do the Verb 49 which - and load the desired initial attitude; so the DAP tried to take it back to the old attitude that we had started up in [a] number of hours to go. That's why we picked up the rates in the other axes. We're going to wait in this attitude for about 20 minutes to damp out the rates again, and then we'll proceed with the Verb 49 and load our attitude that we have at the time - at this time. Over.

a11_0350747.speaker: Collins
a11_0350747.text: Okay. It sounds good, Charlie. When you get to the Verb 49, I'd like for you to give me the three gimbal angles that you want loaded.

a11_0350747.speaker: Duke
a11_0350747.text: And Apollo 11, Houston. We have your fly-by PAD if you're ready to copy. Over.

a11_0350747.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0350747.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Is that P30 PAD?

a11_0350747.speaker: Duke
a11_0350747.text: All right, Buzz. It's - fly-by is the purpose. SPS/G&N: 62815, plus 0.97, minus 0.20; 070:54:59.44; minus 0002.8, plus 0002.3, plus 0006.9; 029, 149, 312; apogee is NA, plus 0022.1; 0007.8, 0:01, 0003.4; sextant star, 01, 218.5, 22.7; boresight star is NA, NA, NA. Latitude is minus 02.65, minus 165.00; 1189.9, 36228, 144:56:47. In the comments: your set stars are Deneb and Vega, 007, 144, 068. No ullage. It's a docked burn using the PTC REFSMMAT. Stand by for your read-back. Over.

a11_0350747.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0350747.text: Okay. Would you give me GET of 0.05g again, please?

a11_0351300.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0351300.text: This is Apollo Control at 35 hours, 13 minutes. Apollo 11 is presently about 93,265 nautical miles [172,727 km] from the Moon and with respect to the Moon is traveling at a speed of about 4,019 feet per second 1,225 m/s. At this time we are receiving the tape playback which Goldstone - the tracking site at Goldstone, California received from the spacecraft in that earlier unscheduled TV transmission. This was a test of the system using the spacecraft on the antennas, the small omnidirectional antennas. Normally transmissions from this distance in space would be - would require the High Gain An

a11_0351300.speaker: Duke
a11_0351300.text: Roger. Say again your roll angle, Buzz. I copy - I read 029. Over.

a11_0351438.speaker: Collins
a11_0351438.text: Houston, Apollo 11. On the seven-tenths rate, the rate loaded into the DAP is one or two tenths.

a11_0352542.speaker: Duke
a11_0352542.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Over.

a11_0352542.speaker: Collins
a11_0352542.text: Houston, Apollo 11.

a11_0352542.speaker: Duke
a11_0352542.text: Roger. We got a little laser visual experiment we'd like to - for you to do for us. If you - if you got the Earth through any of your windows or through the telescope, would you so advise? Over. [Pause.]

a11_0352542.speaker: Collins
a11_0352542.text: Standby one, Charlie. [Pause.]

a11_0352542.speaker: Collins
a11_0352542.text: At this roll attitude, what should our High Gain angles be? Maybe that would help us locate you. We don't see you because of the LM.

a11_0352542.speaker: Duke
a11_0352542.text: Stand by.

a11_0352542.speaker: Duke
a11_0352542.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Those High Gain angles are pitch minus 70, yaw 90. We think the Earth is apparently pretty close to plus Z-axis. Over.

a11_0352542.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0352542.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a11_0352542.speaker: Collins
a11_0352542.text: Okay, Charlie. I got you in the telescope. [Pause.]

a11_0352542.speaker: Duke
a11_0352542.text: Roger, Apollo 11. We've got a laser that we're going to - It's a blue-green laser that we're going to flash on and off at a frequency of on for a second, off for a second. It's coming out of McDonald Observatory near El Paso, which is - should be right on the terminator - or right inside the terminator. We are going to activate that momentarily. Would you please take a look through the telescope and see if you can see it. Over.

a11_0352542.speaker: Collins
a11_0352542.text: Telescope or sextant?

a11_0352542.speaker: Duke
a11_0352542.text: Either one. Over.

a11_0352542.speaker: Collins
a11_0352542.text: Okay, I'll try it with the telescope; and if I don't see it there, then I'll try the sextant.

a11_0352542.speaker: Duke
a11_0352542.text: Roger. We'll give you the word when they've got it turned on. Over.

a11_0352542.speaker: Collins
a11_0352542.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a11_0352542.speaker: Duke
a11_0352542.text: 11, Houston. They don't have it turned on yet. We'll give you the word when they got it turned on. Over.

a11_0352542.speaker: Collins
a11_0352542.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a11_0352542.speaker: Duke
a11_0352542.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We noticed the Cryo pressure dropped a moment ago. Did you stir up the Cryos? Over.

a11_0352542.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0352542.text: Roger. We've finished our cycling operations.

a11_0352542.speaker: Duke
a11_0352542.text: Rog. Copy. Out.

a11_0353353.speaker: Duke
a11_0353353.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. McDonald's got the laser turned on. Would you take a look? Over.

a11_0353353.speaker: Collins
a11_0353353.text: Okay, Charlie.

a11_0353353.speaker: Duke
a11_0353353.text: It's bluish-green.

a11_0353353.speaker: Duke
a11_0353353.text: 11, Houston. We got some shaft and trunnion for you that might tweak it up a little bit. Shaft of 141.5, trunnion of 39.5. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0353353.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0353353.text: Okay. Stand by.

a11_0353353.speaker: Duke
a11_0353353.text: Apollo 11, Houston. If you see it, it should be coming up - appear to be coming up, through the clouds. McDonald reports that there's a break in the clouds that they're beaming this thing through. Over.

a11_0353353.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0353353.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_0353353.speaker: Duke
a11_0353353.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. You can terminate the exercise on the laser. Our rates are steady enough now for to commence the PTC. Over.

a11_0353353.speaker: Collins
a11_0353353.text: Okay, Houston. Neither Neil nor Mike can see it. Incidentally, those shafts and trunnions just missed pointing at the world.

a11_0353353.speaker: Duke
a11_0353353.text: Roger. Thank you. [Pause.]

a11_0353353.speaker: Collins
a11_0353353.text: As we are looking at it through the scanning telescope, it would be about a - oh, maybe a third of an Earth radii high and to the left.

a11_0353353.speaker: Duke
a11_0353353.text: Roger.

a11_0353353.speaker: Collins
a11_0353353.text: But, we did - but we did identify the El Paso area and it appeared to us to be a break in the clouds there, and we looked in that break and saw nothing.

a11_0353353.speaker: Duke
a11_0353353.text: Roger. Thank you much. Out.

a11_0353353.speaker: Collins
a11_0353353.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Over.

a11_0353353.speaker: Duke
a11_0353353.text: Roger. Go ahead. Over.

a11_0353353.speaker: Collins
a11_0353353.text: Were you following that on the DSKY?

a11_0353353.speaker: Duke
a11_0353353.text: Roger. Stand by. [Pause.]

a11_0353353.speaker: Duke
a11_0353353.text: 11, Houston. What's your exact question? Over.

a11_0353353.speaker: Collins
a11_0353353.text: I've followed the procedure through step 7 down to the point where I've got 27303 Enter, and this resulted in an Operator Error light.

a11_0353353.speaker: Duke
a11_0353353.text: Roger. Stand by. [Long pause.]

a11_0353353.speaker: Duke
a11_0353353.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Stand by a moment. We'll have an answer for you momentarily. Over.

a11_0353353.speaker: Collins
a11_0353353.text: Okay. Appreciate it, Charlie. Now the light's gone out without any further DSKY action.

a11_0353353.speaker: Duke
a11_0353353.text: Roger.

a11_0353353.speaker: Collins
a11_0353353.text: Correction. Stand by, that's not so.

a11_0353353.speaker: Duke
a11_0353353.text: Roger.

a11_0355706.speaker: Duke
a11_0355706.text: Roger. We've finally gotten concurrence on our problem here with 50 guys looking at it. When we were sitting in the 50 18, we attempted to load the erasable before you terminated the Verb 49. So, Mike, what we're going to have to do is call up the present CDUs, copy those down, and do a Verb 49, load the present, then do a Proceed, then an Enter, and then we can then set up Attitude Hold in step 6. Over.

a11_0355706.speaker: Collins
a11_0355706.text: Okay. I think that's what we did last time.

a11_0355706.speaker: Duke
a11_0355706.text: It appeared to us that we attempted to load the erasable prior to entering on the Verb 49 which Verb 49 was still running, and it clobbered the CDUs. Over.

a11_0360102.speaker: Collins
a11_0360102.text: Houston, Apollo 11. We're moving at the proper rate.

a11_0360102.speaker: Duke
a11_0360102.text: Hallelujah! [Long pause.]

a11_0360102.speaker: Duke
a11_0360102.text: 11, Houston. It looks great to us now. Over.

a11_0360102.speaker: Collins
a11_0360102.text: It looks fine here, Charlie. The seven-tenths part is the only part I don't find explained yet.

a11_0360102.speaker: Duke
a11_0360102.text: Roger, Mike. We're working on that one right now. We're coming up with a story soon. Over.

a11_0360102.speaker: Collins
a11_0360102.text: Thank you. [Pause.]

a11_0360102.speaker: Duke
a11_0360102.text: 11, Houston. We're handing over comm to Goldst - Correction, from Goldstone to Honeysuckle. Over.

a11_0360102.speaker: Collins
a11_0360102.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a11_0360102.speaker: Collins
a11_0360102.text: Hello, Houston through Honeysuckle. Over.

a11_0360102.speaker: Duke
a11_0360102.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Go ahead. Over.

a11_0360102.speaker: Collins
a11_0360102.text: You sound good to us through Honeysuckle. How do we sound?

a11_0360102.speaker: Duke
a11_0360102.text: Roger. You're five-by, Mike. We'd like the Omni configuration as follows. Omni Alpha, place in Bravo; Omni to Omni, High Gain track to Manual, High Gain yaw 270, pitch... [Long pause.]

a11_0360102.speaker: Duke
a11_0360102.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. How do you read now? Over.

a11_0360102.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0360102.text: Roger. I'm reading you loud and clear. I'm not sure I got all those. I've got S-band Omni B, Omni, track to Manual, and beam wide, pitch - you'd better say that again, and yaw 270. Over.

a11_0360102.speaker: Duke
a11_0360102.text: Roger, Buzz. I broke up at pitch minus 50 at beam wide. Over.[Pause.]

a11_0360102.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0360102.text: Roger. Copy. [Long pause.]

a11_0360102.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0360102.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Are you ready to copy some numbers on status report, et cetera .

a11_0360102.speaker: Duke
a11_0360102.text: Say again. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0360102.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0360102.text: Roger. Are you ready to copy some numbers on the status report, et cetera ?

a11_0360102.speaker: Duke
a11_0360102.text: Rog. Go ahead. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0360102.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0360102.text: Okay. Radiation: CDR, 11005; CMP, 10006; LMP, 09007. Medication negative. And I got some battery and RCS numbers for you.

a11_0360102.speaker: Duke
a11_0360102.text: Go ahead. Over.

a11_0360102.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0360102.text: Battery C, 37.1; Pyro battery A and B, both 37.1. RCS Alpha, 82; Bravo, 84; Cocoa, 85; Delta, 87. Over.

a11_0360102.speaker: Duke
a11_0360102.text: Roger, we copy. Radiation 11005, 10006, 09007; no medication; 37.1, 37.1, 37.1, 82, 84, 85, 87. Over.

a11_0360102.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0360102.text: That's affirmative. And you want a LM/CM Delta-P? It's 1.1 [psi].

a11_0360102.speaker: Duke
a11_0360102.text: Roger. Copy 1.1. [Long pause.]

a11_0360102.speaker: Duke
a11_0360102.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Please verify that four Cryo heaters, Auto; the four fans, Off. Over.

a11_0360102.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0360102.text: Okay. We've been holding the O 2 heater number 1 in the Off position. I believe that was your last instruction. All the other heaters are Auto and all fans are Off. Over.

a11_0360102.speaker: Duke
a11_0360102.text: Roger. Stand by.

a11_0360102.speaker: Duke
a11_0360102.text: 11, Houston. We'd like all heaters, Auto. Over.

a11_0360102.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0360102.text: Roger. All four Auto, all four fans Off. [Long pause.]

a11_0360102.speaker: Duke
a11_0360102.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. As the Sun sinks slowly in the west, the White Team bids you good night. If we get a story on the seven-tenths, we can give it to you in about 15 minutes or so; if not, we'll give it to you in the morning. Over.

a11_0360102.speaker: Collins
a11_0360102.text: Okay. That sounds fine, Charlie. Thanks very much.

a11_0360102.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0360102.text: Hey, you earned your pay today, Charlie. Thank you.

a11_0360102.speaker: Duke
a11_0360102.text: Rog. Good night all.

a11_0362005.speaker: Duke
a11_0362005.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. One request: the optics switch to zero. And we've got a lot of theories on why it maneuvered at seven-tenths a moment ago, Mike, but no real definite answer. We'll be back with you later. Over.

a11_0362005.speaker: Collins
a11_0362005.text: Okay. No rush, Charlie. Thank you.

a11_0362700.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0362700.text: This is Apollo Control. The view that we have at the present time appears to be out the window of the Command Module looking at the Lunar Module docking target.

a11_0362700.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0362700.text: And we seem to have a fairly good view here of the interior of the Command Module. This would look to be the panel, display panel with some of the fuel quantity dials on the right side of the cockpit.

a11_0362700.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0362700.text: At the time these television pictures were transmitted from the spacecraft, Apollo 11 was about 121,000 nautical miles [about 224,000 km] from Earth. Where we do have good signal lock-on, we get amazingly good quality on those little omni antennas. As we had mentioned before, normally the High Gain Antenna would be used for television transmission of this sort.

a11_0362700.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0362700.text: And we could almost make out a face in that one, and somebody's hand down at the instrument panel.

a11_0362700.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0362700.text: That last view, just before we lost picture lock-up, appeared to be the right-center portion of the Main Display Console, main display panel in the Command Module.

a11_0362700.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0362700.text: For a brief moment there we had a picture of a somewhat placid Neil Armstrong closing his eyes momentarily. Another crewman to his left, I'm not sure, at this point, that I can make out who it was. It did appear it might have been Mike Collins.

a11_0362700.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0362700.text: This is Apollo Control. That concludes the replay of the test transmission from Apollo 11. That transmission occurred about 2 hours prior to the regularly scheduled TV transmission this evening. The crew apparently testing out the onboard system, and we received about 52 minutes of intermittant television using the spacecraft omnidirectional antennas. And as you could see, as particularly near the end, this is just - appears to be just about the limit of television reception from the omni antennas. At the time of the transmission, Apollo 11 was about 121,000 nautical miles [about 224,000 km] f

a11_0362700a.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0362700a.text: This is Apollo Control. The view that we have at the present time appears to be out the window of the Command Module looking at the Lunar Module docking target.

a11_0362700a.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0362700a.text: This is Apollo Control. That concludes the replay of the test transmission from Apollo 11. That transmission occurred about 2 hours prior to the regularly scheduled TV transmission this evening. The crew apparently testing out the onboard system, and we received about 52 minutes of intermittant television using the spacecraft omnidirectional antennas. And as you could see, as particularly near the end, this is just - appears to be just about the limit of television reception from the omni antennas. At the time of the transmission, Apollo 11 was about 121,000 nautical miles [about 224,000 km] f

a11_0362700b.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0362700b.text: And we seem to have a fairly good view here of the interior of the Command Module. This would look to be the panel, display panel with some of the fuel quantity dials on the right side of the cockpit.

a11_0362700c.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0362700c.text: At the time these television pictures were transmitted from the spacecraft, Apollo 11 was about 121,000 nautical miles [about 224,000 km] from Earth. Where we do have good signal lock-on, we get amazingly good quality on those little omni antennas. As we had mentioned before, normally the High Gain Antenna would be used for television transmission of this sort.

a11_0362700d.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0362700d.text: This is Apollo Control. The view that we have at the present time appears to be out the window of the Command Module looking at the Lunar Module docking target.

At the time of the transmission, Apollo 11 was about 121,000 nautical miles [about 224,000 km] f

a11_0365210.speaker: Duke
a11_0365210.text: Roger. Mike, I think we can explain that seven-tenths rate. When we - the first time through, you know, we failed to go through the Verb 49, so we had a large error between our actual CDU and desired CDU in roll. And with that situation, the DAP - the vehicle will roll - will maneuver, rather, at a rate that is loaded in, which was three-tenths plus four-tenths rate, and it will limit at four-tenths above the desired rate, so - that is if we have a large enough angle between the desired and the actual, which we did. So, therefore, the rate was four-tenths plus three-tenths to give you the seve

a11_0372100.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0372100.text: At this time, Apollo 11 is 137,219 nautical miles [254,130 km] from Earth. The spacecraft is traveling at a speed of 4,132 feet per second [1,259 m/s]. Here in Mission Control, things have settled down into a rather quiet nightime routine. We said good night to the crew at about 36 hours; 36 hours, 9 minutes to be exact, a little over a hour ago. We did hear from them once or twice since then and we anticipate that at this time they are probably getting settled down to begin their 10-hour sleep period. At 37 hours, 21 minutes; this is Apollo Control.

a11_0382600.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0382600.text: This is Apollo Control; 39 hours, 40 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 11 crew at this time, all three soundly asleep. The space digitals display - stand by. Space digitals display here in Mission Control now showing 82,905 nautical miles [153,540 km] out from the Moon. Velocity; 3,897 feet per second [1,188 m/s] relative to the Moon. Awake time; 7 hours, 19 minutes away. Spacecraft presently over the west-central Pacific, if a line were projected back toward its nearest point on Earth. And at 39 hours, 41 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control.

a11_0394000.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0394000.text: This is Apollo Control; 40 hours, 58 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 11 presently 146,300 nautical miles [270,900 km] out from Earth. Velocity; 3,917 feet per second [1,194 m/s]. Six hours, 1 minute remaining in the sleep period - the ten-hour sleep period scheduled in the Flight Plan. Rather quiet here during the nightwatch, or the Black Team which tonight is being headed up by Flight Director Gerry Griffin who is spelling the usual Black Team Flight Director, Gene Lunney [means Glynn Lunney]. One clock here in Mission Control shows landing time 61 hours, 48 minutes from now. This is simi

a11_0405800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0405800.text: This is Apollo Control; 42 hours, 28 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Crew of Apollo 11 still asleep at this time. Some 4 hours, 31 minutes remaining in the scheduled 10-hour sleep period. Altitude now from the Moon; 76,529 nautical miles [141,732 km]. Velocity from the Moon - toward the Moon; 3,842 feet per second [1,171 m/s]; relative to the Moon that is. And at 42 hours, 28 minutes; this is Apollo Control.

a11_0422800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0422800.text: This is Apollo Control; 43 hours, 29 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 11 presently on the spot directly above or directly out from the Malay Peninsula. Some 3 hours, 30 minutes remaining in the scheduled 10-hour sleep period for the crew. And if the space digitals display were up here at the time, coming out of the computer we would know what the distance and velocity were. So, at 43 hours, 29 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control.

a11_0432900.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0432900.text: This is Apollo Control; 44 hours, 28 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 11 crew has another 2 hours, 31 minutes remaining in their 10-hour sleep period. The spacecraft is now some 72,010 nautical miles [133,363 km] out from the Moon. Velocity continuing to decelerate as we get nearer the changeover point in influence between the Earth and the Moon. Velocity now showing 3,811 feet per second [1,162 m/s]. The spacecraft now calculated to weigh 96,068 pounds [43,576 kg]. At 44 hours, 29 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control.

a11_0442800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0442800.text: This is Apollo Control; 45 hours, 28 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. A little more than an hour remaining in the Apollo 11 crew sleep period. Present velocity; 3,799 feet per second [1,158 m/s]. Distance from Moon; 69,810 nautical miles [129,288 km]. Apollo 11 will continue decelerating as it gets to the point where the Moon's sphere of influence overcomes the Earth's sphere of influence. This point will take place - This event will take place at 61 hours, 39 minutes and 57 seconds Ground Elapsed Time; according to the Flight Dynamics Officer. At this point, the spacecraft-to-Moon distance will b

a11_0452800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0452800.text: This is Apollo Control; 46 hours, 28 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. A little more than half hour remaining in the crew sleep period. Members of the Green Team of flight controllers headed up by prime Flight Director Cliff Charlesworth are coming into the control room at this time, and at each console, a handover is taking place from the Black Watch. At the time - at the present time, the Apollo 11 spacecraft is 67,518 nautical miles [125,043 km] out from the Moon, traveling at a velocity of 3,787 feet per second [1,154 m/s]. Apollo 11 presently is being tracked by the Madrid S-band station. And

a11_0462800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0462800.text: This is Apollo Control at 46 hours, 58 minutes into the mission. The Green Team led by Flight Director Cliff Charlesworth has just relieved Glynn Lunney's Black Team. The Flight Surgeon Dr. Willard Hawkins indicates the crew appears to be still asleep. We're nearing the end of the scheduled rest period. Cliff Charlesworth indicates we will put in a call to the crew within a few minutes. Apollo 11 is 158,681 nautical miles [293,877 km] from Earth. Velocity; 3,578 feet per second [1,091 m/s]. Spacecraft weight is 96,068 pounds [43,576 kg].

a11_0465800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0465800.text: This is Apollo Control at 47 hours, 3 minutes. Cliff Charlesworth has decided to let the crew sleep a little longer. He's just had a conversation with the Flight Surgeon. Dr. Hawkins reports all indications are that the crew is sleeping soundly. The Flight Plan does not warrant awaking them just to get them up. There's no - nothing in the Flight Plan that requires their attention at the present time, so the Flight Director has made a decision to not put in a call to the crew and wake them. Flight Surgeon says that a look at the data throughout the night indicates that the crew slept rather wel

a11_0470300.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0470300.text: This is Apollo Control at 47 hours, 41 minutes into the mission. From all indications the crew is still alseep. We're 41 minutes past the end of the scheduled 10-hour rest period now. Flight Director Cliff Charlesworth has decided to let the crew remain asleep; not awaken them from the ground. There is no need to awaken them. Nothing scheduled in the Flight Plan that requires their attention at this time. Apollo 11 is 160,137 nautical miles [296,574 km] from Earth. Velocity; 3,544 feet per second [1,080 m/s].

a11_0474100.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0474100.text: This is Apollo Control at 48 hours into the Apollo 11 mission. The spacecraft is 160,760 nautical miles [297,728 km] from Earth. The distance from the Moon is 64,115 nautical miles [118,741 km]. Earth-referenced velocity; 3,529 feet per second [1,076 m/s]. The rest period has now lasted an hour longer than the 10-hour period scheduled. It's extended to 11 hours now. Flight Surgeon says there are indications that the commander, Neil Armstrong, may be awakening. Some stirring around. However, we have not yet put in a call to the crew. The midcourse correction-3, scheduled for this afternoon at a

a11_0480000.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0480000.text: This is Apollo Control at 48 hours, 9 minutes. We just put in a call to the crew. Here's that conversation.

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Apollo 11, Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

a11_0480900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0480900.text: Good morning, Houston. Apollo 11.

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Good morning, Apollo 11.

a11_0480900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0480900.text: Nice sleep. Be getting around to the...

a11_0480900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0480900.text: How's everything look up here from the ground?

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Roger. Say again, please.

a11_0480900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0480900.text: Roger. How do all our systems look?

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Roger. They're looking great, and as far as we can tell everything is good from down here. Over.

a11_0480900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0480900.text: Rog. Looks like the attitude held up real well during PTC last night.

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Yes, it did. We were showing you remaining well within a circle of 10 degrees radius throughout the night. Seems to be working beautifully. [Long pause.]

a11_0480900.speaker: Collins
a11_0480900.text: How's the old Green Team this morning? Did you have a quiet night?

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Yeah. It was a very quiet night down here. The old Black Team is complaining they didn't get a chance to make any transmissions. Ron Evans is getting...

a11_0480900.speaker: Collins
a11_0480900.text: Well, we'll be seeing them tomorrow, I guess.

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Yeah. Ron's getting to be known as the silent CapCom.

a11_0480900.speaker: Collins
a11_0480900.text: That's the best kind, Bruce.

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: (Laughter) Okay. [Long pause.]

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: When you feel up to copying, 11, I've got a couple of small items in the way of a Flight Plan update and your morning consumables update. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0480900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0480900.text: Apollo 11.

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Roger, 11. We'd like to perform a waste-water dump at your convenience some time in the near future here. No particular time scheduled. Down there at the time for Midcourse Correction 3, which is about 53:55, we're deleting Midcourse Correction number 3 and all the items associated with it. For your information, the calculated value of the burn for Midcourse number 3 was eight-tenths of a foot per second, that is 0.8 feet per second. Canceling this, if we decide to burn Midcourse Correction-4, this would then give you a burn for Midcourse Correction-4 of 2.0 feet per second. At 53 hours, we ha

a11_0480900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0480900.text: - then we'll get to the waste-water dump [garble].

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Say again, please. You're cutting out.

a11_0480900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0480900.text: [Garble.] Roger. [Garble] for now it looks like [garble].

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: 11, this is Houston. Stand by a minute, please. We're having difficulty receiving you. [Long pause.]

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Radio check. Over.

a11_0480900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0480900.text: Roger, Houston. Read you loud and clear. How me? Over.

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Roger. Reading you the same. We did a minor reconfiguration down here. Stand by. Out.

a11_0480900.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0480900.text: This is Apollo Control. That first conversation was with Buzz Aldrin and Mike Collins joined in. We've not yet heard from Neil Armstrong.

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Okay, 11. This is Houston. We switched your Omni antennas as you rolled through the appropriate position. Did you copy the Flight Plan update item? [No answer.]

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over

a11_0480900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0480900.text: Apollo 11, go ahead.

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Roger, 11. Did you copy the Flight Plan update items? Over.

a11_0480900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0480900.text: Roger. How do you read me now, Bruce?

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Loud and clear, now.

a11_0480900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0480900.text: Okay. The battery charge is in - in the process now and the waste-water dump is in work. MCC-3 has been cancelled. It would have been 0.8 feet per second. MCC-4 now looks like about 2.4 feet per second. At around 53 hours we'll do a P52 in PTC. Over.

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Roger, 11. The magnitudes of the midcourse corrections were just for your information, but Midcourse 4 was down around 2.0 feet per second. Again, for your information, on SPS chamber pressure, it looks like your onboard readout of 87 psi corresponds to 92 psi by our telemetry, and your value of 89 on board corresponds to 94. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Radio check on a new power amplifier in our transmitter. Over.

a11_0480900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0480900.text: Roger. Read you loud and clear. How me? Over.

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Roger. Loud and clear. Did you copy my notes on SPS chamber pressure?

a11_0480900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0480900.text: Negative.

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Okay. Just for your information again, it appears that your readout of 87 psi corresponds to our corrected TM readout of 92 - that's 92 psi, and 89 on board is really 94 psi. Over.

a11_0480900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0480900.text: Roger, I got that you were reading about 5 psi low.

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Roger. And are you ready for the consumables update?

a11_0480900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0480900.text: Ready to copy.

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Okay. Consumables update for GET of 46 plus 00: minus 5.5 percent, minus 6.5 percent, minus 2.5 percent, minus 7.5 percent, minus 5.0 percent, minus 2 pounds hydrogen, plus one pound oxygen, and that minus 5.5 percent on the RCS total corresponds to minus 66 pounds. Over.

a11_0480900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0480900.text: Okay. I copy those, and I'll give you our percentages now: Alpha, 82; Bravo, 84; Cocoa, 85; Delta, 87. Over.

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: This is Houston. We copy your percentages, and do you have a crew status report on sleep for us? [Pause.]

a11_0480900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0480900.text: Roger. In descending order; 8, 9, and 8. Over.

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Houston. Roger. Out.

a11_0480900.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0480900.text: That would be Armstrong, 8; Collins, 9; Aldrin, 8.

a11_0480900.speaker: Collins
a11_0480900.text: Houston, we're getting Cryo pressure warning now in the middle of stirring up the [garble].

a11_0480900.speaker: McCandless
a11_0480900.text: Roger. We copy.

a11_0480900.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0480900.text: This is Apollo Control. The flight surgeon reports that is not a record for sleep. The Apollo 10 crew, during one rest period, logged 10 hours of sleep.

a11_0483235.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0483235.text: Houston, Apollo 11. We've got the continent of Africa right facing toward us right now, and of course, everything's getting smaller and smaller as time goes on. The Mediterranean is completely clear. The Sun looks like it's about to set around Madagascar. The equatorial belt of Africa stands out quite clearly. We're seeing a dark green or a muddy colored green, compared to the sandier colors of the southern tip of Africa and, of course, the Sahara northern coast of Africa. There's a rather remarkable cloud that appears in the vicinity of the border between Afghanistan and Pakistan. It's just a

a11_0483235.speaker: McCandless
a11_0483235.text: Roger, 11. We copy your word description on that. I understand you can see a shadow being cast by that cloud over between Afghanistan and Pakistan. Any estimate on how long that shadow would be? Over.

a11_0483235.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0483235.text: [Garble.] It looks like it's a shadow. [Garble] coming around to - back that way [garble].

a11_0483235.speaker: McCandless
a11_0483235.text: We're getting a lot of background noise now, also. If you will stand by a minute or so until we roll a little further in PTC, I think things will get better.

a11_0483235.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0483235.text: Okay. It's coming around to the number 1 window. We'll get you there.

a11_0483235.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0483235.text: That's Buzz Aldrin with the description.

a11_0483702.speaker: McCandless
a11_0483702.text: 11, this is Houston. The noise on the comm seems to have quieted down now. I guess that we've rotated a new antenna into view and probably also the Earth out of view in your window. Over.

a11_0483702.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0483702.text: Okay. It looks as though the length of the shadow of that cloud is about the same as the width of the Persian Gulf.

a11_0483702.speaker: McCandless
a11_0483702.text: Okay. We copy the width of the Persian Gulf, and I guess that all I can give you first hand is a single isolated data point, and that is that it was clear here in Houston this morning. That's a pretty localized observation. As a result of your waste-water dump, it looks like the PTC mode has been disturbed somewhat. We're showing you about 20 degrees out in pitch right now and about 6 degrees in yaw, which is significantly greater, about twice as much - a little more than twice as much as the deviation you had prior to the waste-water dump. We're watching it down here, though, and we'll let yo

a11_0483702.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0483702.text: Okay. Maybe we ought to - next time split that in half, and put half of it on one side and half on the other or something like that.

a11_0483702.speaker: McCandless
a11_0483702.text: Yeah. We could do that. We were actually pretty interested in seeing what the effect on PTC would be of the waste-water dump. We don't recall ever having performed a waste-water dump during PTC on previous missions. Over.

a11_0484254.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0484254.text: Houston, Apollo 11. I'm looking at that cloud now around Pakistan through the sextant, and it appears to be one single cell in the latter stages of development. There is a smaller, more isolated one just to the south...

a11_0484254.speaker: McCandless
a11_0484254.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. We lost you down in the noise on the comm link here about the time you were describing the single-cell cloud formation over Afghanistan-Pakistan area through the sextant. Over.

a11_0484254.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0484254.text: Rog. It came through a lot clearer through the sextant than with the monocular, and you could definitely tell it was one single cell in the latter stages of development. It must have gone up to over 50,000 feet, though. The eastern Mediterranean is phenomenally clear. You can see all the lakes; the Dead Sea stood out quite well. Over.

a11_0484254.speaker: McCandless
a11_0484254.text: Roger. What appears to be the limit of resolution through that sextant from your current position? Over.

a11_0484254.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0484254.text: Well, I can't see it right now. It's outside the field of view.

a11_0484254.speaker: McCandless
a11_0484254.text: Roger.

a11_0484254.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0484254.text: And, I don't know how you'd really describe the limit of resolution. I'll think about that a little.

a11_0484254.speaker: McCandless
a11_0484254.text: Okay. I guess the smallest object that you could pick out looking through it would give us a pretty good hack.

a11_0484254.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0484254.text: Well, you can see the Nile River going almost up to its source. The lake is obscured by clouds, but you can trace it all the way on up.

a11_0484254.speaker: McCandless
a11_0484254.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a11_0484254.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0484254.text: I guess that's down though, isn't it?

a11_0484254.speaker: McCandless
a11_0484254.text: Apollo 11, Houston.

a11_0484254.speaker: Collins
a11_0484254.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a11_0484254.speaker: McCandless
a11_0484254.text: Roger. We've been working under the assumption that it would take about an hour for the interference from a waste-water dump to dissipate to the point where you could reasonably take star sightings for platform alignment, navigation or something of this sort. If you have a spare minute or two, could you comment on the observation conditions now? Over,

a11_0484254.speaker: Collins
a11_0484254.text: Yeah. Stand by one, Bruce.

a11_0484254.speaker: McCandless
a11_0484254.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a11_0484254.speaker: Collins
a11_0484254.text: My guess would be the telescope's probably pretty useless, but you can differentiate in the sextant between water droplets and stars by the difference in their motions.

a11_0484254.speaker: McCandless
a11_0484254.text: Okay, Mike. And I guess that we've still got - what you're saying is that we've still got a lot of water droplets visible, but you can pick them out and distinguish them in the sextant there.

a11_0484254.speaker: Collins
a11_0484254.text: Right. I think so, but Buzz is looking through it now. Just a second.

a11_0484254.speaker: McCandless
a11_0484254.text: Okay.

a11_0485636.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0485636.text: Houston, Apollo 11. It looks like at this time the sextant would be quite usable for any alignment. There's actually very few particles drifting by.

a11_0485636.speaker: McCandless
a11_0485636.text: Roger, Buzz. How about the telescope? Is it useful now? [Pause.]

a11_0485636.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0485636.text: Well, it's not quite as useful; it never seems to be. Depending on the position of the Sun, it's got that band that seems to go across the center. I don't think it's because of the waste-water particles that it would lack its effectiveness. Over.

a11_0485636.speaker: McCandless
a11_0485636.text: Roger. What - Is this band something that's deposited on the outside of the optics? Over.

a11_0485636.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0485636.text: No. It's the reflection from the Sun.

a11_0485636.speaker: Collins
a11_0485636.text: The Sun bounces off the LM structure. With the LM attached, that telescope is just about useless. Those star charts that MPAD provided us, I think, would be most useful if we had to use the - if for some reason we had to mark through the telescope. We could use those as a guide for what we're looking at and say, 'Well, that bright blob over there has got to be that star because that's the position we're in. But so far, we've been - not been able to pick out any decent star patterns while docked with the LM using the telescope.

a11_0494038.speaker: McCandless
a11_0494038.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Go ahead.

a11_0494038.speaker: Aldrin [underneath McCandless]
a11_0494038.text: Houston, Apollo 11. How do your read? Over.

a11_0494038.speaker: McCandless
a11_0494038.text: Roger. We're reading you loud and clear.

a11_0494038.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0494038.text: Roger. Roger. You're coming back a little scratchy. It looks like our O 2 flow transducer's gotten a good bit worse. I just looked at it at the last water accumulator cycle, and it just barely registered - barely crept up above 0.2. Over.

a11_0494038.speaker: McCandless
a11_0494038.text: 11, this is Houston. At the time of your cyclic accumulator stroking, we were on low-bit-rate data, and consequently not receiving the O 2 flow parameter. We expect that what you're seeing is probably nominal. That is, it's probably what we would expect from a transducer that's malfunctioning in this fashion. It's probably just going to keep on getting worse like that. Nothing to worry about. We'll monitor things on the ground here. Over.

a11_0494038.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0494038.text: Okay. It does look like it's gradually degrading to about zilch.

a11_0495200.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0495200.text: This is Apollo Control at 50 hours, 16 minutes. Apollo 11 is now 165,346 nautical miles [306,221 km] from Earth, traveling at a velocity of 3,423 feet per second [1,043 m/s]. Flight controllers report all systems well within the normal range and operating very satisfactorily.

a11_0501600.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0501600.text: This is Apollo Control at 50 hours, 40 minutes. Apollo 11 is 166,135 miles [307,682 km] from Earth. CapCom is going to take a radio check here, I think, with the crew.

a11_0504000.speaker: McCandless
a11_0504000.text: Apollo 11 CDR, this is Houston. Radio check. Over.

a11_0504000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0504000.text: Roger, Houston. CDR loud and clear.

a11_0504000.speaker: McCandless
a11_0504000.text: Roger. We're reading you the same. Out.

a11_0504000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0504000.text: And would you check with FAO and see where that errata sheet is? We haven't been able to locate that.

a11_0504000.speaker: McCandless
a11_0504000.text: Roger. I understand it's supposed to be the back page in Buzz's operations checklist.

a11_0504000.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0504000.text: FAO is the Flight Activities Officer.

a11_0505300.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0505300.text: This is Apollo Control at 51 hours, 7 minutes. Apollo 7 - Apollo 11's distance is 167,007 nautical miles from Earth. Velocity; 3,386 feet per second.

a11_0510700.speaker: McCandless
a11_0510700.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Did you find it? Over.

a11_0510700.speaker: McCandless
a11_0510700.text: Roger. And I see you're in P00. If you can give us Accept, we'll uplink a new state vector to you and update the CMC clock. Over.

a11_0511244.speaker: McCandless
a11_0511244.text: 11, this is Houston. We're through with the uplink. You can go back to Block.

a11_0511630.speaker: McCandless
a11_0511630.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. We would like to terminate charging Battery Bravo at GET of 51:30. Over. [No answer.]

a11_0511630.speaker: McCandless
a11_0511630.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. We'd like to terminate charging Battery Bravo at 51:30 GET. Over.

a11_0513635.speaker: McCandless
a11_0513635.text: 11, this is Houston. We show you terminating Battery B charge. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0515923.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0515923.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Would you like to have both oxygen and hydrogen purge on? Over.

a11_0515923.speaker: McCandless
a11_0515923.text: 11, this is Houston. Say again. Both what on? Over.

a11_0515923.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0515923.text: On the fuel cell purge: would you like to see both oxygen and hydrogen? Over.

a11_0515923.speaker: McCandless
a11_0515923.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Affirmative. We request hydrogen and an oxygen fuel cell purge. Over.

a11_0515923.speaker: McCandless
a11_0515923.text: Negative. As long as you've got the H 2 purge line heaters on.

a11_0525829.speaker: McCandless
a11_0525829.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Go ahead.

a11_0525829.speaker: Collins
a11_0525829.text: Okay. I am going to go ahead and torque and star angle difference is 0.01, but it's sort of difficult at three-tenths rate. I'm required to use medium speed unresolved, and it's difficult to hold the star centered long enough to get a decent mark on it. [Pause.]

a11_0525829.speaker: McCandless
a11_0525829.text: Roger. We copy. It looks okay to us. [Pause.]

a11_0525829.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0525829.text: This is Apollo Control at 53 hours, 3 minutes into the mission. Apollo 11 is 170,746 nautical miles [316,222 km] from Earth. Velocity; 3,303 feet per second [1,007 m/s]. The crew is now in the process of realigning the spacecraft's inertial platform.

a11_0532000.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0532000.text: This is Apollo Control. We have a correction on the orbital parameters of Luna 15 as given in the news briefing, recently over. The parameters given in that briefing of 72 by 156 nautical miles [133 by 289 km] were based on a - on computations from an orbital period of 2 hours and 30 minutes instead of the correct 2 hours and 30 seconds. The orbit has been recomputed based on the proper numbers and the parameters for Luna 15, based on a period of 2 hours, 30 seconds, are 30 by 110 nautical miles [56 by 204 km], a perilune of 30, apolune of 110 nautical miles.

a11_0535136.speaker: McCandless
a11_0535136.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

a11_0535136.speaker: Collins
a11_0535136.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a11_0535136.speaker: McCandless
a11_0535136.text: Roger. I've got the morning news here if you're interested. Over.

a11_0535136.speaker: Collins
a11_0535136.text: Yeah, we sure are. We're ready to copy and comment.

a11_0535136.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0535136.text: Isn't that 2:30 there?

a11_0535136.speaker: McCandless
a11_0535136.text: Roger.

a11_0535136.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0535136.text: Okay. Go.

a11_0535136.speaker: McCandless
a11_0535136.text: Okay. Here we go. The interest in the flight of Apollo 11 continues at a high level but a competing interest in the Houston area is the easing of watering rules. Mayor Louie Welch promises a lifting of lawn watering restrictions if the rains continue. Friday is partly cloudy, and there is a 30 percent chance of thundershowers in the afternoon. In Washington DC, the Senate Finance Committee approved extension of the income tax surtax, but a Senate vote on the bill...

a11_0535136.speaker: Collins
a11_0535136.text: You cut out, Houston. You cut out.

a11_0535136.speaker: McCandless
a11_0535136.text: Roger. Where do you hold me cutting out? Over.

a11_0535136.speaker: Collins
a11_0535136.text: Houston, Apollo 11.

a11_0535136.speaker: McCandless
a11_0535136.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Over.

a11_0535136.speaker: McCandless
a11_0535136.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. How do you read now? Over.

a11_0535136.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0535136.text: Loud and clear, Houston. Go ahead.

a11_0535136.speaker: McCandless
a11_0535136.text: Roger.

a11_0535136.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0535136.text: Start after the rains in Houston.

a11_0535136.speaker: McCandless
a11_0535136.text: Roger. In Washington, the Senate Finance Committee has approved extension of the income tax surtax, but a Senate vote on the bill currently seems remote. In Austin, State Representative Ray Lemmon of Houston has been nominated as the National Director of the American Society for Oceanography. Lemmon has proposed a study of the possibility of establishing an institute of oceanography in Texas. This would be the first such institute on the western Gulf of Mexico. In Minneapolis, Minnesota, the weather bureau, after recapping today's weather showing a high of 88 and a low of 72, has noted "snowfa

a11_0535136.speaker: McCandless
a11_0535136.text: In sports, the Houston Oilers are showing plenty of enthusiasm in their early pre-season workouts at Kerrville, and Coach Wally Lemm says he is impressed with the fine group of rookies. National League baseball for yesterday, Thursday: St. Louis 11, Philadelphia 3; Montreal 5, over Pittsburg 4; Atlanta 12, Cincinnati 2; San Francisco 14, and Los Angeles 13. American League: we have Baltimore 3, over Cleveland 2; Detroit 4 to Washington's 3; Minnesota 8 to Chicago 5. Boston at New York was rained out. And in Corby, England, an Irishman, John Coyle has won the world's porridge eating championshi

a11_0535136.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0535136.text: Roger. I assume Houston didn't play yesterday.

a11_0535136.speaker: McCandless
a11_0535136.text: That's correct.

a11_0535136.speaker: Collins
a11_0535136.text: I'd like to enter Aldrin in the oatmeal eating contest next time.

a11_0535136.speaker: McCandless
a11_0535136.text: Is he pretty good at that?

a11_0535136.speaker: Collins
a11_0535136.text: He's doing his share up here.

a11_0535136.speaker: McCandless
a11_0535136.text: Let's see. You all just finished a meal not long ago, too, didn't you? [Pause.]

a11_0535136.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0535136.text: I'm still eating.

a11_0535136.speaker: McCandless
a11_0535136.text: Okay. Does that - that...

a11_0535136.speaker: Collins
a11_0535136.text: He's on his - He's on his 19th bowl.

a11_0535136.speaker: McCandless
a11_0535136.text: Roger. Are you having any difficulties with gas in the food bags like the 10 crew reported?

a11_0535136.speaker: Collins
a11_0535136.text: Well, that's intermittently affirmative, Bruce. We have these two hydrogen filters, which work fine as long as you don't hook them up to a food bag. But the entry way into the food bag has enough back pressure to cause the - the filters to start losing their efficiency. A couple of times, I've been tempted to go through that dry-out procedure, but we found that simply by leaving the filters alone for a couple of hours, their efficiency seems to be restored.

a11_0535136.speaker: McCandless
a11_0535136.text: Roger. We copy. [Pause.]

a11_0535136.speaker: Collins
a11_0535136.text: Their efficiency ranges anywhere from darn near perfect to terrible, just depending on the individual characteristics of the food bags we're putting to them. Some of the food bags are so crimped near the entry-way that there's no way we can work them loose to prevent back pressure.

a11_0535136.speaker: McCandless
a11_0535136.text: Roger.

a11_0535136.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0535136.text: That's Mike Collins from the spacecraft.

a11_0543212.speaker: McCandless
a11_0543212.text: Roger, 11 As you've probably noticed, your coning angle in PTC mode is increased substantially as a result of the waste water dump, the fuel cell purge, and natural coupling, so it looks like we are going to have to terminate PTC here in a little while. And we'd like to get your feeling as to whether you're still anticipating trying to send back TV signals from inside the LM. And, if so, we'll try to provide an attitude that you can hold that'll give us High Gain Antenna lock on the Earth during the TV and LM activation period. Over.

a11_0543212.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0543212.text: Yes, we're still planning that activity if the cord lengths work out all right, and we'll accept those attitudes that you work up for us.

a11_0543212.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0543212.text: When you work up an attitude to get High Gain, is there any way that we could get partial Sun in one of the two LM front windows?

a11_0543212.speaker: McCandless
a11_0543212.text: This is Houston. We'll have a look at it.

a11_0543212.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0543212.text: That was Neil Armstrong confirming they will attempt TV at approximately an elasped time of 56 hours, 20 minutes and then the last of the question was by Buzz Aldrin.

a11_0543914.speaker: McCandless
a11_0543914.text: Roger. We have a TV attitude for you if you're ready to copy. [Pause.]

a11_0543914.speaker: McCandless
a11_0543914.text: Okay. We recommend stopping PTC at GET of 54:45:00, and this should put you at just about the right roll angle. The attitude we recommend is roll 263, pitch 090, yaw 000. This gives you the Earth out of window number 1 in the Command Module and places the High Gain Antenna and the CSM window for TV at your convenience. You will also have the Sun shining in - or shining at the hatch on the LM, and if you take down the window shades you should get some sunlight in. We're recommending wide deadband. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0543914.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0543914.text: Roger. Thank you, Houston. We'll look at that.

a11_0544253.speaker: Collins
a11_0544253.text: Houston, Apollo 11. When we pass the proper roll angle, we're not going to be anywhere near zero degrees yaw. Do you want us to just stop at the angle we find ourselves in and then Verb 49 to the three angles you gave us?

a11_0544253.speaker: Duke
a11_0544253.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We'd like you to stop at the proper roll angle, then do a Verb 49 to the roll and pitch. Over. Correction, roll and yaw. [Long pause.]

a11_0544253.speaker: Duke
a11_0544253.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Do you read? Over. [Pause.]

a11_0544253.speaker: Duke
a11_0544253.text: Roger, 11. Do you read me? Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0544253.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0544253.text: Stand by, Charlie. We're going to come out of PTC here at 263 roll and then do a Verb 49 to the recommended attitude.

a11_0544253.speaker: Duke
a11_0544253.text: That sounds fine to us. Over.

a11_0544253.speaker: Duke
a11_0544253.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Before you open the pressure equalization valve, we'd like a LM/CM Delta-P. Over.

a11_0544253.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0544253.text: Okay. Let me check it again. It was about 155.

a11_0544253.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0544253.text: I read it 158 right now, Charlie.

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: Houston, Apollo 11. We're stopping PTC at 263 [garble] 0.

a11_0544951.speaker: Duke
a11_0544951.text: 11, Houston. You're about one-by on this transmission. Say again. Over.

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Do you read?

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: Houston, Apollo 11. How do you read on the High Gain?

a11_0544951.speaker: Duke
a11_0544951.text: 11, how do you read me? Over.

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: Reading you loud and clear, Charlie. We just switched to High Gain, and we stopped PTC at roll 263, pitch 90, yaw 0. How do you read?

a11_0544951.speaker: Duke
a11_0544951.text: Roger, Mike. You're five-by now on the High Gain. We're right between the Omni antennas and pretty horrible Comm on the Omnis. We got you five-by on the High Gain, and we copy the PTC stoppage. Over.

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: Okay, fine. [Long pause.]

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: Houston, we're going to open the Direct O 2 valve and start pumping up the cabin.

a11_0544951.speaker: Duke
a11_0544951.text: Roger. Copy. [Long pause.]

a11_0544951.speaker: Duke
a11_0544951.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We're going to hand over to Goldstone for uplink in about 2 minutes. We might have a momentary drop-out of comm. Over.

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: Alrighty. Can you hear our Master Alarm in the background? That's O 2 Flow High coming through this amplifier.

a11_0544951.speaker: Duke
a11_0544951.text: Roger. Copy. [Pause.]

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: That photoelectric cell is a good device. It's worked very well.

a11_0544951.speaker: Duke
a11_0544951.text: 11, Houston. Say again. Over.

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: I say that photoelectric cell amplifier for the Master Alarm is a good device. It's working very well, and it's a nice pleasing tone.

a11_0544951.speaker: Duke
a11_0544951.text: Rog. Copy. Thank you. [Pause.]

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: Makes you almost glad to get master alarms! [Long pause.]

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: Houston, Apollo 11. As a matter of curiosity, our O 2 flow meter is pegged full-scale High.

a11_0544951.speaker: Duke
a11_0544951.text: Roger, 11. We copy that here. Over.

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: Boy, that transducer's working somewhat.

a11_0544951.speaker: Duke
a11_0544951.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a11_0544951.speaker: Duke
a11_0544951.text: 11, Houston. We'd like to try to attempt to correlate your O 2 flow in transducer with the flow valve that you've got open. How far - How far open would you say you have the Repress O 2 ? Over. Correction, the Direct O 2 .

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: Stand by, Charlie. [Pause.]

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: Okay, Charlie. It's not open very far. It's hard to give you a good reading without shutting it again, but the arrow is about at the one o'clock position. Now I reduced the flow, and I'll let it stabilize here. Right now our onboard reading is about 0.4, and that's with the arrow on the O 2 valve at the two o'clock position. Would you rather have comparisons of O 2 flow readings or would you rather have valve position comparisons?

a11_0544951.speaker: Duke
a11_0544951.text: Roger. Stand by.

a11_0544951.speaker: Duke
a11_0544951.text: EECOMs say they'd like to look at the valve positions. Over.

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: Okay. Well, we're holding steady now at three-tenths of a pound per hour, and our cabin pressure is about 5.4; and I'll close the valve momentarily and then open it again to this position and tell you how much travel is required.

a11_0544951.speaker: Duke
a11_0544951.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: It's about 30 degrees of travel, Charlie, from the closed position, which is with the arrow pointing at about three to three-thirty, four o'clock.

a11_0544951.speaker: Duke
a11_0544951.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: Our flow is stabilized now at 0.6.

a11_0544951.speaker: Duke
a11_0544951.text: Roger. We copy. We're reading the same.

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: Yeah, open it back to the one o'clock position.

a11_0544951.speaker: Duke
a11_0544951.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: Is that enough different positions, or you want more, Charlie?

a11_0544951.speaker: Duke
a11_0544951.text: Mike, that's a good - good enough. We're satisfied now. Over.

a11_0544951.speaker: Collins
a11_0544951.text: Okay.

a11_0550202.speaker: Collins
a11_0550202.text: Houston, Apollo 11. We've terminated direct O 2 , our cabin pressure is 5.7, and, as a matter of curiosity, when we turn the Direct O 2 valve off, we get a master alarm just like they did in the spacecraft testing.

a11_0550202.speaker: Duke
a11_0550202.text: 11, Houston, we have a little update for you. When you go into the LM, we'd like you to unstow and bring back to the Command Module the following items. Over.

a11_0550202.speaker: Duke
a11_0550202.text: Roger. We'd like you to pick up the - out of the flight data file, the surface checklist, the mission rules No-Go card, the DPS, APS, RCS limit cue card. Over.

a11_0550202.speaker: Duke
a11_0550202.text: Apollo 11, Houston. The reason we wanted you to bring those three items back, we'll have some updates for you, for those three. Over.

a11_0551000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0551000.text: Rog. This is just for free. This isn't what we had in mind.

a11_0551000.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0551000.text: That was CapCom, Charlie Duke, advising the crew that we're not quite prepared for television reception at this time. You heard Mike Collins respond that this one's for free. We still intend to get the television transmission during the time the crew is in the Lunar Module; beginning at about 56 hours, 20 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; which would be about 4:52 PM Central Daylight Time.

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: Apollo 11, Houston. It's a pretty good show here. It looks like you almost got the probe out.

a11_0551934.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0551934.text: Yeah, it's loose now.

a11_0551934.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0551934.text: Can you see that?

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: Rog, Neil. It's really good.

a11_0551934.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0551934.text: Not much light up in that area, but apparently the TV set's able to pick it up.

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: There are some bright spots shining on the probe. Apparently Sun shafting on it that just gets just about enough for us to make it out. Over.

a11_0551934.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0551934.text: I think those are the tunnel lights.

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: Oh, Okay. You're right. [Pause.]

a11_0551934.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0551934.text: Okay. It's loose now. Coming down.

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: Looks like it's a little bit easier than doing that in the chamber.

a11_0551934.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0551934.text: You bet. This is the only way...

a11_0551934.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0551934.text: You have to take it easy. It's pretty massive, but it goes where you direct it.

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: 11, Houston. That's a beautiful picture now, we've got. We're looking at a 12-second delay. To us you are just bringing it down by the optics now. [Pause.]

a11_0551934.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0551934.text: Mike must have done a smooth job in that docking. There isn't a dent or a mark on the probe.

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: Rog. [Pause.]

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: We're really getting a great picture here, 11. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: 11, Houston. With a 12-foot cable, we estimate you should have about 5 to 6 feet excess when you get it - the camera into the LM. Over.

a11_0551934.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0551934.text: Roger.

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: We can see the probe now. Correction, the drogue.

a11_0551934.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0551934.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_0551934.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0551934.text: Okay. Drogue removal's coming next.

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: Roger. As we suspected. [Long pause.]

a11_0551934.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0551934.text: Once removal of the drogue is completed, they will have access to the LM hatch and be able to go into the tunnel.

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: 11, Houston. Now it's a good view of the storage area under the couch. [Long pause.]

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: 11, Houston. Looks like you're pretty crowded in there with that drogue. Over.

a11_0551934.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0551934.text: Oh, it's not really bad.

a11_0551934.speaker: Collins
a11_0551934.text: This TV cable is getting in the way. [Pause.]

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: We see lots of arms. [Long pause.]

a11_0551934.speaker: Collins
a11_0551934.text: The only problem, Charlie, is these TV stagehands don't know where to stand.

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: Well, you don't really have a union card, there. We can't really complain too much, I guess. [Long pause.]

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Do you have a little white dot in the bottom of your monitor - TV monitor? Over.

a11_0551934.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0551934.text: Roger. We do.

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: Roger. I guess part of the camera's been burnt out down there. These are really beautiful pictures now, Buzz. Over. Real clear. [Pause.]

a11_0551934.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0551934.text: Okay. We might have got just a little bit of Sun in there. Is it just one small white dot?

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: That's affirmative. [Long pause.]

a11_0551934.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0551934.text: Have a good view here of the computer and display and keyboard assembly with the green lights flashing.

a11_0551934.speaker: Collins
a11_0551934.text: We went up in the tunnel checking the roll angle, Charlie, and it's 2.05 degrees.

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: Roger. Copy. 2.05 on the roll cal.

a11_0551934.speaker: Collins
a11_0551934.text: And that's a plus.

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: Roger. Plus. [Long pause.]

a11_0551934.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0551934.text: The reference to the roll cal, or roll calibration index marker in the tunnel, which shows how far off exact zero the two vehicles were when the docking occurred.

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: 11, Houston. The tunnel looks pretty clear to us. Somebody going up there now. Over.

a11_0551934.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0551934.text: It's Mike checking his connectors up there now.

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: Rog. [Pause.]

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: 11, Houston. The lighting up in there looks very good to us at this time. Over.

a11_0551934.speaker: Collins
a11_0551934.text: Alright, that's mostly the camera. It - it's subdued to say the least. [Pause.]

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: Roger. It's pretty good - It's gathering pretty well to us. We see everything quite clearly up in there. [Long pause.]

a11_0551934.speaker: Collins
a11_0551934.text: Well, the docking latches look good today just like they did yesterday. Everything up in there looks just fine.

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: That sounds fine to us. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: 11, Houston. We can even read the decals up there on the LM hatch.

a11_0551934.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0551934.text: Well, let me zoom it up and see how much you can read.

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: We can see the LM umbilical connection quite well there, Buzz. We see you zooming in on one of the decals now. It's: 'To reset, unlatch handle; latch behind grip and pull back two full strokes'. That's about all we can make out.

a11_0551934.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0551934.text: Hey, you get an A-plus.

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: Thank you very much, sir. At least I passed my eye test.

a11_0551934.speaker: Collins
a11_0551934.text: I'm standing 6 feet from it, Charlie, and you can read it better than I can. There's something wrong with the system.

a11_0551934.speaker: Duke
a11_0551934.text: Rog.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: That's a real good view of the LM hatch handle there, 11. Over.

a11_0553239.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0553239.text: Roger.

a11_0553239.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0553239.text: Looks like we'll be ready to go into the LM early if that's okay with you all down there.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: Roger. It's fine with us, Neil. Go ahead any time you wish. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: 11, Houston. The white spot you see on your monitor, our TV people say it is a burn spot; but they expect it to dissipate after a couple of hours. Over.

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: Roger. Thank you.

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: Okay, the dump valve is actuated.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: Roger. Copy, 11. We see that very clearly. Is that you, Buzz, with your hand on it?

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: Yeah.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: 11, Houston. We're really amazed at the quality of the picture up in the tunnel. It's really superb. Over.

a11_0553239.speaker: Collins
a11_0553239.text: It is, considering the amount of light up in there.

a11_0553239.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0553239.text: Roger. We're about to open our hatch now.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: Rog. [Pause.]

a11_0553239.speaker: Collins
a11_0553239.text: There's that same guy that, when you open up the door, why, he's waiting there for you, and he turns the lights on.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: How about that. Just like the refrigerator. [Long pause.]

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: Buzz, the view in through your - by your right - left shoulder there is so good we can see the ascent engine cover, the Velcro on it, and that's about all we can make out right now. [Long pause.]

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: Now we see the helmet stowage bag...

a11_0553239.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0553239.text: We don't see anything loose up there.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: Well, great. Looks good to us. We see the helmet storage bag.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: Hello, 11. Houston. We got a view of the PLSS there, off the right of our screen.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: 11, Houston. Buzz, you already in? Over.

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: Rog. I'm halfway in. I'm gonna start turning around, I guess.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a11_0553239.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0553239.text: Buzz Aldrin reporting that he's halfway into the LM. This view is inside the LM cabin.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We'd like you to read out the LCG reservoir sight level. Over.

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: Okay. Stand by. [Long pause.]

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: 11, we have a good view of the window there. It looks like the Sun's fairly coming through the shade.

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: Yeah, I'm afraid it's - We're just about plus-Z toward the Sun.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: That's affirmative. This attitude put both windows right toward the Sun for the LM. Over.

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: Well, that may be good in some respects.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: We had a view, Buzz, of the utility light cord.

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: Now let me show you a view looking the other way.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: Rog. And we see right now the utility light or either the floodlight up there.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: I think now I see the utility light still in the stowage bag. Hey, that's a great shot right there. We see you in there. Guess that's Neil and Mike. Better be, anyway. [Long pause.]

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: We see you waving. [Long pause.]

a11_0553239.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0553239.text: Buzz Aldrin has apparently carried the camera into the LM with him, showing us Neil Armstrong and Mike Collins back in the CSM.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: 11, Houston. That's a really a beautiful shot.

a11_0553239.speaker: Collins
a11_0553239.text: Just saying hello.

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: On the LCG sight gauge, you got about - oh, it looks like the white mark that's in the plunger is about a quarter to three-eighths inch out into the green, away from the red. Is that what you'd like to see? Over.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: Stand by. Rog, Buzz. That looks good to us. Thank you much.

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: It is the white index, is it not, that you're interested in comparing whether it's in the red or green?

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: Stand by. That's affirmative, Buzz. It looks good. That's a good reading for us. Over.

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: Okay.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: We had a shot momentar - a moment ago of the suit disconnect valve.

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: I'll open up the windows and see what the lighting condition's going to be like. [Long pause.]

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: 11, Houston. That's a real good view. We have the AOT. You're back now, Buzz, and notice you're taking down one of the window shades. Over.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: The light is superb!

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: How's the Sun coming in? How's the Sun coming in from this direction going to affect what you can see?

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: It made it really super. The lighting is excellent in the - in the LM right now. We can make out the AOT, the ISA, and the left-hand window - there's a little glare off of that, but the LMP side the - with the shade down, it's really excellent. Over.

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: Well, let's - I'm turned around, why I took the shade off my side first.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: Roger. We copy. The light level for the TV is really excellent. Over.

a11_0553239.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0553239.text: Yeah, the lighting in the LM is very nice now, just like completely daylit; and everything is visible. A good bit lighter than the tunnel was earlier.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: Roger. We got a good view now, Neil, of the DEDA; and also Buzz's ACA.

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: Hey, I'm pointing it at the front hatch now. Everything seems to be in place down there.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: Roger, we got the dump valves in view. Over.

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: 11, Houston. We see you removing the ISA now, folding it up, putting it up by the AOT. The instrument panels are coming into view behind.

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: Yeah, I think it'd probably be best, since we've done the SPS burn, to put it back over the instrument panel instead of putting it up over the PLSS on the recharge station. Would you care to comment on that one? We could do either just as easily.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: Stand by. We'll have an answer for you momentarily.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: 11, Houston. That's really a super shot of the main display. [Long pause.]

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: The vehicle is surprisingly free of any debris floating around. It's very clean.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
