a11_0553239.text: 11, Houston. It's pretty hard to describe this view. It's really - really great.

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: Now you know how we feel.

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: Okay. Neil's OPS is about 57, 5,800 [psi].

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: Copy.

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: And mine's about 5,800, also.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: Copy. [Long pause.]

a11_0553239.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0553239.text: Aldrin's hand resting on one of the Portable Life Support Systems which will be used on the Moon's surface.

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: 11, Houston. That's a good shot of Neil's PLSS, there. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0553239.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0553239.text: No, that's mine. [Long pause.]

a11_0553239.speaker: Duke
a11_0553239.text: 11, Houston. That moment - a moment ago, we had a good shot of your PLSS, Buzz, and the two helmet stowage bags. Down behind your left shoulder, Buzz, we have the - the DSKY and the ACA.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: We're going to go ahead and take all the [garble] data on back into the Command Module, Charlie.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0555001.text: This television transmission has now been running about 42 minutes, and the spacecraft now about 176,000 [nautical] miles from Earth.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Buzz, it appears that you're intending to put on the Sun filter and view the Sun through the AOT. Over.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: Yeah, unfortunately it looks like it's down a little bit more towards [garble] than I can be able to see in the AOT.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: We got a beautiful view of the side of the Command Module out of the AOT looking in the left rear detent.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Rog.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: I can see the hatch and all the - all the EVA handrails. First time we've seen the silvery outside of the Command Module.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: I can read the letters on the hatch cover. It's a boost cover release; and the big yellow arrow that points toward the opening - place where the tool B goes.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Rog. Great shot now back down into the...

a11_0555001.speaker: Collins
a11_0555001.text: And left on the...

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Go ahead, Buzz. Over.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: Say again.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: I was just saying we got a great shot looking back into the Command Module.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: [Garble].

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: Okay. And the left detent, I can see the AO - or the rendezvous radar, and I move to the forward detent and that's about all I've got. I'm looking eyeball to eyeball.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: Charlie, is there any concern about the duration that we ought to have the window shades open?

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Stand by.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: We don't have - We don't have any circulation in here, and it might get a little on the warm side.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Rog.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: We'll - We'll put up a couple of hoses in the Command Module here and get a little circulation going.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Sounds like a good idea. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Apollo 11, Houston. As far as the window shades go in this LM, there's nothing except for crew comfort. I don't think we've got any systems problem. Be sure to put them back up when you egress. Over.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: That we will do. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: Charlie, I'll give you a view out of the overhead window, back looking at the Command Module right-hand rendezvous window.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Well, we see it now. Thanks a lot, Buzz. That's a good view through the overhead.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: One washer on...

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: One washer's on by the overhead.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Rog.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: There we go. We got it now.

a11_0555001.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0555001.text: There wasn't very much debris in the Command Module or the LM. We found very few loose particles of bolts, nuts, and screws and lint and things. Very few in each spacecraft. They were very clean.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Roger. Sounds good. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: 11, Houston. We have a good view out of the rendezvous - correction, the overhead window of the LM. We don't see anybody staring back at us, though. Over.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: Charlie, can you see Mike's two eyeballs staring out through the rendezvous window?

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: 11, Houston. Stand by. We haven't picked him up yet.

a11_0555001.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0555001.text: You're looking through a lot of layers of glass.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: 11, Houston. We had a...

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: [Garble] on my monitor.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: We had a slight glimpse of Mike in the rendezvous window at that time. It's pretty murky looking into there, though.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: Okay. Here he is; I've got him. I've got him on the monitor now.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Okay. We see him staring back at us now. Hello, in there. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Our recommendation for the ISA is to stow it back over the instrument panel. Over.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: Roger. Will do.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: 11, Houston. We can make out the markings on the panel. We read System A Ascent Fuel, Ascent Oxidizer. Quad 1, quad 4. The - It's really unbelievable, the definition we're getting down here off that little camera. Over.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: We can even see the barber pole on the talkbacks.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: We can read the markings on the instruments for the glycol pressure, quantity, PCO2. Even read the scale on the eight-ball. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: 11, Houston. We see the cross-feed barber pole, and we have the Velcro patches back up to the RCS systems now. We can see the markings on the meters, green and red bands, in limits. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: We see you raised the cover on the abort stage. We don't recommend that.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: Yeah. We're going to tape that one over.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Rog.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: We're going to tape that one over.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: We concur.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: The restraints in here do a pretty good job of pulling my pants down.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Roger. We haven't quite got that before the 50 million TV audience, yet. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: 11, Houston. That's a good view of the eight-ball. We see - You can even read the Off flag, there.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: You can see the signal strength meter for the radar, read the numbers on it. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: Houston, did you want us to test the cameras in the LM and - I was wondering about that. I saw it in the Flight Plan, but I'm just wondering if you want to do that on CSM power, or do you want us to take both of the 16-mm cameras back in the CSM and test them there? Over.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Stand by, Buzz.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: As an alternative to that, why, we could wait 'til LOI day and do it then when we transfer over to LM power.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Roger. Stand by. We'll have an answer.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: 11, Houston. On that TV, our commentary - The monitor I was looking at was delayed about 12 seconds, 12 to 15 seconds while it went through our color converter. It was probably - You thought I was crazy, but we were looking at it 15 seconds after you broadcast it. 11, Houston.

a11_0555001.speaker: Collins
a11_0555001.text: We understood that, Charlie.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Okay. On the LM cameras, we'd like you to do it on LOI day with the LM power. Over.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: Okay. That's what we'll do. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: Houston, we're showing you something that came out of the Commander's checklist stowage packet. It's got a 16-millimeter camera in it, and it's got this little cylinder; and I guess - I don't understand what it is. Maybe you can tell us.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Roger. Stand by. We can't figure it out either.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: It's got an arrow on the back, and it says turn, but I'm afraid to turn it.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: 11, your friendly geologist says it's the camera cank - crank, excuse me, for the 16-sequence camera if it jams. Over.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: Oh, very well. Thank you. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: There's that word again. The ancillary stowage container.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0555001.text: And we're back with the color.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: The shades didn't quite hack it, there, Buzz. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Collins
a11_0555001.text: Houston, 11. Are you still getting high bit rate off the omnis at this distance?

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Stand by, Mike. [Pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Apollo 11, Houston. About 50 percent of the time, we're getting high bit rate off the omnis when you're in PTC. Over.

a11_0555001.speaker: Collins
a11_0555001.text: Okay. Thank you.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: You're welcome.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Neil, at this attitude you look like you're about 12 feet long.

a11_0555001.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0555001.text: It seems like I always find myself upside-down in whatever I'm doing around here. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Could you give us a few comments on your crew comfort with the CSM hoses moving the air around? Over.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: Well, it's picking up a little bit of circulation in here.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: What do you estimate the temperature is, Buzz? Over. [Pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: Oh, I'd say maybe 73, 75.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Rog.

a11_0555001.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0555001.text: It's hard to tell at this density and pressure of gas, but the comfort level is about the - about the same as the Command Module.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: You probably...

a11_0555001.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0555001.text: It was a little warmer or stuffier when we first got in, but it seems to be improving.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Houston copies. Out. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: 11, Houston.

a11_0555001.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0555001.text: You may be able to see some...

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Go ahead.

a11_0555001.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0555001.text: ...some particles jumping around on your screen. That's just dust particles that are being illuminated by Sun shafting in the window.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Roger. They're very clear now. Over. And that's a good view of Neil's - correction, of Buzz's circuit breaker panel, there. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: I can just barely see the handrail on the front porch from the position on the right-hand window.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: 11, Houston. Our view of the Panel 11 is - gets brighter, then darker. Are you changing the f-stop at all? Over.

a11_0555001.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0555001.text: No, what's happening is, we get pretty close to the window now and then, and it drives the automatic light control into the stop, I think.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: I think that's right. [Pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: Yes, I had the switch on 'Outside' while I was going through the overhead window. That may be what's contributing to some of it.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Roger.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: 11, Houston. We seem to be picking up a few bit more dust particles now. We see them quite clearly in the screen now. Over.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: Yeah, I'm choking on one every so often. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: 11, Houston. Your show is going out to the US now. We're about to get the satellite up. It'll be transmitted to some other countries after that. Over.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: Roger. I'm checking out this window bracket where I'll be putting it for the EVA pictures of Neil going down the ladder.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We keep marveling about the color and the clarity of the picture. It's really difficult to describe. It's - It's just perfect. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: And, 11, it doesn't look like you're having too much trouble with that bracket up there, Buzz. [Pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: I'll tell you, those new knobs really make it easy to twist the thing and get it cinched down quite tight.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Rog.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: 11, Houston. Buzz, how does the alignment look, there?

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: It looks pretty good, as well as I can tell without the gear extended. I can't get a real definitive answer, but you couldn't fix it any place to see much more out of the window without hand-holding it for the whole time.

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: Roger. Looks like to us it's going to work real well.

a11_0555001.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0555001.text: Give it enough room to - Yeah, I think so. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Duke
a11_0555001.text: And Buzz, we see you putting your window guard in place there, and back up to the ISA now. [Long pause.]

a11_0555001.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0555001.text: Houston, ask FAO if the 90-degree bracket isn't stowed in the Commander's stowage assembly.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: 11, Houston. Buzz, you still looking for that 90-degree bracket? Over.

a11_0562335.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0562335.text: Yeah, he is looking for it now.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Roger. We'll have a word for you in just a moment. [Long pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0562335.text: My monitor shows a pretty good, clear picture from this angle. And we found the 90-degree bracket.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Roger, Neil. It's really a super picture. We've got the ACA, your ACA, the good picture of the throttle, the 90-degree bracket. We see the start - your handles, and now over to the bracket. [Long pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0562335.text: That's about the position we'll be putting the camera in, after the initial descent down the ladder, and it'll be taking 1 frame a second for most of the EVA.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Houston copies. Out. That's a real good view of that camera. [Long pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0562335.text: Our monitor is a little bit wavy, so it's hard for us to tell when we're - when we've got a steady picture for you.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: 11, we have no complaints at all. We don't see that waviness on our picture. It's just really great. Over.

a11_0562335.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0562335.text: Do the edges of the window look like straight lines to you?

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: That's affirmative.

a11_0562335.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0562335.text: Okay. They don't in our monitor, and that leads us to make some corrections to the camera, which probably aren't required sometimes.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: 11, we have no complaints at all. It's a magnificent picture.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: What was that, Buzz, you're chasing now?

a11_0562335.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0562335.text: That was - That was me picking up some particles of paint that were floating through the air in front of the camera, there.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Roger, Neil. We got it. It appears to us that Neil's about to check the Velcro mat, there. [Long pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Okay, Buzz. We see the card up now. [Pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0562335.text: Okay. For those of you that don't know, this is where we log most of our data for each of the LM maneuvers, and we have another card like this that the timeline book that we've laid down on the table in front of the data and display keyboard; and it's on this timeline that we have all our procedures, so we obviously have to hold these in place in zero g, so we make use of the Velcro patches on the back and on the table so we can attach these down here; and then we just turn the pages over when we go to new sequences in our timeline of procedures.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Roger.

a11_0562335.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0562335.text: And we're ready to copy DOI PAD.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Rog. We'll have the FIDOs work that one up for you momentarily.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: 11, Houston. That was a good shot of Panel 2. Now we got Panel 3 in view with the Temp Monitor switch. The stabilization station and control panel, we see now, with the Mode Control switches. Now over to the rendezvous radar. Real good. [Pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: 11, that's real good camera work. [Long pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0562335.text: That'll be the most unusual position a cameraman's ever had, hanging by his toes from a tunnel and taking the picture upside-down.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Roger. Well you're doing a super job. We got a good view of the cross pointer, there. Had a good view of the tape meter. [Long pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0562335.text: We're giving you a picture now of the floor of the cabin. I think you can see the - one of the two Portable Life Support System backpacks here in the center, and on each side, we have the two helmet visors. I'll remove one of them and show you a little closer view of what this looks like.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Roger.

a11_0562335.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0562335.text: Inside the helmet visors are the EVA gloves with the blue tips. I'm about to take those out now. [Long pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Roger, Buzz. That's a great shot now that we're getting of the helmet, the EVA visor, and also the - the EVA gloves in the background.

a11_0562335.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0562335.text: Okay. You did say this was going out now, didn't you?

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Stand by. I think so. [Long pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: 11, you got a pretty big audience. It's live in the US. It's going live to Japan, western Europe, and much of South America. Everybody reports very good color. Appreciate the great show. [Pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0562335.text: Roger. Understand. Thank you. [Long pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Buzz, that was a good demonstration of your EVA visor assembly. Appreciate it. [Long pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Hey, that's a good view of Mr. Collins down there. We finally see him again.

a11_0562335.speaker: Collins
a11_0562335.text: Hello there, earthling.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Hello there. [Long pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: 11, Houston. We noticed when you were scanning over Panel 2 a moment ago, 1 and 2, the two eight balls were slightly in disagreement. Control said he'd like a AGS align, there.

a11_0562335.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0562335.text: Yeah. One of them's AGS, one of them's PNGS.

a11_0562335.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0562335.text: The problem is, we don't know whether to align AGS to PNGS or PNGS to AGS.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Stand by. [Pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: 11, Chris said he can tell you.

a11_0562335.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0562335.text: We'll cage them both.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0562335.text: Like old home week, Charlie, to get back in the LM again.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Rog. I can imagine.

a11_0562335.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0562335.text: The traverse from the bottom of the LM to the aft bulkhead of the Command Module must be about, oh, 16, 20 feet. It's not a disorienting one at all, but it's most interesting to contemplate just pushing off from one and bounding on into the other vehicle all the way through the tunnel.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Rog. Must be some experience. Is Collins going to go in and look around? [Pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0562335.text: We're - we're willing to let him go but he hasn't come up with the price of the ticket yet.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Rog. I'd advise him to keep his hands off the switches.

a11_0562335.speaker: Collins
a11_0562335.text: If I can get them to keep their hands off my DSKY, it'd be a fair swap.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Roger.

a11_0562335.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0562335.text: That's why I've been eating so much today. I haven't had anything to do. He won't let me touch it any more.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0562335.text: It appears now that we have a view of Earth out the window.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: 11, Houston. If that's not the Earth, we're in trouble.

a11_0562335.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0562335.text: That's the Earth, and we have a very good view of it today. There are a few more cloud bands on than yesterday when we beamed down to you, but it's a beautiful sight. [Long pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0562335.text: We have some horizontal banding in our TV monitor. Are we transmitting that to you, or do you have a clear picture?

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Neil, we have a very clear picture. The only thing that we see is a little white dot in the bottom of our screen, which is - our TV guys say is an - apparently a burned out spot in the camera, but it should come back. Over.

a11_0562335.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0562335.text: Roger. We have that in our monitor also. [Long pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: 11, Houston. We do have three lines across our TV. I thought it was just a transmission problem, but everybody's telling me now that it's probably - it's on the downlink. Over.

a11_0562335.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0562335.text: No, those are the same three ones that we have.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0562335.text: How far are - out are we now, Charlie?

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Stand by. Give you an exact figure. [Pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0562335.text: Did you notice the difference between yesterday and today? This is as large an image as we - as we can give you.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Roger. It's distinctly smaller. You're now 177,000 miles out. Over.

a11_0562335.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0562335.text: Thank you.

a11_0562335.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0562335.text: That's nautical miles?

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: That's affirmative. 11. We...

a11_0562335.speaker: Collins
a11_0562335.text: That in furlongs?

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Go ahead. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: 11, Houston. We see the - still see the banding along the inter-tropical convergence. I guess the most predominate one now is around the - up in the - around the equator or slightly north of the equator.

a11_0562335.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0562335.text: Yeah, that's the way it looks, Charlie. Same as yesterday.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0562335.text: Just keep the Pacific Ocean nice and clear and calm on splash day. That's all we ask. [Long pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0562335.text: And Charlie, I'd like to say hello to all my fellow scouts and scouters at Farragut State Park in Idaho having a National Jamboree there this week; and Apollo 11 would like to send them best wishes.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Thank you, Apollo 11. I'm sure that, if they didn't hear that, they will get the word through the news. Certainly appreciate that. [Long pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: 11, Houston. We have you - your sub-spacecraft point is just off the western coast of South America directly south of about Mexico City. Over.

a11_0562335.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0562335.text: That - That looks like what we observe from here. [Long pause.]

a11_0562335.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0562335.text: And we're going to turn our TV monitor off now for a short bit while we have some other work to do. Apollo 11 signing off.

a11_0562335.speaker: Duke
a11_0562335.text: Roger, 11. Thank you very much. That was one of the greatest shows we've ever seen. We sure appreciate it. Over.

a11_0562335.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0562335.text: It was a pleasure.

a11_0562335.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0562335.text: This is Apollo Control. That television transmission lasted about 1 hour, 36 minutes according to our first rough calculation. And during that period of time, the spacecraft traveled something over 2,000 nautical miles [3,700 km].

a11_0564550.speaker: Duke
a11_0564550.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Could you give us an idea of about how long it will be before you start close - closing the LM back up? Over.

a11_0564550.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0564550.text: We've got a little more work to do up here, Charlie. We're going to make sure that we have everything transferred around and stowed the way we want it. Try to get a little bit ahead on tomorrow's timeline. I suppose that we could be out of there in another half hour or so if it was necessary.

a11_0564550.speaker: Duke
a11_0564550.text: Roger, Neil. We're not trying to push you. We're just trying to get an idea of - about water dumps and starting up the PTC again. Take your sweet time. Over.

a11_0564550.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0564550.text: Okay. We'd like to get a Flight Plan update from you for the next couple of hours, here. When you think what the various constraints might be and what - what order you might like us to do things.

a11_0564550.speaker: Duke
a11_0564550.text: Roger. Stand by. We'll have that to you in a moment.

a11_0565608.speaker: Duke
a11_0565608.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Mike, we'd like to go ahead and do a waste-water dump. We'd like you to dump it all the way down to zero. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0565608.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0565608.text: Roger. Just noticed that the mast that the EVA light is on is charred brown. It looks as though it took quite a beating during launch.

a11_0565608.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0565608.text: The EVA light still does work.

a11_0565608.speaker: Duke
a11_0565608.text: Roger. We'll let this - the SPAN guys look at this, and we'll be back with you with our - with what we think. Over.

a11_0570021.speaker: Duke
a11_0570021.text: 11, Houston. We were wondering, Neil, with your closing comment on the TV, if you were going to turn it off. It indicated that you might be considering turning it back on. We were wondering whether we want to keep the lines up. Over.

a11_0570021.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0570021.text: Well, we - we want your recommendation on that. I think we would just as soon, ourselves, terminate the TV, but if you have a commitment to keep, we'd be more than willing to turn it back on.

a11_0570021.speaker: Duke
a11_0570021.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We'd like to terminate the TV. We don't - We think we've got a really - a good tape. That hour-and-a-half show was superb. And we'd like to pick up TV - correction - PTC at about 58 hours. Over.

a11_0570021.speaker: Duke
a11_0570021.text: And we'll have the remaining functions in the Flight Plan soon. Over.

a11_0570021.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0570021.text: This is Apollo Control at 57 hours, 3 minutes. The decision, as you heard relayed up to the crew there, that we would go into the Passive Thermal Control mode with the spacecraft in a slow roll at 58 hours in the Flight Plan, would rule out further television for today. I would also like to repeat that the change of shift press conference for the previous shift was cancelled due to the length of that television transmission, and we do expect to have a change of shift briefing following this shift, probably between 11:30 and 12 pm Central Daylight Time. At the present time, Apollo 11 is 178,236

a11_0570021.speaker: Duke
a11_0570021.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Our recommendations on the activities for the next hour or so, as far as Flight Plan goes, are: Continue your LM familiarization as desired until about 58 hours, then ingress to the CSM, close the hatch, and establish PTC shortly thereafter. Over.

a11_0570021.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0570021.text: Okay. Water dump being terminated now.

a11_0691848.speaker: Evans
a11_0691848.text: Say again, Buzz. You were cut out there.

a11_0691848.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0691848.text: Okay. I'll see you at 71 hours.

a11_0691848.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0691848.text: This is Apollo Control. So much for that. Looks like they're going to turn over and go back to sleep. At 69 hours, 19 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control.

a11_0691848.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0691848.text: This is Apollo Control, at 71 hours into the mission.

a11_0710330.speaker: McCandless
a11_0710330.text: Apollo 11, Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

a11_0710330.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0710330.text: Would you like the O 2 purge this morning?

a11_0710330.speaker: McCandless
a11_0710330.text: Yes indeed. O 2 fuel cell purge at 71 hours, and when you feel like copying, I've got a Flight Plan update containing - I guess that and some other items for you.

a11_0710330.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0710330.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Go ahead with the Flight Plan update.

a11_0710330.speaker: McCandless
a11_0710330.text: Roger, 11. This is Houston. At approximately 71 hours to 72 hours, we have you down for an eat period which I imagine is probably in progress already. 71 hours: O 2 fuel cell purge. 72 hours GET: CO 2 filter change number 6, secondary radiator flow check, and we'll send you up a P37 block data on a 2-hour pass - pericynthion pass return mode abort. At 73 hours, 00 minutes, stop PTC at approximately 0 degrees roll, that is when you're coming up on 0 degrees roll angle around 73 hours we'd like you to stop PTC. And perform a P52 option 3 remaining in the PTC REFSMMAT for a drift check. 73 hours,

a11_0710330.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0710330.text: Okay. We'll get started on the fuel cell purge while we're eating. CO 2 canister change number 6; secondary radiator flow check; copy some PADs. Also at 72 hours, stop PTC 0 roll. At 73; do a P52 option 3; we'll get your uplink REFSMMAT for the landing site; and - and at 000 degrees, now was this with the old REFSMMAT or the new REFSMMAT?

a11_0710330.speaker: McCandless
a11_0710330.text: This is with the new REFSMMAT, Buzz.

a11_0710330.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0710330.text: Okay. You want the P52 done at that attitude with the new REFSMMAT?

a11_0711201.speaker: McCandless
a11_0711201.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over. [No answer.]

a11_0711201.speaker: McCandless
a11_0711201.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over. [No answer.]

a11_0711201.speaker: McCandless
a11_0711201.text: Roger, 11. Correction on my last. At 73:20, we uplink you the new REFSMMAT. And at 73:30, we'd like you to maneuver to 0 roll, 0 pitch, 0 yaw in the old REFSMMAT. And then torque around to the new REFSMMAT and run your P52 option 1 in that same inertial attitude. Over.

a11_0711201.speaker: McCandless
a11_0711201.text: And I've got a consumables update, when you're ready to copy.

a11_0711201.speaker: Collins
a11_0711201.text: I just got up, but you didn't catch me on that one.

a11_0711201.speaker: McCandless
a11_0711201.text: I say, I have one for you. [Long pause.]

a11_0711201.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0711201.text: Okay. We're ready to copy that consumable update.

a11_0711201.speaker: McCandless
a11_0711201.text: Roger. As of GET 68:00; RCS total, minus 4.5 percent, corresponding to approximately minus 53 pounds. Alpha, minus 6.0 percent, minus 1.0 percent, minus 7.0 percent, minus 3.0 percent; H 2 total, minus 1.2 pounds; O 2 total, plus 10 pounds. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0711201.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0711201.text: Roger. And our readouts on board are Alpha is 82, Bravo is 84, Cocoa is 84, and Delta is 87.

a11_0711201.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0711201.text: And you want us to cycle the O 2 and H 2 fans, I imagine?

a11_0712326.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0712326.text: Houston, Apollo 11. I have a status report for you.

a11_0712326.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0712326.text: Roger. On sleep, CDR, CMP 7.5, LMP 6.5. Over.

a11_0712326.speaker: McCandless
a11_0712326.text: Roger. 7.5, 7.5 and 6.5. And I got a few words for you here on the SPS engine performance. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0712326.speaker: McCandless
a11_0712326.text: Okay, 11. It turns out that the engine performance during both of your burns so far this mission has been the same as it was on engine acceptance tests. The onboard P C reading is due to a known gauge calibration factor between what you've actually got in the chamber and what you're reading out on the gauge. We expect single-bank operation to be 90 - that is, 90 psi on the gauge with an actual chamber pressure of 95 psi [655 kPa]. In dual-bank operation, the chamber pressure is 94 psi on the gauge with an actual of 99 psi [683 kPa]. 80 psi on the gauge on board correlates to 83 psi [572 kPa] a

a11_0712326.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0712326.text: Apollo 11. Roger. We got all that.

a11_0713308.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0713308.text: Houston. Apollo 11. [Garble].

a11_0713308.speaker: McCandless
a11_0713308.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Go ahead. Over. [No answer.]

a11_0713308.speaker: McCandless
a11_0713308.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Go ahead. Over. [No answer.]

a11_0713308.speaker: McCandless
a11_0713308.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Go ahead. Over.

a11_0713308.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0713308.text: Houston, do you read Apollo 11?

a11_0713308.speaker: McCandless
a11_0713308.text: Roger, 11. We're reading you loud and clear now. We were down in the noise as we switched antennas a minute or so ago. Over.

a11_0713308.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0713308.text: Roger. What sort of settings could you recommend for that solar corona? We've got the Sun right behind the edge of the Moon now.

a11_0713308.speaker: McCandless
a11_0713308.text: Roger.

a11_0713308.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0713308.text: It's quite an eerie sight. There is a very marked three-dimensional aspect of having the Sun's corona coming from behind the Moon the way it is.

a11_0713308.speaker: McCandless
a11_0713308.text: Roger.

a11_0713308.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0713308.text: And it looks as though - I guess what's giving it that three-dimensional effect, the Earthshine. I can see Tycho fairly clearly - at least if I'm right side-up, I believe it's Tycho, in Moonshine - I mean, in Earthshine. And, of course, I can see the sky is lit all the way around the Moon, even on the limb of it where there's no Earthshine or sunshine. [Long pause.]

a11_0713308.speaker: McCandless
a11_0713308.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

a11_0713308.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0713308.text: Go ahead.

a11_0713308.speaker: McCandless
a11_0713308.text: Roger. If you'd like to take some pictures, we recommend using magazine Uniform which is loaded with high speed black and white film, interior lights off, electric Hasselblad with the 80-millimeter lens. And you're going to have to hand-hold this, I guess. We're recommending an f-stop of 2.8, and we'd like to get a sequence of time exposures. Over.

a11_0713308.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0713308.text: Okay. You want magazine Uniform instead of magazine Tango? Over.

a11_0713308.speaker: McCandless
a11_0713308.text: Roger. We're not trying to get you all wrapped up in a procedure here. This is on a not-to-interfere basis, of course. Over.

a11_0713308.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0713308.text: Okay.

a11_0713308.speaker: McCandless
a11_0713308.text: And on the exposures we're looking for an eighth of a second, a half a second. And, if you think you can steady the camera against anything to get longer exposures, 2 seconds, 4 seconds, and 8 seconds. Over.

a11_0713308.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0713308.text: Roger. We copy.

a11_0713308.speaker: McCandless
a11_0713308.text: Roger. Out.

a11_0713915.speaker: McCandless
a11_0713915.text: Roger. We'd like to do a little cryo tank balancing. So, if you could position the Oxygen Tank number 1 heater switch to Off and Hydrogen Tank 2 heater switch to Off, leaving all the rest of the cryo switches the same, we'll let it run that way for a few hours. Over.

a11_0713915.speaker: Collins
a11_0713915.text: Okay. Stand by one, on those switches. We'll get them in a minute.

a11_0713915.speaker: McCandless
a11_0713915.text: Roger. And how far out can you see the corona extending? Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0713915.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0713915.text: Well, its a bit like zodiacal light. It keeps going out farther and farther. We'll talk about it a little more later.

a11_0714246.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0714246.text: We've got quite a few pictures [garble] windows [garble] corresponding [garble].

a11_0714246.speaker: McCandless
a11_0714246.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. I think we have Comm again. We heard you calling. Over. [No answer.]

a11_0714246.speaker: McCandless
a11_0714246.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Were you calling? Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0714246.speaker: Collins
a11_0714246.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Understand you want the heaters Off for Hydrogen Tank 1 and Oxygen Tank 1. Is that affirmative?

a11_0714246.speaker: McCandless
a11_0714246.text: That's negative, Mike. Hydrogen Tank number 2 heaters, Off, and Oxygen Tank number 1 heaters, Off.

a11_0714246.speaker: Collins
a11_0714246.text: I have Hydrogen Tank number 2 heaters, Off. I have Oxygen Tank number 1 heaters, Off.

a11_0715215.speaker: Collins
a11_0715215.text: Houston. Apollo 11. The Earthshine coming through the window is so bright you can read a book by it.

a11_0715600.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0715600.text: And, Houston, I'd suggest that along the ecliptic line we can see corona light out to two lunar diameters from this location. The bright light only extends out about an eighth to a quarter of the lunar radius.

a11_0715600.speaker: McCandless
a11_0715600.text: Roger. Understand that you can see the corona approximately 200 solar diameters out along the ecliptic, and the bright light extends out approximately one-eighth to one-quarter lunar radius. Over.

a11_0715600.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0715600.text: That's two lunar - two lunar diameters along the ecliptic in the bright part - [perhaps acknowledging a suggestion from either Aldrin or Collins] right - [To McCandless] a quarter to an eighth of a lunar radius out, and that's perpendicular to the ecliptic line on the South Pole.

a11_0715600.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0715600.text: That last transmission was from Neil Armstrong.

a11_0715600.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0715600.text: Houston, it's been a real change for us. Now we're able to see stars again and recognize constellations for the first time on the trip. It's - the sky is full of stars. Just like the night side of Earth. But all the way here, we've only been able to see stars occasionally and perhaps through the monocular, but not recognize any star patterns.

a11_0715600.speaker: McCandless
a11_0715600.text: I guess it's turned into night up there really, hasn't it?

a11_0720457.speaker: McCandless
a11_0720457.text: 11, this is Houston. Go ahead. Over.

a11_0720457.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0720457.text: This is Apollo Control at 72 hours, 7 minutes. Apollo 11 is 9,761 nautical miles [18,077 km] from the Moon. Velocity; 4,217 feet per second [1,285 m/s]. Weight; 96,012 pounds [43,550 kg].

a11_0721348.speaker: McCandless
a11_0721348.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Do you read? Over. [No answer.]

a11_0721348.speaker: McCandless
a11_0721348.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. How do you read? Over.

a11_0721348.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0721348.text: Okay. We went to the High Gain. Looks like you had a little trouble getting signal strength there.

a11_0721348.speaker: McCandless
a11_0721348.text: Roger. We missed an Omni switch there. Over.

a11_0721348.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0721348.text: All right. On the secondary loop check when we went to Flow on the secondary radiators, the quantity dropped from 40 percent down to 36 in the first 10 seconds and then stabilized at 36 for the remainder of the 30 seconds. [Long pause.]

a11_0721348.speaker: McCandless
a11_0721348.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. We believe that's normal system operation. The radiators are expected to be very cold right now and apparently the decrease you saw was due to contraction in the fluid. Over.

a11_0721348.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0721348.text: Okay. We'll go ahead with the procedure just as if there were no decrease in accumulator quantity. Right?

a11_0721348.speaker: McCandless
a11_0721348.text: Roger. Press on.

a11_0721348.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0721348.text: And, Houston, the secondary radiator flow check is complete and satisfactory.

a11_0721348.speaker: McCandless
a11_0721348.text: Houston. Roger. Out. [Pause.]

a11_0721348.speaker: Collins
a11_0721348.text: And that's a good deal because we don't have to have any meetings about whether we're going to do it or don't do it any more.

a11_0721348.speaker: McCandless
a11_0721348.text: [Laughter.] That's for sure. [Pause.]

a11_0721348.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0721348.text: That was a Mike Collins' comment.

a11_0721348.speaker: McCandless
a11_0721348.text: The Flight Director says 'ouch!' [Pause.]

a11_0721348.speaker: Collins
a11_0721348.text: No. No 'ouch' intended. I enjoyed every one of those meetings. [Long pause.]

a11_0721348.speaker: McCandless
a11_0721348.text: 11, this is Houston. I have your pericynthion-plus-2 PAD, P30 format, when you're ready to copy. [Pause.]

a11_0721348.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0721348.text: Roger. Stand by. [Long pause.]

a11_0721348.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0721348.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Ready to copy pericynthion-plus-2.

a11_0721348.speaker: McCandless
a11_0721348.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Pericynthion-plus-2 hours PAD. SPS/G&N: 62710, plus 0.98, minus 0.19; GET ignition 077:46:22.48, Delta-V X Noun 81, plus 3214.8, minus 0045.5, minus 1037.7; roll NA, pitch 307, and the remainder of the PAD is NA. GDC align stars; Vega and Deneb. Roll 243, 183, 012; no ullage. Remarks: Assumes landing site REFSMMAT and docked. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0721348.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0721348.text: Roger. SPS/G&N: 62710, plus 0.98, minus 0.19; 077:46:22.48; plus 3214.8, minus 0045.5, minus 1037.7; NA, 307; Vega and Deneb; 243, 183, 012; no ullage. Landing site REFSMMAT, docked. And ya'aven't - change on the LM weight. Over.

a11_0721348.speaker: McCandless
a11_0721348.text: No change in the LM's weight - in the LM weight, and the readback is correct. Out.

a11_0722506.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722506.text: Roger. We're having difficulty getting commands into the spacecraft. We'd like you to cycle your Up Telemetry switch to Command Reset and Off and then back to Normal. Over.

a11_0722506.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0722506.text: We have you on High Gain right now. You want us to switch over to Omni? [Pause.]

a11_0722506.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722506.text: Negative. We'd like to stay on the High Gain if we can. Over.

a11_0722506.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722506.text: Roger. We'd like you to switch to Omni Delta as we show you approximately at the scan limit of the High Gain Antenna. We will then command Omni Delta down here after you advise us you've switched, and then you can select Bravo on board and we'll be back in the Omni antenna commanding business. Over.

a11_0722506.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0722506.text: Okay. We're going to Delta now. [Long pause.]

a11_0722506.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722506.text: 11, Houston. You can go ahead and select Omni Bravo on board now.

a11_0722924.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722924.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. If you have a minute or so free, we can read you up the morning news here.

a11_0722924.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0722924.text: Go right ahead, let's hear it.

a11_0722924.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722924.text: Roger. Hot from the wires of the MSC Public Affairs Office, especially prepared for the crew of Apollo 11. [Pause.]

a11_0722924.speaker: Haise
a11_0722924.text: Okay. First off, looks like it's going to be impossible to get away from the fact that you guys are dominating all the news back here on Earth. Even Pravda in Russia is headlining the mission and calls Neil, the Czar of the Ship. I think maybe they got the wrong mission.

a11_0722924.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722924.text: West Germany has declared Monday to be Apollo Day. School children in Bavaria have been given the day off. Post Office clerks have been encouraged to bring radios to work and Frankfurt is installing TV sets in public places.

a11_0722924.speaker: Haise
a11_0722924.text: BBC in London is considering a special radio alarm system to call people to their TV sets in case there is a change in the EVA time on the Moon.

a11_0722924.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722924.text: And in Italy, Pope Paul VI has arranged for a special color TV circuit at his summer residence in order to watch you, even though Italian television is still black and white.

a11_0722924.speaker: Haise
a11_0722924.text: Back here in Houston, your three wives and children got together for lunch yesterday at Buzz's house. And according to Pat, it turned out to be a gab-fest. The children swam and did some high jumping over Buzz's bamboo pole.

a11_0722924.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722924.text: In Moscow, space engineer Anatol Koritsky was quoted by TASS as saying that Luna 15 could accomplish everything that had been done by earlier Luna spacecraft. This was taken by the press to mean Luna 15 could investigate the gravitational field, photograph the Moon, and go down to the surface to scoop up a bit for analysis.

a11_0722924.speaker: Haise
a11_0722924.text: Even the kids at camp got in the news when Mike Junior was quoted as replying 'yeah' when somebody asked him if his daddy was going to be in history. Then after a short pause he asked: 'What is history?' In Washington, President Nixon is planning to use his executive power to streamline the Interstate Commerce Commission. According to the industry sources, it was reported Nixon would trim the commission from 11 to 7 members by not making new appointments.

a11_0722924.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722924.text: And the big news around Houston today concerns the Astros. In the sports world, the Houston Astros rallied in the ninth inning at Cincinnati to dump the Reds 7 to 4. Going into the ninth however, things looked pretty bleak: the Astros were trailing 4 to 3. Then with one out, Jesus Alou stroked a single to right field. John Edwards hit another single to right, and Sandy Valdespino hit a double to bring in the tying run. Julio Gotay was walked and Joe Morgan dropped a bunt for the game-winning play. A wild throw to the plate allowed another run to score, then a sacrifice fly by Dennis Menke brou

a11_0722924.speaker: Haise
a11_0722924.text: And other games in the National League...

a11_0722924.speaker: Collins
a11_0722924.text: Yes. Those Astros have really been catching those flies since they put a roof on the stadium.

a11_0722924.speaker: Haise
a11_0722924.text: Good work. [Long pause.]

a11_0722924.speaker: Haise
a11_0722924.text: In other games in the National League, New York beat Montreal 5 to 2; Pittsburgh beat St. Louis 4 to 1; and Atlanta over San Diego in the first game of a double header, 6 to 2.

a11_0722924.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722924.text: In the American League, Detroit beat Cleveland 4 to nothing; New York trounced Washington 5 to nothing; Baltimore out hit - Boston out hit Baltimore to score 6 runs to the Orioles' 2; and Chicago beat Kansas City 6 to 1.

a11_0722924.speaker: Haise
a11_0722924.text: Okay. In golf world, Tommy Jacobs, an infrequent competitor in recent years, took the lead in the Philadelphia Golf Classic yesterday. His second round score was 139.

a11_0722924.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722924.text: You might be interested in knowing, since you are already on the way, that a Houston astrologer, Ruby Graham, says that all the signs are right for your trip to the Moon. She says that Neil is clever, Mike has good judgment, and Buzz can work out intricate problems. She also says Neil tends to see the world through rose-colored glasses, but he is always ready to help the afflicted or distressed. Neil, you are also supposed to have, quote, intuition that enables you to interpret life with feeling, unquote. Buzz is to be very sociable and cannot bear to be alone in addition to having excellent c

a11_0722924.speaker: Haise
a11_0722924.text: And last but not...

a11_0722924.speaker: Collins
a11_0722924.text: Who said all that?

a11_0722924.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722924.text: [Laughter] Ruby Graham, an astrologer here in Houston. Now we check with Flight Operations for all the signs for the mission, and then we, of course, had to make sure that everything was really all set. [Long pause.]

a11_0722924.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0722924.text: Houston, 11. You're cutting out [garble].

a11_0722924.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722924.text: Apollo 11, Apollo 11, this is Houston. We're switching Omnis. Can you stand by for about 2 minutes?

a11_0722924.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0722924.text: Houston, 11. Radio check.

a11_0722924.speaker: Haise
a11_0722924.text: 11, Houston. Go ahead.

a11_0722924.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0722924.text: Roger. You cut out after Tommy Jacobs and I guess we got into antenna switching problems.

a11_0722924.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722924.text: Okay. Following Tommy Jacobs, we have the hot smoking word from a local Houston astrologer by the name of Ruby Graham. She says that all the signs are right for your trip to the Moon. Neil is clever, Mike has good judgement, and Buzz can work out intricate problems. She also says Neil tends to see the world through rose-colored glasses but is always ready to help the afflicted or distressed. Neil, you are also supposed to have, quote, intuition that enables you to interpret life with feeling, unquote. Buzz is supposed to be very sociable and cannot bear to be alone in addition to having excell

a11_0722924.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0722924.text: Thank you much there, Bruce and Fred Show, we appreciate that.

a11_0722924.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722924.text: Roger.

a11_0722924.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0722924.text: That was Fred Haise alternating with Bruce McCandless on that newscast.

a11_0722924.speaker: Collins
a11_0722924.text: Did you hear our comment about the Astros?

a11_0722924.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722924.text: The one about the roof?

a11_0722924.speaker: Collins
a11_0722924.text: Yep. [Long pause.]

a11_0722924.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722924.text: Hey, Mike, the game was at Cincinnati there, and we think that they're still using Crosby Field up there. I don't believe it has a roof on it. [Pause.]

a11_0722924.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0722924.text: You got him on that one.

a11_0722924.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722924.text: Right...

a11_0722924.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0722924.text: I think they're just getting to be a good team in the clinch.

a11_0722924.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722924.text: They certainly seem to be.

a11_0722924.speaker: Collins
a11_0722924.text: Well, if they can do that well without a roof, think of what they're going to do with a roof.

a11_0722924.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722924.text: Roger. Out.

a11_0722924.speaker: Collins
a11_0722924.text: They're trying. [Long pause.]

a11_0722924.speaker: Collins
a11_0722924.text: An old Oiler fan is trying to comment on an alien game. [Long pause.]

a11_0722924.speaker: Collins
a11_0722924.text: You tell Michael Junior, history or no history, he'd better behave himself.

a11_0722924.speaker: McCandless
a11_0722924.text: Roger. We'll pass that along, Mike.

a11_0724858.speaker: McCandless
a11_0724858.text: Apollo 11, Houston. If it's convenient with you, we have an LOI-1 PAD that we can pass up to you now. Over.

a11_0724858.speaker: Collins
a11_0724858.text: Houston, Apollo 11. The next time we pass through roll 0, we're going to stop PTC and that'll give us 90 degrees pitch. Now, I understand you want us to move from 90 degrees pitch to 0 degrees pitch for the platform align, option 1. Is that affirmative? [Long pause.]

a11_0724858.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0724858.text: And we're ready to copy on the LOI-1. [Long pause.]

a11_0724858.speaker: McCandless
a11_0724858.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. When you stop at 0 roll, you'll be in approximately 90 pitch, 0 yaw, and 0 roll. We'd like you to run the first P52, that is, the P52 option 3, from that attitude. Then we'll uplink you a new REFSMMAT, either before or while you're maneuvering to 000, then you can torque the platform around and run the second REFSMMAT. Over. Run the second P52. Over.

a11_0724858.speaker: McCandless
a11_0724858.text: And I copied you're ready for the LOI-1 PAD. Over.

a11_0724858.speaker: McCandless
a11_0724858.text: LOI-1, SPS/G&N: 62710, plus 0.98, minus 0.19, GET ignition 075:49:49.65; minus 2889.7, minus 0394.4, minus 0068.6; roll 358, pitch 226, 347; 0169.2, plus 00610; 2917.3, 6:02, 2910.8; sextant star 31, 1066, 358. Remainder of the PAD is NA. GDC align, Vega and Deneb, 243, 183, 012. No ullage. The horizon will be visible just below the upper edge of the hatch window 2 minutes prior to the LOI burn. It will not be visible in the rendezvous window on the left-hand side. LOS at 75 hours, 41 minutes, 23 seconds. AOS at 76:15:29. AOS without the LOI burn, 76:05:30. The values which you would see on No

a11_0724858.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0724858.text: Roger. LOI-1, SPS/G&N: 62710, plus 0.98, minus 0.19; 075:49:49.65; minus 2889.7, minus 0394.4, minus 0068.6; 358, 226, 347; 0169.2, plus 0061.0; 2917.3, 6:02, 2910.8; 31, 106.6, 35.8. GDC align, Vega and Deneb, 243, 183, 012. No ullage. Horizon in the hatch window 2 minutes before T IG . AOS with an LOI, 76:15:29; AOS without an LOI, 76:05:30. H A before the burn, 431.3; H P , minus 128.2. Say again LOS time.

a11_0724858.speaker: McCandless
a11_0724858.text: 11, this is Houston. Readback correct. Out.

a11_0724858.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0724858.text: That was Neil Armstrong with the readback of the Lunar Orbit Insertion burn number 1 PAD. The ignition time for that burn; 75 hours, 49 minutes, 49 seconds. That's 2 hours, 57 minutes, 49 seconds from this time. Duration of that burn; 6 minutes, 2 seconds retrograde, and the change in velocity; 2,917.3 feet per second [889.2 m/s]. The expected orbit following that maneuver is 169.2 by 61 nautical miles [313.4 by 113.0 km]. To repeat the LOS/AOS times; we will lose signal with Apollo 11 at 75 hours, 41 minutes, 23 seconds as it goes behind the Moon. Given a successful Lunar Orbit Insertion numb

a11_0730438.speaker: McCandless
a11_0730438.text: Roger. Apparently we missed getting your onboard readouts on battery Charlie and Pyro batteries Alpha and Bravo last night. I wonder if you could give us some fresh numbers. Over.

a11_0730438.speaker: McCandless
a11_0730438.text: Yes, please. If it's convenient for you. [Long pause.]

a11_0730438.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0730438.text: Okay. All three of the them are still 37.1 [Volts].

a11_0730914.speaker: Collins
a11_0730914.text: Houston, Apollo 11. The P52 option 3 is complete. We're maneuvering to 000.

a11_0730914.speaker: McCandless
a11_0730914.text: Roger. We observe your maneuvering, and we'll have some uplinks for you in a couple of minutes here.

a11_0731313.speaker: McCandless
a11_0731313.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. We observe you're in P00. If you'll give us Accept, we'll start our uplinks.

a11_0731651.speaker: McCandless
a11_0731651.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

a11_0731651.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0731651.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a11_0731651.speaker: McCandless
a11_0731651.text: Roger. We're on low bit rate at the present time so it's going to take us a little bit longer than normal to get this stuff up to you. Over.

a11_0731651.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0731651.text: I guess we're in no rush.

a11_0731651.speaker: McCandless
a11_0731651.text: Okay. We're here, if you're there. [Pause.]

a11_0731651.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0731651.text: The view of the Moon that we've been having recently is really spectacular. It fills about three-quarters of the hatch window, and of course, we can see the entire circumference, even though part of it is in complete shadow and part of it's in Earthshine. It's a view worth the price of the trip.

a11_0731651.speaker: McCandless
a11_0731651.text: Well, there are a lot of us down here that would be willing to come along. [Pause.]

a11_0731651.speaker: Collins
a11_0731651.text: I hope you get your turn, and soon. [Long pause.]

a11_0731651.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0731651.text: One of these days, we'll be able to bring the whole MOCR along, I hope. Save a lot of antenna switching.

a11_0731651.speaker: McCandless
a11_0731651.text: Say again, 11.

a11_0731651.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0731651.text: One of these days, we could bring the whole MOCR along, and then that'll save a lot of antenna switching.

a11_0731651.speaker: McCandless
a11_0731651.text: That's jolly.

a11_0731651.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0731651.text: The MOCR is the Mission Operations Control Room. That's the control center here.

a11_0731651.speaker: McCandless
a11_0731651.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

a11_0731651.speaker: Collins
a11_0731651.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a11_0731651.speaker: McCandless
a11_0731651.text: 11, this is Houston. We're showing you...

a11_0731651.speaker: Collins
a11_0731651.text: The Czar is brushing his teeth, so I'm filling in for him.

a11_0731651.speaker: McCandless
a11_0731651.text: Say again, please.

a11_0731651.speaker: Collins
a11_0731651.text: I said the Czar is brushing his teeth, so I'm filling in for him. What can we do for you?

a11_0731651.speaker: McCandless
a11_0731651.text: Roger. Well, if you don't get in the way of the Czar while he's brushing his teeth, we'd like you to bring up the primary accumulator quantity a little bit. We're showing the quantity now at 20.6 percent on TM. Seems to have gone down a bit since you've gone into the shadow. We'd like it serviced to bring the quantity up to between 30 and 40 percent, preferably 35 percent. Over.

a11_0731651.speaker: Collins
a11_0731651.text: Okay.

a11_0731651.speaker: McCandless
a11_0731651.text: The computer is yours, 11. The loads are in and verified. You can go back to Block.

a11_0731651.speaker: Collins
a11_0731651.text: We're in Block.

a11_0731651.speaker: McCandless
a11_0731651.text: 11, this is Houston. On the basis of your last P52 alignment, the platform looks like it's indeed performing very well. No problems there, no updates required, and no PIPA bias update is required either. Over.

a11_0731651.speaker: Collins
a11_0731651.text: Sounds good.

a11_0731651.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0731651.text: This is Apollo Control at 73 hours, 25 minutes. Apollo 11 is 6,522 nautical miles [12,079 km] away from the Moon; approaching at a velocity of 4,483 feet per second [1,366 m/s].

a11_0734051.speaker: McCandless
a11_0734051.text: 11, this is Houston. Loud and clear. Over.

a11_0734051.speaker: Collins
a11_0734051.text: Okay. Just checking. Do you want the High Gain?

a11_0734051.speaker: McCandless
a11_0734051.text: Roger. If you can give it to us.

a11_0734051.speaker: Collins
a11_0734051.text: Houston, Apollo 11. How do you read on the High Gain?

a11_0734051.speaker: McCandless
a11_0734051.text: Loud and clear on the High Gain.

a11_0734051.speaker: Collins
a11_0734051.text: Same here. We've completed the P52 option 1.

a11_0734051.speaker: McCandless
a11_0734051.text: Roger. We've been looking over your shoulder by TM. [Pause.]

a11_0735837.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0735837.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Standing by to copy TEI-1 and TEI-4. Over.

a11_0735837.speaker: McCandless
a11_0735837.text: Roger. I've got the 1 and 4 PADs here, right now. I'll be ready to read them up to you in just a second. [Long pause.]

a11_0735837.speaker: McCandless
a11_0735837.text: 11, this is Houston. I'm ready with the TEI-1 and 4 PADs. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0735837.speaker: McCandless
a11_0735837.text: Roger. TEI-1, SPS/G&N; 38658, minus 0.54, plus 0.65, T IG , 078:02:03.45; plus 2918.0, plus 0377.9, minus 0132.5; roll NA, pitch 041. The balance of the PAD is NA. Ullage; two jets, 19 seconds. TEI-4 PAD, SPS/G&N:, 38658, minus 0.54, plus 0.65, T IG , 084:29:50.59; plus 3137.3, plus 0376.0, minus 0096.8; roll NA, pitch 034. The rest of the PAD is NA. Ullage; two jets, 19 seconds. Both of these PADs are for an undocked maneuver. TEI-plus-4 PAD assumes no LOI-2. Over. Make that TEI-4 PAD assumes no LOI-2. [Long pause.]

a11_0735837.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0735837.text: Roger. TEI-1, SPS/G&N; 38658, minus 0.54, plus 0.65; 078:02:03.45; plus 2918.0, plus 0377.9, minus 0132.5; roll NA, pitch 041; two jets, 19 seconds; undocked. TEI-4: 38658, minus 0.54, plus 0.65, 084:29:50.59, plus 3137.3, plus 0376.0, minus 0096.8; roll NA, pitch 034; two jets, 19 seconds; undocked; assumes no LOI-2.

a11_0735837.speaker: McCandless
a11_0735837.text: ...11, this is Houston. Readback correct. Out.

a11_0735837.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0735837.text: That was Buzz Aldrin with the readback of that information which was for contingency Trans-Earth Injection burns if required shortly after Lunar Orbit Insertion.

a11_0735837.speaker: McCandless
a11_0735837.text: Roger. At GET of 74:30, we'd like you to cycle the fans in all four Cryo tanks and position the heaters in all four Cryo tanks to the Auto position. We're doing this in advance of LOI in order to ensure that you don't have any destratification as a result of the burn, which might result in giving you a master Caution and Warning during the burn. Over.

a11_0735837.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0735837.text: Okay. Was that 74:30 you want us to cycle the heaters and turn - cycle the fans and turn all the heaters on?

a11_0735837.speaker: McCandless
a11_0735837.text: All the heaters to Auto; cycle the fans at 74:30, about 25 minutes from now. Over.

a11_0743200.speaker: McCandless
a11_0743200.text: 11, this is Houston. Radio check. Over.

a11_0743200.speaker: McCandless
a11_0743200.text: Roger. Loud and clear now. [Long pause.]

a11_0743200.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0743200.text: Apparently this is not a very good Omni attitude for you. We're ready to start our TVC check. [Long pause.]

a11_0743200.speaker: McCandless
a11_0743200.text: 11, this is Houston. We're ready, except that we'd like to get the High Gain Antenna prior to this test. Over.

a11_0743200.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0743200.text: Can you give us a couple of pointing angles?

a11_0745101.speaker: McCandless
a11_0745101.text: Apollo 11, Apollo 11, this is Houston. Radio check. Over. [No answer.]

a11_0745101.speaker: McCandless
a11_0745101.text: Apollo 11, Apollo 11, this is Houston. Radio check. Over. [No answer.]

a11_0745101.speaker: McCandless
a11_0745101.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Do you read? Over.

a11_0745101.speaker: McCandless
a11_0745101.text: Roger. We're reading you weak but clear.

a11_0745101.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0745101.text: Roger. We put our - our roll for MSFN track in on the wrong sign. Going to continue rolling around until we get High Gain here. And, we'll delete the - the pitch that was scheduled after the TVC check.

a11_0745101.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0745101.text: Roger. We put the wrong sign in...

a11_0745101.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0745101.text: ...for the roll correction to get MSFN High Gain, and we're continuing rolling around to get the proper attitude for High Gain at this time. We will delete the pitch maneuver that was scheduled subsequent to - subsequent to the TV check since we already have those pictures.

a11_0745101.speaker: McCandless
a11_0745101.text: Roger. We copy. And [pause] and we recommend that you go ahead and complete your TVC test on board. If you have problems, we'll talk to you when you get around further into the High Gain Antenna attitude. Over.

a11_0745859.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0745859.text: Houston, how do you read on High Gain?

a11_0745859.speaker: McCandless
a11_0745859.text: Oh, loud and clear on High Gain, 11.

a11_0745859.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0745859.text: This is Apollo Control at 75 hours into the mission. Apollo 11 is 2,241 nautical miles away from the Moon. Velocity; 5,512 feet per second. We're 41 minutes away from Loss Of Signal as Apollo 11 goes behind the Moon. We're 49 minutes away from the Lunar Orbit Insertion maneuver number 1.

a11_0745859.speaker: McCandless
a11_0745859.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. We observed your gimbal test down here, and it looked good to us. Over.

a11_0751500.speaker: McCandless
a11_0751500.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Radio check. Over.

a11_0751500.speaker: McCandless
a11_0751500.text: Roger. And your systems are looking good from down here.

a11_0751500.speaker: Collins
a11_0751500.text: Yeah. Looks good up here too, Bruce.

a11_0752600.speaker: McCandless
a11_0752600.text: 11, this is Houston. You are Go for LOI. Over.

a11_0752600.speaker: McCandless
a11_0752600.text: And we're showing about 10 minutes and 30 seconds to LOS. I would like to remind you to enable the B/D roll on the Auto RCS switches. Over.

a11_0752600.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0752600.text: Roger. And confirm you want PCM Low [bit-rate] going over the hill. Over.

a11_0752600.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0752600.text: That was Buzz Aldrin confirming the Go.

a11_0753555.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0753555.text: Houston, do you want to give me a time check, please?

a11_0753555.speaker: McCandless
a11_0753555.text: Roger. I'll give you a Mark at 13 minutes and 30 seconds to ignition.

a11_0753555.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0753555.text: Okay. And then a GET, please.

a11_0753555.speaker: McCandless
a11_0753555.text: I'll give you a time hack on the GET at 75 hours, 37 minutes and I'll try to bias it about a second and a half to allow for the time of flight.

a11_0753555.speaker: McCandless
a11_0753555.text: And I'll give you a time hack on time to ignition at 12 minutes to ignition. Over.

a11_0753555.speaker: McCandless
a11_0753555.text: Stand by for a Mark at T IG minus 12.

a11_0753555.speaker: Collins
a11_0753555.text: You were right on, Bruce. Thank you.

a11_0753555.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0753555.text: We're 3 minutes away from Loss Of Signal. Apollo 11 is 425 nautical miles [787 km] from the Moon. Velocity 7,368 feet per second [2,246 m/s]. Weight; 96,012 pounds [43,550 kg].

a11_0753555.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0753555.text: Okay, 41:23. One minute to LOS. Mark that.

a11_0753555.speaker: McCandless
a11_0753555.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. All your systems are looking good going around the corner. We'll see you on the other side. Over.

a11_0753555.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0753555.text: How much time have we got, Mike?

a11_0753555.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0753555.text: Well, let's let them look at the main bus ties coming on, alright?

a11_0753555.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0753555.text: How soon are we going to...

a11_0753555.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0753555.text: 1 second early. Okay. Main Bus Ties...

a11_0753555.speaker: Collins
a11_0753555.text: I'm going to turn my S-Band Volume down, so you can [garble].

a11_0753555.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0753555.text: Main Bus Tie A coming On. Have you got TVC Gimbal Drive - Pitch and Yaw to Auto, huh?

a11_0753555.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0753555.text: And we've had Loss Of Signal as Apollo 11 goes behind the Moon. We were showing a distance to the Moon of 309 nautical miles [572 km] at LOS. Velocity; 7,664 feet per second [2,336 m/s]. Weight was 96,012 pounds [43,550 kg]. We're 7 minutes, 45 seconds away from the LOI number 1 burn, which will take place behind the Moon, out of communications. Here in the control center, two members of the backup crew, Bill Anders and Jim Lovell, have joined Bruce McCandless at the CapCom console. Fred Haise, the third member of the backup crew, has just come in, too, and Deke Slayton, Director of Flight Cre

a11_0753555.speaker: Collins
a11_0753555.text: TVC Gimbal Drive, Pitch and Yaw to Auto.

a11_0753555.speaker: Collins
a11_0753555.text: He's not going to have the Sun in your eyes - I mean, on this thing, why don't we [garble]?

a11_0753555.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0753555.text: Now, you may have the Sun in your eyes coming around the corner. Now, you've got your patch ready in case you want it?

a11_0753555.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0753555.text: Okay, TVC Servo Power 1, to AC 1,

a11_0753555.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0753555.text: Rotation Control Power, Normal, number 2, to AC.

a11_0753555.speaker: Collins
a11_0753555.text: Okay, stand by. Rotational Control Power is Normal, number 2, to AC.

a11_0753555.speaker: Collins
a11_0753555.text: Rotational Hand Controller, number 2, is Armed.

a11_0753555.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0753555.text: It's going to have to get up pretty high to [garble]. Alright, time check.

a11_0754900.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0754900.text: 35 seconds; DSKY's blank, EMS Mode, Normal. Okay.

a11_0754900.speaker: Collins
a11_0754900.text: Yes, the Moon is there, boy - in all its splendor.

a11_0754900.speaker: Collins
a11_0754900.text: Plaster of paris gray to me.

a11_0754900.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0754900.text: Don't look at it. Here we come up...

a11_0755100.speaker: Collins
a11_0755100.text: g feels sort of pleasant, doesn't it? We're measuring just a shadow over zero g on the g-meter.

a11_0755100.speaker: Collins
a11_0755100.text: Okay. The chamber pressure is holding steady as a rock. It's holding - it's building up a little bit, actually; it's up around 96 now. Gimbals are sure a little bit busier than I would have guessed.

a11_0755100.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0755100.text: That's a little more chamber pressure than they were predicting.

a11_0760530.speaker: Collins
a11_0760530.text: Oh, golly, let me have that camera back. There's a huge, magnificent crater over here. I wish we had the other lens on, but God, that's a big beauty. You want to look at that guy, Neil?

a11_0760615.speaker: Collins
a11_0760615.text: Well, don't miss that first one.

a11_0760615.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0760615.text: It's very quiet here in the control room. Most of the controllers seated at their consoles, a few standing up, but very quiet.

a11_0760615.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0760615.text: See how am I doing. Yes, you're right.

a11_0760615.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0760615.text: We'll need - we need to catch it about 10.

a11_0760615.speaker: Collins
a11_0760615.text: Shoot, you're going to have plenty of passes.

a11_0760930.speaker: Collins
a11_0760930.text: Yes, there's a moose down here you just wouldn't believe. There's the biggest one yet. God, it's huge! It is immense! It's so big I can't even get it in the window. You want to look at that? That's the biggest one you ever seen in your life. Neil? God, look at this central mountain peak.

a11_0760930.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0760930.text: And that time is the initial acquisition time, but it could take a little longer to lock onto the signal for voice communications.

a11_0761220.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0761220.text: There's a good view of that...

a11_0761220.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0761220.text: Looks hotter than hell to me. Boy, look at the size of that one.

a11_0761400.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0761400.text: About another minute and a half.

a11_0761400.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0761400.text: [Coughing.]

a11_0761400.speaker: Collins
a11_0761400.text: I rolled too slow.

a11_0761400.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0761400.text: Doubt that we'll make it.

a11_0761400.speaker: Collins
a11_0761400.text: Oh, look at that [garble].

a11_0761400.speaker: Collins
a11_0761400.text: Golly damn! A geologist up here would just go crazy.

a11_0761400.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0761400.text: You want the Flight Plan?

a11_0761400.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0761400.text: Yeah, please.

a11_0761400.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0761400.text: 30 seconds.

a11_0761400.speaker: Collins
a11_0761400.text: Okay, we shouldn't take any more pictures on this roll until Earth comes, I don't think. This is...

a11_0761400.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0761400.text: About out?

a11_0761400.speaker: Collins
a11_0761400.text: ...just about out and it's on our last color roll, so we'll switch to black and white as soon as we get to Earth.

a11_0761400.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0761400.text: We might make it in time.

a11_0761400.speaker: Collins
a11_0761400.text: Yeah.

a11_0761400.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0761400.text: There it is, it's coming up!

a11_0761400.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0761400.text: What?

a11_0761400.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0761400.text: The Earth.

a11_0761400.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0761400.text: See it?

a11_0761400.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0761400.text: Yeah. Beautiful.

a11_0761400.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0761400.text: It's halfway up.

a11_0761400.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0761400.text: We ought to have AOS now. You got your...

a11_0761400.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0761400.text: Right over the LM.

a11_0761400.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0761400.text: Are you set up?

a11_0761400.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0761400.text: Just about to be cut off by the LM. Boy, does that ever look beautiful in the sextant.

a11_0761400.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0761400.text: Have you got...

a11_0761400.speaker: Collins
a11_0761400.text: Okay, how about MSFN...

a11_0761400.speaker: Collins/Aldrin
a11_0761400.text: You got them.

a11_0761400.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0761400.text: Madrid AOS, Madrid AOS.

a11_0761400.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0761400.text: We're in Omni...

a11_0761400.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0761400.text: Down Voice Backup.

a11_0761400.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0761400.text: ...Bravo.

a11_0761400.speaker: McCandless
a11_0761400.text: Apollo 11, Apollo 11, this is Houston. Do you read? Over.

a11_0761400.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0761400.text: Yeah, we sure do, Houston. The LOI-1 burn just nominal as all getout, and everything's looking good.

a11_0761400.speaker: McCandless
a11_0761400.text: Apollo 11, Apollo 11, this is Houston. Do you read? Over.

a11_0761400.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0761400.text: Telemetry indicates that the crew is working on the antenna angles to bring the High Gain Antenna to bear.

a11_0761400.speaker: Spacecraft
a11_0761400.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Over.

a11_0761400.speaker: McCandless
a11_0761400.text: Apollo 11, Apollo 11, this is Houston. We are reading you weakly. Go ahead. Over.

a11_0761400.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0761400.text: Roger. Burn status report follows. Delta-T IG zero, burn time 5:57, [garble] on the PAD. V GX minus 0.1, V GY minus 0.1, V GZ plus 0.1, Delta-V C minus [garble] point eight, fuel [garble] plus 390 [garble]. Over.

a11_0761400.speaker: McCandless
a11_0761400.text: 11, this is Houston. These residuals, do you have minus 0.17 [garble], V GX minus 0.1, V GY minus 0.1, V GZ 1.1, and a burn time of 5 plus 57. Stand by, maybe the comm will improve a little bit. Over.

a11_0761400.speaker: McCandless
a11_0761400.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Are you in the process of acquiring with the High Gain Antenna? Over.

a11_0761400.speaker: McCandless
a11_0761400.text: Apollo 11, Apollo 11, this is Houston. How do you read?

a11_0761400.speaker: Collins
a11_0761400.text: Reading you loud and clear, Houston. How us?

a11_0761400.speaker: McCandless
a11_0761400.text: Roger. Reading you the same, now. Could you repeat your burn status report? We copied the residuals and burn time, and that was about it. Send the whole thing again, please.

a11_0761400.speaker: Collins
a11_0761400.text: It was like - it was like perfect!

a11_0761400.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0761400.text: Delta-T IG zero, burn time 5:57, PAD values on the angles, V GX minus 0.1, V GY minus 0.1, V GZ plus 0.1, no trim, minus 6.8 on Delta-V C , fuel was 38.8, ox 39.0, plus 50 on balance. We ran an increase on the PUGS. Noun 44 showed us in a 60.9 by 169.9.

a11_0761400.speaker: McCandless
a11_0761400.text: Roger. We copy your burn status report. And the spacecraft is looking good to us on telemetry.

a11_0761400.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0761400.text: Roger. Everything looks good up here.

a11_0761400.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0761400.text: That burn report was by Neil Armstrong.

a11_0761400.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0761400.text: This is Apollo Control. We're showing spacecraft weight in lunar orbit of 72,004 pounds [32,660 kg].

a11_0763434.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0763434.text: Apollo 11 is getting its first view of the landing approach. This time we are going over the Taruntius crater, and the pictures and maps brought back by Apollos 8 and 10 have given us a very good preview of what to look at here. It looks very much like the pictures, but like the difference between watching a real football game and one on TV. There's no substitute for actually being here.

a11_0763434.speaker: McCandless
a11_0763434.text: Roger. We concur, and we certainly wish we could see it first hand, also.

a11_0763434.speaker: Armstrong
