a11_0763434.text: We're going over the Messier series of craters right at the time, looking vertically down on them, and Messier A, we can see good-sized blocks in the bottom of the crater. I don't know what our altitude is now, but in any case, those are pretty good-size blocks.

a11_0763434.speaker: McCandless
a11_0763434.text: Okay. Just roughly, it looks like you're about 120 miles or 130 miles right now. Make that 127 [nautical] miles [235 km].

a11_0763434.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0763434.text: We're approaching PDI point now, over... [Pause.]

a11_0763434.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0763434.text: We're over Mount Marilyn at the present time, and it's ignition point.

a11_0763434.speaker: McCandless
a11_0763434.text: Roger. Thank you. And our preliminary tracking data for the first few minutes shows you in a 61.6 by 169.5 orbit [114.1 by 313.9 km]. Over.

a11_0764129.speaker: McCandless
a11_0764129.text: 11, Houston. During your SPS burn as played back on tape down here, we've observed the nitrogen tank Bravo pressure in the SPS system dropping a little bit more than we anticipated. It's holding steady right now. We'll continue to watch it and keep you posted if anything comes up. Over.

a11_0764129.speaker: McCandless
a11_0764129.text: Right. And it has held steady...

a11_0764129.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0764129.text: And Boot Hill, Duke Island, Sidewinder, looking at Maskelyne W, that's the yaw round checkpoint, and just coming into the terminator. At the terminator it's ashen gray. As you get further away from the terminator, it gets to be a lighter gray, and as you get closer to the subsolar point, you can definitely see browns and tans on the ground, according to the last Apollo limb observation anyway.

a11_0764129.speaker: McCandless
a11_0764129.text: Roger, 11. We're recording your comments for posterity.

a11_0764129.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0764129.text: And again, that was Neil Armstrong with the report.

a11_0764129.speaker: Collins
a11_0764129.text: Did somebody in the background - do they accuse us of being compromisers?

a11_0764129.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0764129.text: And the landing site is well into the dark here. I don't think we're going to be able to see anything of the landing site this early.

a11_0764129.speaker: McCandless
a11_0764129.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. When you have a free minute, could you give us your onboard readout of N 2 tank Bravo, please. And we'd like to make sure you understand that ever since you stopped thrusting with the SPS, the temperature in this tank has remained steady. Over. Make that the pressure has remained steady.

a11_0764129.speaker: Collins
a11_0764129.text: Rog. We understand tank pressure has stayed steady. Thank you.

a11_0764129.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0764129.text: Roger. We're showing the N 2 tank pressure in tank Bravo to be 1,960, something like that, and Alpha is, oh, about 22 - about 2,250. Over.

a11_0764129.speaker: McCandless
a11_0764129.text: Roger. We show 2,249 in Alpha and 1,946 down here.

a11_0765319.speaker: Collins
a11_0765319.text: Houston, Apollo 11. How about coming up with some roll, pitch, and yaw angles in which to stop this so-called Orb-Rate that I'm doing.

a11_0765319.speaker: McCandless
a11_0765319.text: We'll have them for you in a minute, 11.

a11_0765319.speaker: Collins
a11_0765319.text: Okay. And time to stop also, please.

a11_0765319.speaker: McCandless
a11_0765319.text: Roger. We show you, in the Flight Plan, staying in orbital rate until about 79 hours, 10 minutes. Do you have some particular attitude or reason for wanting to go inertial? Over.

a11_0765319.speaker: Collins
a11_0765319.text: No, that's fine. I just wanted to confirm that. Until 79:10, then we'll breeze around here in orbit.

a11_0765319.speaker: McCandless
a11_0765319.text: Roger. And we've got an observation you can make if you have some time up there. There's been some lunar transient events reported in the vicinity of Aristarchus. Over.

a11_0765319.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0765319.text: Roger. We just went into spacecraft darkness. Until then, why, we couldn't see a thing down below us. But now, with Earthshine, the visibility is, oh, pretty fair. Looking back behind me, now, I can see the corona from where the Sun has just set. And we'll get out the map and see what we can find around Aristarchus.

a11_0765319.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0765319.text: We're coming upon Aristarchus right now...

a11_0765319.speaker: McCandless
a11_0765319.text: Okay. Aristarchus is at Tango Echo 9 on your ATO chart. It's about 394 miles north of track. However, at your present altitude, which is about 167 nautical miles, it ought to be over - that is within view of your horizon: 23 degrees north, 47 west. Take a look and see if you see anything worth noting up there. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0765319.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0765319.text: That was Buzz Aldrin discussing the Earthshine.

a11_0770301.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0770301.text: Houston, 11. It might help us a little bit if you could give us a time of crossing of 45 west.

a11_0770301.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0770301.text: You might give us a time of crossing of 45 west, and then we'll know when to start searching for Aristarchus.

a11_0770301.speaker: McCandless
a11_0770301.text: Roger. You'll be crossing 45 west at 77:04:10 or about 40 seconds from now. Over. Thirty seconds from now.

a11_0770301.speaker: McCandless
a11_0770301.text: Apollo 11, when we lose the S-band, we'd like to get Omni Charlie from you. And update my last, that 77:04 was the time when Aristarchus should become visible over your horizon. 77:12 is point of closest approach south of it. Over.

a11_0770301.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0770301.text: Okay. That sounds better because we're just - just went by Copernicus a little bit ago.

a11_0770301.speaker: McCandless
a11_0770301.text: Roger. We show you at about 27 degrees longitude right now.

a11_0770301.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0770301.text: Houston, when a star sets up here, there's just no doubt about it. One instant it's there, and the next instant it's just completely gone.

a11_0770921.speaker: McCandless
a11_0770921.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. We request you use Omni Charlie at this time. Over.

a11_0771157.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0771157.text: Houston, Apollo 11.

a11_0771157.speaker: McCandless
a11_0771157.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Go ahead.

a11_0771157.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0771157.text: Roger. Seems to me since we know orbits so precisely, and know where the stars are so precisely, and can time the setting of a star or a planet to a very fine degree, that this might be a pretty good means of measuring the altitude of the horizon.

a11_0771157.speaker: McCandless
a11_0771157.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_0771157.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0771157.text: Hey, Houston. I'm looking north up toward Aristarchus now, and I can't really tell at that distance whether I really am looking at Aristarchus, but there's an area there that is considerably more illuminated than the surrounding area. It just has - seems to have a slight amount of fluorescence to it as a crater can be seen, and the area around the crater is quite bright.

a11_0771157.speaker: McCandless
a11_0771157.text: Roger, 11. We copy. [Long pause.]

a11_0771157.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0771157.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Looking up at the same area now and it does seem to be reflecting some of the Earthshine. I'm not sure whether it was worked out to be about zero phase to - Well, at least there's one wall of the crater that seems to be more illuminated than the other, and that one - if I'm lining up with the Earth correctly, does seem to put it about at zero phase. That area is definitely lighter than anything else that I could see out this window. I am not sure that I am really identifying any phosphorescence, but that definitely is lighter than anything else in the neighborhood.

a11_0771157.speaker: McCandless
a11_0771157.text: 11, this is Houston. Can you discern any difference in color of the illumination, and is that an inner or an outer wall of the crater? Over.

a11_0771157.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0771157.text: Rog. That's an inner wall of the crater.

a11_0771157.speaker: Collins
a11_0771157.text: No, there doesn't appear to be any color involved in it, Bruce.

a11_0771157.speaker: McCandless
a11_0771157.text: Roger. You said inner wall. Would that be the inner edge of the northern surface?

a11_0771157.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0771157.text: I guess it would be the inner part of the west-northwest part, the part that would be more nearly normal if you were looking at it from the Earth.

a11_0771157.speaker: McCandless
a11_0771157.text: 11, Houston. Have you used the monocular on this? Over.

a11_0771157.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0771157.text: Stand by one.

a11_0771157.speaker: Collins
a11_0771157.text: Like you to know this quest for science has caused me to lose my lunch. Floating around in here somewhere, but I can't find it.

a11_0771157.speaker: McCandless
a11_0771157.text: 11, this is Houston. We're - we're hearing only a partial comm. Say again please.

a11_0771157.speaker: Collins
a11_0771157.text: I think [garble] [Long pause.]

a11_0771157.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0771157.text: Houston, we'll give it a try if we have the opportunity on next rev, when we're not in the middle of lunch, and trying to find the monocular.

a11_0771157.speaker: McCandless
a11_0771157.text: Roger. Copied you that time. Expect in the next rev you'll probably be getting ready for LOI-2.

a11_0771157.speaker: McCandless
a11_0771157.text: So, let's wind - wind this up, and we've got some other things to talk to you about in a few minutes.

a11_0771157.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0771157.text: Okay.

a11_0771157.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0771157.text: Apollo 11 will be in acquisition for another 20 minutes during its first revolution of the Moon.

a11_0772244.speaker: McCandless
a11_0772244.text: 11, this is Houston. We're targeting, or planning to make the LOI-2 burn now using bank A only. We'll have the PAD and everything for you next time around. Just trying to economize a little on bank B. Bank B is holding, though.

a11_0773153.speaker: McCandless
a11_0773153.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

a11_0773153.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0773153.text: Go ahead.

a11_0773153.speaker: McCandless
a11_0773153.text: 11, Houston. In order to improve the communications a little bit here, we'd like to try to get you on the High Gain Antenna. We're recommending a pitch angle of 0, yaw 355 - I say again 355, the Track switch to Manual, and Wide Beamwidth. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0773153.speaker: Collins
a11_0773153.text: Okay. You ready to switch to High Gain now?

a11_0773153.speaker: McCandless
a11_0773153.text: That's affirmative. [Long pause.]

a11_0773153.speaker: McCandless
a11_0773153.text: 11, Houston. Do you read? [Pause.]

a11_0773153.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0773153.text: Roger. We read you. It seems to be rather marginal on the High Gain.

a11_0773153.speaker: McCandless
a11_0773153.text: Roger. We concur. [Long pause.]

a11_0773153.speaker: Collins
a11_0773153.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Could you give us a time of crossing the prime meridian 150 west? Over.

a11_0773153.speaker: McCandless
a11_0773153.text: Roger. Stand by about a half a second, here. Okay. Your time of crossing the 150 west meridian will be 77:50:05. Over.

a11_0773153.speaker: Collins
a11_0773153.text: Thank you. [Long pause.]

a11_0773153.speaker: McCandless
a11_0773153.text: 11, this is Houston. We have about 6 minutes remaining until LOS, and in order that we may configure our ground lines, we'd like to know if you're still planning to have the TV up with the beginning of the next pass. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0773153.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0773153.text: Roger, Houston. We'll try to have it ready.

a11_0773153.speaker: McCandless
a11_0773153.text: This is Houston. We are inquiring if it is your plan to. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0773153.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0773153.text: It never was our plan to. But it's in the Flight Plan, so I guess we'll do it.

a11_0773153.speaker: McCandless
a11_0773153.text: Houston. Roger. Out. [Long pause.]

a11_0773153.speaker: McCandless
a11_0773153.text: 11, Houston.

a11_0773153.speaker: Collins
a11_0773153.text: Roger. Go ahead.

a11_0773153.speaker: McCandless
a11_0773153.text: For use in connection with that time on the prime meridian crossing, you have an orbital period now of 2 hours, 8 minutes and 37 seconds. Over.

a11_0773153.speaker: Collins
a11_0773153.text: Thank you.

a11_0773153.speaker: McCandless
a11_0773153.text: Roger. Out.

a11_0773153.speaker: McCandless
a11_0773153.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. A little over 2 minutes to LOS. All your systems parameters and orbit are looking good from the ground. We have AOS on the other side at 78:23:31. Over.

a11_0773153.speaker: McCandless
a11_0773153.text: Roger. That was 31 on the end.

a11_0773153.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0773153.text: Okay.

a11_0773153.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0773153.text: This is Apollo Control. We've had Loss Of Signal from Apollo 11 on its first lunar revolution. We will acquire the spacecraft on the next revolution at 78 hours, 23 minutes, 31 seconds. The orbital period for Apollo 11's present orbit; 2 hours, 8 minutes, 37 seconds; and as you heard we passed up to the crew information that we would perform the LOI-2 burn using only bank A. The banks are the drive mechanisms for the ball valves in the Service Propulsion System. They open and close these ball valves and the valves allow the fuel and oxidizer to flow into the engine. There are redundant valves

a11_0773153.speaker: Collins
a11_0773153.text: That's why I'm trying to get it out.

a11_0773153.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0773153.text: No alignment this rev, huh?

a11_0774800.speaker: Collins
a11_0774800.text: Oh, shit! This pitch here is no good. 32, huh? Pitch 315 I want to be at, huh? Alright. They keep - all they do is they say Orb-rate and that little attitude right there and right there applies to the rest of this page, all of that page, and over to this page.

a11_0774800.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0774800.text: Okay, so that's the one we'll do.

a11_0774800.speaker: Collins
a11_0774800.text: Okay, that's the way I'm rolling.

a11_0774800.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0774800.text: And we'll take the - we'll have High Gain...

a11_0774800.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0774800.text: ...and we'll get the camera out of the center window, if that looks reasonable.

a11_0774800.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0774800.text: We'll have to give them pictures of the Moon.

a11_0774800.speaker: Collins
a11_0774800.text: We'll have a gauge as to where we are.

a11_0781800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0781800.text: Mark. 2 minutes now from time of predicted acquisition in Mission Control Center. We're standing by.

a11_0782210.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0782210.text: ...and you could be busy getting up supplies if you...

a11_0782210.speaker: Collins
a11_0782210.text: About a minute from AOS.

a11_0782210.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0782210.text: Okay, let's get out of this. Let me get Verb 62. Okay, Mike?

a11_0782210.speaker: Collins
a11_0782210.text: Oh, I really need these [garble], Buzz. I really need these goddam [garble].

a11_0782210.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0782210.text: Well, we're not going to have much of a TV unless we get High Gain.

a11_0782210.speaker: Collins
a11_0782210.text: Alright.

a11_0782210.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0782210.text: Mark. 1 minute now from time of predicted acquisition. Continuing to stand by in Mission Control Center, Houston.

a11_0782210.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0782210.text: I'll give it back to you - [garble].

a11_0782210.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0782210.text: You got yourself some rates going about, like, what you want?

a11_0782210.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0782210.text: You got - you got High Gain right now, I mean the angles, right now.

a11_0782210.speaker: Collins
a11_0782210.text: And we're 23 - we're 30 seconds from AOS, so those angles should be okay. You reading them?

a11_0782210.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0782210.text: Minus 30 pitch...

a11_0782210.speaker: Collins
a11_0782210.text: Yes.

a11_0782210.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0782210.text: ...150 yaw, okay.

a11_0782210.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0782210.text: No, that's not 150 - that's 15. Isn't it?

a11_0782210.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0782210.text: Just a second. Yes, minus - I'm sorry, minus 31 and plus 15. Right. You got it?

a11_0782210.speaker: Collins
a11_0782210.text: Yes.

a11_0782210.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0782210.text: Mark. 10 seconds away now. Standing by for acquisition. We've - we've had AOS by Goldstone. Television is now on. That's Bruce McCandless, our Cap...

a11_0782210.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0782210.text: I don't know what f-stop I ought to be at. Well - see what it's doing, Mike?

a11_0782210.speaker: Collins
a11_0782210.text: [Garble].

a11_0782210.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0782210.text: The flicker I don't know about, the white dot is...

a11_0782210.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0782210.text: Yes, the flicker...

a11_0782210.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0782210.text: ...the flicker is what I'm - Nothing I can...

a11_0782210.speaker: Collins
a11_0782210.text: Okay, we got it solid.

a11_0782210.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0782210.text: ...nothing you can do about the flicker?

a11_0782210.speaker: McCandless
a11_0782210.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

a11_0782210.speaker: Collins
a11_0782210.text: Got it solid on Auto.

a11_0782210.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0782210.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Are you picking up our signals okay?

a11_0782210.speaker: McCandless
a11_0782210.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Affirmative. We're reading you loud and clear on voice and we have a good clear TV picture, a little bright crater in the...

a11_0782210.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0782210.text: ...No, no, no. That's...

a11_0782210.speaker: McCandless
a11_0782210.text: ...the bottom of the picture. I guess that's the spot on the tube.

a11_0782210.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0782210.text: I'm sorry about that one.

a11_0782210.speaker: McCandless
a11_0782210.text: And if you could give us P00 and Accept, we'll uplink a new state vector and target load to you.

a11_0782210.speaker: Collins
a11_0782210.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a11_0782210.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0782210.text: Houston, Apollo 11. One of the larger craters on the back side - I noticed a small, dark speck on the outer wall, and putting the monocular on it, I was able to see - oh, an area maybe a quarter of a mile in diameter. It was really a fresh looking dark-colored pit, and that seems to be in contrast with all the other fresh little craters or holes that you can perceive on the walls of any of these craters. Around this particular one there seems to be two or three of these - especially the one that caught my attention. Quite remarkable. Over.

a11_0782530.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0782530.text: Houston, Apollo 11. One of the larger craters on the back side - I noticed a small, dark speck on the outer wall, and putting the monocular on it, I was able to see - oh, an area maybe a quarter of a mile in diameter. It was really a fresh looking dark-colored pit, and that seems to be in contrast with all the other fresh little craters or holes that you can perceive on the walls of any of these craters. Around this particular one there seems to be two or three of these - especially the one that caught my attention. Quite remarkable. Over.

a11_0782530.speaker: McCandless
a11_0782530.text: Roger. Do you have a location on that one? [Pause.]

a11_0782530.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0782530.text: No, not a precise one. I've got several pictures of it, though.

a11_0782530.speaker: McCandless
a11_0782530.text: Roger. We copy. [Pause.]

a11_0782530.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0782530.text: This - That was Buzz Aldrin making a report, geological report on back-side pass.

a11_0782530.speaker: McCandless
a11_0782530.text: We're getting a beautiful picture in down there now, 11. The color's coming in quite clearly, and we can see the horizon and the relative blackness of space, and without getting into the question of grays and browns, it looks, at least on our monitor, sort of a brownish-gray.

a11_0782530.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0782530.text: That's a good, reasonable way of describing it. It appears to me as though it made a difference just sitting back in the tunnel and gazing at all windows; it makes a difference which one you're looking out of. For example, the camera right now is looking out the number 5 window, and it definitely gives a rosier or tanner tinge, especially when you look straight through it and not at an angle. Over.

a11_0782530.speaker: McCandless
a11_0782530.text: Roger.

a11_0782530.speaker: Flight
a11_0782530.text: GNC, Flight. [Under Aldrin] Okay, your tank - nitrogen tank [garble] is okay? Still holding?

a11_0782530.speaker: Collins
a11_0782530.text: Oh, we're about 95 or 100 degrees east. Coming up on Smyth's Sea.

a11_0782530.speaker: Flight
a11_0782530.text: Okay.

a11_0782530.speaker: McCandless
a11_0782530.text: Say again, 11?

a11_0782530.speaker: Collins
a11_0782530.text: I'd say again we're about 95 degrees east, coming up on Smyth's Sea.

a11_0782530.speaker: McCandless
a11_0782530.text: Roger. And for your information, we show you at an altitude of about...

a11_0782530.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0782530.text: Houston...

a11_0782530.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0782530.text: Okay.

a11_0782530.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0782530.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Did you observe a difference in the N 2 pressures before LOI? It seems to me as though the two were not equal on the [garble]...

a11_0782530.speaker: Flight
a11_0782530.text: Standby.

a11_0782530.speaker: Flight
a11_0782530.text: Yeah, I think that's right. Ah...

a11_0782530.speaker: Collins
a11_0782530.text: I'm flying it in SCS minimum impulse, Houston, and it's rather difficult to keep it on a constant theta. The LM wants to wander up and down. I'm not sure if it's in response to mascons or what, but I can get it completely stabilized in theta and let it alone, and in another couple of minutes it will have developed its own rate.

a11_0782530.speaker: McCandless
a11_0782530.text: This is Houston. Roger.

a11_0782530.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0782530.text: That was Mike Collins making that report.

a11_0782530.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0782530.text: Houston, we'll be moving shortly from the side window to the hatch window, and we'll try and pick up some of the landmarks that we'll be looking at as we approach powered descent. Over.

a11_0782530.speaker: McCandless
a11_0782530.text: 11, this is Houston. Roger. And we're through with the uplink; the computer is yours. You can go to Block and we'll have the information on nitrogen for you shortly. Over.

a11_0782530.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0782530.text: Roger. Copy. [Pause.]

a11_0782530.speaker: Collins
a11_0782530.text: Okay, Houston. Several minutes ago I was exactly steady on theta, and since then I have been moving toward the LM, pointed straight down toward the radius vector, and that's been despite a number of down minimum-pitch impulses.

a11_0782530.speaker: McCandless
a11_0782530.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_0782530.speaker: Collins
a11_0782530.text: We're over Smyth's Sea right now.

a11_0782530.speaker: McCandless
a11_0782530.text: Roger.

a11_0782530.speaker: Collins
a11_0782530.text: We're about 88 degrees east, I would estimate.

a11_0782530.speaker: McCandless
a11_0782530.text: We show you about south of the - southwest of the crater Jansky right now. [Long pause.]

a11_0782530.speaker: Collins
a11_0782530.text: Smyth Sea doesn't look very much like a sea. It - The area which is devoid of craters, of which there's not very much, is sort of a hilly looking area. It's not like the maria at all.

a11_0782530.speaker: McCandless
a11_0782530.text: Roger. We copy that about the sea, and it looks like you were just giving us a view of the crater Neper, the large crater on the left, and Jansky on the right. [Long pause.]

a11_0782530.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0782530.text: That exchange between CapCom Bruce McCandless and Mike Collins aboard the Apollo 11 spacecraft.

a11_0782530.speaker: Collins
a11_0782530.text: We think you're close, but no cigar.

a11_0782530.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0782530.text: Apollo Control, Houston. We acquired TV at 78 hours, 24 minutes, 11 seconds. Currently our orbital parameters show 104 altitude [193 km] - an apolune of 170.2 [315.2 km], a perilune of 61.3 [113.5 km] - nautical miles, those are.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: 11, this is Houston. Would you care to comment on some of these craters as we go by?

a11_0783252.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0783252.text: Roger. We're approaching the approach path to ignition. This is equivalent to 13 minutes before ignition, and we're at about 80 degrees east, I guess - 83 degrees east. [To crewmate] That correspond to the location you're holding there presently?

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger. We're showing your present position as about 77 - 76 degrees east looking back towards the east. [Pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: Hey, you should be looking back at Smyth Sea now.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger.

a11_0783252.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0783252.text: We've now heard from all three Apollo 11 crewmembers during this television pass. The individual talking earlier was Neil Armstrong.

a11_0783252.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0783252.text: Okay.

a11_0783252.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0783252.text: Houston, what you're seeing in the middle of the screen now is the crater Schubert and Gilbert U is in the center right now; and this comes up at about - a little over 12 minutes before powered descent. Instead of me looking - Instead of looking back at it, we'd be looking straight down at that time.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: And we show you at an altitude now of about 110 [nautical] miles [204 km]. And, of course, you'll be considerably lower at the initiation of powered descent. [Long pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: Okay, Houston. Look at register 3 on the DSKY data. This data is increasing toward my desired of 315; and I'll let the hand controller alone here, and I'll bet you it reverses itself. [Long pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger, 11. We're watching the DSKY now, and it's still coming in beautifully on the TV. [Pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0783252.text: Okay. There's - on the right side of the screen at the present time, there's a triple crater with - with a small crater between the first and second; and the one at the bottom of the screen is Schubert Y. [Long pause.] Zoom in - it does have a central peak in Schubert Y. Actually, several of them, and you can observe those, plus the rim craters at the bottom of your screen.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger. We're seeing the central peak quite clearly now. [Long pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0783252.text: Okay. We're zooming in now on a crater called Schubert N. Schubert N, very conical inside walls and the bottom appears to be nearly flat.

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: Look at data on the DSKY. It's stabilized and is holding steady now.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger.

a11_0783252.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0783252.text: Looking out the window I can see a number of small craters on the bottom of Schubert N.

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: We're coming up on the Foaming Sea where I'll be doing some P22 marking on a crater of my choice; name of crater, KAMP.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Okay. We'll be watching for KAMP.

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: And notice register 3 has reversed itself, and it's heading back the other way now without any pitch thruster firing.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger, Mike. We confirm that you've changed the direction of your pitch rate. [Long pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: Generally speaking the...

a11_0783252.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0783252.text: The crater...

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: ...The tendency seems to be to pull the LM down toward the center of the Moon as in a gravity gradient experiment.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger, 11. We copy...

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: It may have something to do with mascons or it may...

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger. We copy...

a11_0783252.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0783252.text: [Garble.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: It may have something to do with Mascons or it may just be the peculiarity of the DSKY display.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Okay. We've observed the behavior of your DSKY, and I think we've got the data here to work on it. Let us grind around a little while on it, and we'll report back to you, probably in a rev or two.

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: Okay. Well, in the meantime, I'm going to pitch down toward 315.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0783252.text: Three craters - three horizontal craters that you now have in the field of view are immediately underneath the ground track. The right-hand, and the largest crater that you see, is Dubiago P. [Pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger. We concur on the identification of that crater. [Pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: And we show you coming up on landmark Alpha 1 here shortly.

a11_0783252.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0783252.text: Roger. Mike's having his first look at Alpha 1 at the present time. [Pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: Yeah. It's a great bright crater. It's not a large one but an extremely bright one. It looks like a very recent and, I would guess, impact crater with rays streaming out in all directions which should make my... Correction - the Foaming Sea easy to see coming up on it now. Crater KAMP is one of the smaller ones out on the - on the floor of the Foaming Sea. [Long pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0783252.text: We've been some 17 minutes now into this television pass and standing by, continuing to monitor.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Here we show you over the Sea of Fertility now, and we ought to have Langrenus down south of track a few degrees, about 9 degrees south of track.

a11_0783252.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0783252.text: Now the crater that's in the center of the screen now is Webb. We'd be looking straight down on it at about 6 minutes before powered descent. It has a relatively flat bottom to the crater, and you can see maybe two or three craters that are in the bottom of it. On the western wall, the wall that's now nearest to the - the camera, near the bottom of the screen, we can see a dimple crater, just on the outside. And then coming back toward the bottom of the screen and to the left, you can see a series of depressions. It's this type of connected craters that give us most interest to discover why th

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger. We're observing the dimple crater now. The central peak we can see on the Orbiter photos doesn't seem to stand out very well here.

a11_0783252.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0783252.text: Well, they're not central peaks. They're depressions in the center.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger.

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: And you'll notice on the pitch thruster activity, I've still - I've put in, oh, a dozen minimum impulses in pitch down, and I'm still far from correcting back to 315.

a11_0783252.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0783252.text: We're moving the camera over to the right window now to give you Langrenus, its - its several central peaks and...

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger. We got Langrenus in our screen now. [Long pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Okay, 11. This is Houston. We're getting a beautiful picture of Langrenus now with its rather conspicuous central peak.

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: The Sea of Fertility doesn't look very fertile to me. I don't know who named it.

a11_0783252.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0783252.text: Well, it may have been named by a gentleman whom this crater was named after, Langrenus. Langrenus was a cartographer to the King of Spain and made one of the - one of the early reasonably accurate maps of the Moon.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger. That's very interesting...

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: I'll have to admit it sounds better for our purposes than the Sea of Crises.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Amen to that.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Okay. It looks like you're coming inside now on the camera.

a11_0783252.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0783252.text: Well, I can't get behind to see the monitor. I'll bring the focus in, but we're going to be looking down past one of the LM quads and one of the antennas, almost straight down at the ground track that we'll be seeing coming in now. I guess this is maybe 2 or 3 minutes before powered descent. [Long pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0783252.text: Alright, that should put the LM structure about in focus, and I'm going to move it out to infinity and then expand the field of view. [Long pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: Crater Secchi is out my window now, window number 2. [Pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Apollo 11. This is Houston. We show you coming up on the terminator at 78:53, about 7 minutes from now, and we've also got the LOI-2 and TEI-5 PADs ready for you after the TV, whenever you want to terminate. Over.

a11_0783252.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0783252.text: Roger.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: And we're getting a good view of the track leading into the landing site now. [Long pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Okay. And it looks like we got Secchi K, went by about 10 seconds ago. Coming up on Apollo Ridge. [Long pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: And in the right-hand portion of our screen right now, we can see Messier Alpha and Bravo with the light-colored rays streaming off in one direction. [Long pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: I don't know if you can make out, but in the Sea of Fertility there are a number of craters that are just barely discernible. Old, old craters whose outlines are just barely able to be seen.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger. I think we can make them out. The color really enhances our ability to discern features and craters over what we see in real time on our black and white monitor.

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: Right. The - At these low Sun angles, there's no trace of brown, it's now returned to a very gray appearance and, like the 8 crew said, it has a look of plaster of Paris to it at this Sun angle, which is completely lacking at higher Sun angles.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0783252.text: We're now some 25 minutes into our television pass.

a11_0783252.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0783252.text: Okay. This is very close to ignition point for powered descent. Just passing Mount Marilyn that - that triangular-shaped mountain that you see in the center of the screen at the present time with crater Secchi Theta on top of the far northern edge of the mountain.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger. We're getting a good view of Mount Marilyn and of Secchi Theta. [Pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0783252.text: And now we're looking at what we call Boot Hill; occurs 20 seconds into the descent. [Long pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0783252.text: Watching this pass with a great deal of interest in Mission Control Center is Pete Conrad, the commander for the Apollo 12 mission.

a11_0783252.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0783252.text: The bright, sharp-rimmed crater at the very right edge of the screen, Censorinus T. [Pause.] Now passing the - the 1-minute point in powered descent.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger. And for your information, your current altitude is 148 nautical miles [274 km] above the surface. [Pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: I'm unable to determine altitude at all looking out the window. I couldn't tell whether we were down at 60 or up at 170 [111, 315 km resp.].

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: I bet you could tell if you were down at 50,000 feet.

a11_0783252.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0783252.text: [Garble].

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: I wouldn't be surprised. [Long pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0783252.text: We're passing some steep ridges here, the edges of old craters that were photographed by Apollo 10. And those - the crew of Apollo 10 was very impressed with the steepness of these ridges when they came over them at about 50,000 feet.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger. We can observe they're also steep even from this altitude. You got quite a shadow being cast by the Sun at these low angles.

a11_0783252.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0783252.text: The entire surface is getting considerably darker than the surface that we looked at previously when the Sun was quite high above us. The crater in the - bright crater in the center of the screen, - well, the smaller one is Censorinus.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger. And we show you a little over 1 minute from the terminator at the present time. [Long pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0783252.text: How's the brightness of the picture you're receiving? You think we ought to open up the f-stop some as we approach the terminator?

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Yeah. The brightness is still doing quite well. You can go ahead and open it up a stop or two. The automatic light level compensation seems to be working beautifully. [Long pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0783252.text: There's a good picture of Boot Hill.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger. We're...

a11_0783252.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0783252.text: Three minutes and 15 seconds into the descent.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger. We're seeing Boot Hill now.

a11_0783252.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0783252.text: And the next crater coming into the bottom, that's Duke Island right there, and to the left, the crater - the largest of the craters near the center of the picture right now is Maskelyne W. This is a position check during descent at about 3 minutes and 39 seconds, and it's our downrange position check and cross-range position check prior to yawing over face-up to acquire the landing radar. Past this point, we would be unable to see the surface below us until getting very near the landing area.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger. I imagine you get a - you'll get a real good look at that tomorrow afternoon. [Pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0783252.text: Sinuous Rille is the one that was referred to in Apollo 10 as Sidewinder.

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: That's a good name, too: Sidewinder and Diamondback. It looks like a couple of snakes down there in a lake bed. [Long pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0783252.text: And we're approaching the terminator now. See the...

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger.

a11_0783252.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0783252.text: ...contrast has increased and only the sunlit side of these ridges remain illuminated, while the dark sides and the shadow will become completely black.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: 11, this is Houston. The picture's getting a little grainy now. You might go ahead and open up the f-stop. [Long pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: Landing point is just barely in the darkness. That one crater, the upper part of which you see, lower part completely in darkness - the small, well-defined crater is Moltke, which is about abeam of the landing site.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger. We can just see - it looks like a little less than half of its rim right now. [Pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: And we can make out, just barely, some features on the surface, maybe from Earthshine. [Pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Are you wide open on the f-stop at this time?

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins/Aldrin
a11_0783252.text: Affirmative, we are.

a11_0783252.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0783252.text: Yeah. And it looks like we're just about to get the Sun coming into the lens, so we'll have to move the camera away.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger.

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: We can't see any Earthshine or any surface features at all in Earthshine now, due to the fact that the LM is very bright and is causing our pupils to contract.

a11_0783252.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0783252.text: It's a very fantastic view to see the terminator as you look along the edge of it. I think you'll agree that some of these craters that you're seeing in the picture now are really accentuated by the lengthening of the shadows as they approach the terminator.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Yes. It's a very beautiful and a rugged sight that we've got on the screen now. [Pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: And I think you've got some interesting data on thruster firings versus pitch angle. It looks like that LM just wants to head down towards the surface, is all.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger. I have a comment here that says that's what the LM was built for.

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: I believe! [Long pause.]

a11_0783252.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0783252.text: And as the Moon sinks slowly in the west, Apollo 11 bids good day to you.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger. We sort of thought it was the Sun setting in the east.

a11_0783252.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0783252.text: There you have it. Our first glimpse of the lunar surface during the Apollo 11 mission. The eleven crew took us on a guided tour of the front side, plus talked their way through the powered descent that lies ahead in tomorrow's activities. At 78 hours, 58 minutes into the flight of Apollo 11; this is Apollo Control, Houston, continuing to monitor.

a11_0783252.speaker: Collins
a11_0783252.text: Well, it depends on your point of view.

a11_0783252.speaker: McCandless
a11_0783252.text: Roger. Out.

a11_0785858.speaker: McCandless
a11_0785858.text: Roger on the inertial. And here we go on the LOI-2 PAD. LOI-2, SPS/G&N: 38320, plus 1.66, minus 0.81; T IG 080:11:36.03. Noun 81; minus 0140.8, minus all balls, minus 0074.3. Roll, all balls, 196, 359; 0065.7, plus 0053.7. Delta-V T ; 0159.2, 0:17, 0153.1. Sextant star; 23, 116.0, 13.8. The rest of the PAD is NA. GDC align; Vega and Deneb, 243, 183, 012. Ullage; two jets, 19 seconds. Remarks: On your DAP load, we would like in R1, 20101 vice the value which appears in the Flight Plan. In making the sextant star check, this must be done between GET of 79:30:10, at which time the star comes abov

a11_0785858.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0785858.text: Roger, LOI-2: SPS/G&N: 38320, plus 1.66, minus 0.81; 080:11:36.03; minus 0140.8, minus all balls, minus 0074.3. All zeros, 196, 359; 0065.7, plus 0053.7; 0159.2, 0:17, 0153.1; 23, 116.0, 13.8. Vega, Deneb, 243, 183, 012; two jet, 19 seconds. DAP; R1, 20101. Sextant star between 79:30:10 and 79:52:10. Attitude is heads down, retrograde pitched up 28 degrees. H A after the burn - Was that Noun 42 for H A and 64.6 and H P 54.6? Over.

a11_0785858.speaker: McCandless
a11_0785858.text: Roger. On the Noun 42 value, the last stuff you gave, H A is 65.6, H P is 54.6. Otherwise, I readback correct. I'm standing by with your TEI-5 PAD. Over.

a11_0785858.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0785858.text: Roger. H A 65.6 for Noun 42. And ready to copy.

a11_0785858.speaker: McCandless
a11_0785858.text: 11, this is Houston. TEI-5 SPS/G&N: 37201, minus 0.60, plus 0.47; T IG 086:09:36.66. Noun 81; plus 3352.1, plus 0344.1, minus 0145.8; roll NA; pitch, 032. The rest of the PAD is NA. Ullage; two jets, 16 seconds, undocked. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0785858.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0785858.text: Roger. TEI-5 SPS/G&N: 37201, minus 0.60, plus 0.47; 086:09:36.66; plus 3352.1, plus 0344.1, minus 0145 - 458, NA, 032. The rest is NA. Two jets, 16 seconds, undocked. Over.

a11_0785858.speaker: McCandless
a11_0785858.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Readback is correct. Out. [Long pause.]

a11_0785858.speaker: Collins
a11_0785858.text: Houston, you want us back on downvoice backup? Over.

a11_0785858.speaker: McCandless
a11_0785858.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. That's affirmative on the downvoice backup. We'd like you to confirm your Uptelemtry switch in the Normal position. Over.

a11_0785858.speaker: Collins
a11_0785858.text: Roger. It's in Block. Did you get us the - You got us a new CSM state vector and an LOI-2 target load in between all that television, didn't you?

a11_0785858.speaker: McCandless
a11_0785858.text: And what I'm asking for is the switchover to...

a11_0785858.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0785858.text: The Up-telemetry switch is in Normal. Over.

a11_0785858.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0785858.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 79 hours, 9 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 11. We currently read an apolune of 170.2 nautical miles [315.2 km], a perilune of 61.2 nautical miles [113.3 km]. Those listing of figures that you heard passed up to the crew were maneuver PAD updates. The first group for LOI-2. We're now looking at the time of burn of 80 hours, 11 minutes, 36 seconds; which should revise our orbital parameters to 65.7 nautical miles by 53.7 nautical miles [121.7 by 99.5 km]. A Delta-V of 159.2 feet per second [48.5 m/s], and a burn duration of 17 seconds, some 17 seconds. S

a11_0790900.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0790900.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 79 hours, 18 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 11. A quiet period at this time, as the Apollo 11 spacecraft continues its pass around the front side of the Moon. Our current altitude, very close to apolune, now reading 166.7 nautical miles [308.7 km]. Our orbital parameters; 170.2 by 61.2 nautical miles [315.2 by 113.3 km]. Current spacecraft weight in orbit; 71,622 pounds [32,487 kg]. We'll continue to keep the line up and continue to monitor the Apollo 11 crew. No doubt, at this time, preoccupied very probably with the alignment of their G&N platform.

a11_0792151.speaker: McCandless
a11_0792151.text: Roger. During the LOI-1 burn, your engine burned a little bit more propellant than we predicted, and consequently, we'd like to update - or send you a new TEI-4 PAD. Over.

a11_0792151.speaker: Collins
a11_0792151.text: Our chamber pressure onboard was higher that time, too. It's all on the onboard tape, the time entry, and the chamber pressure. But to make a long story short, it worked its way up to 100.

a11_0792151.speaker: McCandless
a11_0792151.text: And down here, we showed a chamber pressure of, on the order of, 103 to 104 psi during your burn on playback.

a11_0792151.speaker: McCandless
a11_0792151.text: Roger. TEI-4 revised: SPS/G&N: 38320, minus 0.55, plus 0.60; 084:30:27.49; plus 3138.0, plus 0347.5, minus 0103.2; roll NA: pitch, 034. Rest of the PAD is NA. Ullage, two jets, 16 seconds, undocked. No LOI-2. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0792151.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0792151.text: Understand; TEI-4 SPS/G&N: 38320, minus 0.55, plus 0.60; 084:30:27.49; plus 3138.0, plus 0347.5, minus 0103.2; NA, 034. All the rest of the PAD's NA. Two jets, 16 seconds, undocked. No LOI-2.

a11_0792151.speaker: McCandless
a11_0792151.text: 11, this is Houston. Readback correct. Out.

a11_0792151.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0792151.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 79 hours, 25 minutes. That maneuver PAD that was transmitted to the crew - that was TEI for Trans-Earth Injection burn for the fourth revolution, is a contingency PAD only, only to assure that it is properly onboard the spacecraft, if in the unlikely event it should become necessary to return. At the present time we read an altitude of 157.7 nautical miles [292.1 km] descending from apolune at this time. And our orbital parameters read 170.2 nautical miles [315.2 km], 61.2 nautical miles [113.3 km]. We're some 23 minutes away at the present time from Loss Of

a11_0793219.speaker: McCandless
a11_0793219.text: Roger. We've been looking at your systems data on playback, and everything is looking good. In particular, the SPS looks good. We'd like to remind you, though, of a request to perform this burn on the Bank A ball valves only, and you are Go for LOI-2. Also, we have currently in the Flight Plan, you scheduled tomorrow to start entering the LM at about 96 hours GET, and we'd like to know if you have any plans to initiate this ingress into the LM earlier. If so, we can call the people in ahead of time. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0793219.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0793219.text: Well, we didn't have any plans to, no. We just wanted to be ready at that time.

a11_0793219.speaker: McCandless
a11_0793219.text: Roger. We just wanted to make sure that we were ready when you were ready. Over.

a11_0793219.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0793219.text: Okay. And to get the sextant star in LOI-2, that's roll zero. Is that affirm?

a11_0793219.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0793219.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. We're some 14 minutes away now from Loss Of Signal with the Command and Service Module of Apollo 11. At 79 hours, 34 minutes; this is Apollo Control, Houston, standing by.

a11_0793219.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0793219.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 79 hours, 38 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 11. Apollo 11 now 130.4 nautical miles in altitude [241.5 km]. Current velocity reading; 5,131 feet per second [1,564 m/s]. Orbital parameters: apolune, 170.2 nautical miles [315.2 km] with a perilune reading 61.3 nautical miles [113.5 km]. Apollo 11, at this time, has completed its platform alignment and is maneuvering the spacecraft to its burn attitude. We're some 33 minutes away now from time of ignition for the Lunar Orbit Insertion number 2 burn; and we're 9 minutes, 40 seconds away from Loss Of Signal

a11_0794330.speaker: McCandless
a11_0794330.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Five minutes 'til LOS. And with respect to your request for the nitrogen bottle pressures pre-burn. Just before the burn, we were showing 2,270 pounds per square inch [15.7 MPa] on bottle Alpha and 2,350 [16.2 MPa] on bottle Bravo. Over.

a11_0794623.speaker: McCandless
a11_0794623.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Two minutes to LOS. Your AOS on the other side is 80:33:21, and the friendly White Team will see you when you come out from behind the Moon.

a11_0794623.speaker: Collins
a11_0794623.text: Okay. I don't blame you, Hank.

a11_0794623.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0794623.text: Mark. 30 minutes - 30 seconds now from predicted time of Loss Of Signal. Standing by.

a11_0794623.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0794623.text: This pitch angle is quite a bit off nominal; 196 instead of 212.

a11_0794623.speaker: Collins
a11_0794623.text: Yes, Shaffer screwed up - got to get his eccentric orbit.

a11_0794623.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0794623.text: Apollo 11 should now be passing out of range.

a11_0795100.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0795100.text: Yes, here we go - [garble] doesn't look bad.

a11_0795100.speaker: Collins
a11_0795100.text: No, I just got through aligning it a little while ago.

a11_0795100.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0795100.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 79 hours, 51 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 11. We're some 20 minutes away, at this time, for our time of ignition for Lunar Orbit Insertion burn number 2. This the fine-tune second burn in the series of two as we have inserted into lunar orbit. For LOI-2, the Apollo 11 will be heads down. The burn will be initiated near perilune as the spacecraft passes over the far side of the Moon. Retrograde, like LOI-1, but unlike Apollo's 8 and 10, the burn will not be targeted to place a spacecraft into a precise circular orbit. Taking what was learned on Apoll

a11_0795100.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0795100.text: Man Att, three, to Rate Command.

a11_0795100.speaker: Collins
a11_0795100.text: Okay, Manual Attitude, three, Rate Command. And - sunrise.

a11_0795100.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0795100.text: Sunrise's going to be 52:10 - and I missed [garble].

a11_0795100.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0795100.text: Man Att, three, to Rate Command, you got that?

a11_0795100.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0795100.text: BMAG Mode, three of them, to Rate 2.

a11_0795100.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0795100.text: Rot Control Power, Direct, two of them, Off.

a11_0795100.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0795100.text: SCS TVC, two, to Rate Command.

a11_0795100.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0795100.text: TVC Gimbal Drive, Pitch and Yaw, Auto.

a11_0795100.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0795100.text: Okay, what time do you have?

a11_0795100.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0795100.text: That TVC gimbal drive's taking up the power?

a11_0795100.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0795100.text: No. The TVC Gimbal Drive, Pitch and Yaw, to Auto. That didn't do anything, did it?

a11_0795100.speaker: Collins
a11_0795100.text: No. No, that didn't do a thing. Servo power's what takes it.

a11_0795100.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0795100.text: You know not to leave them on too long.

a11_0795100.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0795100.text: What did you get out of P30 as far as H A and H P ?

a11_0801036.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0801036.text: Mark. 30 seconds. Continuing to monitor - or read those displays that gave us our final readout prior to our passage to the backside of the Moon.

a11_0801036.speaker: Collins
a11_0801036.text: EMS Mode, Normal. Stand by for ullage. [Garble].

a11_0801036.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0801036.text: Mark. 5 seconds. We won't know for sure how the burn comes out until we reacquire.

a11_0801036.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0801036.text: Mark. Planned time for ignition. At 80 hours, 12 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 11, this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a11_0801036.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0801036.text: She's holding - she's holding - [garble] looks good.

a11_0803121.speaker: Collins
a11_0803121.text: That's it, I think, there, Neil - so pitch down.

a11_0803121.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0803121.text: Thank you. Is that right, Buzz?

a11_0803121.speaker: Collins
a11_0803121.text: All that - Where'd you ever hear that one, Buzz?

a11_0803121.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0803121.text: Oh, that's a bright one. I got to get that one [garble].

a11_0803121.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0803121.text: 150 - you don't want to take too many on this.

a11_0803121.speaker: Collins
a11_0803121.text: No. Might as well put the other one back on.

a11_0803121.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0803121.text: Mark. 2 minutes from time of predicted acquisition of the Apollo 11 spacecraft. During this upcoming pass, we'll have our second excursion on the part of the Apollo 11 crew into - into the Lunar Module. The LM is to be pressurized by a valve in the tunnel hatch and, as a point of interest, will remain pressurized following this period of activation and after the members of the Apollo 11 crew return to the Command Module. For this period of activation, it's definitely planned that Buzz will go into the LM and there is a distinct possibility that Commander Neil Armstrong could - could exercise h

a11_0803121.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0803121.text: Well, you might save that for some Earth shots.

a11_0803121.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0803121.text: I think it focused the second one a little bit better. I think it's beautiful. Just fabulous. Not really sure what you're looking at - but there's some mighty big fresh rocks down in that crater.

a11_0803121.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0803121.text: Mark. 10 seconds from predicted time of acquisition.

a11_0803121.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0803121.text: The walls actually look pock-marked. Sure enough, and they're not filled in. Pock-marked, and it looks like somebody's painted white paint vertically down the edges and then it's been eaten away.

a11_0803121.speaker: Collins
a11_0803121.text: Here is the Earth. Hey, I got the view over here.

a11_0803121.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0803121.text: I guess I'd better get the High Gain off, hadn't I?

a11_0803121.speaker: Collins
a11_0803121.text: Do we still got High Gain?

a11_0803121.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0803121.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston, standing by at this time at 80 hours, 35 minutes.

a11_0803530.speaker: Duke
a11_0803530.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We're standing by. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_0803530.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0803530.text: Do you want to talk to them?

a11_0803530.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0803530.text: ... Roger, Houston. Burn status report follows: Delta-T IG . zero; burn time, 17; angle through the pad values, Delta-V GX was plus 0.3...

a11_0803530.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0803530.text: ...V GY minus 0.0, V GZ minus 0.1, Delta-V C minus 5.2, fuel 362, Ox 364, unbalance plus 50, and our postburn Noun 94's, 66.1 by 54.4. Go ahead.

a11_0803530.speaker: Duke
a11_0803530.text: Roger. We copy, Neil. Would you say again the Delta-V Z ? We missed that. Over.

a11_0803530.speaker: Duke
a11_0803530.text: Roger. Copy the burn report. Sounds good.

a11_0803530.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0803530.text: It all looked good up here. [Long pause.]

a11_0803530.speaker: Duke
a11_0803530.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We missed your Delta-T IG and also your Delta Burn Time. Over.

a11_0803530.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0803530.text: Delta-T IG was zero and the burn time was 17 seconds.

a11_0803530.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0803530.text: You heard that report from Commander Neil Armstrong indicating that LOI-2 was all - came off almost precisely as planned.

a11_0803530.speaker: Duke
a11_0803530.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We'll be satisfied if you pump up the cabin to 5.4. Over.

a11_0803530.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0803530.text: Okay. We're showing about 5.2 right now.

a11_0803530.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0803530.text: And, Charlie, the LM/CM Delta-P is just over 1 pound right now.

a11_0804348.speaker: Duke
a11_0804348.text: Apollo 11, Houston. If you read, please attempt to acquire on the High Gain. We're having trouble locking up on the TM and we have no voice. Over.

a11_0804348.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0804348.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. You copied that report. We're standing by for Apollo 11 spacecraft to acquire on the High Gain Antenna. Meanwhile, onboard readings on orbital parameters were 66.1 nautical miles [122.4 km] by 54.4 nautical miles [100.7 km]; very close to - very close to the planned altitudes that were predicted prior to the LOI-2 burn. At 80 hours, 46 minutes; continuing to monitor; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a11_0804723.speaker: Duke
a11_0804723.text: Roger. We're reading you five-by. Go ahead. Over.

a11_0804723.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0804723.text: Roger. We have you on High Gain now.

a11_0804723.speaker: Duke
a11_0804723.text: Rog. We lost the TM and the voice for about 5 minutes here. We were - attempted a handover and fouled it up in some manner, but we got you back now. Thank you much.

a11_0804723.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0804723.text: Okay. We're pressurizing the LM at this time.

a11_0804723.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0804723.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 80 hours, 48 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 11. Very preliminary ground readings indicate an apolune of 65.6 [121.5 km]. Perilune; 53.7 [99.5 km].

a11_0805051.speaker: Duke
a11_0805051.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We have a P22 Auto optics update for you, if you're ready to copy. Over.

a11_0805051.speaker: Duke
a11_0805051.text: Rog, Mike. It's landmark Alpha 1: T1, 82:37:35; T2, 82:42:50. We're 7 miles north. Over. [Pause.]

a11_0805051.speaker: Collins
a11_0805051.text: Copy. P22. T1 time, 82:37:35; T2, 82:42:50. And the target is 7 miles north. Thank you.

a11_0805051.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0805051.text: That was passed up to Mike Collins, the Command Module Pilot, who will occupy himself during this pass on the - over the front side with landmark tracking activities. At 80 hours, 53 minutes into the flight, Apollo 11; we continue to monitor.

a11_0805532.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0805532.text: I get the distinct impression, Charlie, that mare surface laps up over the edge of the mountains at the shoreline.

a11_0805532.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0805532.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston, at 80 hours, 56 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 11. Our current velocity reading; 5,334 feet per second [1,626 m/s]. Current weight of the spacecraft in orbit, 70,505 pounds [31,981 kg].

a11_0805532.speaker: Duke
a11_0805532.text: Houston. On your comment about the mare lapping up to the terrain - mountainous terrain, is that an impression like a lava flow coming in around a prominence, Neil, or is it more - looks like it's sloping up at that point? Over.

a11_0805532.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0805532.text: It isn't true everywhere, but there's certainly places where there seems to be a slope downward towards the shoreline on the mare. In other words, from the mare down to the shoreline is a downward slope indicating that it might be a lava front.

a11_0805532.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0805532.text: That was Commander Neil Armstrong talking to our Capsule Communicator Charles Duke. Our current orbital readings show an apolune of 65.5 [121.3 km], a perilune of 53.7 nautical miles [99.5 km]. At 80 hours, 58 minutes into the flight; we continue to monitor and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a11_0805532.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0805532.text: Crossing Duke Island and Maskelyne W.

a11_0805532.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0805532.text: We just crossed Duke Island and Maskelyne W.

a11_0805532.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0805532.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston, at 81 hours into the flight of Apollo 11. A period of relative quiet. No doubt the Apollo 11 crew quite preoccupied in preparation for the activation of the LM. During this period of relative quiet, we'll pass along heart rates from the LOI-1 burn; that's LOI-1, not LOI-2. We have yet to receive those numbers. The heart rate for the Commander Neil Armstrong read 106; for the Command Module Pilot Mike Collins, 66; and for the Lunar Module Pilot Buzz Aldrin, we have a reading of 70. At 81 hours, 1 minute into the flight of Apollo 11; this is Apollo Control, Houst

a11_0805532.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0805532.text: Apollo Control, Houston; at 81 hours, 5 minutes into the flight. Still a period of relative quiet. Our ground readings indicate that the Apollo 11 spacecraft has completed its program 52, that's to align the inertial platform. Indications from the ground are that it - this activity went very well. And at 81 hours, 6 minutes, continuing to monitor; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a11_0810500.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0810500.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston, at 81 hours, 15 minutes. It's been an extremely quiet pass. No doubt, the Apollo 11 crew quite busy at this time. We expect at the time entry is made into the Lunar Module, Apollo 11, as a matter of fact, will be out of acquisition, traversing over the far side of the Moon. At the present time, we read an altitude, current altitude reading of 56.7 nautical miles [105.0 km]. Our ground displays indicate an apolune of 65.4 [121.1 km], a perilune of 53.8 [99.6 km] and a spacecraft velocity of 5,364 feet per second [1,635 m/s]. Continuing to monitor, this is Apollo

a11_0812257.speaker: Duke
a11_0812257.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We're wondering if you've started into the LM yet. Over.

a11_0812257.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0812257.text: We have the CSM hatch out, the drogue and probe removed and stowed, and we're just about ready to open the LM hatch now.

a11_0812257.speaker: Duke
a11_0812257.text: Roger. Thank you much, Neil. We'll be standing by.

a11_0812257.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0812257.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 81 hours, 24 minutes now into the flight. The silence of conversation between Mission Control Center, Houston and the crew has broken there moments ago. Charlie Duke called up Apollo 11 and spoke with Neil Armstrong, who indicated that the hatch was out and the probe and drogue removed, and they were about ready to open the Lunar Module hatch. Our current altitude shows 54.7 nautical miles [101.3 km], apolune 65.4 [121.1 km], perilune 53.8 [99.6 km]. Interestingly enough, the part of the LM activation which we will follow most closely will be at time of reac

a11_0812257.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0812257.text: Okay, Charlie. We're in the LM. The docking index mark is the same.

a11_0812257.speaker: Duke
a11_0812257.text: Roger. We copy. [Long pause.]

a11_0812257.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0812257.text: You heard that report from Neil Armstrong. They are now in the Lunar Module.

a11_0812257.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0812257.text: Charlie, there just doesn't seem to be any slow way to get that Repress to Auto without making a big bang.

a11_0812257.speaker: Duke
a11_0812257.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Say again. Over.

a11_0812257.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0812257.text: Roger. There just doesn't seem to be any slow way to get the Repress from Closed to Auto and avoid a big bang. Over.

a11_0812257.speaker: Duke
a11_0812257.text: Oh, we copy, Buzz. Thank you much. Out.

a11_0812257.speaker: Duke
a11_0812257.text: We concur with that, Buzz. [Pause.]

a11_0812257.speaker: Duke
a11_0812257.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We'll have LOS 81:45, next AOS - Stand by.

a11_0812257.speaker: Duke
a11_0812257.text: Next AOS 82:32. Over.

a11_0812257.speaker: Collins
a11_0812257.text: Houston, Apollo 11. I'm going to start a maneuver to P22 attitude at this time.

a11_0812257.speaker: Duke
a11_0812257.text: 11. Roger. We copy. Over.

a11_0812257.speaker: Collins
a11_0812257.text: Okay. We're noticing some water inside the Command Module for the first time. There's a little puddle of it on the aft bulkhead sort of like 101 had.

a11_0812257.speaker: Duke
a11_0812257.text: Roger.

a11_0812257.speaker: Collins
a11_0812257.text: I'd like to know how EECOM wants to get rid of it. There are a number of different ways and what does he think is the best one?

a11_0812257.speaker: Duke
a11_0812257.text: We'll be with you in a moment, Mike. Stand by.

a11_0812257.speaker: Collins
a11_0812257.text: No big rush. It'll wait until the next rev or two.

a11_0812257.speaker: Duke
a11_0812257.text: All right.

a11_0812257.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0812257.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 81 hours, 30 minutes now into the flight, Apollo 11. The Apollo 11 Commander and Lunar Module pilots appear to be a little bit ahead on their time lines in the LM activation period. Meanwhile, Command Module Pilot Mike Collins proceeding further with his landmark tracking exercises. Mike also reported a little puddle of water inside the Command Module near the aft bulkhead. His reference to 'like 101' referred to the Apollo 7 spacecraft which was commanded by Walter Schirra. Our current altitude, 54 nautical miles [100 km]; current apolune, 65.4 [121.1 km]; our

a11_0814100.speaker: Collins
a11_0814100.text: Both of those - those things are in here.

a11_0814100.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0814100.text: [Garble] worry about nothing goes in there [garble].

a11_0814100.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0814100.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. We're now some five minutes away from Loss Of Signal with the Apollo 11 spacecraft. We currently show an altitude of 54.2 nautical miles [100.4 km], apolune 65.4 [121.1 km], perilune 53.9 nautical miles [99.8 km]. Flight Director Milt Windler now talking with various members of his flight control team. We would expect a final bit of conversation prior to Loss Of Signal with the Apollo 11 spacecraft. We'll keep our line up and continue to monitor conversations that could transpire prior to Loss Of Signal. Standing by at 81 hours, 41 minutes into the flight, Apol

a11_0814100.speaker: Duke
a11_0814100.text: Hello, Apollo 11, Houston. We've played back the LOI-2 burn. It looked really good to us. The systems were all good. We got an orbit on the limited amount of tracking at 65.4 by a 53.9. Over.

a11_0814100.speaker: Collins
a11_0814100.text: Sounds good, Houston.

a11_0814100.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0814100.text: I need that film now.

a11_0814100.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0814100.text: Okay.

a11_0814100.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0814100.text: [Garble].

a11_0814100.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0814100.text: Okay, want to get film. It's a long trip to the film container.

a11_0814100.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0814100.text: Mark. 3 minutes now from predicted time of Loss Of Signal.

a11_0814100.speaker: Collins
a11_0814100.text: You want something?

a11_0814100.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0814100.text: Oh, shoot. I'm going to have trouble getting in there.

a11_0814100.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0814100.text: Mark. 2 minutes now from time of LOS.

a11_0814100.speaker: Collins
a11_0814100.text: How's it going, Neil? You getting any?

a11_0814100.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0814100.text: [Garble].

a11_0814100.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0814100.text: Well - Buzz, the 70-millimeter container's only got one black and white and one color in it - Isn't it supposed to...

a11_0814100.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0814100.text: Mark. 1 minute now from time of LOS.

a11_0814100.speaker: Collins
a11_0814100.text: That's - that's not - that's mine.

a11_0814100.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0814100.text: You've got the wrong one.

a11_0814100.speaker: Collins
a11_0814100.text: No, that's not the right one.

a11_0814100.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0814100.text: The one...

a11_0814100.speaker: Collins
a11_0814100.text: The one you want, Neil, is way over here in - R-13.

a11_0814100.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0814100.text: No, it's not in there. It was on my girth shelf.

a11_0814100.speaker: Collins
a11_0814100.text: Okay.

a11_0814100.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0814100.text: Oh, okay, there it is. Did you get that one put back?

a11_0814100.speaker: Collins
a11_0814100.text: No, but I will.

a11_0814100.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0814100.text: Okay, appreciate it. I had it in my mind that - our...

a11_0814100.speaker: Collins
a11_0814100.text: You want to do something to the polarizing filter, Neil?

a11_0814100.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0814100.text: Uh...

a11_0814100.speaker: Collins
a11_0814100.text: I'll stick it up there on the ceiling. There's a...

a11_0814100.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0814100.text: ...not really.

a11_0814100.speaker: Collins
a11_0814100.text: ...we got room for it up there.

a11_0814100.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0814100.text: We've now had Loss Of Signal with Apollo 11. At 81 hours, 45 minutes into the flight; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a11_0814100.speaker: Collins
a11_0814100.text: You want the 16-millimeter while you're down here, Neil?

a11_0814100.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0814100.text: Yes.

a11_0814100.speaker: Collins
a11_0814100.text: The 16-millimeter bag as well?

a11_0814100.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0814100.text: Yes, I'll take that one, too.

a11_0814100.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0814100.text: Okay.

a11_0814100.speaker: Collins
a11_0814100.text: Well, that - damn stuff won't stick. Haven't got a piece of Velcro on there yet.

a11_0814100.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0814100.text: You're not [garble].

a11_0822933.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0822933.text: But I can't see [garble] - I see the Earth, but it's a lousy picture.

a11_0822933.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0822933.text: We have acquisition. We are receiving telemetry data at this time. Hawaii and Goldstone both have acquired.

a11_0822933.speaker: Collins
a11_0822933.text: Could you wait just one? I'm right in the middle of the event-timer setting.

a11_0822933.speaker: Duke
a11_0822933.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We're standing by. Out.

a11_0822933.speaker: Collins
a11_0822933.text: Okay, Houston. We'll be doing P22 in just a couple of minutes here.

a11_0822933.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0822933.text: You want to come in, Neil? Going in?

a11_0822933.speaker: Duke
a11_0822933.text: Roger. We copy all that. You're looking good.

a11_0822933.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0822933.text: That was Mike Collins indicating he would be doing a little additional landmark tracking. We shall hear further from him shortly.

a11_0823800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0823800.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 82 hours, 38 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 11. Only a single contact with Apollo 11 thus far this pass, when Mike Collins identified he was still involved with program 22, the auto optics landmark tracking activity. We expect additional conversation as the pass transpires. Presently we're reading on our orbit displays an altitude of 65.1 nautical miles [120.6 km], apolune 65.3 nautical miles [120.9 km], a perilune of 54 nautical miles [100 km]. We currently show a velocity on the Apollo 11 spacecraft of 5,318 feet per second - 5,318 feet per second [1,6

a11_0824701.speaker: Collins
a11_0824701.text: Roger. You copy that Noun 49 on your downlink? If you've had enough time, I'll proceed.

a11_0824701.speaker: Duke
a11_0824701.text: We got it. Go ahead, Mike.

a11_0824701.speaker: Collins
a11_0824701.text: Look, what gimbal angle was that when - on the pitch - when that activity started, just out of curiosity?

a11_0824701.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0824701.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston, at 82 hours, 48 minutes now into the flight, Apollo 11. Our air/ground sounding somewhat noisy, this being because we're utilizing the Omni antenna for downlink. This, a requirement because of the attitude required for landmark tracking for Program 22. At 82 hours, 48 minutes continuing to monitor; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a11_0824701.speaker: Collins
a11_0824701.text: Okay, now, the Flight Plan says where we want to stop [garble], that says so right here - pitch 229 is where we want to stop.

a11_0824701.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0824701.text: Okay, we've gone by that, however, quite a ways.

a11_0825027.speaker: Duke
a11_0825027.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We see a Noun 89. You can do the Verb 34 now. Over. Beat me to it.

a11_0825027.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0825027.text: A beautiful view out here, Neil.

a11_0825027.speaker: Collins
a11_0825027.text: Okay, we didn't waste any gas by doing what we did, but what we wasted gas by was that goddamn DAP activity. I don't understand that. Just like the simulator.

a11_0825027.speaker: Collins
a11_0825027.text: You got a good view there, Neil?

a11_0825027.speaker: Collins
a11_0825027.text: All that procedure for P22 seemed to work very well. The only thing that was a little odd, is that there was some DAP thruster activity. I had pitch in Accel Command, and roll and yaw in Rate Command, and somehow, roll and yaw got excited and the DAP went into a flurry of thruster firing. We've noticed the same thing in the CMS, and just written it off as a CMS peculiarity.

a11_0825027.speaker: Duke
a11_0825027.text: Roger. We saw that activity, Mike. We'll see if we can track it down and let you know. Over.

a11_0825027.speaker: Collins
a11_0825027.text: Well, one P22 out of the way. Ho, ho, ho!

a11_0825027.speaker: Collins
a11_0825027.text: ...they're sort of inconclusive because I marked - see, they gave me...

a11_0825027.speaker: Duke
a11_0825027.text: Apollo 11, Houston. You can proceed to the sleep attitude now. Over.

a11_0825027.speaker: Collins
a11_0825027.text: Hey, how about holding this for just a little bit?

a11_0825027.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0825027.text: Yes, let's hold this attitude a little bit. I want to look at the...

a11_0825027.speaker: Collins
a11_0825027.text: Boy, that's beautiful out there, isn't it?

a11_0825027.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0825027.text: ...TPI approach. Man, this is really something, you ought to look at this. You want to watch our approach into the landing site. You got to watch right through this window. We're coming over - we just passed Mount Marilyn. We're coming up on Maskelyne series here - straight out ahead, coming into the landing area.

a11_0825027.speaker: Collins
a11_0825027.text: Houston, we're holding inertial a little while to study the approach to the landing zone.

a11_0825027.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0825027.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 82 hours, 55 minutes. Our current spacecraft altitude, 62.1 nautical miles [115.0 km]. Our orbital parameters, essentially the same at 65.3 [120.9 km], 53.9 [99.8 km]. So at 82 hours, 55 minutes; we continue to monitor and this Apollo Control, Houston.

a11_0825027.speaker: Collins
a11_0825027.text: There go Sidewinder and Diamondback. God, if you ever saw checkpoints in your life, those are it.

a11_0825027.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0825027.text: But [garble] we don't get to see them.

a11_0825027.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0825027.text: No, we roll over right here at this little - well, you see Boot Hill coming up right here?

a11_0825027.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0825027.text: And just beyond it that's - that crater right on track there, the big one?

a11_0825027.speaker: Collins
a11_0825027.text: That's Mount Marilyn? Past Boot Hill?

a11_0825027.speaker: Collins
a11_0825027.text: Oh God, look at that Moltke, he's my favorite [garble]. Look at that son of a bitch. You see all those roads - triangular roads leading right past him?

a11_0825650.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0825650.text: Houston, this is Apollo 11, in the Eagle. Apollo 11 in the Eagle. And I got a beautiful view of the whole landing area.

a11_0825650.speaker: Duke
a11_0825650.text: Apollo 11, Houston. You are breaking up badly. Say again. Over.

a11_0825650.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0825650.text: Roger. I can see the entire landing area from the position I'm in, looking out the left window in the LM.

a11_0825650.speaker: Duke
a11_0825650.text: Roger, Buzz. Understand you can see the entire landing area looking out the LM windows. Over.

a11_0825650.speaker: Collins
a11_0825650.text: [Garble].

a11_0825650.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0825650.text: That's right.

a11_0825650.speaker: Mission Control
a11_0825650.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. That was a report from Lunar Module Pilot Buzz Aldrin, that he could see the entire landing area out the window. At 82 hours, 58 minutes; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a11_0825650.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0825650.text: Boy, that sure is eerie looking.

a11_0825650.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0825650.text: Isn't that something?

a11_0825650.speaker: Unidentified speaker
a11_0825650.text: [Garble].

a11_0825650.speaker: Collins
a11_0825650.text: [Garble] enough of a shot down there, but you can't find a single spot on the surface that doesn't look [garble] 1-degree sun angle, that's - that's just a lousy sun angle.

a11_0825650.speaker: Armstrong
a11_0825650.text: That's spectacular out there - Looks like you're flying right into the side of a mountain, doesn't it?

a11_0825650.speaker: Collins
a11_0825650.text: Yes, sure does.

a11_0825650.speaker: Aldrin
a11_0825650.text: I missed taking a picture of it, [garble].

a11_0825650.speaker: Collins
