a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Like an AGS to PGNS align? Over.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. We're standing by for it. (Long Pause) [Armstrong - "Clearly, we were trying to initialize AGS so that, if we would have to use it, we would have taken some of the drift out of it."]

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Propellant quantity (garbled)

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Eagle, Houston. You are Stay for T2. Over.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Correction, you're...

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. Stay for T2. We thank you.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger, sir. [Comm Break]

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Tranquility Base, Houston. We recommend you exit P12. Over. [Comm Break. Houston is calling polite attention to the fact that Neil and Buzz have forgotten to exit program P12.] 102:55:16 Armstrong: Hey, Houston, that may have seemed like a very long final phase. The Auto targeting was taking us right into a football-field-sized crater, with a large number of big boulders and rocks for about one or two crater diameters around it, and it required us going in P66 and flying manually over the rock field to find a reasonably good area. 102:55:49 Duke: Roger. We copy. It was beautiful from here, Tra

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1024746-1033957.text: We'll get to the details of what's around here (later), but it looks like a collection of just about every variety of shape, angularity, granularity, about every variety of rock you could find. The color is...Well, it varies pretty much depending on how you're looking relative to the zero-phase point. There doesn't appear to be too much of a general color at all. However, it looks as though some of the rocks and boulders, of which there are quite a few in the near area... It looks as though they're going to have some interesting colors to them. Over. [The point on the horizon directly opposite

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. Copy. Sounds good to us, Tranquility. We'll let you press on through the simulated countdown, and we'll talk to you later. Over.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Okay. This one-sixth g is just like the airplane.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Rog. Tranquility. Be advised there're lots of smiling faces in this room and all over the world. Over.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Well, there are two of them up here.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Rog. That was a beautiful job, you guys.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Collins
a11a1024746-1033957.text: And don't forget one (smiling face) in the command module.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Rog. (Long Pause) [In his extraordinary book, Carrying the Fire, Mike recalls that, because he was hearing Neil and Buzz on a relay from Houston, it was two and a half seconds before he heard Neil say "Well there are two of them (smiling faces) up here." Mike wrote that, as soon as he heard Neil, "I say 'And don't forget one in the Command Module'; but, in the meantime Houston has heard Neil and has answered him, 'Roger. That was a beautiful job, you guys.' I was more than a little embarrassed to hear their message coming in as I was mouthing mine. It sounded like I was asking them not to forg

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: That's confirmed by our local observation.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. (Pause) [Because of the uneven terrain, the LM is tilted slightly backward. However, this is the smallest pitch/roll deviation of any of the landed LMs. Table 9.6.IV in the Apollo 11 Mission Report gives the orientation of the LM on the surface as indicated by the PGNS and AGS : pitch, +4.4 degrees (tilted back); roll, +0.5 degrees (Buzz's side of the spacecraft slightly higher than Neil's; and yaw, +13.3 degrees (a counterclockwise rotation around the vertical axis, hiding the LM shadow from Neil's view).]

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Collins
a11a1024746-1033957.text: And thanks for putting me on relay, Houston. I was missing all the action.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. We'll enable MSFN (Manned Spaceflight Network) relay. (Pause)

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Collins
a11a1024746-1033957.text: I just got it, I think. [Mike is in an orbit 60 nautical miles (110 km) above the surface, with a period of about 1 hour 58 minutes. In that orbit, he could maintain line-of-sight communications with the LM until he was below the Tranquility Base horizon, which would happen about 20/360ths of an orbit after passing over the landing site, or about 6.5 minutes. He passed over the landing site about about 102:41 which, because Eagle was decelerating throughout powered descent, was about five minutes before Eagle landed. He lost direct comm with the LM one or two mintues later and, thereafter, had

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Rog, Columbia. This is Houston. Say something. They (the LM crew) ought to be able to hear you. Over.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Collins
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. Tranquility Base, it sure sounded great from up here. You guys did a fantastic job.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Thank you. Just keep that orbiting base ready for us up there now.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Collins
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Will do. (Long Pause)

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Columbia, Houston. LOS (Loss of Signal) 103:27; AOS (Acquisition of Signal) 104:13 . Over.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Collins
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Thank you. [Mike will go behind the Moon in about a half hour and re-emerge about forty-five minutes later.] [Comm Break.] 103:00:44 Duke: Tranquility Base, Houston. All your consumables are solid. You're looking good in every respect. We copy the DPS (Descent Propulsion System) venting. Everything is copasetic. Over.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Thank you, Houston. [Comm Break. They want to depressurize the propellant tanks so that any heating of the LM while it sits on the surface won't pressurize and possibly rupture a tank. The tanks are depressurized by venting the helium in the descent stage.] ["Copasetic" is a word meaning "very satisfactory" which originate in about 1919 and was a part of popular, coffee-house culture during the early and mid-1950s when Charlie was in high school and the US Naval Academy.]

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Houston, the guys that said that we wouldn't be able to tell precisely where we are, are the winners today. We were a little busy worrying about program alarms and things like that in the part of the descent where we would normally be picking out our landing spot; and aside from a good look at several of the craters we came over in the final descent, I haven't been able to pick out the things on the horizon as a reference as yet.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Rog, Tranquility. No sweat. We'll figure out...We'll figure it out. Over. (Long Pause) [During our 1991 mission review in Santa Fe, Buzz wanted to talk about the decision to do a simulated countdown at this point in the mission.] [Aldrin - "I've always had a question that I've never gotten around to posing to the other crews. Jack (Schmitt) and I had gotten involved in some of the timeline discussion - oh, maybe a year or less (before Apollo 11) - about what one ought to be doing right after you land. And it occurred to me that it would have been a number of days since we last trained in the s

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: You might be interested to know that I don't think we notice any difficulty at all in adapting to one-sixth g. It seems immediately natural to move in this environment.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger, Tranquility. We copy. Over. [They have probably removed the waist-to-floor tethers that they wore during the landing to keep them firmly in place.] [Aldrin - "I can't remember hooking the tethers up before lift-off (from the Moon)."] [Armstrong - "I remember hooking them up, but I can't recall when that was."] [The relevant item is "Attach Restraints", which is the second line of Surface Checklist page Sur-58 .] [Aldrin - "You remember hooking yours up; I don't remember hooking mine up. But, I didn't notice that I was floating around when we got into orbit, either."] [During the landing

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: The area out the left-hand window is a relatively level plain cratered with a fairly large number of craters of the 5- to 50-foot variety; and some ridges (which are) small, 20, 30 feet high, I would guess; and literally thousands of little, 1- and 2-foot craters around the area. We see some angular blocks out several hundred feet in front of us that are probably two feet in size and have angular edges. There is a hill in view, just about on the ground track ahead of us. Difficult to estimate, but might be a half a mile or a mile.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger, Tranquility. We copy. Over. [The 'hill' can be seen just to the left of the LM shadow in AS11-37- 5451 , which Neil took out his window prior to the EVA, and in AS11-37- 5454 and 5455 , which Buzz took out his window. These hills are discussed in section 4.5.4 in a new photogrammetric investigation of Tranquility Base by Journal Contributor Vlad Pustynski. The hills are raised portions of the rim of a 200m crater and are about 200m from the LM.]

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Collins
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Sounds like it looks a lot better than it did yesterday...

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: (Garbled under Mike)

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Collins
a11a1024746-1033957.text: ...at that very low sun angle. It looked rough as a (corn) cob then. [With the Sun very low in the sky, even shallow, rimless craters are filled with shadow while those with rims cast long shadows on the surrounding terrain.]

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: It really was rough, Mike. Over the targeted landing area, it was extremely rough, cratered, and large numbers of rocks that were probably some - many - larger than 5 or 10 feet in size.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Collins
a11a1024746-1033957.text: When in doubt, land long.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: That's what we did. (Long Pause)

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Tranquility, Houston. After you get through this P57, we'd like an E-memory dump. Over. [P57 is the platform alignment, beginning with a gravity alignment and followed by an alignment done with star sightings. The E-memory dump is simply a transmission to Houston of the contents of the computer's erasable memory. See Eldon Hall's Journey to the Moon: History of the Apollo Guidance Computer .]

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. After this first P57, you want an E-memory dump.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: That's affirmative. (Pause) Columbia, Houston. We have a P22 update for you, if you're ready to copy. Over.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Collins
a11a1024746-1033957.text: At your service, sir. [For the LM, P22 is the program which uses the rendezvous radar ( LM-9 photo by Randy Attwood) to track the Command Module as it passes overhead.] [Aldrin - "His P22 was different than our P22. What he was trying to do was look in the sextant and try to see us."] [Armstrong - "I assume that what they're sending him are pointing angles for the sextant." (True)]

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Rog, Mike. T1, 104:32:18; T2, 104:37:28. And that is 4 miles south. This is based on the targeted landing site. Over. [The statement "4 miles south" indicates that Houston thinks the landing site is four miles south of Mike's ground track. Figure 5-14 in the Apollo 11 Mission Report shows the sextant targets that Mike tried on various passes over the landing site. Each of the small squares is 1 kilometer on a side and the circles, which represent the approximate sextant field-of-view, are each about 3.2 km (2 miles) in diameter. This first sextant target circle is, in fact, the only one that c

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Collins
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Okay. Roger. Understand. Based on the targeted landing site; T1, 104:32:18; T2, 104:37:28, and 4 miles south.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Collins
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Do you have any idea whether they landed left or right of center line? Just a little bit long, is that all we know?

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Apparently that's about all we can tell. Over.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Collins
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Okay. Thank you. (Long Pause)

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Tranquility, Houston...

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: And, Houston, our mission timer is now reading 902:34:47 and static. [The timer is giving a nonsense reading and isn't advancing.]

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. Copy your mission timer's now static. It...Say again the time.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. Copy, Tranquility. That gravity align looked good to us. We see you recycling.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Well, no. I was trying to get time, (Verb)16 (Noun) 65, out, and somehow it proceeded on to the 06 22 before I could do a Verb 32 Enter. I want to log a time here, and then I'd like to know whether you want me to proceed on the torquing angles or to go back and reenter again before torquing. Over. [David Woods tells us that Verb 16 - monitor in decimal form - and Noun 65 - time from the computer - would give Buzz the current Ground Elapsed Time. Buzz is doing the gravity alignment P57, on checklist page Sur-2 , which includes a step (Verb) 06 (Noun) 22, which displays the gimbal angles. Eviden

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Rog, Buzz. Standby. [Comm Break] [Armstrong - "We needed to establish an initial attitude for the (inertial) platform. And the technique is to use a local vertical for one axis and use gravity to do that alignment. And the second is to use a star to align the platform in yaw, essentially."] [Jones - "In other words, what you need to know is the absolute orientation of the platform so that, when you're ready to leave, the spacecraft will know which way to go."] [Armstrong - "Precisely."]

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Tranquility, Houston. We'd like you to recall P57 and run through the gravity align one more time. Over.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. I concur with that. [Armstrong - "This type of alignment had never previously been done, and it was our interest, I think - since that would have to be done before launch - to get a chance to check that procedure out if we needed it for the first revolution (that is, needed to return to orbit when Mike came around again) or, if not, to have at least have gone through it before we had to do it the next day."] [Aldrin - "If you're going to have problems, it's best to have them happen now when you've got a lot of time."]

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger, Tranquility. For the mission timer, two suggestions. Check the circuit breaker, panel 11; also, Reset and attempt to start. That nine in the first digit might have something to do with it. Over. [Circuit breaker panel 11 ( CB(11) ) is at Neil's left shoulder while panel 16 ( CB(16) ) is at Buzz's right shoulder on the other side of the spacecraft.]

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Okay. We've tried both of those. If the circuit breaker is in, when I put it in Reset, I get 902:04:40. When I release it now, I get 902:04:49. I'm going to cycle the circuit breaker.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: I cycled the circuit breaker and got all nines. (Pause) And it will not now reset from all nines.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. (Long Pause) [Journal Contributor Frank O'Brien writes, "Also, the reason why cycling the breaker worked was most likely because a weak solder joint expanded from the heat, opening the circuit. Pulling the breaker allowed the equiment to cool off, reseal the cracked joint and continue operation."]

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Tranquility, Houston. We'll research this problem and be back with you momentarily on the mission event time - correction - the mission timer.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Okay. (Long Pause) 103:12:44 Armstrong: I'd say the color of the local surface is very comparable to that we observed from orbit at this Sun angle - about 10 degrees Sun angle, or that nature. It's pretty much without color. It's gray; and it's a very white, chalky gray, as you look into the zero-phase line. And it's considerably darker gray, more like ashen gray as you look out 90 degrees to the Sun. Some of the surface rocks in close here that have been fractured or disturbed by the rocket engine plume are coated with this light gray on the outside; but where they've been broken, they displa

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. Tranquility, we see the Noun 93. (Pause) Verb 34.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. I assume you want us (to)... (Hears "Verb 34") Roger. (Long Pause) [Buzz is at the bottom of Sur-2 . David Woods writes, "Noun 93 is the delta gyro angles which give the differences between the prealignment and post-alignment orientation of the platform. It is essentially a measure of how much the platform had to move to achieve proper alignment." The Greek letter delta ( Δ / δ), the ancestor of the modern Latin letter ' D / d', is often used in mathematics to indicate a difference, in this case, a difference in gyro angles.] 103:14:32 Duke: Tranquility, Houston. Please vent

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Okay. Ox going now. (Pause)

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Tranquility, Houston. You can open both fuel and Ox vent now. Over.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Okay.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Houston, Tranquility standing by for Go on AGS to PGNS align and a lunar align. Over.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Stand by. (Pause) Tranquility, Houston. You are Go for the AGS to PGNS align, and then the lunar align. Over. 103:15:26 Aldrin: Roger. (Long Pause) [Buzz is at the end of the top paragraph on Sur-3 . Houston will look over the proposed alignment before it is loaded.] [Aldrin - "You've got the previous alignment in the AGS and you've just re-aligned the PGNS and, if that (new PGNS alignment) isn't very good, you don't want to screw up the one in the AGS. If it is (good), you store it in the AGS."]

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Tranquility, Houston. Please vent the fuel. It's increasing rapidly. Over. (Pause)

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: We show 30 psi in the fuel and 30 in the oxidizer (which are not unusual readings).

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. We're reading somewhat different than that. Standby.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: The fuel temperature is reading 64 in the descent, and the oxidizer...(Clarifying what he has just said) That's descent (tank) 2. And the oxidizer is off-scale low. Descent 1 is showing 61 in the fuel and 65 in the oxidizer.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. Standby. (Pause) Tranquility, Houston. Please take the fuel vent switch and hold it open. Over. [Armstrong - "That switch was momentary to the vent position, which would account for why you couldn't just leave it open."]

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Okay. We're holding it open. Indicating about 24 psi on board.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. (Long Pause)

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Now indicating 20 psi on the fuel side.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: And 22 in the OX.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. [Comm Break]

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Now indicating 15 psi in both tanks.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. (Long Pause)

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Tranquility, Houston. If you haven't done so, you can release the fuel vent switch now. Over.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. [Comm Break] [Aldrin - (Chuckling) "You were holding the switch all that time?"] [Armstrong - "Yes."]

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Tranquility, Houston. We have an indication that we've frozen up the descent-fuel helium heat exchanger - and with some fuel trapped in the line between there and the valves...And the pressure we're looking at is increasing there. Over.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. Understand. (Long Pause) [Later, the NASA Public Affairs commentator tells the press that there is a small amount of fluid trapped in a line and, if the pressure had continued to increase, the worst that could have happened would have been a small leak which would then have relieved the pressure. A fuller discussion is linked here .]

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Tranquility Base, Houston. If you have not done so, please close both Fuel and Ox vents now. Over.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: They're closed.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Thank you, sir. (Long Pause)

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: From the surface, we could not see any stars out the window; but out my overhead hatch (means the overhead rendezvous window), I'm looking at the Earth. It's big and bright and beautiful. Buzz is going to give a try at seeing some stars through the optics. 103:22:54 Duke: Roger, Tranquility. We understand. Must be a beautiful sight. Over. [Comm Break] [Gene Cernan says that, while standing in the shadow of the Apollo 17 LM, he could see some stars while he was outside. I asked the 11 crew if they had made any such experiment.] [Armstrong - "I don't recall doing it on the surface. We tried a go

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Columbia, Houston. Two minutes to LOS. You're looking great going over the hill. Over. (Pause)

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Collins
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Okay. Thank you. Glad to hear the system's looking good. You have a suggested attitude for me? This one here seems all right.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Stand by. (Pause)

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Collins
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Let me know when it's lunch time, will you?

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Say again.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Collins
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Ah, disregard.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Columbia, Houston. You got a good attitude right there. 103:25:37 Collins: Okay. Thank you. [Long Comm Break. NASA Public Affairs announces to the media that Neil's heart rate at PDI was 110; at touchdown it was 150; now it is in the 90s. While they were in the spacecraft, only one of them could be monitored at a time and, for obvious reasons, it was always the Commander who was monitored during the landing. Of all of the landing-mission Commanders, Neil had the highest heart rate at touchdown. See figure 12-1 in the Apollo 11 Mission Report.] [Armstrong - "That's not surprising."] [Pete Conra

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Tranquility Base, Houston. If you want me to, I can give you a hack on the mission time, every 30 minutes. Over. (Long Pause) Tranquility, Houston. I'm counting down to T3 time. If you'd like to give me a hack, we can set up an event timer. Over. [T3 is the next pre-programmed launch opportunity, in this case a chance to catch Mike when he passes overhead on his second post-landing pass.]

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Okay. How about counting up?

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. You want it counting up? Stand by. [Comm Break. While Buzz is doing the star sightings, they have shades drawn over the LM windows, hence the lack of commentary by Neil about the view outside.]

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Tranquility, Houston. On my Mark, 62:30. Mark. 62:30 past PDI. (Pause)

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: What we're looking for, Charlie, is the time counting up to T2 that'll be equal to 60 minutes...(Correcting himself) Or, at T3 be equal to 60 minutes at T3.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger. We'll have it for you. (Long Pause) [They have an event timer on the control panel - essentially a stopwatch - and they want to set it so that it reaches 60:00 at T3. The reason for doing this is so that, if they have lost comm with Houston and need to launch, they will know when to do so for a relatively easy rendezvous with Mike.]

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Tranquility Base, Houston. Reset the event timer to zero. And, on my Mark at 103:39:41, we'll give you a hack, and it'll be 1 hour (prior to T3). Over.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Roger.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Duke
a11a1024746-1033957.text: And we've got almost 3 minutes to go, Neil. Over.

a11a1024746-1033957.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1024746-1033957.text: Okay. [Comm Break]

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Tranquility, Houston. We see the star-angle difference. Looks good.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Okay. That last star was Navi , and it wasn't too well distinguishable. I can see where that error could come in. I think for the gravity alignment with one star, Rigel will be quite good.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. Stand by on the Noun 93. (Long Pause) Hello, Tranquility Base. Houston. We'd like you to torque that. Over. [Comm Break. They are about two-thirds of the way down Surface Checklist page Sur-5 .]

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Houston, this is Tranquility. Do you want us to accept this position? Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Tranquility, Houston. We're looking at it. Stand by. We'd like you to pull the circuit breaker on panel 11 for the mission timer. Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Rog. I've already done that, Charlie.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Okay. (Long Pause) [The reason for pulling the circuit breaker is to let the cracked solder joint cool down enough that it will stay closed the launch and ascent - which it does.]

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Tranquility, Houston. We'd like you to reject that RLS (Reference Landing Site). Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: And, Tranquility Base, Houston. We'd like you to call...After this, call P00 and give us a E(rasable)-memory dump. (Long Pause)

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Okay. Here comes the E-memory dump.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. (Long Pause) [They are at the bottom of Sur-5 and, once they are done, they will raise the shades and take photographs out Neil's window to the south and out Buzz's window to the north.]

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: And we got 1106. [O'Brien - "A program alarm 1106 is an error during an E-memory dump."]

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. (Long Pause) Hello, Tranquility Base; Houston. Did I copy Program Alarm 1106 from you? Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Rog. That's affirmative.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Okay. Stand by.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Could that, by any chance, be due to the fact that I flashed the updata link switch to Data while that was going on? Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Stand by. (Pause) Hello, Tranquility Base; Houston. The SPAN guys think that's conceivable. Stand by. I think we want another Verb 74.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Okay. Standing by. (Pause)

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Hello, Tranquility Base; Houston. We'd like another Verb 74. Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. Here it comes. (Long Pause)

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Tranquility Base, Houston. On my Mark it will be GET (Ground Elapsed Time) 103:53 [That is, Ground Elapsed Time 103:53:00 since launch. He actually means 103:54.]

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Mark. 53...Correction, 54.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Hello, Tranquility. Houston. We have the LM ascent Pad. If you're ready to go. Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Stand by. (Pause) [Before doing the photography, they are completing the tasks on Sur-7 . Specifically, they are copying down data they would need for a launch at T-3. Buzz will write the data on some pre-printed forms.]

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. Ready to copy the LM ascent Pad.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Rog, Tranquility. Tig, 104:39:47:00, 55358, 00322, plus 0022. DEDA 47, plus 37130, minus 70615, plus 58620, plus 56936. Over. [Next, Buzz will do a readback to be certain that he has copied the numbers correctly.]

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. LM ascent Pad: 104:39:47:00, 55358, 00322, plus 0022, plus 37130, minus 70615, plus 58620, plus 56936. Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger, Tranquility. Good readback. We also have a CSI Pad if you are ready to copy. (Pause)

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Okay. We are ready to go.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. Coming at you with a CSI: Noun 11, 105:35:3700; 107:11:3000, 0538, minus all zeros. FDAI is NA; 0937...Correction, 09356; 10315; plus 0538, minus all zeros, plus 0012. Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. Say again Rl and Noun 86.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. Rl is plus 0538, and we have a load for you. Will you please give us P00 and Data? Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. Before I do that I would like to designate the rendezvous radar up to plus-X.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. (Long Pause) [By putting the computer in Program 00 and Data, they will be able to accept memory updates radioed up from Houston. In moving the rendezvous radar "up to plus X", Buzz will be pointing it at the zenith.]

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Okay. CSI readback: Noun 11, 105:35:3700, 107:11:3000, 0538, minus all zeros, NA, 09356, 10315. Noun 86, plus 0538, plus all zeros, and the last one was 0012. And what's the sign of that, please? (Long Pause)

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Tranquility, Houston. The Delta-VY is minus all zeros. The Delta-VZ is plus 0012. Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. Plus 0012.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Rog. Good readback. (Long Pause)

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Houston, Tranquility Base. The DSKY 's yours, and updata link to Data. 103:59:47 Duke: Roger. Thank you, Tranquility. [Comm Break. Buzz is telling Houston that he has put the computer in P00 and Data. Neil and Buzz may now be taking pictures out the windows. A discussion of the window photography is linked here .] [I noted that Houston has just read up a long Pad of data and is now sending more data electronically and asked why.] [Aldrin - "We copied the data down that was useful to us in the normal sense for the activities that were going to be happening. CSI (for example), was a maneuver aft

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Okay.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Stand by. Mark. Thirty-seven minutes 'til T3.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Okay; thank you. (Long Pause)

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Tranquility, this is Houston. It's your computer. We got the load in. You can start your P57.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger; thank you. [Comm Break] [Neil and Buzz are about to start another platform alignment. They probably have taken pictures out the windows during the last few minutes, as per Surface Checklist page Sur-6 . They have three magazines onboard the LM: two color (HCEX) magazines, 37/R and 40S, and one black-and-white magazine, 39/Q. The pre-EVA window photos are AS11-37- 5449 to 5459, AS11-39- 5737 to 5791, and AS11-40- 5847 to 5849. On the whole, the B&W pictures capture detail better than the color pictures. They also had two Hasselblad cameras: a black IVA camera and a silver-colored EVA cam

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Houston, Tranquility Base. Does somebody down there have a mike button keyed? Over. [Buzz is asking if anyone connected to the audio circuit has a microphone switched on (keyed). Normally, the CapCom is the only person who transmits to the astronauts, but there are others who have the ability to do so if appropriate. Among these are the Flight Director and, designated individuals at the three tracking stations. See, for example, John Saxon's account of his conversation with the Apollo 16 crew when a communications link between Houston and the Honeysuckle Creek receiving station went down short

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Stand by, and we'll check. (Long Pause) Tranquility, Houston. Do you still hear it now? Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: I still hear it. It sounds like somebody's banging some chairs around in the back room.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. That's a VOGAA that you hear for the CSM to keep the noise down on the loop. Maybe we got a MSFN relay or something. Stand by.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Okay. (Long Pause)

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Tranquility, Houston. We got the MSFN relay in. You're hearing the VOGAA, which is a noise suppression device. We'll try to take it out. Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: All right. Thank you. [Comm Break]

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Tranquility, Houston. It ought to be a little quieter up there now. We disabled the MSFN relay.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Okay. I think the noise has stopped now. Thank you, Charlie.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. [Long Comm Break]

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Tranquility Base, Houston. On my Mark, 25 minutes 'til T3. Stand by. Mark. 25 minutes until T3.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. Thank you, Charlie. (Pause)

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Collins
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Houston, Columbia. How's it going?

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Columbia, Houston. We're reading you about three-by. Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Collins
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. I'm on Omni Charlie. How's it going? [There are four omni-directional antennas on the Command Module: A, B, C (Charlie), and D.] 104:15:13 Duke: Roger. Understand. Omni Charlie. Mike, be advised we have an update for you on the P22 for the LM. We estimate he landed about 4 miles downrange. Your T1 times are updated and your T2, if you're ready to copy. Over. [In about two minutes, Charlie tells Mike that he will give him a map location, but never does. On the copy of landing site map LAM-2 flown in the Command Module and bearing Mike's handwritten notes, the grid spacing is one kilomete

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Collins
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Ready to copy.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Okay. Roger, Columbia. T1 104:32:24, 104:37:33, 2 miles south. Time of closest approach is 104:39:08 . (Pause)

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Hello, Tranquility Base. Houston. We copy the Noun 93. You can torque them. Over. [Comm Break. They may be on page Sur-10 , in the paragraph just above the box.]

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Collins
a11a1033957-1050000.text: You said 4 miles long, is that correct, Houston?

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: That's affirmative,...

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Houston, do you have an updated LM weight for us? Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: ...Columbia. It's about 4 miles long. Stand by. We'll have you a map location momentarily. Over. (Long Pause)

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Houston, Tranquility Base. Do you have an updated LM weight for us? Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: That's affirmative. Stand by on the DAP (Digital Auto Pilot). Our DAP Pad for you is LM weight 10906 (terrestrial pounds). Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. 10906.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Rog. (Long Pause) [O'Brien - "One of the many tasks of the Digital AutoPilot is to calculate the firing times of the RCS thrusters for a given rotational rate. Because the LM's moment-of-inertia changes significantly with changes in weight, the DAP needs the most up-to-date value for optimal performance."] [Neil and Buzz are near the top of Sur-11 in the simulated countdown.]

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Columbia, Houston. With a latitude (and) longitude-over-two update for LM position. Over. (Pause) Columbia, Houston. Over. [Neil thought that, perhaps, they used the actual longitude divided by two to get more significant digits.] [Armstrong - "But why? I don't know."] [O'Brien - "The choice of 'longitude-over-two' was a way to realize three decimal digits of precision. As the computer display was limited to only five digits, it could not display the full range of longitude (plus or minus 180 degrees) plus the necessary three decimal digits. By dividing the longitude by two, a precision of +/-

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Collins
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger, Mike. We got an update on the lat(itude)/longitude for the LM, if you're ready to copy. Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Collins
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Go ahead. Go ahead. 104:20:42 Duke: Roger. Columbia, it's plus 7 - correction - plus 0.799 for the Lat, plus 11.730 for the longitude-over-two. Over. [The difference between 23.46 degrees (2 x 11.730) and 23.433 degrees is 0.023 degrees or 0.6 kilometers on the ground. The difference in latitude corresponds to 2.8 kilometers on the surface. With the actual LM location at map coordinates J.65/7.52 , the latitude/longitude Charlie has just given to Mike correspond to map coordinates of M.5/8.0. See the discussion following 104:42:48 .]

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Collins
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Thank you. The altitude remain unchanged?

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Say again. Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Collins
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Does the altitude remain unchanged? I guess it would.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: That's affirmative. (Long Pause) Hello, Tranquility Base; Houston. You are stay for a T3. We have some surface block data if you're ready to copy. Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. Understand we're stay for T3. Stand by. (Long Pause) Okay, Houston. Go ahead with your block data. [The following are estimated launch times for successive Command Module passes over the landing site.]

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Rog, Tranquility. Stand by one. (Pause) Tranquility, Houston. Say again your T4 copy. Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. Correction on T4: 106:38:02. Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. [Comm Break]

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Hello, Columbia. Houston. We will not come up on the MSFN relay. We'd like you to come on (control) panel 9 (and) turn on your VHF to TR. Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Collins
a11a1033957-1050000.text: (Faint) Okay. I'm on panel 9. Ready to receive. You want me to transmit for some reason with it?

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Say again, Mike...

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Houston; Tranquility Base. I have...(Listens) I'll wait. Go ahead.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: ...You're about two-by.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Collins
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. Panel 9 is configured VHF, Receive. You want me to transmit with the VHF for some reason? Why do you want me in TR?

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Columbia, this is Houston. We don't want you to transmit, Mike. We just want you in that position in case you want to talk to Tranquility. Break. Tranquility, Houston. Say again. Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. I have a fairly good-sized difference between battery volts on (batteries) 5 and 6; 6 is reading 33.5 and 5 is reading 36.5. Is that what you expect? Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Duke
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. Stand by. (Pause) Tranquility, Houston. They are both coming up in voltage. No problem. We're still Go. Over.

a11a1033957-1050000.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1033957-1050000.text: Roger. [Long Comm Break. Buzz is now on page Sur-16 , near the bottom of the box on that page. Batteries 5 and 6 are Ascent Stage batteries.]

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Columbia, Houston. You were unreadable. Say again please.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Collins
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Disregard. (Long Pause)

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Columbia, Houston. Several items for you. Over.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Collins
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Ready to copy.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Columbia, Houston. First of all, we'd like a waste water dump to 10 percent on the backside. Secondly, it does not look like we are going to need any plane change at this time, so we will not be uplinking a new REFSMMAT. Third item, I would like all of your Cryo heaters to Auto, and we are ready for a battery charge, battery Bravo; it will last about 7 hours. If you should go to sleep, we will be terminating that Batt charge, but at the moment, we can go ahead and start the Batt charge on Batt Bravo. And a final item, for your SM RCS configuration for your rest period, register 1 for the DAP i

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Collins
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Roger. Dump waste water to 10 percent on the backside. Use prior REFSMMAT, CRYO heaters on to AUTO, battery B charge until I go to sleep. DAP is 11111, 01100. Select quads A pitch only on, C and D all up. Over.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Columbia, Houston. Roger. (Long Pause)

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Columbia, Houston. We will have a state vector update for you a little later. We are not prepared with it right now. And on another subject, from Tranquility Base, they are prepared to begin the EVA early. They expect to begin Depress operations in about 3 hours at 108...approximately 108 GET (Ground Elapsed Time). Over.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Collins
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Sounds good to me. Tell them to eat some lunch before they go. [Comm Break. The hatch will come open at 109:07:33.]

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Columbia, Houston. We'd like your PRD readouts when possible, and we've checked over your EM (Erasable-Memory) dump. It all looks okay. (Pause)

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Tranquility Base, Houston. Over.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Tranquility, Houston. We'd like your PRD (Personal Radiation Dosimeter) readout, and we have double-checked your EM dump. It all looks okay. Over.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Roger. Understand our E-memory dump was good. CDR's dosimeter is 11014. (Pause)

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1050000-1055217.text: And LMP is 09011.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Roger, Tranquility. Break. Columbia, we would like for you to Re-acq(uire) with your high gain; attempt a manual lock-on. Over.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Collins
a11a1050000-1055217.text: In work.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Houston, Tranquility here. The LMP's (PRD) readout may possibly be 09017. Over.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Tranquility, Houston. Roger. 09017 is an update on your readout.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Collins
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Columbia's on high gain.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1050000-1055217.text: I'll let you know for sure when it goes to either 12 or 18.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Tranquility, Houston. Roger. The medics report your latter reading, "17", appears to be the correct one. Over.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Roger. (Pause)

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Collins
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Columbia's on the high gain.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Roger, Columbia. You're sounding much better now. (Long Pause)

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Columbia, Houston. Request P00 in Accept, and we'll uplink another state vector. Over.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Collins
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Roger. Going P00 in Accept. [Comm Break]

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Columbia, Houston. Suggest you put Batt A on your Batt relay bus. Over.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Collins
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Okay.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Columbia, Houston. We're through with your computer. You can go to Block.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Collins
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Roger. Block. [Comm Break]

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Tranquility Base, Houston. Over.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Go ahead, Houston. Tranquility Base.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Tranquility Base, Houston. We've reviewed the checklist, and about the only change in order to advance the EVA that we've found is that you'll want to delay your lithium hydroxide change until after the EVA rather than before. Over.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Roger. We'd just as soon make a change and jettison the old one. Over. [Comm Break. During the 1991 mission review, I noted that this exchange seemed a bit strange to me in light of the crew's prior comment that they had been planning to make an early EVA if everything was going well.] [Aldrin - "I don't know if they (meaning the people in the Mission Control Room) were all that privy to our plan."] [Armstrong - "They probably were going by the book."] [The Environmental Control System ( ECS ) contains two lithium hydroxide canisters to remove carbon dioxide from the cabin air. As detailed on

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Tranquility Base, Houston. We would like to delay that (primary) LiOH change until after the EVA. There is a possibility you could jettison the canister when you jettison your PLSS. Over.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1050000-1055217.text: All right. We'll plan it that way. Over.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Roger, Tranquility. [Comm Break.]

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Columbia, Houston. Over.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Collins
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Houston, Columbia.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Columbia, Houston. We show your EVAP OUT temperature running low. Request you go to manual temperature control and bring it up. You can check the procedures in ECS MAL 17. Over.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Collins
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Roger, Houston.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Columbia, Houston. I have a P22 update for you.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Collins
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Columbia. Go ahead. 105:19:59 Garriott: Columbia, Houston. Your P22 AUTO - AUTO optics landmark ID on LM. T1, 106 plus 30 plus 31; T2, 106 plus 35 plus 41, 2 nautical miles south. Your TCA, 106 plus 37 plus 16. Shaft angle 357.9 and trunnion angle 44.3. Over.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Collins
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Roger. Thank you.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Garriott
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Columbia, Houston. We have your LOS in 3 minutes. AOS will be 106 plus 11. Over.

a11a1050000-1055217.speaker: Collins
a11a1050000-1055217.text: Roger. [Long Comm Break.]

a11a1055217-1061725.speaker: Collins
a11a1055217-1061725.text: Houston, Columbia. How do you read?

a11a1055217-1061725.speaker: McCandless
a11a1055217-1061725.text: Columbia, Columbia. This is Houston... 106:11:14 Armstrong: Houston, this is Tranquility Base. We are beginning our EVA Prep.

a11a1055217-1061725.speaker: McCandless
a11a1055217-1061725.text: Tranquility Base, this is Houston, Roger. Copy. You're beginning EVA Prep. Break. Break. Columbia, Columbia. This is Houston. Reading you loud and clear. Over 106:11:35 Collins: You're loud and clear. The waste-water dump is down to 10 percent. I have a question on the P22. Do you want me to do another P22, or is all that information just for my own use in tracking the LM for photographic purposes? 106:11:49 McCandless: Columbia, this is Houston. We request that you perform another P22. We'd like you to let the Auto optics take care of the tracking and devote your energies to trying to pick ou

a11a1055217-1061725.speaker: Collins
a11a1055217-1061725.text: Okay. Fine. I'll do it. [Owen Garriott gave Mike the Auto Optics settings at 105:19:59 .] [Armstrong - "There were a couple of reasons for trying to find the LM on the surface. I would say, first, they wanted to find out if they could see it from the Command Module. Second, they wanted to try to help in establishing its position. A lot of people were interested in where we landed, particularly those people who were involved in the descent guidance trajectory controls. After all, in later flights, we were going to try to go to specific spots on the surface and we needed to get all the informati

a11a1055217-1061725.speaker: Collins
a11a1055217-1061725.text: And on the ECS system, whatever the problem was, it seems to have gone away without any changing of J52 sensors or anything like that. My glycol evaporator outlet Temp is up above 50 now, and it's quite comfortable in the cockpit; so we'll talk more about that one later.

a11a1055217-1061725.speaker: McCandless
a11a1055217-1061725.text: Roger, Columbia. Did you shift into manual control, or did the problem resolve itself under Auto control? Over.

a11a1055217-1061725.speaker: Collins
a11a1055217-1061725.text: The problem went away under Auto.

a11a1055217-1061725.speaker: McCandless
a11a1055217-1061725.text: Roger. That's the best type. Out.

a11a1055217-1061725.speaker: Collins
a11a1055217-1061725.text: I did cycle out of Auto into Manual, back into Auto.

a11a1055217-1061725.speaker: McCandless
a11a1055217-1061725.text: Houston. Roger. Out. [Long Comm Break] Audio Clip from the Public Affairs loop, starting at about 106:17:25. Clip courtesy John Stoll, ACR Senior Technician at NASA Johnson.  Click to load audio in new, pop-up window.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Tranquility Base. Tranquility Base. This is Houston. Over.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Tranquility, this is Houston. We need a second set of PRD readings so that we may establish a rate. Over.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Okay. Stand by. (Pause) CDR is reading 11014. (Pause)

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1061725-1070202.text: LMP is reading 09017 and three-quarters.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: (Guffaws over the "3/4") Tranquility, this is Houston. We copy your readings. Out. [The readings are unchanged since the landing.] [Long Comm Break]

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Houston, Columbia. How do you read on Omni D, Dog?

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Columbia, this is Houston. We're reading you loud with background noise on Omni D. Over.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Okay. I'll stay on D here for a while. I'm about to go into P22 (a tracking program which keeps the sextant pointed at the targeted spot on the ground while he passes overhead).

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Roger. Out. [Long Comm Break]

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Houston, Columbia. I'm coming up on my time for the first pass when I may be able to see the LM. Do you have any topographical cues that might help me out here? Auto optics is tracking between two craters. One of them, as the LM sees it, would be long at 11 o'clock. The other would be short and behind him at 5 o'clock. (Pause) These are great big old craters (or) depressions.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Stand by. (Long Pause) Columbia, this is Houston. The best we can do on topo features is to advise you to look to the west of the irregularly shaped crater, and then work on down to the southwest of it. Over. (Pause) Columbia, Houston. Another possibility is the southern rim of the southern of the two old-looking craters. Over. [Unlike later Command Module Pilots, Mike is not attempting to make any formal geologic observations from orbit - and for good reason, as Neil explained during the 1991 mission review.] [Armstrong - "I think Mike's view - and I share it - was that his responsibility was

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Roger, Houston. Columbia. No joy. I kept my eyes glued to the sextant that time hoping I'd get a flash of specular light off the LM, but I wasn't able to see any in my scan areas that you suggested.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Roger. On that southern of the old craters, there's a small bright crater on the southern rim. One plot would put him slightly to the west of that small bright crater, about 500 to 1000 feet. Do you see anything down there? Over.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: It's gone past now, Bruce, but I scanned that area that you are talking about very closely, and no, I did not see anything.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Roger. Out. (Long Pause) Columbia, this is Houston. Over.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Go ahead.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Columbia, this is Houston. On your LAM-2 map , we'd like to confirm the topographical area in which you were looking on this last period of sightings. As we understand you, you were looking in the vicinity of Papa 7 to November 8. Is that correct? Over.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Stand by one.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Roger. [Comm Break] [Papa 7 is the intersection of the P horizontal line with the 7 vertical line. The actual landing site is near J0.7 and 7.4; that is, seven tenths of the way from the J line to the K line and four tenths from the 7 line to the 8 line. Note that the lines are a kilometer apart.]

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Houston, Columbia.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Go ahead, Columbia. 106:43:08 Collins: One of the craters I was talking about is located exactly at Mike 6.7 (on LAM-2 ). [This crater is in the southwestern part of the hand-drawn ellipse .]

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Roger. We found that one.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: The other one is located at 7...(Listens) The other one is located at 7.2, two-thirds of the way from Mike to Nan. [This crater is in the northeastern part of the hand-drawn ellipse .]

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Roger. We believe you were looking a little too far to the west and south. Over. (Long Pause)

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Roger. Understand. I was looking where auto optics was tracking, on the average; and (I) understand that it should have been more to the north and more to the west; actually a tiny bit outside the circle, huh? 106:44:17 McCandless: More to the north and a little more to the east. The feature that I was describing to you - the small bright crater on the rim of the large, fairly old crater - would be about Mike 0.8 and 8.2 . Over. [This crater about 200 meters east of the 'tiny crater' Mike circled at M.7/8.0.]

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Well, just give me your best estimate as to his location in this coordinate system, and I'll plot it on my map and go from there.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Roger. [Long Comm Break]

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Tranquility Base, this is Houston. Can you give us some idea of where you are in the surface checklist at the present time? Over 106:49:07 Aldrin: Okay. We're on the top of page 27 .

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Roger. Out. [Comm Break] [On checklist page Sur-25 , the notation "BTH" means "Both". UCTA is Urine Collection and Transfer Assembly. They are both wearing condom-like urine collection sleeves which, via a short hose, empty into a collection bag. In turn, the collection bag is connected to a valve/connector on the right thigh which can be connected to an external hose/bag assembly. Here, they are emptying the in-suit collection bags. They will place the external bag into a jettison bag for disposal. The PGA is the Pressure Garment Assembly or, more simply, the suit. The chest-mounted PGA diver

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Houston, Columbia. Over.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Go ahead, Columbia.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Roger. I finally got you back on Omni D. I've been unsuccessfully trying to get you on the high gain, and I've gone Command Reset to Process. How do you read me now?

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Roger. Reading you loud with background noise. Understand that's Omni Delta or Omni Bravo? Over.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Omni Delta and you were cut out. I never got your coordinates on estimated LM position. Over.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Columbia, this is Houston. Estimated LM position is latitude plus 0.799, longitude-over-two plus 11.730. On your chart we would place it...Stand by on the charts and (give me a) readback on the latitude and longitude.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Yeah. The latitude and longitude over two: 799 and 11730 are the ones that I('ve) been using in P22. But what I'm interested in is grid coordinates on that map we're using.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Roger. We'll have them for you in a second.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Thank you. (Long Pause) Houston, Columbia. Could you enable the S-band relay at least one-way from Eagle to Columbia so I can hear what's going on?

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Roger. There's not much going on at the present time, Columbia. I'll see what I can do about the relay. (Pause) Columbia, this is Houston. Are you aware that Eagle plans the EVA about 4 hours early? Over.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Affirmative. When's hatch open time in GET estimated?

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Roger. Somewhere around 108 hours. We'll have an update for you on that a little later.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Okay. I haven't heard a word from those guys, and I thought I'd be hearing them through your S-band relay.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Roger. They're on about page Surface 27 in the checklist, proceeding in good time.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Glad to hear it. You got a crowd there in MCC (Mission Control Center)? (Long Pause)

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: "Roger" your last (transmission), Columbia.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Roger. I'd expect you probably have about nine CapComs and eleven Flight Directors with no place to plug in (to the consoles).

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: (With a smile in his voice) Roger. Out. [NASA Photo S69-39600 shows Pete Conrad and Al Bean, and, behind them, their backups, Dave Scott (behind Al) and Jim Irwin, monitoring Apollo 11 activities after the landing.]

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: That ratio might even be reversed. (Long Pause) Glycol evaporator outlet temperature is 50 degrees (Fahrenheit, 10 C) and the comfort in here is just fine.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Roger. We copy 50 degrees on the glycol, and comfort index fine. (Long Pause)

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: Collins
a11a1061725-1070202.text: And, if you'll excuse me a minute, I'm going to have a cup of coffee.

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Roger. (Pause) Apollo...(Correcting himself) Columbia, this is Houston. Your map coordinates (for the LM) are Papa decimal 2 and 6 decimal 3 on the LAM-2 chart . Over. (No answer; Long Pause) Columbia, this is Houston. Did you copy the coordinates for the LM? Over. (No answer) [There is nothing drawn on the flown map at this location.] [Comm Break]

a11a1061725-1070202.speaker: McCandless
a11a1061725-1070202.text: Columbia. Columbia. This is Houston. If you read, we request high-gain antenna yaw 180, pitch 0. I say again, yaw 180, pitch 0 on the high gain. Over. (No answer) [Long Comm Break] Audio Clip from the Public Affairs loop, starting at about 107:02:02. Clip courtesy John Stoll, ACR Senior Technician at NASA Johnson.  Click to load audio in new, pop-up window.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: McCandless
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Columbia, Columbia, this is Houston. Do you read? Over. [Comm Break]

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Houston, Columbia on the high gain.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: McCandless
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Columbia, this is Houston reading you loud and clear. Over.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Reading you loud and clear, Bruce.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: McCandless
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Roger, Mike. I have the coordinates...

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: What's new? 107:05:31 McCandless: Well, what's new is I think we have some more coordinates for you on the LM location. Over.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Ready to copy.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: McCandless
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Roger, Mike. Papa 0.2 and 6.3 on your LAM-2 chart . Over.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Roger. Papa 0.2 and who decimal three?

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: McCandless
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Six decimal three, I say again, six decimal three. (Pause)

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Thank you. Papa 0.2 and 6.3. I'll try it.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: McCandless
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Roger. (Long Pause) [The actual landing site is at about Juliett 0.7 and 7.4 (on LAM-2 ). West Crater is at about Juliett 0.5 and 8.1. Note that each of the boxes on LAM-2 represents a square kilometer. Because of the local terrain rises toward the west, the LM shadow, which is its most visible manifestation, is only about 20 meters long.]

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Okay. What you are saying is, if you look at the Cat's Paw, then that's just about, oh, his middle finger; a little bit...one to two o'clock from his middle finger. Is that right? [This location (P.2/6.3) is marked on a detail from LAM-2G and, as can be seen in Figure 5-14 from the Apollo 11 Mission Report, it is far enough outside the landing ellipse that none of the sextant field-of-view was inside the landing ellipse.] [As mentioned in the commentary after 102:55:49 a feature centered just west of the landing elipse on a portion of the Descent Monitoring Chart and labled Cat's Paw is more t

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: McCandless
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Roger. About one to two o'clock from the middle finger if you're using 12 o'clock being to the west. Over.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: (Joking) That must be the way cats face (on the Moon). Okay. I'm with you. [Mike may have mentioned the "middle finger" to ensure he and Bruce were reading the map the same way. Evidently, he's a bit amused that they are trying to pinpoint a location based on a pattern that only faintly resembles a cat's paw print.] [Phil Stooke notes that, in an untitled, post-flight, Manned Spacecraft Center graphic he found in the library at the Lunar and Planetary Institute in Houston, the larger craters in the area Mike and Bruce have been discussing, especially the largest one that is shaped like a half-

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: McCandless
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Okay. And I got LOS and AOS times for you.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Go ahead. (Pause) Go ahead, Houston.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: McCandless
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Roger. Your LOS at 107 plus 23 plus 08. AOS at 108 plus 09 plus 06. The next pass for COAS tracking: your time of closest approach is 108:35:28. Look 3 miles south of track. Over. [Armstrong - "I think COAS means 'optical alignment sight' or something like that. (To Buzz) Do you remember?"] [Aldrin - "I didn't have one." (General laughter)] [In addition to the COAS (Crewman Optical Alignment Sight) in the Command Module, there is one in the LM - mounted over Neil's window. The COAS is prominent in a detail from pre-flight photo 69-H-134 . Journal Contributor Marv Hein notes that anyone interes

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: I understand all that, but with this new information would you like me to try P22 and look for him in a different spot?

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: McCandless
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Stand by a minute, please.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Okay. Because I was looking in the wrong place last time. Auto optics was not pointing me at the coordinates you gave.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: McCandless
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Roger. [Comm Break]

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: McCandless
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Columbia, this is Houston. Over.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Go ahead. 107:10:15 McCandless: On your next pass, Columbia, rather than performing a P22 as such, we would like you to look in the vicinity of the coordinates that we gave you, which is our best analysis based on math/physics and the trajectory. And we also have another set of coordinates that we would like you to search in the vicinity of. This last one being based on an interpretation of the geological features that were seen by the crew on their way down. The coordinates of this second site are Mike 0.7 and 8.0. I say again, Mike 0.7 and 8 (garbled) I say again, Mike 0.7 and 8.0. Over. [Th

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Roger. Copy. Mike 0.7 and 8.0. The only thing is, my best tool for looking is the sextant and if I'm going to crank the sextant up, I might as well let P22 go at the same time, or don't you think so?

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: McCandless
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Roger. If you want to go that way, crank it up, and then you can drive it around and look where you want.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Okay.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: McCandless
a11a1070202-1073041.text: And if you can find the LM, then by all means, track it or make a note of where it was, and we can track it on the next Rev. If you're ready, we have a REFSMMAT update that we can pass up to you at this time, if you will give us P00 and Accept. Over. (Pause) [By going to Program 00 and Accept, Mike will allow Houston to radio up changes to some of the data in his computer.]

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Okay. P00 and Accept you got. And this is an updated landing site REFSMMAT. We still believe that a plane change is not required. Is that affirmative?

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: McCandless
a11a1070202-1073041.text: That's affirmative, Columbia.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Good show. [Long Comm Break. Public Affairs reports that the LM cabin pressure is 4.86 psi and the temperature is 63F.]

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: McCandless
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Columbia, this is Houston. We are through with the uplink. It's your computer.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Roger. Thank you. [Long Comm Break]

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Houston, Columbia.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: McCandless
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Go ahead, Columbia.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Roger, (on the) next pass, I'd appreciate the S-band relay mode. Over.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: McCandless
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Roger. We're working on that. There haven't been any transmissions from Tranquility Base since we last talked to you. We cannot give you a full S-band relay without being assured of high-gain antenna. We're working on the partial relay for you. Over.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Okay. Understand, Bruce. Thank you very much. (Long Pause)

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: McCandless
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Columbia, this is Houston. Approximately 2 minutes to LOS. All your systems are looking good from down here. Over.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Does it look to you like the two-forty controller is properly controlling the glycol evaporator outlet Temp? It looks all right up here. [David Woods tells us that the unit known as two-forty ( or 2.40 ) is a glycol evaporator control, which is to the left of center and slightly down in the large diagram on page 2.7-25 (PDF page 25) in the Block II Apollo Operations Handbook . David writes, "I suspect the function of this controller is to adjust the valve that controls the steam pressure in the steam vent of the evaporator. This steam pressure affects how much heat is lost through evaporation.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: McCandless
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Roger, Columbia. During this pass on the front side, it looked okay to us.

a11a1070202-1073041.speaker: Collins
a11a1070202-1073041.text: Okay. Thank you. [Long Comm Break] The First Lunar Landing Apollo 11 Journal EVA Preparations

a11a1073041-1080053.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1073041-1080053.text: Okay. We are on about the middle of page 28, Surface (checklist page) 28.

a11a1073041-1080053.speaker: McCandless
a11a1073041-1080053.text: Roger, Tranquility. We copy. [Very Long Comm Break with occasional unintentional keys.] [They are getting Buzz into his PLSS. NASA Public Affairs informs the press that the crew is running about 30 minutes behind schedule.] [Armstrong, from the 1969 Technical Debrief - "Now, a preliminary comment (on the EVA Preps) has to do with the longer time that it took than during our simulations. It is attributable to the fact that, when you do simulations of EVA Prep, you have a clean cockpit and you have all the things that you're going to use there in the cockpit and nothing else. In reality, you hav

a11a1073041-1080053.speaker: McCandless
a11a1073041-1080053.text: Tranquility Base, this is Houston. Over.

a11a1073041-1080053.speaker: McCandless
a11a1073041-1080053.text: Roger, Tranquility. We're coming up in about 6 minutes on GET of 108. If you'd like to start your event timer, we can give you a hack at 108:00. Over.

a11a1073041-1080053.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1073041-1080053.text: Wilco (meaning "Will comply"). [Long Comm Break. During either this comm break or the prior one, Neil and Buzz installed the electrical fitting that connected the PLSS to the RCU .] [Aldrin, from the 1969 Technical Debrief - "We had problems with this one particular electrical connector, the one that joins the RCU to the PLSS, ever since the first time we'd ever seen it."] [Armstrong, from the 1969 Technical Debrief - "It's about a 50-pin Bendix connector."] [Aldrin, from the 1969 Technical Debrief - "It's just very difficult to get the thing positioned properly so that the three pins on the o

a11a1080053-1082505.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1080053-1082505.text: Houston, Tranquility. We're ready to start with the electrical checkout. We're going to S-band modulate FM. Over. [Journal Contributor Phil Karn writes, "The normal S-band mode, PM (phase modulation), carried voice, telemetry and ranging but could not support TV. Switching to FM (frequency modulation) enabled television. It also disabled ranging but this was not needed on the lunar surface. Switching to FM also meant that the large 210-foot dishes at Goldstone and Parkes were now necessary even to receive voice from Eagle; in the PM mode the smaller 85-foot antennas sufficed for voice. Needles

a11a1080053-1082505.speaker: McCandless
a11a1080053-1082505.text: Roger. Tranquility, this is Houston. We copy. Go ahead with the FM. And we missed the mark at 108. Do you want us to try and give you one at 108:05? Over.

a11a1080053-1082505.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1080053-1082505.text: I think we've got the timer going. We've got 1 minute and 30 seconds. Mark.

a11a1080053-1082505.speaker: McCandless
a11a1080053-1082505.text: Roger. We copy, and you're in sync with us. [Long Comm Break with occasional accidental triggers of the microphones.] [Armstrong - "Someone asked me if I had left my wristwatch in the Lunar Module during the EVA as a backup to the mission timer; and I couldn't remember. But that seemed like a logical suggestion."] [Aldrin - "That jibes with what I remember: your electing not to take it out on the surface was because of (the mission timer)."] [Journal Contributor Ulli Lotzmann notes that, according to an Omega brochure, Neil mentioned leaving his watch in the LM to NASA Historian Alan A. Nelson

a11a1080053-1082505.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1080053-1082505.text: That's got it. (Long Pause)

a11a1080053-1082505.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1080053-1082505.text: Fastest VOX in the west. (Pause) [The VOX is the voice-activated comm system. They seem to have been checking it and finally have it working. Neil is making a joking reference to gunfighters in the American Old West, possibly referring to his own slow response to Buzz.]

a11a1080053-1082505.speaker: Aldrin
a11a1080053-1082505.text: (Garbled).

a11a1080053-1082505.speaker: Armstrong
a11a1080053-1082505.text: Well, we've got antennas down and (garbled) not real good (garbled)
