a11_1260727.text: Unfortunately, the chart doesn't agree with it, because the range-rate at 36 minutes was off the chart.

a11_1260727.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1260727.text: Apollo Control here. Less than a minute remaining until the Constant Delta Height or CDH maneuver. We'll continue to monitor the air-ground. This a small magnitude radial burn to put Eagle in a orbit that's concentric with - Here we go. Thirty seconds.

a11_1261648.speaker: Evans
a11_1261648.text: Eagle, Houston. When you get a chance, are your LCGs hooked up? And if so, what does the LCG accumulator show? [Long pause.]

a11_1261648.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1261648.text: This is Apollo Control. Range now showing 91.3 nautical miles [169.1 km]. Range-rate, rate of closure, 119 feet per second [36 m/s].

a11_1261648.speaker: Collins
a11_1261648.text: Eagle, Columbia. Passing over the Landing Site. It sure is great to look down there and not see you.

a11_1261648.speaker: Evans
a11_1261648.text: Roger. Did you copy on the LCG, there, and the reading on the water accumulator?

a11_1261648.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1261648.text: Yeah. Roger. I did. I'm getting [garble].

a11_1261648.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1261648.text: Houston, the water accumulator is right on the line between the red and the green. Over.

a11_1262413.speaker: Evans
a11_1262413.text: Roger. On the water problem there, we can't add anything more to it, except the fact that it looks like the water accumulators are up to speed, to us down here.

a11_1262413.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1262413.text: Okay. It's not going to be too much trouble.

a11_1262413.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1262413.text: It's just in one suit, too, for some reason.

a11_1262413.speaker: Evans
a11_1262413.text: Columbia, Houston. Our comm problem was traced to a ground station here.

a11_1262413.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1262413.text: This is Apollo Control. Range between Eagle and Columbia now showing 67.5 nautical miles [125.0 km]. Range-rate, closure rate, 121 feet per second [37 m/s].

a11_1263149.speaker: Collins
a11_1263149.text: I have a TPI T IG when you guys want to compare them.

a11_1263149.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1263149.text: Go ahead, Mike. What have you got?

a11_1263149.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1263149.text: You're about 32 seconds later than we are.

a11_1263149.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1263149.text: This is Apollo Control. Some 25 minutes now until the TPI, Terminal Phase Initiation burn, just before Loss Of Signal as both spacecraft go over the hill.

a11_1263149.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1263149.text: This is Apollo Control. The Black Team of flight controllers here in Mission Control are more or less in an advisory capacity during this rendezvous sequence. They're actively computing maneuver times, but in the final analysis, it's onboard computations by the crew of Columbia and Eagle which really bring about the rendezvous. Standing by at 126 hours, 37 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; some 24 minutes away from ignition on the thrust along the line of sight for Terminal Phase Initiate.

a11_1263912.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1263912.text: [Garble.] [Garble] mark and I'll do it. [Long pause.]

a11_1263912.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1263912.text: [Garble] want to get another [garble] I can get a data update in the AGS [garble] barely touches [garble]. [Long pause.]

a11_1263912.speaker: Collins
a11_1263912.text: Buzz, I'd like to confirm that your TPI T IG is 127:02:02. Over.

a11_1263912.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1263912.text: We haven't settled on a final one yet. The last one was - stand by. [Long pause.]

a11_1263912.speaker: Collins
a11_1263912.text: Just as soon as you know what TPI T IG 's going to be, I'd appreciate a call.

a11_1263912.speaker: Collins
a11_1263912.text: Last I got was 32 seconds earlier than mine which would make it 127:02:02. [Pause.]

a11_1263912.speaker: Collins
a11_1263912.text: Thank you. Are you going to be revising that one?

a11_1263912.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1263912.text: I think probably so. How late - How late can you take a revision? [Pause.]

a11_1263912.speaker: Collins
a11_1263912.text: Well, to stay on my time line, I should have it in the next couple of minutes.

a11_1264807.speaker: Evans
a11_1264807.text: Roger. In the event of the possibility that we may have had some water channeling in those hydroxide canisters, we recommend you stay in the cabin mode from now on. Over.

a11_1265125.speaker: Evans
a11_1265125.text: Roger. I'd better clarify that cabin mode a little bit there. What we mean is you go ahead and stay in the cabin mode. Helmets and gloves on are your option. And we really have no concern with the CO 2 . Over.

a11_1265125.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1265125.text: Mike, you already loaded that time? We've got a final one here.

a11_1265125.speaker: Collins
a11_1265125.text: I've already loaded it. I don't think it'll make much difference.

a11_1265125.speaker: Evans
a11_1265125.text: Roger, Mike. You can go ahead and arm your logic anytime you want to, and we'll give you a Go so that you can hit your Pyro Arm at your convenience.

a11_1265125.speaker: Collins
a11_1265125.text: That's a good idea, babe. You standing by to watch the logic?

a11_1265125.speaker: Evans
a11_1265125.text: Columbia, Houston. We need the SECS Arm circuit breakers closed.

a11_1265125.speaker: Collins
a11_1265125.text: Okay. Going in SECS Arm Batt A, and Batt B. [Long pause.]

a11_1265125.speaker: Evans
a11_1265125.text: Columbia, Houston. Logic looks good. You can arm your Pyros at your convenience.

a11_1265125.speaker: Collins
a11_1265125.text: Eagle, Columbia's starting to maneuver to TPI attitude.

a11_1265125.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1265125.text: This is Apollo Control; about 6½ minutes to ignition on the Terminal Phase Maneuver in which the crew of Eagle will thrust along the line of sight toward Columbia. Distance now between the two spacecraft, some 38.6 nautical miles [71.5 km], closing at a rate of 110 feet per second [34 m/s].

a11_1265125.speaker: Evans
a11_1265125.text: Eagle and Columbia, Houston. All your solutions look good to us. Out. [Long pause.]

a11_1265125.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1265125.text: And, Mike, if you want our target Delta-V, I'll give it to you.

a11_1270025.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1270025.text: I'm showing a good bit of out-of-plane velocity on my cross-pointers, Mike.

a11_1270025.speaker: Collins
a11_1270025.text: Rog. I have no indication of it.

a11_1270025.speaker: Collins
a11_1270025.text: Coming up on 1 minute to T IG , Neil. How's it looking?

a11_1270025.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1270025.text: That out-of-plane was in the AGS, not in the radar.

a11_1270025.speaker: Evans
a11_1270025.text: Eagle, Houston. Aft Omni, low-bit rate, and we'll see you at 127 plus 51.

a11_1270025.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1270025.text: This is Apollo Control. We've apparently had Loss Of Signal with Columbia and Eagle as they went behind the Moon on the 26th revolution. Next maneuver scheduled for about 33 minutes from now. While both vehicles are behind the Moon, this will be the braking series of maneuvers coming down to docking, or station-keeping first, and then docking at about 128 hours Ground Elapsed Time. And at 127 hours, 6 minutes Ground Elapsed Time in the flight of Apollo 11; this is Mission Control.

a11_1270025.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1270025.text: Well - say when [garble] Oh, wait a minute.

a11_1275000.speaker: Collins
a11_1275000.text: [Garble].

a11_1275000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1275000.text: Hope you know how to roll.

a11_1275000.speaker: Collins
a11_1275000.text: Yes, I do. I [garble].

a11_1275000.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1275000.text: This is Apollo Control; 127 hours, 50 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Less than a minute now away from acquisition of the spacecraft, Columbia. Hopefully flying within a few feet of it, will be Eagle. Docking should take place about 10 minutes from now, according to the Flight Plan. However, this is a crew option matter. We're standing by for word that data is coming in from the two spacecraft.

a11_1275000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1275000.text: You want to end up with that window - opposite his right window so you don't want to roll right. Right?

a11_1275000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1275000.text: Yes.

a11_1275000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1275000.text: The only trouble is, it's towards - towards 90, isn't it?

a11_1275000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1275000.text: You could - you...

a11_1275000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1275000.text: If I roll 120 - it'll roll left

a11_1275000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1275000.text: 90, huh? [Garble] 60?

a11_1275000.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1275000.text: This is lunar revolution number 27 for Columbia.

a11_1275000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1275000.text: Well, why don't I start to roll...

a11_1275000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1275000.text: Yes, I think if you roll up 60...

a11_1275000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1275000.text: I'll be looking into his left window when I pitch up.

a11_1275000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1275000.text: I don't think so. If you did it right now you'd...

a11_1275000.speaker: Collins
a11_1275000.text: [Garble] I got the Earth coming up already. It's fantastic!

a11_1275000.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1275000.text: Have LM AOS.

a11_1275000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1275000.text: Okay. You've got me.

a11_1275000.speaker: Evans
a11_1275000.text: Eagle and Columbia, Houston. Standing by.

a11_1275000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1275000.text: Roger. We're station-keeping.

a11_1275000.speaker: Evans
a11_1275000.text: Roger.

a11_1275000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1275000.text: Pitch up then when we translate up just a little, you got a better view - bottom side - [garble] - move back.

a11_1275000.speaker: Collins
a11_1275000.text: [Garble] - that's right.

a11_1275000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1275000.text: Okay. I'm getting about into the right attitude, I think. [Garble].

a11_1275000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1275000.text: Yes.

a11_1275000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1275000.text: That roll's pretty far. I don't know just how much - so that's - Oh, it's going to go gimbal lock!

a11_1275000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1275000.text: That's it - going to AGS?

a11_1275000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1275000.text: Yes, [garble] Att Deadband.

a11_1275000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1275000.text: Okay, Mike, I'll get - try to get in position here, and then you got it.

a11_1275000.speaker: Collins
a11_1275000.text: Okay.

a11_1275000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1275000.text: How does the roll attitude look?

a11_1275000.speaker: Collins
a11_1275000.text: [Garble].

a11_1275000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1275000.text: Let's see how the DSKY thinks it looks.

a11_1275000.speaker: Collins
a11_1275000.text: Have you stopped rolling yet?

a11_1275000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1275000.text: I'll stop. Matter of fact, I can stop right here, if you like that.

a11_1275000.speaker: Collins
a11_1275000.text: Need a little bit more. That's the way, keep it going. Need a little more [garble]. That's the way, keep going - go a little bit more - go ahead - go ahead - okay, stop. Okay, I got it now.

a11_1275000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1275000.text: You got the [garble] in [garble]?

a11_1275000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1275000.text: Yes. Right there. Okay, [garble] I...

a11_1275000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1275000.text: Well, we might need to at least have a platform [garble].

a11_1275000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1275000.text: Yes.

a11_1275000.speaker: Collins
a11_1275000.text: Okay, now, Neil, when you feel us contact, you're going to turn [garble] seconds, is that right?

a11_1275000.speaker: Evans
a11_1275000.text: Eagle, Houston. Middle gimbal. And you might pass to Columbia, we don't have him yet.

a11_1275000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1275000.text: That's right.

a11_1275000.speaker: Collins
a11_1275000.text: Okay, Buzz.

a11_1275000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1275000.text: We got a platform to make.

a11_1275000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1275000.text: Okay.

a11_1280050.speaker: Collins
a11_1280050.text: Okay. [Pause.] Okay, I have thrusters B3 and C4 safetied.

a11_1280050.speaker: Collins
a11_1280050.text: I'm pumping up cabin pressure. [Long pause.]

a11_1280050.speaker: Collins
a11_1280050.text: That was a funny one, you know. I didn't - I didn't feel a shock, and I thought things were pretty steady. I went to Retract there, and that's when all hell broke loose. [Pause.] Were you guys - did it appear to you to be - that you were jerking around quite a bit during the retract cycle?

a11_1280050.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1280050.text: Ah yeah. It seemed to happen at the time I put the plus-X thrust to it, and apparently it wasn't centered, because somehow or other I accidentally got off in attitude and then the attitude hold system started firing.

a11_1280050.speaker: Collins
a11_1280050.text: Yeah. I was sure busy there for a couple of seconds. [Pause.]

a11_1280050.speaker: Collins
a11_1280050.text: Are you hearing me all right? I got a horrible squeal.

a11_1280050.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1280050.text: Yeah. I agree with that, but we hear you okay.

a11_1280536.speaker: Collins
a11_1280536.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Over.

a11_1280536.speaker: Evans
a11_1280536.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Go.

a11_1280536.speaker: Collins
a11_1280536.text: Roger. I'm supposed to adjust the oxygen flow in this thing to six-tenths of a pound per hour, but being as how this transducer is not working right, could you give me an updated number?

a11_1280536.speaker: Evans
a11_1280536.text: Affirmative. You want to go ahead and adjust your O 2 flow until it just goes off the peg, and then crank the direct O 2 valve back down about 5 degrees. Over.

a11_1280536.speaker: Collins
a11_1280536.text: Boy, you're really waiting for that one, aren't you? Okay, Ron. Thank you. [Long pause.]

a11_1280536.speaker: Collins
a11_1280536.text: Houston, I did that, and I believe we are flowing oxygen, but the gauge is just pegged Full Scale Low.

a11_1280536.speaker: Evans
a11_1280536.text: Roger. That's fine. That's what we expect.

a11_1280536.speaker: Collins
a11_1280536.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a11_1280536.speaker: Collins
a11_1280536.text: Okay. I'm going to go ahead with the tunnel leak check.

a11_1280536.speaker: Evans
a11_1280536.text: Columbia, Houston. I have a new LM weight for you whenever you're ready to copy. [Pause.]

a11_1280536.speaker: Collins
a11_1280536.text: No, not right now, Ron. Remind me of it later, would you please?

a11_1280536.speaker: Evans
a11_1280536.text: Roger. We'll stand by.

a11_1280536.speaker: Collins
a11_1280536.text: Houston, Apollo 11. I let P47 run longer than I should. I may have deteriorated our state vector slightly.

a11_1280536.speaker: Evans
a11_1280536.text: Roger, Apollo 11. That's okay. We'll get it later.

a11_1280536.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1280536.text: This is Apollo Control. Communications are somewhat scratchy with Apollo 11. Columbia and Eagle now reunited to become Apollo 11 again. Our best estimate on the time of docking is some 3 minutes after the pre-mission time of 128 hours. Continuing to monitor this 27th lunar orbit for the two-way communications between the two spacecraft.

a11_1280536.speaker: Collins
a11_1280536.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Go ahead with your DAP up, please.

a11_1280536.speaker: Evans
a11_1280536.text: Roger. Your LM weight, 5785. For an R1 we'd like to have 61102; R2, 01111. Use B/D roll. Over.

a11_1280536.speaker: Collins
a11_1280536.text: Roger. I'm configured now at panel 8 for B/D roll, and I have thrusters C4 and B3 turned off, and I copy Register 1 61102, 01111 and LM weight 5785. Thank you.

a11_1280536.speaker: Evans
a11_1280536.text: Roger, Columbia.

a11_1280536.speaker: Collins
a11_1280536.text: Houston, Columbia has completed the leak check, and proceeding with opening the hatch dump valve.

a11_1280536.speaker: Evans
a11_1280536.text: Roger, Columbia. Understand you're doing the leak check. I missed anything after that.

a11_1280536.speaker: Collins
a11_1280536.text: I say the leak check is complete, and I'm proceeding with opening the hatch dump valve.

a11_1280536.speaker: Evans
a11_1280536.text: Eagle - Columbia, Roger.

a11_1282003.speaker: Collins
a11_1282003.text: My hatch is removed. You can open yours, and I'll start passing stuff up to you.

a11_1282003.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1282003.text: This is Apollo Control. Still rather noisy communications here on the 27th lunar revolution. 39 minutes remaining until Apollo 11 goes behind the Moon. We'll leave the circuit up and try to monitor the conversation between the two spacecraft or between Apollo 11 and the ground for the remainder of this pass - try to ascertain the status onboard as far as transferring the crew and other items back into the Command Module. The clean-up in the LM getting all the items dusted off prior to bringing them back into the Command Module. At 128 hours, 25 minutes Ground Elapsed Time and standing by; this

a11_1282830.speaker: Collins
a11_1282830.text: Yeah, everything is going fine. Be with you in just a sec.

a11_1282830.speaker: Evans
a11_1282830.text: Roger. Any time prior to jettison there, we'd like an AGS to PGNS align: 400 plus 30 000. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1282830.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1282830.text: Okay. Any particular attitude you'd like the PGNS in when we do that? [Pause.]

a11_1282830.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1282830.text: No. We're not getting any. Could you give us some course align gimbal angles to move the PGNS to, and then we'll align the AGS to the PGNS. Over.

a11_1282830.speaker: Evans
a11_1282830.text: Roger. Eagle. We concur. Stand by on the gimbal angles. And also, Eagle, while we've got the Command Module direct O 2 on there, there's a possibility that your cabin relief might relieve if we get on up around cabin pressure of about 5.4 or 5.5. [Pause.]

a11_1282830.speaker: Evans
a11_1282830.text: Roger. All we're trying to do is get PGNS and AGS aligned together. Doesn't make any difference on the gimbal angles. [Long pause.]

a11_1282830.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1282830.text: Okay. We're pretty close to 000. Is that all right?

a11_1282830.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1282830.text: Now, you might want to take into account what'll happen when the CSM maneuvers to jettison attitude.

a11_1282830.speaker: Evans
a11_1282830.text: Eagle, Houston. We don't care what the - All we are trying to do is get a drift rate and see how long it takes them to drift apart on the thing after you jettison.

a11_1282830.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1282830.text: Okay. Will we be jettisoning at about this attitude? That's okay. I'll align the AGS to the PGNS. You can tell me a little later if you need some help.

a11_1283631.speaker: Collins
a11_1283631.text: Houston, Columbia. You want me to roll over and get High Gain or anything like that?

a11_1283631.speaker: Evans
a11_1283631.text: Columbia, Houston. I can give you some Reacq angles for the High Gain on the LM jettison attitude. Then you can go there whenever you want to. The angles are pitch minus 50, and yaw zero. [Pause.]

a11_1283631.speaker: Collins
a11_1283631.text: Okay.

a11_1283631.speaker: Collins
a11_1283631.text: Houston, Columbia. Say the jettison roll, pitch, and yaw, please. [Long pause.]

a11_1283631.speaker: Evans
a11_1283631.text: Columbia, Houston. Roll zero, pitch 025, and yaw zero. Over.

a11_1283631.speaker: Collins
a11_1283631.text: Roger. Understand roll zero, pitch 025, yaw zero.

a11_1283631.speaker: Evans
a11_1283631.text: Affirmative. [Long pause.]

a11_1283631.speaker: Collins
a11_1283631.text: Maneuver in progress. We've moving. Houston. [Long pause.]

a11_1283631.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1283631.text: Houston, Eagle. Over.

a11_1283631.speaker: Evans
a11_1283631.text: Eagle, Houston. Go.

a11_1283631.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1283631.text: Roger. It doesn't appear as though the red hose is going to be much of a competitor to the leading vacuum cleaner brands. Over.

a11_1283631.speaker: Evans
a11_1283631.text: There's a little noise there, Buzz. Say again.

a11_1283631.speaker: Evans
a11_1283631.text: Eagle, Houston. [Pause.]

a11_1283631.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1283631.text: Roger. Go ahead.

a11_1283631.speaker: Evans
a11_1283631.text: Roger. Just a reminder to be sure and zero the AGS errors before you enable AGS attitude hold there after you get in burn attitude. [Long pause.]

a11_1283631.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1283631.text: Roger. You mean Sep attitude? [Long pause.]

a11_1283631.speaker: Collins
a11_1283631.text: Houston, how do you read Columbia on the High Gain now?

a11_1283631.speaker: Evans
a11_1283631.text: Hey, Columbia, Houston. Mighty fine, loud and clear.

a11_1283631.speaker: Collins
a11_1283631.text: Same here, Ron. Thanks.

a11_1283631.speaker: Evans
a11_1283631.text: And Eagle, Houston. Your steerable antenna angles for jettison attitude are - Over. [Long pause.]

a11_1283631.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1283631.text: Roger. Go ahead.

a11_1283631.speaker: Evans
a11_1283631.text: Roger. Pitch 165, yaw 68. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1283631.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1283631.text: Roger. Pitch 165, yaw 68.

a11_1283631.speaker: Evans
a11_1283631.text: Eagle, Houston. Correct.

a11_1283631.speaker: Evans
a11_1283631.text: Columbia, Houston.

a11_1283631.speaker: Collins
a11_1283631.text: Columbia. Go ahead.

a11_1283631.speaker: Evans
a11_1283631.text: Roger, Mike. You want to tweak the O 2 flow up just a bit there?

a11_1283631.speaker: Collins
a11_1283631.text: Okay. Coming up. [Pause.] Houston, do you have any preferences as to what you want us to do with the probe? Over.

a11_1283631.speaker: Evans
a11_1283631.text: Columbia, Houston. Stand by one.

a11_1283631.speaker: Collins
a11_1283631.text: Okay. Eagle says they've got a place for it inside there, so no - no problem.

a11_1283631.speaker: Evans
a11_1283631.text: Roger. That's what we were assuming. [Long pause.]

a11_1283631.speaker: Evans
a11_1283631.text: Eagle, Houston. [Long pause.]

a11_1283631.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1283631.text: Eagle. Go ahead.

a11_1283631.speaker: Evans
a11_1283631.text: Roger. Neil, it looks like your steerable's good. You can put your Track mode to Slew and high bit rate, please. Over.

a11_1283631.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1283631.text: Okay. Track mode to Slew and high bit rate. [Long pause.]

a11_1283631.speaker: Collins
a11_1283631.text: Okay. Stand by just one, please. [Long pause.]

a11_1283631.speaker: Collins
a11_1283631.text: Okay. Shoot them on down.

a11_1283631.speaker: Evans
a11_1283631.text: Eagle, Houston.

a11_1283631.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1283631.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a11_1283631.speaker: Evans
a11_1283631.text: Roger. Neil, just a reminder again, ACA out of detent, to zero the AGS error there just in case you go to Attitude Hold shortly.

a11_1283631.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1283631.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a11_1283631.speaker: Collins
a11_1283631.text: You say you wanted the probe now?

a11_1283631.speaker: Collins
a11_1283631.text: Okay.

a11_1285346.speaker: Evans
a11_1285346.text: Roger. That ACA out of detent didn't quite do it because the mode control switches were off. Request Guidance Control to PGNS and then back to AGS, and that will zero the AGS, there. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1285346.speaker: Evans
a11_1285346.text: Roger. Request Guidance Control switch to PGNS and then back to AGS. Over.

a11_1285346.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1285346.text: Okay. We still have both mode control switches off. Over.

a11_1285346.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1285346.text: And I thought I'd just take about 5 seconds here and see if I could get 000 gone, since we're fairly close to gimbal lock right now.

a11_1285346.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1285346.text: This is Apollo Control. Some 6 minutes, 40 seconds remaining until Apollo 11 goes behind the Moon on the 27th revolution. The signal from the passive seismometer, which was left on the Moon by the crew of Eagle, was lost for 30 minutes beginning about 5 minutes before Eagle took off this morning. The signal was lost because of a equipment problem at the Canary Island tracking station. The seismic equipment is back on line now, and is beginning to record lunar day surface temperatures. The dust detector recorded zero dust after Eagle lift-off. The laser ground stations have not yet acquired a r

a11_1285346.speaker: Evans
a11_1285346.text: Columbia and Eagle, Houston. About 5 minutes to LOS. Your LM jett time will be 131 plus 52, and I have the rest of the maneuver PAD if you want it now, or I can give it to you on the next time around. [Pause.]

a11_1285346.speaker: Collins
a11_1285346.text: Could you read it around the next time around, please?

a11_1285346.speaker: Evans
a11_1285346.text: Sure, Mike. That's fine. We'll get it to you then.

a11_1290152.speaker: Evans
a11_1290152.text: Apollo 11, Houston. About a minute and a half to LOS. You're looking great. It's been a mighty fine day.

a11_1290152.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1290152.text: This is Apollo Control. We've had Loss Of Signal as Apollo 11 went around the back side of the Moon on the 27th rev. We'll have acquisition with Apollo 11 approximately 45 minutes from now. At - let's see - would you believe they don't have the next tables up for the next rev. At any rate, 45 minutes from now. And at 129 hours, 4 minutes Ground Elapsed Time, this is Apollo Control.

a11_1290152.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1290152.text: Now, here are a couple of bags - and I think it's self-explanatory what goes in them.

a11_1291300.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1291300.text: This is Apollo Control at 129 hours, 13 minutes. Apollo 11 is now 36 minutes, 40 seconds from coming around the other side of the Moon for reacquisition on the 28th revolution. We're nearing the end of the 27th revolution at this time on the back side of the Moon. Armstrong and Aldrin should be involved in preparing for transferring back to the Command Module with Mike Collins, and they'll be cleaning up equipment and vacuuming off any particles of dust that remain before transferring to the Command Module. About 15 minutes after we reacquire, we would expect Neil Armstrong to be ready for the

a11_1291300.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1291300.text: What did you do with that checklist?

a11_1291300.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1291300.text: Yes, there's some rocks in it, too. You can feel them, but you can't see them; they're covered with that - graphite.

a11_1295055.speaker: Duke
a11_1295055.text: Hello, Eagle. Houston. Do you read? Over.

a11_1295055.speaker: Collins
a11_1295055.text: Houston, this is Columbia. Reading you loud and clear. We're all three back inside. The hatch is installed. We're running a pressure check - leak check. Everything's going well.

a11_1295055.speaker: Duke
a11_1295055.text: Roger, Eagle. Correction - Roger, Columbia. We copy. You guys are speedy; you beat us to the punch here. We had a couple of things for you.

a11_1295055.speaker: Duke
a11_1295055.text: Oh, it was just - We wanted you to close the CO 2 sensor breaker and give us an RCS onboard read-out out of Eagle, but that's all. Columbia, Houston. We've got a state vector for you if you'll give us P00 and Accept. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_1295055.speaker: Collins
a11_1295055.text: Buzz says the CO 2 sensor circuit breaker is in.

a11_1295055.speaker: Collins
a11_1295055.text: The RCS quantity was approximately 60 at A and 45 percent at B.

a11_1295055.speaker: Collins
a11_1295055.text: And we're going P00 and Accept.

a11_1295055.speaker: Duke
a11_1295055.text: Columbia, Houston. Your friendly White Team's going to be on till we get you on the way home, and we'd like to congratulate everybody on a successful rendezvous and a beautiful EVA. It was a great show for everybody. Over.

a11_1295055.speaker: Collins
a11_1295055.text: Thank you, sir. I'll tell Neil and Buzz. [Long pause.]

a11_1295055.speaker: Collins
a11_1295055.text: Houston, the hatch passes its integrity check. I'm going to go to LM tunnel Vent now, and leave it there.

a11_1295055.speaker: Duke
a11_1295055.text: Roger, Columbia. We copy. That's good, and we'd like a readout on the GET of about the time you - that Eagle selected the secondary loop. Over.

a11_1295055.speaker: Duke
a11_1295055.text: Hello, Columbia. Houston. We got the load in. You can do the Verb 66 and the computer's yours. Over.

a11_1300213.speaker: Duke
a11_1300213.text: Rog, Mike. It looks like if we move up this jettison time and give you a new load, it would require a new attitude, and we can't do that due to the LM already closed out. It would fight us all the way around and we'd lose comm with it. We're thinking about separating in P47 in about 10 minutes. We're looking at trajectories and we'll be right with you momentarily. Over.

a11_1300213.speaker: Collins
a11_1300213.text: Okay. It's no big thing with me either way.

a11_1300213.speaker: Duke
a11_1300213.text: Hello, Columbia. Houston. We'd like you to start down your jettison checklist. We recommend picking up page F11-12 and we'd like to jettison at ten minutes, that'll be 130:14:45. Over.

a11_1300213.speaker: Duke
a11_1300213.text: Columbia, Houston. If you can't - If that doesn't - not satisfactory, let us know. Over.

a11_1300213.speaker: Collins
a11_1300213.text: Houston, Columbia. How about a Go for Logic Bus Arm.

a11_1300213.speaker: Duke
a11_1300213.text: Columbia, Houston. You've got a Go.

a11_1301600.speaker: Duke
a11_1301600.text: Columbia, Houston. Would you start a maneuver to about a pitch of 230 for this little tweak burn? Over.

a11_1301600.speaker: Duke
a11_1301600.text: Rog, Mike. And verify track mode in Auto for the High Gain.

a11_1301600.speaker: Collins
a11_1301600.text: We're in Reacq. Is that alright?

a11_1301600.speaker: Collins
a11_1301600.text: Say again. We're in Reacq - Auto Reacq.

a11_1301600.speaker: Duke
a11_1301600.text: Roger. We need Auto, please, sir.

a11_1301600.speaker: Duke
a11_1301600.text: Right now, that's what we're looking at. Stand by. We might have you roll so we can keep the High Gain. Stand by.

a11_1301649.speaker: Duke
a11_1301649.text: Columbia, Houston. Would you start a maneuver to about a pitch of 230 for this little tweak burn? Over.

a11_1301649.speaker: Duke
a11_1301649.text: Rog, Mike. And verify track mode in Auto for the High Gain.

a11_1301649.speaker: Collins
a11_1301649.text: We're in Reacq. Is that alright?

a11_1301649.speaker: Collins
a11_1301649.text: Say again. We're in Reacq - Auto Reacq.

a11_1301649.speaker: Duke
a11_1301649.text: Roger. We need Auto, please, sir.

a11_1301649.speaker: Duke
a11_1301649.text: Right now, that's what we're looking at. Stand by. We might have you roll so we can keep the High Gain. Stand by.

a11_1301649.speaker: Duke
a11_1301649.text: Oh! Rog, Apollo 11! We got you going to a posigrade attitude and we want you - this burn will be using the minus-X thrusters at about 2 or 3 feet per second, and we got a load for you. We'll send it up momentarily. Over.

a11_1301649.speaker: Duke
a11_1301649.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Would you give us P00 and Accept? We have a load for you. Over.

a11_1301649.speaker: Duke
a11_1301649.text: Roger, Mike. And our pitch attitude's a little wrong here. If you're ready to copy, I'll give you the Sep PAD. Over.

a11_1301649.speaker: Duke
a11_1301649.text: Roger. Starting with Noun 33: 130:30:00.00, plus 00020, plus all zeros, plus all zeros. Roll, all zeros; pitch, 230; yaw, zero. Noun 44 is NA. Delta-V T 00020, burn time 0:07, Delta-V C 00020. We have - the rest of the PAD is NA.

a11_1303024.speaker: Collins
a11_1303024.text: Okay. Burn complete. Residuals: plus three balls 40, plus four balls 7, plus four balls 2, Delta-V counter 102.1. Over.

a11_1303024.speaker: Duke
a11_1303024.text: Copy, Apollo 11. Looks good to us. Over.

a11_1303324.speaker: Collins
a11_1303324.text: Houston, Apollo 11. How about coming up with a good communications attitude for us to go to between now and the time we maneuver to TEI attitude.

a11_1303324.speaker: Duke
a11_1303324.text: Hello, Apollo 11, Houston. A couple of things for you. Over.

a11_1303324.speaker: Duke
a11_1303324.text: Okay. Mike, you can maneuver to your preliminary TEI attitude as shown on page 3-98 of the Flight Plan , and the High Gain angles are good as shown in the Flight Plan, and we'd like you to dump the waste water at 131:05 down to 10 percent. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1303324.speaker: Collins
a11_1303324.text: Okay. Understand I'm going to go to roll 1.1, pitch zero - or 52.6, and yaw 13.8, and you want a waste-water dump 10 percent starting at 131:05.

a11_1304014.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1304014.text: This is Apollo Control at 130 hours, 46 minutes. That Command Module separation maneuver, which occurred at 130 hours, 30 minutes; was a 2-foot-per-second [0.6 m/s] retrograde burn. Burn duration was 7 seconds. The Flight Dynamics Officer reports that at Trans-Earth Injection, which is scheduled to occur as per the Flight Plan, at about 135 hours, 25 minutes; and at that time, the CSM will be about 20 miles [37 km] ahead of the LM and about 1 mile [1.85 km] below.

a11_1304600.speaker: Collins
a11_1304600.text: Apollo 11 on the High Gain. How do you read?

a11_1304600.speaker: Duke
a11_1304600.text: Five-by, 11. How me? Over.

a11_1304600.speaker: Collins
a11_1304600.text: You're loud and clear, Charlie. What - What numbers are you looking at for TEI T IG preliminary? 135 hours, 23 minutes; something like that?

a11_1304600.speaker: Duke
a11_1304600.text: That's affirmative, Mike. We're looking at about nominal time. We've considered kicking it up a rev, but we don't think this rev-track is going to be any good since we had the RCS burn and we need some more tracking to get you a good TEI. Over.

a11_1304600.speaker: Collins
a11_1304600.text: That's what we're looking for.

a11_1304600.speaker: Duke
a11_1304600.text: All right, sir. [Pause.]

a11_1304600.speaker: Duke
a11_1304600.text: 11, Houston. Looks like it's going to be pretty relaxed time here for the next couple of hours. We'll have you a PAD, of course, the next rev or so, and we'll keep you posted on TEI. Looks like nominal time. Over.

a11_1304600.speaker: Collins
a11_1304600.text: Thank you, Charlie.

a11_1304600.speaker: Duke
a11_1304600.text: And your little maneuver back here a moment ago will put you about 20 miles ahead of the LM at TEI.

a11_1304600.speaker: Collins
a11_1304600.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a11_1304600.speaker: Collins
a11_1304600.text: Imagine the place has cleared out a little bit after that rendezvous. You can find a place to sit down almost, huh?

a11_1304600.speaker: Duke
a11_1304600.text: Roger. Our MOCR's about empty right now. We're taking it a little easy. How does it feel up there to have some company?

a11_1304600.speaker: Collins
a11_1304600.text: Damn good, I'll tell you.

a11_1304600.speaker: Duke
a11_1304600.text: I'll bet. I bet, you'd almost be talking to yourself up there after 10 revs or so.

a11_1304600.speaker: Collins
a11_1304600.text: No, no. It's a happy home up here. It'd be nice to have some company. Be - As a matter of fact, it'd be nice to have a couple of hundred million Americans up here.

a11_1304600.speaker: Duke
a11_1304600.text: Rog. Well, they were with you in spirit.

a11_1304600.speaker: Collins
a11_1304600.text: Let them see what they're getting for their money.

a11_1304600.speaker: Duke
a11_1304600.text: Rog. They were with you in spirit anyway, at least that many. We heard on the news today, 11, that last night after you - yesterday after you made your landing, New York Times came out with a - headlines, the largest headlines they've ever used in the history of the newspaper.

a11_1304600.speaker: Collins
a11_1304600.text: Save us a copy. [Pause.]

a11_1304600.speaker: Collins
a11_1304600.text: I'm glad to hear it was fit to print.

a11_1304600.speaker: Duke
a11_1304600.text: It was great.

a11_1304600.speaker: Unidentified speaker, may be Slayton or Shepard
a11_1304600.text: That's why we didn't read you up any newscast. There really wasn't anything to talk about.

a11_1304600.speaker: Collins
a11_1304600.text: Hello, there, boss.

a11_1304600.speaker: Duke
a11_1304600.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We've got 10 minutes to LOS. See you over the hill at 131:48. Over.

a11_1304600.speaker: Collins
a11_1304600.text: Okay, Charlie. I'll dump the water as soon as we go around the corner.

a11_1304600.speaker: Duke
a11_1304600.text: Rog. Everything's looking real good now.

a11_1305708.speaker: Duke
a11_1305708.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Coming up to about 4:30 LOS. You're looking great on all your systems. Eagle is purring right along on a - After an hour and thirty [minutes] on, without any cooling, the PNGS is still looking good. Over.

a11_1310026.speaker: Duke
a11_1310026.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Would you verify that your Rendezvous Radar transponder is off? Over.

a11_1310026.speaker: Collins
a11_1310026.text: It's not, but I'll get it off.

a11_1310026.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1310026.text: Okay.

a11_1310026.speaker: Duke
a11_1310026.text: Rog. We were seeing some - believe it or not, we were seeing some funnies on the Eagle's Rendezvous Radar...

a11_1310026.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1310026.text: What do you do with it?

a11_1310026.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1310026.text: Hey - what do you do with it?

a11_1310026.speaker: Collins
a11_1310026.text: Just turn it down to off.

a11_1310026.speaker: Collins
a11_1310026.text: Good theory.

a11_1310026.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1310026.text: This goes off...

a11_1310026.speaker: Collins
a11_1310026.text: No, no, no, no, that's not the one - it's this switch right next to that IMU...

a11_1310026.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1310026.text: Oh.

a11_1310026.speaker: Collins
a11_1310026.text: ...Buzz. Okay, that one. Just turn it to - turn it to Position 1 - extreme left - that one. There you go. Thank you.

a11_1310026.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1310026.text: I thought you were going to be doing VHF Ranging on the darn thing because we had it set up for - VHF [garble].

a11_1310026.speaker: Collins
a11_1310026.text: I don't know where [garble] other than that.

a11_1310026.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1310026.text: That was to...

a11_1310026.speaker: Collins
a11_1310026.text: You ought to check the Flight Plan, it doesn't mention the [laughter] probe or the drogue. It says I remove my hatch, and then I notify you that you're clear to open your hatch.

a11_1310026.speaker: Collins
a11_1310026.text: Huh?

a11_1310026.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1310026.text: Oh, no.

a11_1310026.speaker: Collins
a11_1310026.text: So, that's just the contingency.

a11_1310026.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1310026.text: This is Apollo Control. We've had Loss Of Signal now. At the present time, we show Apollo 11 in an orbit with a high point of 62.6 nautical miles [115.9 km] and a low point or pericynthion of 54.9 [101.7 km]. The spacecraft is traveling at a speed of 5,355 feet per second [1,632 m/s]. We'll reacquire the spacecraft in a little over 45 minutes on the 21st [means 29th] revolution. At 131 hours, 3 minutes, this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a11_1310026.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1310026.text: No, negative.

a11_1310026.speaker: Collins
a11_1310026.text: That's the contingency.

a11_1310026.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1310026.text: We move the drogue there. [Garble].

a11_1310026.speaker: Collins
a11_1310026.text: We've got to reach down and grab that extension handle and all that good stuff.

a11_1310026.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1310026.text: That was alright, we understand.

a11_1314800.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1314800.text: Boy, I thought for a while there that some of those might get a little [garble] - [garble]. I'd re-set the program alarm in time for a [garble] out of there.

a11_1314800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1314800.text: This is Apollo Control at 131 hours, 48 minutes. We're standing by to reacquire Apollo - Apollo 11. Acquisition should come in about 5 seconds. This revolution should be relatively quiet. We don't have a great deal of activity scheduled. The crew may have time here to get something to eat, and here on the ground, we'll be computing the information needed for their Trans-Earth Injection burn. We do have data now from the spacecraft. We'll stand by for a call to the crew.

a11_1314800.speaker: Duke
a11_1314800.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We're standing by. Everything is looking great here. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1314800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1314800.text: This is Apollo Control. We suspect that the crew are having something to eat at this time which probably accounts for the relatively quiet period. One of the things that we're watching with interest here in Mission Control is the Lunar Module. At the time Aldrin and Armstrong left the LM and came back into the Command and Service Module, they switched over to the secondary coolant loop as part of a test that we are running to determine just how long the Primary Guidance and Navigation System will last without cooling. The primary guidance system is not cooled on the secondary loop which provid

a11_1315600.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1315600.text: This is Apollo Control at 132 hours, 15 minutes. We have some preliminary figures on the Trans-Earth Injection maneuver scheduled to occur about 3 hours, 8 minutes from now. The time of ignition is - stand by just a moment. The time of ignition would be 135 hours, 23 minutes, 41 seconds.

a11_1321500.speaker: Duke
a11_1321500.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. If you guys want it, we've got some news, here, we can read up. Over.

a11_1321500.speaker: Duke
a11_1321500.text: Rog, Neil. Starting off: Congratulatory messages on the Apollo 11 mission have been pouring into the White House from world leaders in a steady stream all day. Among the latest are telegrams from Prime Minister Harold Wilson of Great Britain and the King of Belgium. The world's press has been dominated by news of Apollo 11. Some newsmen estimate that more than sixty percent of the news used in papers across the country today concerned your mission. The New York Times, which we mentioned before, has had a - such a demand for its edition of the paper today, even though it ran 950,000 copies, tha

a11_1321500.speaker: Duke
a11_1321500.text: And Mrs. Robert Goddard said today that her husband would have been so happy. He wouldn't have shouted or anything. He would just have glowed. She added: 'That was his dream, sending a rocket to the Moon.' People around the world have had - had many reasons to be happy about the Apollo 11 mission. The Italian police reported that Sunday night was the most crime-free night of the year. And in London, a boy who had the faith to bet $5 with a bookie that a man would reach the Moon before 1970 collected $24,000. Pretty good odds.

a11_1321500.speaker: Duke
a11_1321500.text: You're probably interested in the comments your wives have made. Neil, Jan had said about yesterday's activities: 'The evening was unbelievably perfect. It is an honor and a privilege to share with my husband, the crew, the Manned Spacecraft Center, the American public, and all mankind, the magnificent experience of the beginning of lunar exploration.' She was then asked if she considered the Moon landing the greatest moment in her life. She said: 'No, that was the day we were married.' And Mike, Pat said simply: 'It was fantastically marvelous.' Buzz, Joan said - apparently couldn't quite bel

a11_1321500.speaker: Duke
a11_1321500.text: In other news, and there was a little bit, another explorer, Thor Heyerdahl, had to give up his attempt to sail a papyrus boat across the Atlantic. The storm-damaged boat was abandoned about 650 miles from Bermuda. The speed of the craft had been reduced to about 25 miles a day, and Heyerdahl said the object of the voyage had not meant to provide an endurance test for the crew.

a11_1321500.speaker: Duke
a11_1321500.text: Looking at the world of sports, let's see here. While you were busy the other day, Joe Namath and football Commissioner Pete Rozelle made the announcement that Broadway Joe had agreed to sell his interest in the Bachelors III restaurant and report to the New York Jets. And Joe arrived at the Jets' training camp today and had his first workout. Several other Jet players, who had held out along with Joe, also reported. And Davy Hill, from Jackson, Michigan, won his third major golf in as many starts in the past week. He won the Philadelphia Classic. Hill has won four tournaments so far this year

a11_1321500.speaker: Duke
a11_1321500.text: 11, Houston. We've got a preliminary TEI-30 PAD, if you're ready to copy. [Long pause.]

a11_1321500.speaker: Duke
a11_1321500.text: Rog. Coming at you. TEI-30, SPS/G&N: 36691; minus 0.61, plus 0.67; 135:23:41.49. Noun 81, plus 3202.0, plus 0671.3, minus 0277.3; 181, 054, 013. Noun 44, H A is NA, plus 0023.0; 3283.3, 2:28. Delta-V C , 3262.5; 24, 151.0 35.5. Next three lines are NA. Noun 61 plus 11.03, minus - minus 172.37; 1180.6, 36275, 195:04:52. Your set stars are Deneb and Vega, 242, 172, 012. We like two-jet ullage for 16 seconds. And the horizon will be on the 11-degree mark at T IG minus 2 minutes. And in the other comments: your sextant star is visible after GET of 134:50. Ready for your readback. Over.

a11_1321500.speaker: Collins
a11_1321500.text: Roger. We have a TEI-30, SPS/G&N: 36691, minus 0.61, plus 0.67; 135:23:41.49. Plus 3202.0, plus 0671.3, minus 0277.3; 181, 054, 013. NA, plus 0023.0; plus 3283.3, 2:28, 3262.5; 24, 151.0, 35.5. NA three times. Plus 11.03, minus 172.37; 1180.6, 36275, 195:04:52. Deneb and Vega, 242, 172, 012. Two-jet ullage, 16 seconds. Horizon 11-degree line at T IG minus 2 minutes. Sextant star visible after 134:50. Over.

a11_1325302.speaker: Duke
a11_1325302.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Seven minutes to LOS. Next AOS 133:46. You're looking good going over the hill. Out.

a11_1325302.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1325302.text: This is Apollo Control. We're now about 30 seconds from Loss Of Signal with Apollo 11 on the 29th revolution. We'll be reacquiring in about 46 minutes as the spacecraft comes around on its 30th revolution. That will be the next to the last full revolution in lunar orbit. The Trans-Earth Injection maneuver will be performed at the end of the 30th revolution, just after - actually, just after beginning the 31st revolution of the Moon. Apollo 11 is now in an orbit with a high point of 62.6 nautical miles [115.9 km] and a low point of 54.2 [100.4 km]. The current spacecraft velocity is 5,356 feet

a11_1325900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1325900.text: Are you staying in this inertial attitude? Let's just leave it in Reacq then. It works just like a charm.

a11_1334500.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1334500.text: We've acquired the signal from the spacecraft.

a11_1334500.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1334500.text: You got something [garble]?

a11_1334500.speaker: Collins
a11_1334500.text: Yes. Right across the breach. Okay. Look at that. [Garble]

a11_1334500.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1334500.text: We're standing by at this time for a call from the crew; or for CapCom Charlie Duke to put in a call to the crew from the ground. We presently show the Lunar Module in an orbit 63.3 by 56 nautical miles [117.2 by 103.7 km]. The Command and Service Module is in an orbit 63.2 by 53.9 [117.0 by 99.8 km]. At the time of the Trans-Earth Injection burn we expect that the Command Module will be about 1 mile below the LM and about 20 miles in front of it.

a11_1334500.speaker: Duke
a11_1334500.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We're standing by. [Pause.]

a11_1334500.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1334500.text: Roger. Apollo 11.

a11_1334500.speaker: Duke
a11_1334500.text: Rog. We'd like you, sometime at your convenience, to stir up the cryos on this pass. And wondering if you got the fuel cell purge. Over.

a11_1334500.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1334500.text: Roger. The [garble] fuel cell purge is complete.

a11_1334500.speaker: Duke
a11_1334500.text: Say again. You're breaking up.

a11_1334500.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1334500.text: Roger. The O 2 fuel cell purge is complete.

a11_1334500.speaker: Duke
a11_1334500.text: Rog. Copy.

a11_1334500.speaker: Duke
a11_1334500.text: Hello, Apollo 11, Houston. We've got a load for you, if you give us P00 and Accept. The load consists of a CSM pre-TEI state vector that's going in the CSM slots, and a post-TEI state vector that'll go into the LM slots, if that's okay. And also a TEI target load. Any comments? Over.

a11_1334500.speaker: Collins
a11_1334500.text: Very good. Thank you very much.

a11_1334500.speaker: Duke
a11_1334500.text: Yes, sir.

a11_1334500.speaker: Collins
a11_1334500.text: P00 and Accept. You got it.

a11_1334500.speaker: Duke
a11_1334500.text: Thank you. [Long pause.]

a11_1334500.speaker: Duke
a11_1334500.text: And, 11, Houston. A reminder. You can scratch the Verb 66 at 134:30.

a11_1334500.speaker: Collins
a11_1334500.text: Understand. [Long pause.]

a11_1334500.speaker: Duke
a11_1334500.text: And, 11, Houston. For your information, Eagle, we had an ISS fail light came on at about 3:19 due to a CDU overheating. And at about this time, at AOS, it looks like we're about to lose the platform.

a11_1334500.speaker: Unidentified crewmember
a11_1334500.text: Roger.

a11_1334500.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1334500.text: This is Apollo Control. At this time the crew should be involved in their pre-Trans-Earth Injection status checks. They'll also be aligning the platform on their spacecraft guidance system and we'll be passing up the final information for the Trans-Earth Injection burn computed on the ground. A few minutes ago you heard Charlie Duke advise the crew that we show the LM platform is about to go. We'd mentioned that prior to leaving the Lunar Module, the crew had deactivated the primary coolant loop, placing the secondary coolant loop in operation aboard the LM. This means that the primary guidanc

a11_1335742.speaker: Duke
a11_1335742.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We got the load in. You can have the computer...

a11_1335742.speaker: Collins
a11_1335742.text: 11. Are you through with the computer?

a11_1335742.speaker: Duke
a11_1335742.text: That's affirmative, Buzz.

a11_1335742.speaker: Collins
a11_1335742.text: All right. That's timing for you. [Long pause.]

a11_1335742.speaker: Duke
a11_1335742.text: And, Apollo 11, Houston. Your friendly White Team has your coming home information, if you're ready to copy. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1335742.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1335742.text: Stand by. [Long pause.]

a11_1335742.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1335742.text: Apollo 11. Ready to copy.

a11_1335742.speaker: Duke
a11_1335742.text: Rog, 11. Got two PADs for you, TEI-30 and then a TEI-31. TEI-30, SPS/G&N: 36691, minus 0.61, plus 0.66; 135:23:41.56. Noun 81: 32 - correction, plus 3201.1, plus 0681.8, minus 0265.0; 181, 054, 014. Apogee is NA, perigee, plus 0023.0; 3286 - correction, 32836; burn time 2:28, 3262.8; 24, 151.1, 35.7. Next three lines are NA. Noun 61: plus 11.03, minus 172.37; 1180.6, 36275, 195:04:52. Set stars are Deneb and Vega, 242, 172, 012. We'd like ullage from two jets for 16 seconds, and the horizon is on the 10-degree line at T IG minus 2 minutes, and your sextant star is visible after 134 plus 50. St

a11_1335742.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1335742.text: Roger. TEI-30, SPS/G&N: 36691, minus 0.61, plus 0.66; 135:23:41.56; plus 3201.1, plus 0681.8, minus 0265.0; 181, 054, 014. Apogee NA, plus 0023.0; 32836, 2:28, 32628; 24, 151.1, 35.7. NA three times. Plus 11.03, minus 172.37; 1180.6, 36275, 195:04:52. Deneb and Vega, 242, 172, 012. Two-jet ullage, 16 seconds. Horizon out-of-the-window, 10 degrees, T IG minus 2 minutes. Sextant star at 134:10. Over.

a11_1335742.speaker: Duke
a11_1335742.text: Roger, Buzz. Good readback. You're very weak. If you're ready to copy, I got a TEI-31 for you. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_1335742.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1335742.text: All right. Go ahead. [Pause.]

a11_1335742.speaker: Duke
a11_1335742.text: Apollo 11, Houston. You were cut out. Say again. [Pause.]

a11_1335742.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1335742.text: Roger. Stand by one.

a11_1335742.speaker: Duke
a11_1335742.text: Rog. [Pause.]

a11_1335742.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1335742.text: All right. Go ahead. I'm ready to copy.

a11_1335742.speaker: Duke
a11_1335742.text: Roger, 11. TEI-31, SPS/G&N: 36691, minus 0.61, plus 0.66, 137:22:39.85. Plus 3283.8, plus 0684.5, minus 0248.7. NA, pitch 052. Rest of the PAD is NA. Ready for your readback. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1335742.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1335742.text: Roger. TEI-31, SPS/G&N: 36691; minus 0.61, plus 0.66; 137:22:39.85. Plus 3283.8, plus 0684.5, minus 0248.7. NA, pitch 052. The rest is NA. Over.

a11_1335742.speaker: Duke
a11_1335742.text: Roger. Good readback. And, Buzz, did you say sextant star is visible after 134:50? [Pause.]

a11_1335742.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1335742.text: No. I wrote down 134:10. I wasn't real sure about that.

a11_1335742.speaker: Duke
a11_1335742.text: Roger. It went by me there. Retro caught it. It's 134:50. Over.

a11_1335742.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1335742.text: Okay. 134:50. Thank you.

a11_1335742.speaker: Duke
a11_1335742.text: Yes, sir.

a11_1335742.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1335742.text: This is Apollo Control at 134 hours, 10 minutes. We have about 47 minutes, 30 seconds before losing contact with Apollo 11 as it goes behind the Moon in preparation for the Trans-Earth Injection burn. With the burn, we would reacquire the spacecraft at 135 hours, 34 minutes, 11 seconds. Without the Trans-Earth Injection burn on the upcoming revolution, we would reacquire at 135 hours, 43 minutes, 50 seconds. The final figures on that burn as passed up to the crew a few minutes ago are as follows: ignition will occur at 135 hours, 23 minutes, 42 seconds. The burn duration will be 2 minutes, 28

a11_1341653.speaker: Duke
a11_1341653.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. After the burn, we'd like you to trim X and Z. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1341653.speaker: Duke
a11_1341653.text: Rog. And that's to two-tenths of a foot per second, as shown in the Flight Plan. [Long pause.]

a11_1341653.speaker: Collins
a11_1341653.text: Sounds like there's a story behind that one, too.

a11_1341653.speaker: Duke
a11_1341653.text: We'll tell you when you get back.

a11_1342022.speaker: Duke
a11_1342022.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Would you verify that you've stirred up the Cryos? Over.

a11_1342022.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1342022.text: This is Apollo Control at 134 hours, 32 minutes. Flight Director Gene Kranz just requested his flight controllers to review all of their data, take a good look at the spacecraft, and be prepared to make Go/No-Go recommendations shortly for the Trans-Earth Injection burn. That maneuver now 51 minutes, 27 seconds away. All systems on the spacecraft looking good at this point. The cabin temperature, been running about 72 degrees [Fahrenheit, 22°Celsius]. At this time, the crew is aligning the platform on their guidance system, the stable platform used as a attitude reference for the upcoming burn

a11_1343753.speaker: Duke
a11_1343753.text: Apollo 11, Houston. You are Go for TEI. Over.

a11_1343753.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1343753.text: This is Apollo Control at 134 hours, 48 minutes. It continues very quiet here in Mission Control. The flight controllers have been observing the crew inputs to their computer, monitoring as the crew prepares for the Trans-Earth Injection burn, scheduled to occur at about 35 minutes from now. We have now 9 minutes, 20 seconds until Loss Of Signal. The spacecraft currently traveling at a speed of 5,329 feet per second [1,624 m/s] and the altitude is 62.5 nautical miles [115.8 km]. At the time of the Trans-Earth Injection burn, the Lunar Module, Eagle, should be about 20 miles [37 km] behind the

a11_1344800.speaker: Duke
a11_1344800.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. You've got about 8 minutes 'til LOS. Your AOS with the burn, 135:34:05, no burn 135:44. Over.

a11_1344800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1344800.text: The crew has a Go for the Trans-Earth Injection at the beginning of the 31st revolution and all systems on the spacecraft are looking very good at this point. You heard CapCom Charlie Duke advise Mike Collins that we'll reacquire the spacecraft on the other side of the Moon; with the burn, at a Ground Elapsed Time of 135 hours, 34 minutes and 5 seconds. Without the burn we would reacquire at 135 hours, 44 minutes, 3 seconds. We now have 6 minutes, 50 seconds until Loss Of Signal. We'll continue to monitor.

a11_1345635.speaker: Duke
a11_1345635.text: Apollo 11, Houston. One minute to LOS. Go sic 'em.

a11_1345635.speaker: Collins
a11_1345635.text: Thank you, sir. We'll do it.

a11_1345635.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1345635.text: Thirty seconds now until Loss Of Signal. We've had a last status check from the Flight Director and all around the room the word is Go. We're now 26 minutes, 23 seconds from the Trans-Earth Injection maneuver - 20 minutes [means seconds] until Loss Of Signal.

a11_1345635.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1345635.text: Yes. We can get Verb 64 before we come over the hill and see what looks good.

a11_1345635.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1345635.text: Okay. I'm ready to proceed now.

a11_1345635.speaker: Collins
a11_1345635.text: Say, you guys ready - you got anything you want to do?

a11_1345635.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1345635.text: And we have Loss Of Signal now. We should next reacquire Apollo 11 at 135 hours, 34 minutes, 5 seconds. And we're now 25 minutes, 38 seconds from Trans-Earth Injection.

a11_1345635.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1345635.text: I got to make a star check, yet.

a11_1345635.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1345635.text: You're not going to fool around with that camera any more, are you?

a11_1345635.speaker: Collins
a11_1345635.text: I'll take care of it for you.

a11_1345635.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1345635.text: Post - we might run it post - after PDI if you can put it somewhere where you can get at it, going away from the Moon. I just didn't want it in my way...

a11_1353310.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1353310.text: Alright, I've seen enough of Verb 83, Mike...

a11_1353310.speaker: Collins
a11_1353310.text: Here you go.

a11_1353310.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1353310.text: ...unless you want to call a Verb 89.

a11_1353310.speaker: Collins
a11_1353310.text: Not me. I'd rather take pictures.

a11_1353310.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1353310.text: What time is AOS?

a11_1353310.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1353310.text: Haven't the foggiest.

a11_1353310.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1353310.text: That's right now.

a11_1353310.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1353310.text: Give me a Verb 51.

a11_1353310.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1353310.text: Anybody got any choice greetings they want to make to Houston?

a11_1353310.speaker: Collins
a11_1353310.text: No, I - the best burn I've ever seen in my life, I'll tell you. I guess you guys have seen two good ones today.

a11_1353310.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1353310.text: Oh, a couple.

a11_1353310.speaker: Collins
a11_1353310.text: Yes, more than two. AOS.

a11_1353310.speaker: MCC Speaker
a11_1353310.text: AOS.

a11_1353310.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1353310.text: And there's the cue, we have Acquisition Of Signal.

a11_1353310.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1353310.text: And we have data right on schedule.

a11_1353310.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1353310.text: Yes, we sure as hell have.

a11_1353310.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1353310.text: Get the burn status.

a11_1353310.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1353310.text: Hey, I hope somebody's getting the picture of the Earth coming up.

a11_1353310.speaker: Collins
a11_1353310.text: [Garble]. Not quite pitched far enough. Well, maybe I can get it out...

a11_1353310.speaker: MCC Speaker
a11_1353310.text: Rog. Zero - minus 0.7, minus 0.2.

a11_1353310.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1353310.text: I can get around to here.

a11_1353310.speaker: Collins
a11_1353310.text: [Garble] your window.

a11_1353310.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1353310.text: Upside down, turn the camera upside down. Then it'll look right.

a11_1353310.speaker: Duke
a11_1353310.text: Hello Apollo 11. Houston. How did it go? Over.

a11_1353310.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1353310.text: Tell 'em to open up the LRL doors, Charlie.

a11_1353310.speaker: Duke
a11_1353310.text: Roger. We got you coming home. It's well stocked.

a11_1353310.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1353310.text: Okay, Burn status: Delta-T IG was zero, burn time was 2 plus 30. PAD angles: Delta-V GX after trim was 0.1, V GY 0.9, V GZ 0.1. Delta-V C minus 17.9, fuel 10.6, Ox 10.4, unbalance minus 50.

a11_1353310.speaker: Duke
a11_1353310.text: Roger. Copy, Neil. Sounds good to us. [Long pause.]

a11_1353310.speaker: Duke
a11_1353310.text: And Apollo 11, Houston. You - All your systems look real good to us. We'll keep you posted.

a11_1353310.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1353310.text: Rog.

a11_1353310.speaker: Collins
a11_1353310.text: Hey, Charlie boy, looking good here. That was a beautiful burn. They don't come any finer.

a11_1353310.speaker: Duke
a11_1353310.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a11_1353310.speaker: Duke
a11_1353310.text: Apollo 11, Houston. I wondered if you've compared your pre-T - your state vector after TEI with the one in the LM slots? Over.

a11_1353310.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1353310.text: Yes, sir, and that one looked very nice. Verb 83 was plus 00070 and minus 00008.

a11_1353310.speaker: Duke
a11_1353310.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a11_1353310.speaker: Duke
a11_1353310.text: 11, Houston. I was looking at your bank Bravo nitrogen tank. It didn't leak a bit - correction - didn't leak a bit this time. Over.

a11_1353310.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1353310.text: Roger. Looked good here.

a11_1353310.speaker: Collins
a11_1353310.text: Chamber pressure was hanging in there around 100. The latter part of the burn, it started oscillating a little bit and got down a little bit below 100.

a11_1353310.speaker: Duke
a11_1353310.text: Roger.

a11_1353310.speaker: Collins
a11_1353310.text: 96 or so.

a11_1353310.speaker: Duke
a11_1353310.text: Roger.

a11_1353310.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1353310.text: Most of the conversations so far has been from Neil Armstrong and Mike Collins. That last comment came from Collins. Our first report after acquisition was from Neil Armstrong.

a11_1353310.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1353310.text: That Trans-Earth Injection burn was very close to nominal. At this time we show the spacecraft traveling at a speed of 7,603 feet per second [2,317 m/s]. The velocity already beginning to drop off and we're at an altitude of 445 nautical miles [824 km] now from the Moon.

a11_1353310.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1353310.text: This is Apollo Control. We now show the spacecraft traveling at 7,378 feet per second [2,249 m/s]. Altitude; 568 nautical miles [1,052 km]. The next order of business will be to get the crew to sleep. Flight Director Gene Kranz requested his flight controllers, prior to Acquisition Of Signal, to review their procedures and to take as many steps as possible to get the crew to sleep as soon as possible. There will be a press conference in the Building 1 auditorium. We estimate the time on that at about 12:30 Central Daylight Time.

a11_1353310.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1353310.text: And our LM telecommunications engineer reports that we've just had Acquisition Of Signal from Eagle which is still in lunar orbit. The last fix that we had on Eagle's orbit showed an apogee of 64.1 and a peri - apocynthion rather of 64.1 [118.7 km] and a pericynthion of 54.4 nautical miles [100.7 km]. The spacecraft altitude has now climbed to almost 700 nautical miles [1,300 km] from the Moon. We show a weight of 26,510 pounds [12,025 kg]; about 10,000 pounds [4,500 km] less than what we had - actually about 1,100 or 11,000 pounds - let's correct that - about 10,100 pounds [4,580 kg] less tha

a11_1354724.speaker: Duke
a11_1354724.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Would you give us P00 and Accept? We've got a REFSMMAT for you. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1355007.speaker: Duke
a11_1355007.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We've got the load in. You can go back to Block. Over.

a11_1355007.speaker: Collins
a11_1355007.text: Your Command Module film seems to be working out pretty well, Charlie, the amount we carried. Looks like we carried just about what we needed.

a11_1355007.speaker: Collins
a11_1355007.text: We have one 16-millimeter roll of the ASA-1000 color interior film. We were thinking of shooting that during the entry, out window number 4 on a bracket, and you might get the camera guys sometime in the next couple of days to give us all the good settings for that.

a11_1355007.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1355007.text: This is Apollo Control. The Flight Dynamics Officer reports that the burn was very nominal; almost precisely as planned. The burn duration was about 3 seconds long, but the velocity change was almost precisely what we had been expecting. At the present time, Apollo 11 is 1,076 nautical miles [1,993 km] from the Moon. The velocity continuing to drop off; down now to 6,698 feet per second [2,042 m/s].

a11_1355446.speaker: Duke
a11_1355446.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Wondered if, during the TEI burn, you utilized the oxidizer flow valve on the PUGS? Over.

a11_1355446.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1355446.text: Yes, we did. Based on your very excellent briefing I was expecting the thing to continue desiring increase for the whole time, so we started out with it in Increase. I saw that we pretty quickly crossed the line and started falling about 6, 7 percent behind, so I was still expecting it to move up, and I went down to Full Decrease and brought it back down to a difference of 2 percent. Over.

a11_1355446.speaker: Duke
a11_1355446.text: Rog. Thank you very much, Buzz.

a11_1355446.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1355446.text: Two-tenths of a percent, I'm sorry.

a11_1355937.speaker: Duke
a11_1355937.text: Apollo 11, Houston. You can go to PTC attitude and torque at your con - and do the P52 and torque at your convenience. Over.

a11_1355937.speaker: Collins
a11_1355937.text: Hey, we got to take some more pictures, Charlie. Is there any constraint, normally, in staying here for a while?

a11_1362037.speaker: Collins
a11_1362037.text: How does that tracking look, or is it too early to tell?

a11_1362037.speaker: Duke
a11_1362037.text: Apollo 11, Houston. FIDOs are looking at the data. It's too early to tell yet exactly. It's looking real good so far. We'll have you some answers shortly on trajectory. Over.

a11_1362808.speaker: Duke
a11_1362808.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Mike, did you notice any transients at ignition on TEI? Over.

a11_1362808.speaker: Collins
a11_1362808.text: Yeah. The transients were more noticeable than on previous burns, Charlie. I just wrote it off on the fact we had a light Command Module, but there was considerable roll activity which dampened down after the first, oh, 20 seconds, I would guess, of the burn. But there - there was also some pitch and yaw activity. I don't believe it was abnormal, and seemed to be deadbanding rather crisply in roll plus or minus about 8 degrees either side of center line. And after the first couple of - oh, after the first 20 seconds or so, the gimbals were quiet, and pitch and yaw were relatively quiet. Before

a11_1362808.speaker: Duke
a11_1362808.text: Roger. Thank you much. We were looking at the playback, and we saw some things that - right at start up. We'll be back with you later on that.

a11_1364226.speaker: Duke
a11_1364226.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Have you finished taking pictures? Over.

a11_1364226.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1364226.text: About to get started on a P52 here pretty soon.

a11_1364400.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1364400.text: This is Apollo Control. That brings us up to date with the taped conversation. We'll stand by for any further live communication from the crew before they begin their sleep period. We've gotten some preliminary figures from the Flight Dynamics Officer on that Trans-Earth Injection burn after a review of the telemetry data and it shows that our change in velocity was a nominal 3,283.5 feet per second [1,000.8 m/s]. We also show a nominal burn time of 2 minutes, 28 seconds. The crew reported the burn time about 2 to 3 seconds long based on their onboard data. The ground data shows the burn to ha

a11_1364940.speaker: Duke
a11_1364940.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. You can crank up on the PTC at any time. Over.

a11_1364940.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1364940.text: All right-oh. [Long pause.]

a11_1364940.speaker: Slayton
a11_1364940.text: Apollo 11, Houston.

a11_1364940.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1364940.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a11_1364940.speaker: Slayton
a11_1364940.text: Rog, 11. This is the original CapCom. Congratulations on an outstanding job. You guys have really put on a great show up there. I think it's about time you powered down and got a little rest, however. You've had a mighty long day here. Hope you're all going to get a good sleep on the way back. I look forward to seeing you when you get back here. Don't fraternize with any of those bugs en route , except for the Hornet.

a11_1364940.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1364940.text: Okay. Thank you, boss. We'll - We're looking forward to a - to a little rest and a restful trip back. And see you when we get there.

a11_1364940.speaker: Slayton
a11_1364940.text: Rog. You've earned it. [Long pause.]

a11_1364940.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1364940.text: That exchange was between Donald K. 'Deke' Slayton, Director of Flight Crew Operations at the Manned Spacecraft Center and astronaut Neil Armstrong.

a11_1364940.speaker: Duke
a11_1364940.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We'd like you to turn off O 2 Tank Number 1 heaters. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1364940.speaker: Collins
a11_1364940.text: It's off. Thank you.

a11_1364940.speaker: Duke
a11_1364940.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a11_1364940.speaker: Duke
a11_1364940.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. For your information, the LGC in Eagle just went belly up at 7 hours. Over.

a11_1364940.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1364940.text: Okay. Very good. That was the death of a real winner, there. [Long pause.]

a11_1364940.speaker: Collins
a11_1364940.text: Charlie, we're going to rotate about pitch 270 degrees on the way home vice 1 - or 090 on the way out. Right?

a11_1364940.speaker: Duke
a11_1364940.text: Right, sir.

a11_1364940.speaker: Collins
a11_1364940.text: Okay. Verb 49 maneuver to that attitude is in progress.

a11_1364940.speaker: Duke
a11_1364940.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a11_1364940.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1364940.text: Houston, crew status report. Radiation: CDR 11017, CMP 10019, LMP 09020. No medication.

a11_1364940.speaker: Duke
a11_1364940.text: Say again, please, Neil. We - you were breaking up. We missed that. Over.

a11_1364940.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1364940.text: Okay. This is a crew status report. Radiation: CDR 11017, CMP 10019, LMP 09020. No medication.

a11_1364940.speaker: Duke
a11_1364940.text: Roger. Thank you.

a11_1364940.speaker: Duke
a11_1364940.text: And we didn't get a crew status report from you this morning. Wondered if you could give us an estimate of sleep last night. Over.

a11_1364940.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1364940.text: Okay [garble]. [Long pause.]

a11_1364940.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1364940.text: Okay. We'll take a guess, Charlie, and try to give an equivalent amount and call it CDR 3 and LMP 4.

a11_1364940.speaker: Duke
a11_1364940.text: Rog. Thank you very much. [Long pause.]

a11_1364940.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1364940.text: And, Charlie, you want the fans cycled, I think that's right?

a11_1364940.speaker: Duke
a11_1364940.text: That's affirmative, and we'd like you to disable quads Charlie and Delta. Over.

a11_1364940.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1364940.text: Okay. Charlie and Delta. [Long pause.]

a11_1364940.speaker: Duke
a11_1364940.text: Apollo 11, Houston. If it's convenient, we'd like to go through your onboard readout. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1364940.speaker: Collins
a11_1364940.text: Of what?

a11_1364940.speaker: Duke
a11_1364940.text: Oh, excuse me. It's on the Flight Plan, 3-102. We'd like Batts and RCS. Over.

a11_1364940.speaker: Collins
a11_1364940.text: Stand by.

a11_1364940.speaker: Collins
a11_1364940.text: Ready to copy, Houston?

a11_1364940.speaker: Duke
a11_1364940.text: Roger. Go ahead.

a11_1364940.speaker: Collins
a11_1364940.text: Batt Charlie 37.0, Pyro Batt A 37.0, Batt B 37.0. RCS; 55, 65, 64, and 62. Over.

a11_1364940.speaker: Duke
a11_1364940.text: Roger. We copy all that. Thank you much.

a11_1364940.speaker: Collins
a11_1364940.text: Roger.

a11_1371701.speaker: Duke
a11_1371701.text: Apollo 11, Houston. A couple of questions for the Moonwalkers, if you got a second. Over.

a11_1371701.speaker: Duke
a11_1371701.text: Rog, Neil. We're seeing some temperature rises on the Passive Seismic Experiment that are a little higher than normal and were wondering if you could verify the deployed position. We understand it's about 40 feet from the LM in the eleven o'clock position. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1371701.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1371701.text: No. It's about in the nine or nine-thirty position, and I'd say it's about 50 or 60 feet.

a11_1371701.speaker: Duke
a11_1371701.text: Roger. Copy. Also, did you notice - was there any indication of any dust cloud as you lifted off? Over.

a11_1371701.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1371701.text: Not very much. There was quite a bit of Kapton and parts of the LM that went out in all directions, usually for great distances, as far as I can tell. But I don't remember seeing anything of a dust cloud to speak of.

a11_1371701.speaker: Duke
a11_1371701.text: Roger. Understand all you could see was parts of the LM going out. What was your - your first - first comment? Over.

a11_1371701.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1371701.text: I don't remember. Just could see Kapton and other parts of the LM staging scattering all around the area for great distances, but I didn't see much dust.

a11_1371701.speaker: Collins
a11_1371701.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Could you keep me honest on the lithium hydroxide changes? When do you have the next one scheduled for?

a11_1371701.speaker: Duke
a11_1371701.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Mike, on that canister, we had you due to change one at 133 before TEI, and it's on page 3-99 . The next one we got is at 147. Over.

a11_1372531.speaker: Duke
a11_1372531.text: Hello, Apollo 11, Houston. We'd like to extend our damping period for another 5 minutes. Let the rates get way down. Over.

a11_1372531.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1372531.text: This is Apollo Control at 137 hours, 27 minutes. At this time, Apollo 11 is traveling at a speed of about 4,982 feet per second [1,519 m/s]. At - Is about 5,900 nautical miles [10,900 km] from the Moon, and about 198,900 nautical miles [368,400] from Earth. A short while ago, you heard Neil Armstrong make a few descriptive comments of the scene on the lunar surface at the time the LM ascent stage lifted off. Armstrong reported seeing very little dust, but quite a bit of debris from the LM. He referred to the Kapton, which is a plastic-like insulation material generally silver or gold in color

a11_1372531.speaker: Collins
a11_1372531.text: Roger, Charlie. Like to bring you up to date on our chlorination status. In compartment B4, we have one, two, three, four, five, six, seven - correction, we have eight pockets for chlorine and buffer ampules, of which - let me correct that. We have seven pockets, of which one is empty and always has been empty, leaving six remaining. On the other side over there in B7, we have another container with seven pockets, so we have a total of seven plus six, and those are filled with six chlorines and seven buffers. Now, I've been using one chlorine and one buffer per day which, at this point in time

a11_1372531.speaker: Duke
a11_1372531.text: Rog. We copy, Mike. Stand by.

a11_1373721.speaker: Duke
a11_1373721.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Check in A1, Mike, and see what you can find in there. Over.

a11_1373721.speaker: Duke
a11_1373721.text: We think you might have some more chlorine up in A1. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_1373721.speaker: Duke
a11_1373721.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Do you read? You're breaking up. Over.

a11_1373721.speaker: Duke
a11_1373721.text: Roger, 11. You're breaking up. Mike, please look in compartment A1. We think there might be some more chlorine up there. Over.

a11_1373721.speaker: Duke
a11_1373721.text: 11, Houston. Reading you about one-by. Over.

a11_1373721.speaker: Duke
a11_1373721.text: 11, Houston. We're having a downlink problem, the reason we can't read you. We're switching sites. Stand by. [Long pause.]

a11_1373721.speaker: Duke
a11_1373721.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. How do you read now? Over. [Pause.]

a11_1373721.speaker: Duke
a11_1373721.text: Rog. You're five-by now, too, Mike. Thank you much. Did you copy that about A1 on that chlorine?

a11_1374526.speaker: Duke
a11_1374526.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We're having a little trouble getting the yaw rate damped out to appropriate value. We'd like y'all to be quiet like mice for a couple of minutes and let's see if that'll help it out. Over.

a11_1374526.speaker: Duke
a11_1374526.text: 11, Houston. You did great work there. We're ready to spin it up. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_1374526.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1374526.text: Yeah. We read you, Charlie. Would you stand by a minute?

a11_1374526.speaker: Duke
a11_1374526.text: 11, Houston. Shift change time, here. White Team bids you good night. We'll see you tomorrow. Over.

a11_1374526.speaker: Duke
a11_1374526.text: Adios. Thanks again for a great show, you guys.

a11_1374526.speaker: Collins
a11_1374526.text: Thanks for a great job down there.

a11_1374526.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1374526.text: This is Apollo Control at 137 hours, 52 minutes. Apollo 11 crew has signed off for the night, starting a long, well-deserved rest period. Duration of the rest period is programmed for 10 hours, however, the wake up time is not critical. It's very likely we'll let them sleep 'til - 'til they wake up of their own accord. At this time Columbia is 7,045 nautical miles [13,047 km] away from the Moon, headed toward home at a velocity of 4,868 feet per second [1,484 m/s].

a11_1375200.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1375200.text: This is Apollo Control at 138 hours, 2 minutes. CapCom Owen Garriott has just put in a call to the crew and is passing up some antenna information to them. Here's that conversation.

a11_1380200.speaker: Garriott
a11_1380200.text: Howdy there, Mike. We're ready to go ahead and have you switch to your Omni positions for your sleep period, and we would like the following High Gain switch positions: your High Gain antenna in Manual, beam width Wide, pitch is minus 50, and yaw is a plus 270. And just follow the Flight Plan for remaining Comm configuration. Over.

a11_1380200.speaker: Collins
a11_1380200.text: You Purple people keep funny hours.

a11_1380200.speaker: Garriott
a11_1380200.text: Your Comm is pretty weak at this point, Mike. Please say again.

a11_1380200.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1380200.text: This is Apollo Control. Ten minutes ago we logged what we expect to be our last contact with Eagle in lunar orbit. That coming at 137 hours, 55 minutes Elapsed Time. At that time the battery power fell below the level where the secondary guidance system could hold the attitude of the vehicle within the steerable antenna limits. We do not expect to establish contact with Eagle again. We'll continue to stand by here live. There may be a little bit more conversation before the crew turns in for the night.

a11_1380620.speaker: Garriott
a11_1380620.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We'd like for you to go ahead and put your S-band antenna Omni to Omni and Omni B. Over.

a11_1380620.speaker: Garriott
a11_1380620.text: Apollo 11, Houston. How do you read me through Honeysuckle now? Over. [Pause.]

a11_1380620.speaker: Garriott
a11_1380620.text: Very good. Reading you better now. And did you copy we'd appreciate going S-band Omni and Omni B at this time? Over.
