a11_1380620.speaker: Collins
a11_1380620.text: I'll tell you. Purple people keep funny hours.

a11_1380620.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1380620.text: This is Apollo Control at 138 hours, 11 minutes. We do not intend to contact the crew during this rest period again. We'll take this line down now and come back up if there is further conversation. This is Mission Control, Houston.

a11_1474711.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1474711.text: Good afternoon, Houston. Apollo 11 up. [Long pause.]

a11_1474711.speaker: McCandless
a11_1474711.text: Good morning, 11. This is Houston. Over.

a11_1474711.speaker: McCandless
a11_1474711.text: Roger. 8, 8 and 8.5. When you're ready, we've got a small Flight Plan update for you. [Long pause.]

a11_1474711.speaker: McCandless
a11_1474711.text: Roger. At about 148 hours, if you've not already done so, a CO 2 filter change, and the H 2 purge line heater on 20 minutes before the O 2 and H 2 purge. At 148 hours, we'd like you to initiate a charge on Battery Alpha instead of at 151 hours, and leave the charge on until we notify you further. At 150 hours GET, waste-water dump to 10 percent. We do plan to burn Midcourse Correction 5. It will be an RCS burn about 5 feet per second [1.5 m/s] at about the nominal time in the Flight Plan. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_1474711.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1474711.text: Roger. Understand. We'll be accomplishing the filter change shortly, the purge line heater is on, and we'll take care of O 2 and H 2 purge shortly, and at 148 will initiate a charge on Battery A until you notify us further. 150 hours, waste-water dump to 10 percent. And we're looking forward to Midcourse Correction 5 at about 5 feet per second at the nominal time. Over.

a11_1474711.speaker: McCandless
a11_1474711.text: Roger. I've got your consumables update, if you're ready to copy. [Pause.]

a11_1474711.speaker: McCandless
a11_1474711.text: Okay. At GET of 147 plus 00, RCS total minus 2.0 per cent, which is about minus 14 pounds. Alpha minus 12.0, Bravo plus 10.0, minus 3.0, minus 2.0. Hydrogen total, minus 1.5 pounds; O 2 total, plus 20 pounds. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1474711.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1474711.text: Roger. I copy, and our onboard readouts - Alpha 53 percent, Bravo 54 percent, Cocoa's 64 percent, Delta 61 percent. Over.

a11_1474711.speaker: McCandless
a11_1474711.text: Roger, 11. Would you read that quad Alpha again, please, Buzz. You're cutting out. It may be - are you operating on VOX? Over.

a11_1474711.speaker: McCandless
a11_1474711.text: 11, from down here on telemetry, all your systems look to be in good shape.

a11_1480151.speaker: McCandless
a11_1480151.text: Roger. Would you ask Buzz to check his biomedical TM sensors for a loose or dried out sensor? We're getting erratic electrocardiogram readings. That would be one of the three sternal leads. Over.

a11_1480151.speaker: McCandless
a11_1480151.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Say again your last, please.

a11_1480151.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1480151.text: This is Apollo Control at 148 hours, 7 minutes. In about 24 seconds from now, the spacecraft will pass the imaginary line into the Earth's sphere of influence.

a11_1480700.speaker: McCandless
a11_1480700.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Stand by for a Mark leaving the lunar sphere of influence.

a11_1480700.speaker: McCandless
a11_1480700.text: You're leaving the lunar sphere of influence. Over.

a11_1480700.speaker: Collins
a11_1480700.text: Roger. Is Phil Shaffer down there?

a11_1480700.speaker: McCandless
a11_1480700.text: Negative. But we've got a highly qualified team on in his stead.

a11_1480700.speaker: Collins
a11_1480700.text: Rog. I wanted to hear him explain it again at the press conference.

a11_1480700.speaker: Collins
a11_1480700.text: That's old Apollo 8 joke but tell him the spacecraft gave a little jump as it went through the sphere.

a11_1480700.speaker: McCandless
a11_1480700.text: Okay. I'll pass it on to him. Thanks a lot, and Dave Reed is sort of burying his head in his arms right now.

a11_1480700.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1480700.text: Those guys down there in the trench did a pretty good job this flight.

a11_1480700.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1480700.text: We don't want them to give up yet, though.

a11_1480700.speaker: McCandless
a11_1480700.text: No. They'll hang in there for about another 47 hours or so.

a11_1480700.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1480700.text: This is Apollo Control at 148 hours, 21 minutes. At the time the spacecraft crossed from the Moon's sphere of influence to the Earth's sphere of influence, that point at which the Earth is computed as having the dominant influence on the spacecraft trajectory, Apollo 11 was about 33,800 nautical miles [62,600 km] from the Moon, and about 174,000 nautical miles [322,000 km] from Earth. At the present time, the spacecraft is traveling at a speed of 3,994 feet per second [1,217 m/s] with respect to the Earth. After awakening this morning, Neil Armstrong reported all three crewmen getting at least

a11_1482100.speaker: McCandless
a11_1482100.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. If you're not busy now, I can read you up the morning news.

a11_1482100.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1482100.text: Roger. We're all listening. Go ahead.

a11_1482100.speaker: McCandless
a11_1482100.text: Roger. From the hot wires of the Public Affairs Office, Apollo 11 still dominates the news around the world. Only four nations - Communist China, North Korea, North Vietnam, and Albania - have not yet informed their citizens of your flight and landing on the Moon. One newsman said that he has run out of ways to describe your success. Tonight, President Nixon is scheduled to watch the All Star baseball game in Washington. After the game, he will depart for the Pacific recovery area. Wednesday evening, he will fly from Johnston Island by helicopter to the Navy communications ship Arlington. Then

a11_1482100.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1482100.text: Would you look up the Dow Jones Industrials for us.

a11_1482100.speaker: McCandless
a11_1482100.text: Roger. Stand by a minute, please.

a11_1483345.speaker: McCandless
a11_1483345.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. We see you in P00. When you can give us Accept, we have a state vector and target load uplink ready for you. [Long pause.]

a11_1483345.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1483345.text: Roger, Houston. Go ahead. You've got the computer.

a11_1483841.speaker: McCandless
a11_1483841.text: Apollo 11, we've completed the uplink. The computer's yours.

a11_1484341.speaker: McCandless
a11_1484341.text: Roger. With respect to the Dow Jones Industrials, since closing on Tuesday afternoon the 15th up to about 1:05 p.m. Houston time this afternoon, why, the effect has been a net drop. That is, minus 6 points on the industrial average. So far today since opening, the Dow Jones industrial average has gone down by 11.05 after rising 1½ shortly after opening. Today's performance on the utilities is a drop of 1.63; and railroads, a drop of 1.58. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1484341.speaker: Collins
a11_1484341.text: Yeah. Every flight has to have some disadvantages, I guess.

a11_1484341.speaker: McCandless
a11_1484341.text: Roger. Some speculation that you all are responsible for that 1½-point rise right after opening. [Pause.]

a11_1484341.speaker: Collins
a11_1484341.text: Well, don't blame the 11-point drop on us, anyway.

a11_1484341.speaker: McCandless
a11_1484341.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. If you have a minute or so free, I wonder if we could get Mike to give us a little bit of clarification on what happened around about the time of docking. We copied him as mentioning that contact was very smooth, almost imperceptible, and we're a little bit inquisitive or curious about his remarks as to what happened after probe retraction. Over.

a11_1484341.speaker: Collins
a11_1484341.text: Roger. I docked in CMC Auto, and as I said, I wasn't really sure of the moment of contact. I kept cross-checking the docking probe indicators. I got two barber poles indicating that the three capture latches - not capture latches, but the three giz-maches had made, and we were soft docked. And at that time the situation looked very stable. So, I went to CMC Free, glanced back out the window. It still looked stable and I fired primary 2 bottle. And at that time, a gyration began between the two vehicles due I'm not sure to what. Perhaps the LM thrusting or perhaps it was building up prior, and

a11_1484341.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1484341.text: And on the LM side, we were in AGS Min deadband Att Hold, and at contact, I thrusted plus-X. And shortly after that we had a sizable attitude oscillation and thruster firing, so we opened up the deadband to Max and manually flew the vehicle into stable attitude during the retraction. And we went to Off after [garble] completion of retraction.

a11_1484341.speaker: McCandless
a11_1484341.text: Roger. Thank you very much. Out.

a11_1485048.speaker: McCandless
a11_1485048.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. I have your Midcourse Correction 5 PAD available when you're ready to copy.

a11_1485048.speaker: McCandless
a11_1485048.text: 11, this is Houston. Midcourse Correction number 5. RCS/G&N: 26025, pitch and yaw trim NA, T IG 150:29:54.53; minus 0004.8, plus all balls, plus 0000.1; 075, 159, 328. H A is NA; H P , plus 0023.0. 0004.8, 0:11, 0004.8. Sextant star 03, 090.8, 38.2. Boresight star block, none available. Latitude plus 11.02, minus 172.04; 1180.3, 36275, 195:03:33; GDC align, Deneb and Vega, 007, 144, 068; no ullage of course, four-quad thrusting. Over. Read back.

a11_1485048.speaker: Collins
a11_1485048.text: Roger. Midcourse number 5. RCS/G&N: 26025, pitch and yaw NA, 150:29:54.53, minus 0004.8, plus all zeros, plus 0000.1; 075, 159, 328. NA, plus 0023.0; 0004.8, 0:11, 0004.8. 03, 090.8, 38.2. NA three times. Plus 11.02, minus 172.04, 1180.3, 36275, 195:03:33; Deneb and Vega, 007, 144, 068; and four quads for the burn. Over.

a11_1485048.speaker: McCandless
a11_1485048.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Readback correct. Out.

a11_1485048.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1485048.text: This is Apollo Control at 148 hours, 58 minutes. The series of numbers passed up to the crew a few minutes ago was for Midcourse Correction number 5. That is scheduled to occur at 150 hours, 29 minutes, 54 seconds. It will be a Reaction Control System burn using the spacecraft Reaction Control System thrusters, with a velocity change of 4.8 feet per second, and that will be retrograde. Primary purpose of the maneuver will be to adjust the entry conditions which is - would primarily be for corridor control, controlling the flight path angle at entry. And the current predicted splash time in the

a11_1490311.speaker: McCandless
a11_1490311.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Over.

a11_1490311.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1490311.text: Roger. Go ahead, Houston.

a11_1490311.speaker: McCandless
a11_1490311.text: Roger. If Neil has a free minute, we've got a question or two regarding the CO 2 partial pressure and water in the suit loop discrepancies noted yesterday. Over.

a11_1490311.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1490311.text: Go ahead.

a11_1490311.speaker: McCandless
a11_1490311.text: Roger, 11. Was water noted in both suits or only in yours, Neil?

a11_1490311.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1490311.text: I think only in my suit.

a11_1490311.speaker: McCandless
a11_1490311.text: Okay. Can you locate that occurrence for us in time when you first noticed water in the suit, either by mission time or relation to any particular event? [Long pause.]

a11_1490311.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1490311.text: I think it was after insertion sometime, Bruce. I don't remember exactly when. I - It was when we were in orbit and had our - after we took our helmets off.

a11_1490311.speaker: McCandless
a11_1490311.text: Roger. Did you call it to us when you first noticed it, or was it some time after, when you called it?

a11_1490311.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1490311.text: I'd guess it might have been probably 20 minutes after I noticed it that I mentioned it to you.

a11_1490311.speaker: McCandless
a11_1490311.text: Roger. Was this noticing the water accompanied by erratic CO 2 partial pressure readings, or was that a separate problem? Over. [Pause.]

a11_1490311.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1490311.text: Well, the water problem evidenced itself before we noted any erratic motions of the PCO 2 gauge.

a11_1490311.speaker: McCandless
a11_1490311.text: Roger. And what was the relative sequence on selecting water separator number 2 and the secondary CO 2 canister? That is, did you go to the secondary water separator first and then the secondary CO 2 ? Over. [Pause.]

a11_1490311.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1490311.text: I believe we went to secondary CO 2 first.

a11_1490311.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1490311.text: Secondary hydroxide - lithium hydroxide.

a11_1490311.speaker: McCandless
a11_1490311.text: Roger. We copy. And was there any change in your suit loop...

a11_1490311.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1490311.text: No.

a11_1490311.speaker: McCandless
a11_1490311.text: Go ahead.

a11_1490311.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1490311.text: I should mention, Bruce, that when I went to water secondary - water separator to secondary there, I didn't notice any change. But about after 15 minutes or 20 minutes, the water stopped coming out. So maybe that was just water that was already in the loop that was still blowing out, but the secondary water separator was operating properly.

a11_1490311.speaker: McCandless
a11_1490311.text: Roger. Did you make any changes in the suit loop configuration after you went from the egress mode to the cabin mode after insertion? That is, in particular, they're interested in knowing if you recall changing the diverter valve position to Egress at any time while you were on the secondary canister? Over.

a11_1490311.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1490311.text: No. I don't believe we did that at all, Bruce.

a11_1490311.speaker: McCandless
a11_1490311.text: Okay, 11. Thank you. That sums up our questions for now, and we'll crank these back into the engineering pipeline and see what we can come up with.

a11_1490311.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1490311.text: Okay. Are you satisfied that the CO 2 circuit breaker was in on jettison? Over.

a11_1490311.speaker: McCandless
a11_1490311.text: Say again, please?

a11_1490311.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1490311.text: Roger. On LM jettison, are you satisfied that the CO 2 circuit breaker was in? Over.

a11_1490311.speaker: McCandless
a11_1490311.text: Yes. It was in.

a11_1490311.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1490311.text: Roger. Could you confirm that? I thought there was some question after we got into the Command Module as to whether that had been left in or not. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1490311.speaker: McCandless
a11_1490311.text: Roger, 11. It was in and confirmed in, and the readings after jettison stayed about 0.1 to 0.2.

a11_1492424.speaker: McCandless
a11_1492424.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. We have not noticed any change in the signal coming through on the LMP's EKG. When he has a little free time, we'd like him to check into it again. Over.

a11_1492424.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1492424.text: Roger. I looked at all three of the upper chest center ones, and they appear to be fairly tight. I'll push them back in again. Over.

a11_1492424.speaker: McCandless
a11_1492424.text: Roger. On the TM here, we noticed some fluctuations that may have been attributed to your moving the sensors around or pushing on them, but the erratic problem seems to be persisting.

a11_1492424.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1492424.text: This is Apollo Control at 149 hours, 41 minutes. We're now about 49 minutes away from the first midcourse correction on this trans-Earth leg of the Apollo 11 flight. That maneuver will be a 4.8-foot-per-second burn of the spacecraft Reaction Control System thrusters and is scheduled to occur at a Ground Elapsed Time of 150 hours, 29 minutes, 54 seconds. At this time, Apollo 11 is 171,017 nautical miles [316,723 km] from the Earth and the spacecraft velocity is 4,043 feet per second [1,232 m/s].

a11_1494427.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1494427.text: Roger. I wonder if you've noticed any change in the Biomed return you're getting. Over.

a11_1494427.speaker: McCandless
a11_1494427.text: Negative, Buzz. It still looks kind of bad. Apparently, when you move around, it's cutting in and out. Have you checked the little electrical connector where it goes into the signal conditioner? Over.

a11_1494427.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1494427.text: Yes. They're all about as tight as can be. I tell you what - I'll take them off and put them back on again and see if that makes any difference.

a11_1494427.speaker: McCandless
a11_1494427.text: Okay. If you would, at your convenience. We'll be watching it down here.

a11_1494427.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1494427.text: This is Apollo Control at 150 hours, 4 minutes. Telemetry data at this time shows the spacecraft in the proper attitude for the upcoming midcourse correction maneuver. The crew will soon be verifying their attitude by taking a sighting on a star through the sextant and then be running some tests on the Guidance and Control system and the Reaction Control System before the maneuver takes place. That burn now scheduled to come in a little over 25 minutes. Apollo 11 is now 170,102 nautical miles [315,029 km] from the Earth and the spacecraft velocity is 4,058 feet per second [1,237 m/s].

a11_1501019.speaker: McCandless
a11_1501019.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. We'd like you to try acquisition on the High Gain Antenna for us at pitch minus 90, yaw 270. Over.

a11_1501019.speaker: McCandless
a11_1501019.text: 11, this is Houston. We're showing about 6.8 percent on waste water on our telemetry now. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1501019.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1501019.text: Okay. Got about 9, up here. Over.

a11_1502831.speaker: McCandless
a11_1502831.text: 11, Houston. We're standing by for your burn. Everything's looking good from down here.

a11_1502831.speaker: Collins
a11_1502831.text: Thank you, Bruce. You've got about a minute and 20 seconds.

a11_1502831.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1502831.text: One minute now until Midcourse Correction number 5. That will be a 10.9-second burn of the spacecraft Reaction Control System thrusters giving a change of velocity retrograde of 4.8 feet per second. The primary purpose of this maneuver will be to control the spacecraft flight path angle at Entry Interface. We're now less than 30 seconds from the initiation of the burn.

a11_1502831.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1502831.text: They should be burning at this time.

a11_1502831.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1502831.text: And we show the burn off.

a11_1502831.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1502831.text: Houston, you copy our residuals? [Long pause.]

a11_1502831.speaker: McCandless
a11_1502831.text: Roger. We've got your residual. Do you have a counter reading for us.

a11_1502831.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1502831.text: That midcourse correction was performed at a distance of about 169,000 nautical miles [313,000 km] from the Earth. The spacecraft velocity; 4,075.6 feet per second [1,242.2].

a11_1502831.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1502831.text: This is Apollo Control at 150 hours, 35 minutes. Our telemetry data here on the ground shows that midcourse correction maneuver [was] just about nominal; burn duration, 10.5 seconds. Prior to the maneuver, we were predicting a splashdown time of 195 hours, 17 minutes, 25 seconds. And we expect there will be some modification to that after we've had a chance to do some tracking following this midcourse correction maneuver. Apollo 11 is now 168,843 nautical miles [312,697 km] from the Earth, traveling at a speed of 4,078 feet per second [1,243 km], and we're continuing to see a very slow build-u

a11_1504334.speaker: Collins
a11_1504334.text: Roger. We're in PTC attitude and would you please give us a call when our thruster activity has subsided sufficiently?

a11_1505641.speaker: McCandless
a11_1505641.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. We're going to hand over from Madrid to Goldstone at 151 hours even. If you should lose lock on the High Gain at this time, you may reacquire at pitch minus 45, yaw 270. Break. We're still watching your rates. Over.

a11_1510849.speaker: McCandless
a11_1510849.text: 11, we're still seeing rates on your spacecraft above those that we'd like for any - continuation of the PTC mode. We're still monitoring it, and we'll advise you when it's settled down. Over.

a11_1510849.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1510849.text: This is Apollo Control at 151 hours, 11 minutes. The crew is presently setting up the spacecraft for Passive Thermal Control. Once it stabilizes out, it will begin a slow roll rate of three revolutions per hour to maintain temperature control. At the present time, Apollo 11 is 167,448 nautical miles [310,114 km] from the Earth and the velocity is 4,101 feet per second [1,250 m/s].

a11_1512151.speaker: McCandless
a11_1512151.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. You are go for the spin-up on PTC. Over.

a11_1512151.speaker: Collins
a11_1512151.text: Rog. It didn't like it that time. When I got down to the entry 27303 Enter, it took off in roll at a high rate in excess of 1 degree per second. Over. I've stopped it now, and we are going to have to go back and do it over again. I'd like to try to find out the reason why it did that.

a11_1512151.speaker: McCandless
a11_1512151.text: Roger. You might as well start setting up for it, and we'll be working the problem here.

a11_1512151.speaker: Collins
a11_1512151.text: Okay. Do you have us on high bit rate here now?

a11_1512151.speaker: Collins
a11_1512151.text: Okay, good. I'll maneuver back to PTC initiation attitude while you guys look at the data and see what you think.

a11_1512151.speaker: Collins
a11_1512151.text: Houston, Apollo 11. I think the reason is in having 16 20 on the DSKY during the subsequent entries, or at least that's one possibility.

a11_1513333.speaker: McCandless
a11_1513333.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. While you're waiting for the CSM to settle down and for us to look at the tapes on your latest maneuver, would you feel like answering some more questions with relation to the lunar surface? Over. [Pause.]

a11_1513333.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1513333.text: Go ahead.

a11_1513333.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1513333.text: Go ahead, Bruce.

a11_1513333.speaker: McCandless
a11_1513333.text: Roger. For 64 thousand dollars, we're still trying to work out the location of your landing site, Tranquillity Base. We think it is located on LAM-2 chart at Juliet 0.5 and 7.8. Do you still have those charts on board? Over.

a11_1513333.speaker: Collins
a11_1513333.text: Yeah. Stand by one. They're packed.

a11_1513333.speaker: McCandless
a11_1513333.text: Roger. You may not have to unpack it. The position which I just gave you is slightly west of West Crater. I guess it's about two-tenths of a kilometer west of it, and we were wondering if Neil or Buzz had observed any additional landmarks during descent, lunar stay, or ascent which would confirm or disprove this. One thing that we're wondering about is that if you were at this position, you would have seen the Cat's Paw during ascent just up to the north of your track. Over.

a11_1513333.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1513333.text: We were looking for the Cat's Paw, too, thinking we were probably downrange, beyond the Big V. But I think that it's likely that that might have been West Crater that we went across in landing, but - Stand by. [Long pause.]

a11_1513333.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1513333.text: We're hoping, Bruce, that our 16-mm film was working at that point in descent, and we'll be able to confirm our touchdown position. We thought that during ascent we might be able to pick up some recognizable objects close to the landing site, and we did see a number of small craters, and crater rows, and things like that, which we may be able to pick out after the fact, but we haven't been able to yet.

a11_1513333.speaker: McCandless
a11_1513333.text: Roger. And the next question from our panel is for Buzz. We recall that he reported seeing a laser upon AOS of the Earth the first time after - the first rev after ascent, and we're wondering what color the beam was and if he could determine at the approximate location with respect to the Earth. Over.

a11_1513333.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1513333.text: It was mostly white, perhaps a tinge of yellowish color to it. And it seemed to be - as I recall it, the terminator of the Earth was toward the horizon and seemed to be about a quarter to a third of the way down from - down towards the terminator of the Earth - from the opposite horizon. That's a third to a quarter Earth radii. Over.

a11_1513333.speaker: McCandless
a11_1513333.text: Roger. And that puts it in the light side? Over.

a11_1513333.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1513333.text: Roger. Yes, it was in the light side. The Earth was about - a two-thirds lit Earth, with the terminator down toward the horizon. And now coming from the opposite limb of the Earth, the sunlit limb, coming down about one-quarter to one-third of a radius in from the limb. Generally, centrally located with respect to a line drawn perpendicular to the terminator that goes through the center. Over.

a11_1513333.speaker: McCandless
a11_1513333.text: Roger, Buzz. We copy.

a11_1513333.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1513333.text: And I got pictures of that. I'm sure that'll show up.

a11_1513333.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1513333.text: And I saw that, too. It was a very bright spot of light and I confirm Buzz's observation of its position.

a11_1513333.speaker: McCandless
a11_1513333.text: Okay, 11. Very good. Now, with respect to the documented sample container - on television it appeared to us as though the samples for that container were in fact being given - being selected in accordance with some thought or consideration being given to the rocks themselves. And we were wondering if you could give any further details from memory about any of these samples, and the context of the material or the surface from which they were taken. Over.

a11_1513333.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1513333.text: Yes. You remember I initially started on the cut side of the LM that the TV camera was on, and I took a number of samples of rocks on the surface, and several that were just subsurface - about 20 - 15 to 20 feet north of the LM. And then I recalled that that area had been probably swept pretty well by the exhaust of the descent engine, so I crossed over to the southern side of the LM and took a number of samples from the area around the elongate double crater that we commented on and several beyond that and tried to take as many different types - of rock types as I could see by eye, as I could

a11_1513333.speaker: McCandless
a11_1513333.text: Roger. Did you observe any small craters with conspicuously blocky rims? Over.

a11_1513333.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1513333.text: Well, aside from the real big one that we went over, I guess there were none in our area. I took a stroll back after putting up the PSEP [Passive Seismic Experiment Package], and while Buzz was starting to unpack [likely means 'pack up'] the documented sample, took - took a stroll back to a crater behind us that was maybe 70 or 80 feet in diameter and 15 or 20 feet deep, and took some pictures of it. It had rocks in the bottom of pretty good size, considerably bigger than any that were out on the surface, but there was no - we apparently, at 15 feet or so, had not gotten below the regolith. We

a11_1513333.speaker: McCandless
a11_1513333.text: Roger. We copy. [Long pause.]

a11_1513333.speaker: McCandless
a11_1513333.text: Okay. Thank you, Neil. That about wraps up the questions we have on hand for now.

a11_1513333.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1513333.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a11_1513333.speaker: Collins
a11_1513333.text: My compliments to the chef. The food is outstanding. This cream of chicken soup I give at least three spoons.

a11_1513333.speaker: McCandless
a11_1513333.text: Okay. Cream of chicken, three spoons.

a11_1514622.speaker: McCandless
a11_1514622.text: 11, we concur that having Verb 16, Noun 20 up on the DSKY may well have had some effect on your PTC initiation. It looks like this would give - let the computer work with a knowledge of the actual CDU angles. What we'd like you to do is, do a CDU zero which is Verb 40, Noun 20, Enter, and then start the PTC procedure again at Step 2 with loading Verb 6, Noun 22, desired attitude in the Auto maneuver, and all that. Over.

a11_1514622.speaker: Collins
a11_1514622.text: Okay. The only thing I don't understand about that is why it took off at the rate it did. What rate should it have taken off at under that theory?

a11_1515217.speaker: McCandless
a11_1515217.text: Mike, over here on page 9-7 of your checklist where we're setting up PTC, there's been a note penciled in after: 'Wait 20 minutes for rates to damp. Do not monitor Verb 16, Noun 20.' It turns out that the significance of that is that, if you are monitoring 16 Noun 20, then when you get down here in step 7, the second time you do a Verb 24, you've got to reload the Noun 01, to make it 'Verb 24, Noun 01, Enter', before you load the three registers. Over.

a11_1515217.speaker: Collins
a11_1515217.text: Roger, that. I was just questioning the rate at which the maneuver would begin if that were not done.

a11_1515217.speaker: McCandless
a11_1515217.text: Roger. We're still working on computing the rate for you. [Long pause.]

a11_1515217.speaker: McCandless
a11_1515217.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. We'd like you to select Reacq mode on the High Gain Antenna. Looks like we're about to lose you. Over.

a11_1515217.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1515217.text: This is Apollo Control at 152 hours, 9 minutes. At this time, the crew is getting the spacecraft set up to reinitiate the Passive Thermal Control. Apollo 11 currently 165,143 nautical miles [305,849 km] from the Earth and traveling at a speed of 4,142 feet per second [1,262 m/s]. The Flight Plan has relatively few activities scheduled for now through the beginning of the crew's sleep period tonight. We do have a television transmission scheduled. I believe, the time on that is a little after 8:00 pm Central Daylight Time. And we show the sleep period to begin at about 160 hours Ground Elapsed

a11_1521713.speaker: McCandless
a11_1521713.text: Apollo 11, Apollo 11, this is Houston broadcasting in the blind. If you read us, attempt to acquire on Omni antennas. Attempt to acquire us on Omni antennas, if you read. This is Houston. Out. [No answer.]

a11_1521713.speaker: McCandless
a11_1521713.text: Apollo 11, Apollo 11, this is Houston broadcasting in the blind. If you read, attempt acquisition on an Omni antenna. Attempt acquisition using an Omni antenna. Over. [No answer.]

a11_1521713.speaker: McCandless
a11_1521713.text: Apollo 11, Apollo 11, this is Houston broadcasting in the blind. If you read, attempt contact using Omni antennas, using an Omni antenna. This is Houston. Out. [No answer.]

a11_1521713.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1521713.text: This is Apollo Control at 152 hours, 29 minutes. In the process of re-establishing the Passive Thermal Control with the spacecraft in a slow rotation, we have apparently lost High Gain lock-on and we expect that the crew will reacquire lock with the antenna once the Passive Thermal Control is re-established. At the present time Apollo 11 is 164,320 nautical miles [304,321 km] from the Earth and the velocity is up now to 4,156 feet per second [1,267 m/s]. We'll continue to stand by here for reacquisition of the spacecraft, for re-establishment of High Gain lock-on.

a11_1523508.speaker: McCandless
a11_1523508.text: Apollo 11, Apollo 11, this is Houston broadcasting in the blind. If you read us, attempt acquisition using an Omni antenna. Attempt acquisition using an Omni antenna. This is Houston. Out. [No answer.]

a11_1524348.speaker: McCandless
a11_1524348.text: Apollo 11, Apollo 11, this is Houston. Radio check. Over. [No answer.]

a11_1524348.speaker: McCandless
a11_1524348.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. How do you read? Over.

a11_1524348.speaker: Collins
a11_1524348.text: Loud and clear, Bruce. How me?

a11_1524348.speaker: McCandless
a11_1524348.text: Roger. What antenna are you using? [Long pause.]

a11_1524348.speaker: Collins
a11_1524348.text: Houston, Apollo 11 is calling you on the High Gain. How do you read? Over.

a11_1524348.speaker: McCandless
a11_1524348.text: Roger. Loud and clear on the High Gain. [Long pause.]

a11_1524348.speaker: McCandless
a11_1524348.text: Oh, we were wondering what was new with you up there.

a11_1524348.speaker: Collins
a11_1524348.text: All very quiet. We're just sitting here letting the thruster firing damp down. When they get good enough, let us know, and we'll start this PTC.

a11_1524348.speaker: Collins
a11_1524348.text: Nice to sit here and watch the Earth getting larger and larger and the Moon smaller and smaller.

a11_1524348.speaker: McCandless
a11_1524348.text: Roger. We'll give you a call when your rates have damped down sufficiently, and we're unable at the present time to predict what rate you should have seen at your last attempt to initiate PTC. We saw about 2½ degrees per second. Over.

a11_1524348.speaker: Collins
a11_1524348.text: Buzz thinks we should have a PTC program built into the computer. He could very well be right.

a11_1524348.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1524348.text: This is Apollo Control at 153 hours, 7 minutes. At the present time, we are changing shifts here in Mission Control. Flight Director Gene Kranz will be coming on to relieve Flight Director Clifford Charlesworth. The Capsule Communicator on this shift will be astronaut Charlie Duke. There will be a change of shift briefing in the news center, in the Building 1 auditorium in about 10 minutes. At the present time, Apollo 11 is traveling at a speed of 4,185 feet per second [1,276 m/s]. The spacecraft is about 162,700 nautical miles [301,300 km] from the Earth. During the change-of-shift briefing,

a11_1531917.speaker: Collins
a11_1531917.text: Rog. Just checking the radios, and how is the thruster activity coming?

a11_1531917.speaker: McCandless
a11_1531917.text: 11, Houston. The radios are still in good shape, and we're still waiting for your rates to decay. We've got 0.03 degrees per second in pitch now.

a11_1531917.speaker: Collins
a11_1531917.text: Okay. We're - we're in no rush. This is a very pleasant attitude, as a matter of fact. The Sun is down in the LEB, so it's not shining through the windows and heating the place up. We've got the Earth steady out Window 1. We have the Moon steadily out Window 3 and, of course, we're locked up on the High Gain. So as long as the thermal people are happy, we're happy.

a11_1533327.speaker: McCandless
a11_1533327.text: Okay, 11. We're about ready to start PTC. I'd like to give you some High Gain Antenna angles, though. We'd like to operate in the Reacq mode, and do you plan on spinning up in the positive or negative direction? Over.

a11_1533327.speaker: Collins
a11_1533327.text: We can do it either way. I had planned the positive.

a11_1533327.speaker: McCandless
a11_1533327.text: Okay. For positive, the High Gain Antenna setting should be pitch plus 30, yaw 270, and in Reacq. Over.

a11_1533327.speaker: Collins
a11_1533327.text: Understand. Reacq, pitch plus 30, yaw 270. Thank you.

a11_1533327.speaker: McCandless
a11_1533327.text: Roger. And if you would, when you're making your DSKY entries to set up for PTC, go a little slower, and we'll try to follow each entry from down here. Over.

a11_1534305.speaker: McCandless
a11_1534305.text: 11, Houston. We observe the PTC to be fairly well established here, and we'll keep you posted on how it's going, and your friendly White Team commentator is taking over now.

a11_1534305.speaker: Collins
a11_1534305.text: Okay. Thanks to all you Black Team.

a11_1534305.speaker: Collins
a11_1534305.text: Correction, all you Green Team - correction, Green Team. Excuse me.

a11_1534305.speaker: Collins
a11_1534305.text: How could I forget? I used to be a Green one.

a11_1535312.speaker: Duke
a11_1535312.text: Apollo 11, Houston. You sure you don't have anybody else in there with you?

a11_1535312.speaker: Duke
a11_1535312.text: We had some strange noises coming down on the downlink, and it sounded like you had some friends up there.

a11_1535312.speaker: Collins
a11_1535312.text: Where - where do the White Team go during their off hours anyway?

a11_1535312.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1535312.text: This is Apollo Control. Still no explanation, the weird noises emanating from Apollo 11, if indeed it is from Apollo 11 and it's reported from Network that it's being received on the downlink at two different stations in the Manned Space Flight Network. Perhaps it will all shake out later in the mission as to what these strange noises are. We'll come back up again as conversation is resumed with Apollo 11; now 160,410 nautical miles [297,079 km] out from Earth, traveling at 4,228 feet per second [1,289 m/s]. At 154 hours, 5 minutes Ground Elapsed Time, this is Apollo Control.

a11_1544058.speaker: Duke
a11_1544058.text: Roger. Would you ver - We've lost comm with you for about the last 10 minutes. Would you verify that the S-band track switch is in Reacq? Over.

a11_1544058.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1544058.text: Negative. It's not. Last time we broke lock, we went to Auto, and I left it there. Sorry.

a11_1544058.speaker: Duke
a11_1544058.text: Rog. We'd like to - have you to put it in Reacq, and monitor. In about 2 minutes, we'll be coming up on the High Gain. Would you monitor the Reacq? If it doesn't take, acquire manually. Over.

a11_1544058.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1544058.text: Okay. Say again the angles you'd like.

a11_1544058.speaker: Duke
a11_1544058.text: We'll - we'll try to switch it ourselves. Stand by on the angles.

a11_1544058.speaker: Duke
a11_1544058.text: Buzz, the - it's pitch plus 30, yaw 270. Over.

a11_1544611.speaker: Duke
a11_1544611.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Would you please terminate battery charge now? Over.

a11_1545051.speaker: Duke
a11_1545051.text: Hello, Apollo 11, Houston. Any special attitude you'd like us to look at for the TV? Over. [Pause.]

a11_1545051.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1545051.text: I don't guess we have a requirement there, Charlie.

a11_1545051.speaker: Duke
a11_1545051.text: Roger. We have an attitude that we can get the Earth out of a window or the Moon. We're trying to look at - find one that we can get both, if that's what you'd like. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1545051.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1545051.text: Our 50-degree roll attitude will probably give us that, Charlie.

a11_1545051.speaker: Collins
a11_1545051.text: That's a good one because it puts the Earth out window 1 and the Moon out window 3 and puts the Sun down in the LEB, so the lighting in here remains relatively constant.

a11_1552308.speaker: Duke
a11_1552308.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We'll have High Gain coverage about 155:30. At that time, you can turn on the TV if you desire, and continue your roll around 'til you get 50 degrees roll. Over.

a11_1552825.speaker: Duke
a11_1552825.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We were going to give you the All Star game tonight, but it was rained out. Over.

a11_1552825.speaker: Duke
a11_1552825.text: 11, Houston. We're on the High Gain. You can warm up the FM amp if you like. Over.

a11_1552825.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1552825.text: This is Apollo Control; still standing by for the incoming television signal from Columbia. Still nothing but the color-bar test pattern as of now. Continuing to stand by on air-ground and television links.

a11_1553452.speaker: Duke
a11_1553452.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We're ready for the TV, we're all configured. At your convenience. Over.

a11_1553452.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1553452.text: This is Apollo Control. While we're waiting for the television pictures to come in, we have in the control room here, a vase full of long-stemmed red roses, the card saying: 'To one and all concerned. Job superbly done. From a moonstruck Canadian.' Continuing to stand by as we wait for the pictures to come from Columbia. Here they come.

a11_1553452.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1553452.text: Are you picking up our TV signals?

a11_1553452.speaker: Duke
a11_1553452.text: That's affirmative. We have it up on the Eidophor now. The focus is a little bit out. We see Earth in the center of the screen. Still have a little white dot in the bottom of the camera, apparently. And see some land masses in the center, at least I guess that's what it is. It's very hazy at this time on our Eidophor. Over.

a11_1553452.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1553452.text: Believe that's where we just came from.

a11_1553452.speaker: Duke
a11_1553452.text: It is, huh? Well, I'm really looking at the bad - at a bad screen here. Stand by one. [Pause.] Hey, you're right.

a11_1553452.speaker: Duke
a11_1553452.text: [As if] it's not bad enough, not finding the right landing spot...

a11_1553452.speaker: SC
a11_1553452.text: Hey, it should be getting [garble]-er on your screen now.

a11_1553452.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1553452.text: It's not bad enough, not finding the right landing spot, when you haven't even got the right planet!

a11_1553452.speaker: Duke
a11_1553452.text: I'll never live that one down.

a11_1553452.speaker: Collins
a11_1553452.text: We're making it get smaller and smaller here to make sure that it really is the one we're leaving.

a11_1553452.speaker: Duke
a11_1553452.text: Aww, that's enough you guys. [Long pause.]

a11_1553452.speaker: Duke
a11_1553452.text: 11, that was a good picture there.

a11_1553452.speaker: Collins
a11_1553452.text: Okay. That's enough of the Moon.

a11_1553452.speaker: Collins
a11_1553452.text: Okay. That's enough of the Moon, Charlie. We're getting set up now for some inside pictures.

a11_1554032.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1554032.text: We know there's a lot of scientists from a number of countries standing by to see the lunar samples, and we thought you'd be interested to see them as they really are here. These two boxes are the sample return containers. They - They are vacuum-packed containers that were closed in a vacuum on the lunar surface, sealed and then brought inside the LM and put inside these fiberglass bags, zippered and re-sealed around the out - around the outside and placed in these receptacles in the side of the Command Module. These are the two boxes, and as soon as we get onto the ship, I'm sure these boxes

a11_1554032.speaker: Duke
a11_1554032.text: Roger, Neil. Thank you much for that description. We've got a pretty dark picture down here. Could you check your f-stop? We'd like to have it - See if you can open it up a little bit. Over.

a11_1554032.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1554032.text: Okay. Our monitor showed that to be very bright.

a11_1554032.speaker: Duke
a11_1554032.text: Roger.

a11_1554032.speaker: Collins
a11_1554032.text: ... We're down around between, well, around f:4, which we thought would be plenty light. Well, we'll lighten it up some more.

a11_1554032.speaker: Duke
a11_1554032.text: Well, we'd appreciate it. It's pretty dark on all our monitors here.

a11_1554032.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1554032.text: Okay. Fine.

a11_1554032.speaker: Duke
a11_1554032.text: That's looking a lot better now, Neil.

a11_1554032.speaker: Duke
a11_1554032.text: There's Buzz. [Long pause.]

a11_1554032.speaker: Duke
a11_1554032.text: 11, Houston. We have an excellent picture now. Over.

a11_1554032.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1554032.text: Okay. How do you read me, Charlie?

a11_1554032.speaker: Duke
a11_1554032.text: Five-by now, Buzz. Over.

a11_1554032.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1554032.text: Okay. The more mundane affairs, now that we've left the Moon, I'd like to trace through them a little bit for you; developments that have taken place in the food department. I'm sure you've already [voice cut out] type of a drink container. A little later, Mike will show you how the water gun operates with its new filter to take out the hydrogen. Essentially, this water gun is put in in this end and fills up this bag with water, and the drink then dissolves in the water, and this end of the [voice cut out] outfeeding. Likewise, we have other foods that are more solid nature. You can probably s

a11_1554032.speaker: Duke
a11_1554032.text: 11, Houston. Buzz, you're breaking up badly. Will you check your Vox? Over.

a11_1554032.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1554032.text: Roger. How am I coming through now, Charlie?

a11_1554032.speaker: Duke
a11_1554032.text: Rog. You're very clear when you come through. It's just that your Vox is not keying at every word. Over.

a11_1554032.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1554032.text: Okay. These bite-sized objects were designed to remove the problem of having so many crumbs floating around in the cabin, so they designed a particular size that would be able to go into the mouth all at once. I think since all of our experience, we've discovered that we can progress a good bit further than that, back to some of the type meals that we have on Earth. As a matter of fact, on this flight we've carried along pieces of bread, and along with the bread we have a ham spread. And I'll show you, I hope, how easy it is to spread some ham [in the] environment of zero g. [Long pause.]

a11_1554032.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1554032.text: I think we've discovered that it is quite easy to [voice cut out] all very familiar with. [Long pause.]

a11_1554032.speaker: Duke
a11_1554032.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We notice your roll rate increasing. Will you please see if you can bring that down to about zero for us or we'll be losing the High Gain shortly. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1554032.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1554032.text: You can also use zero gravity to demonstrate many things that we've all learned in school. I'd like to demonstrate briefly how easy it is to explain the action of the gyroscope. If I spin this can, we know that according to the equations of motion that we would expect that once this is given a spin, about - and has a spin axis in this direction, if we give it a particular torque, and if I - I'll do this by pushing my hands against it in this fashion once it's spinning. By the equations we can predict that, as I put this torque on it, it will in fact rotate this direction. Let's see how well th

a11_1554032.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1554032.text: See that as I apply the torque this way, it's rotated this way. [Long pause.]

a11_1554032.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1554032.text: Too close, I think. [Long pause.]

a11_1554032.speaker: Duke
a11_1554032.text: 11, Houston. It's a pretty good demonstration. [Long pause.]

a11_1554032.speaker: Collins
a11_1554032.text: Houston, this next is a little demonstration for the kids at home, all kids everywhere, for that matter. I was going to show you how you drink water out of a spoon, but I'm afraid I filled the spoon too full and if I'm not careful, I'm going to spill water right over the sides. Can you see the water slopping around on the top of the spoon, kids?

a11_1554032.speaker: Duke
a11_1554032.text: That's affirmative, 11.

a11_1554032.speaker: Collins
a11_1554032.text: Okay. Well, as I said, I was gonna show you but I'm afraid I filled it too full and it's gonna spill over the sides. I'll tell you what. I'll just - I'll just turn this one over and get rid of the water and start all over again. Okay?

a11_1554032.speaker: Duke
a11_1554032.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a11_1554032.speaker: Collins
a11_1554032.text: And you can see, up here we don't know where over is. One up is as good as another. That really is water, though. I'll show you. [Long pause.]

a11_1554032.speaker: Collins
a11_1554032.text: That's really not the way we drink. We really have a water gun which I'll show you. [Pause.]

a11_1554032.speaker: Collins
a11_1554032.text: Here's the water gun. This cylindrical thing on the end of it is a filter with several membranes. One allows water to pass, but not any gas. The other allows gas to pass, but not any water. So, by routing the gaseous water which comes from our tank through this filter, we're enabled to drink purified water without the gas in it, filtered water. And, of course, all we do to - to get it started, is just pull the trigger. [Long pause.]

a11_1554032.speaker: Collins
a11_1554032.text: It's sort of messy. I haven't been at this very long. It's sort of the same system that the Spaniards used to drink out of wineskins at bull fights, only I think this is even more fun. Well, be seeing you, kids.

a11_1554032.speaker: Duke
a11_1554032.text: Thank you from all us kids in the world, here in the MOCR, who can't tell the Earth from the Moon.

a11_1554032.speaker: Collins
a11_1554032.text: Roger. Stand by one, and we'll get you that Earth quick.

a11_1554032.speaker: Duke
a11_1554032.text: Looks like you need a wine skin up there, Mike.

a11_1554032.speaker: Collins
a11_1554032.text: That'd be nice.

a11_1554032.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1554032.text: Okay.

a11_1554032.speaker: Duke
a11_1554032.text: Okay. 11, Houston...

a11_1554032.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1554032.text: You have a picture now, Houston?

a11_1554032.speaker: Duke
a11_1554032.text: That's affirmative. I refuse to bite on this one, though. You tell us.

a11_1554032.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1554032.text: Okay. This should be getting larger, and if it is, it's the place we're coming home to.

a11_1554032.speaker: Duke
a11_1554032.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_1554032.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1554032.text: No matter where you travel, it's always nice to get home.

a11_1554032.speaker: Duke
a11_1554032.text: We concur, 11. We'll be happy to have you back.

a11_1554032.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1554032.text: This is Apollo 11. Signing off.

a11_1554032.speaker: Duke
a11_1554032.text: Roger. Thank you very much, 11. That was a good demonstration and a good show. We appreciate it very much.

a11_1554032.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1554032.text: This is Apollo Control. Still up live with the air-to-ground circuit to Apollo 11 homeward bound. Now in the Passive Thermal Control mode, or barbecue mode. Charlie Duke is going to make another call to the crew. Let's listen in, in a moment. He's discussing with Flight Director Pete Frank, who tonight is spelling Gene Kranz on this shift, although Gene is here. They're discussing some adjustments to the Passive Thermal Control mode. Apollo 11 has left the Moon some 53,666 miles [99,389 km] behind it. And relative to the Moon, Apollo 11 is traveling now at 4,306 feet per second [1,312 m/s]. Co

a11_1555700.speaker: Duke
a11_1555700.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We were curious to see if there was any excess moisture up around the tunnel hatch area as we saw on 10. Over.

a11_1555700.speaker: Collins
a11_1555700.text: It just so happens that's what we were talking about now. There is a little bit of dampness around the outside edge of the hatch, but a very, very slight amount. We've got a hose up there that we're hoping will sort of help keep it a little bit dry.

a11_1555700.speaker: Duke
a11_1555700.text: Roger, Mike. Thank you much. Have you seen any more water collecting on the aft bulkhead? Over.

a11_1555700.speaker: Collins
a11_1555700.text: No, we haven't, as a matter of fact. It's been dry in that area since we got rid of that last time.

a11_1555700.speaker: Collins
a11_1555700.text: Apollo 11 is back in PTC attitude. Standing by for thruster quieting.

a11_1555700.speaker: Duke
a11_1555700.text: Rog. We see that. Thank you much, Mike.

a11_1555700.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1555700.text: This is Delta Launch Control. We have postponed the launch of the Delta vehicle tonight, the launch of Intelsat 3, 24 hours. The reason for this postponement is to examine the second stage propellant ground equipment. There is a slight chance that the acid used in the second stage for an oxidizer, inhibited red fuming nitric acid, could have contained an excessive level of contaminants. This possibility is remote but there is a desire to make the examination. During fueling today, it was noticed that the transfer of the inhibited red fuming nitric acid took longer than expected, or longer than

a11_1555700.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1555700.text: This is Apollo Control. Apparently, there will be little conversation during the next half hour or so. Apollo 11 now 155 thousand... as you were - Yes, 155,906 nautical miles [288,738 km] out from Earth. Approaching at a velocity of 4,316 feet per second [1,316 m/s]. And at 156 hours, 6 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control.

a11_1560720.speaker: Collins
a11_1560720.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Could you get a little summary of the evening news for us?

a11_1560720.speaker: Duke
a11_1560720.text: Yes, sir. We'll have it for you momentarily. Also, a little Flight Plan update, Mike. If you - On page 3-113, you can delete the O 2 fuel cell purge. Over.

a11_1560720.speaker: Collins
a11_1560720.text: Will do. [Pause.]

a11_1560720.speaker: Duke
a11_1560720.text: There is a flurry of activity in the PAO site for the evening news.

a11_1560720.speaker: Collins
a11_1560720.text: Bully. [Pause.]

a11_1560720.speaker: Collins
a11_1560720.text: How's the weather down there? You got any rain?

a11_1560720.speaker: Duke
a11_1560720.text: Rog. We've been having a little bit, thunderstorm-type, in the last couple of days. We had a pretty good rain today, and it's been overcast. A slow storm system's been moving through the area in the last couple of days, and primarily evening and afternoon thundershowers.

a11_1560720.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1560720.text: Rog. We were watching a few clouds in your area through the monocular along the Texas Gulf Coast this afternoon, and we also noticed there were clouds over Baja California, which is a little bit unusual.

a11_1560720.speaker: Duke
a11_1560720.text: We - Rog. Thank you for the weather report. We can't quite see that far. Uh, the, uh, it seems to have cleared up outside now, uh, we - according to some of the people coming in. This constant overcast in the MOCR here is a little hard to see outside.

a11_1560720.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1560720.text: Yeah. We also noticed there was a little overcast down over - in the Antarctic ice cap, too.

a11_1560720.speaker: Duke
a11_1560720.text: Rog. It's apparently raining pretty hard up...

a11_1560720.speaker: Collins
a11_1560720.text: How's that for one-upsmanship? [sic]

a11_1560720.speaker: Duke
a11_1560720.text: Yeah. [Laughter].

a11_1560720.speaker: Collins
a11_1560720.text: He may know that, but he doesn't even know whether his grass is wet or dry. [Pause.]

a11_1560720.speaker: Duke
a11_1560720.text: It's apparently raining fairly hard up in Washington where the All Star game was to be played tonight. They started out, I understand, and then it was rained out and they called it off.

a11_1560720.speaker: Collins
a11_1560720.text: They need a roof on their stadium so they can catch all those flies.

a11_1560720.speaker: Duke
a11_1560720.text: Rog.

a11_1560720.speaker: Collins
a11_1560720.text: In the rain.

a11_1560720.speaker: Duke
a11_1560720.text: Touché. [Long pause.]

a11_1560720.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1560720.text: Hey, Charlie, what's the preliminary outlook for the weather in our recovery area?

a11_1560720.speaker: Duke
a11_1560720.text: Stand by, Buzz. It looks pretty good as far as I can tell, We got the - along the tropical convergence line there, there's a few clouds shown on the weather map I'm looking at here, but nothing of significance. Right now - Stand by. Let's see, right now in the mid - yeah, at the MPL, we've got 3000 scattered, visibility 10, wave height 3 feet, is the present weather. I don't think there's anything forecast to be of significance. There are a couple of - Flight just informed me that what I just gave you was the forecast. There are a couple of tropical storms in the - well, not in the area of lan

a11_1560946.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1560946.text: Hey, Charlie, what's the preliminary outlook for the weather in our recovery area?

a11_1561403.speaker: Duke
a11_1561403.text: 11, Houston. The RETROs were wondering if you could fill us in on any non-nominal stowage that we have on board. Just the location and weight is about all they're interested in. Over.

a11_1561403.speaker: Collins
a11_1561403.text: Roger. We'll - we'll do some work on that and let you know, Charlie.

a11_1561403.speaker: Duke
a11_1561403.text: And, Apollo 11, Houston. Would you please place O 2 Tank 1 Heater to Auto? Over.

a11_1561702.speaker: Collins
a11_1561702.text: What we'll do Charlie, tomorrow, is go through and reconfigure our stowage as closely as possible to nominal. Some things that will not be nominal are as follows: the EVA visors were brought back into the Command Module, and we have not yet found a home for them. We'll let you know where they go. In addition, there's about 5 pounds of miscellaneous weight from the LM in compartment Able-8, and it's taking the place of the LCGs which we moved from A-8 into the suit bag. We got rid of one miscellaneous trash bag, mostly old food wrapping and also old underwear and that helmet protective visor of

a11_1561702.speaker: Duke
a11_1561702.text: Thank you very much. We appreciate it. Out.

a11_1562212.speaker: Duke
a11_1562212.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We got the rates looking copacetic. You can go ahead and initiate PTC. Over.

a11_1562212.speaker: Collins
a11_1562212.text: Okay. Thank you.

a11_1562212.speaker: Duke
a11_1562212.text: And Buzz, we're still not getting any data from your EKG. It looks like the only way we're gonna be able to get any is if, at your convenience, you would take your - change out your EKG leads, which are the center ones that are connected to the blue pin. And there's a spare one in the medical box. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1562212.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1562212.text: Roger. How many do you want me to change?

a11_1562212.speaker: Duke
a11_1562212.text: Just the center ones. I'll get the right nomenclature from the Doc. Stand by. It's called the sternal EKG, which are the three center ones, and it's got - they lead into a - into the blue-stringed lead ones. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1562212.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1562212.text: Okay. There's three of them, is that right?

a11_1562212.speaker: Duke
a11_1562212.text: That's affirmative.

a11_1562212.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1562212.text: And you want me to change all three.

a11_1562212.speaker: Duke
a11_1562212.text: That's affirmative and they're all hooked together from the picture I'm looking at, and they go into the center belt signal conditioner, and it's got the blue strain relief on it.

a11_1562212.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1562212.text: Yes. I checked the connectors at both ends on that. I don't guess we have a spare signal conditioner or anything like that, do we?

a11_1562212.speaker: Duke
a11_1562212.text: No. We do not. [Pause.]

a11_1562212.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1562212.text: Well, I can assure you my heart's still working.

a11_1562212.speaker: Duke
a11_1562212.text: We believe it. [Long pause.]

a11_1562212.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1562212.text: Charlie, what we suggest here is, before we start that, turn our two suit powers off and plug his blue lead into my blue signal conditioner and see if we get his signal through my signal conditioner. Okay?

a11_1562212.speaker: Duke
a11_1562212.text: Roger. That's a good suggestion, Neil. We concur. Over.

a11_1562212.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1562212.text: Okay, Charlie. We're transmitting, and let's see if you get any EKG signal on the CDR at this point.

a11_1562212.speaker: Duke
a11_1562212.text: Roger, Stand by. [Pause.]

a11_1562212.speaker: Duke
a11_1562212.text: 11, Houston. We get some data, but it's got the same problem that we had through Buzz's signal conditioner, so apparently the lead is broken and we'd like you to change it out if you could. Over.

a11_1562212.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1562212.text: Okay.

a11_1562212.speaker: Duke
a11_1562212.text: Thank you.

a11_1563812.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1563812.text: Roger. I think the problem was that the - the center lead had dried out. I'll go ahead and put the new one on, and see how that works. Over.

a11_1563812.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1563812.text: I can't tell you how good it feels to get it off.

a11_1564841.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1564841.text: Roger. How do you read my EKG now?

a11_1564841.speaker: Duke
a11_1564841.text: Stand by. We'll let the docs look at it. [Pause.] Buzz, we're on low bit rate. We'll get you on the High Gain momentarily, and we'll let you know then. Over.

a11_1564841.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1564841.text: Okay. I got my High Gain Antenna coming out.

a11_1564841.speaker: Duke
a11_1564841.text: Roger. Just leave it on Reacq. We'll get you.

a11_1564841.speaker: Duke
a11_1564841.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Buzz, your EKG looks good now. The doc said thanks a lot.

a11_1570355.speaker: Duke
a11_1570355.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Based on our tracking since the midcourse, we're showing a gamma of minus 6.57. This is preliminary, though, and we think that after some more tracking it should come on in, and we could tweak it right on into the corridor. We're just about in the center of the corridor. Everything's looking fine. We'll have you an Entry PAD in a couple of hours before you go to sleep. And from our friends in the Public Affairs, a few headlines, other than your flight. You're still dominating the news. However, there are some other things of interest for you. As I mentioned earlier, the All

a11_1570355.speaker: Duke
a11_1570355.text: And back in Washington, the House Ways and Means Committee agreed to tax changes affecting oil companies, banks, and utilities that could add nearly 2 billion a year to federal revenue. And, also today, NASA announced that it will launch a large orbital workshop in 1972, with a cut-down version of the Saturn V. And your television pictures attracted a lot of interest. They were shown live throughout just about the whole world, and - but we're expecting hundreds of telephone calls from mothers all over the world complaining that their youngsters are trying to drink milk from spoons, thanks to y

a11_1570355.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1570355.text: This is Apollo Control. Things are beginning to quieten down aboard Apollo 11 as they get nearer their sleep period. [There] probably won't be too many more exchanges between spacecraft communicator Charlie Duke here in Mission Control and the crew aboard Columbia. Entry countdown clock now showing 37 hours, 53 minutes. This may be refined a few times between now and splash time, or entry. Apollo 11 now is 153,080 nautical miles [283,504 km] out from Earth, approaching at 4,373 feet per second [1,333 m/s]. And at 157 hours, 10 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control.

a11_1575337.speaker: Duke
a11_1575337.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Buzz, you brought the surgeon right out of his chair. We see you exercising. Over.

a11_1575337.speaker: Duke
a11_1575337.text: We see you exercising. Is that correct, Buzz?

a11_1575337.speaker: Duke
a11_1575337.text: Rog. We've got his heartbeat way up.

a11_1575632.speaker: Collins
a11_1575632.text: White Team's really got a busy one tonight, huh, Charlie?

a11_1575632.speaker: Duke
a11_1575632.text: Say again, Mike. Over.

a11_1575632.speaker: Collins
a11_1575632.text: Say, the old White Team's really got a busy one tonight, huh?

a11_1575632.speaker: Duke
a11_1575632.text: Oh, boy. We're really booming along here with all this activity. Can barely believe it.

a11_1575632.speaker: Collins
a11_1575632.text: What are you doing? Sitting around with your feet up on the console drinking coffee?

a11_1575632.speaker: Duke
a11_1575632.text: [Laughter.] You must have your X-ray eyes up. You sure can see a long way.

a11_1575632.speaker: Collins
a11_1575632.text: Yeah. We're watching you as well, you know.

a11_1575632.speaker: Duke
a11_1575632.text: All right. [Long pause.]

a11_1575632.speaker: Collins
a11_1575632.text: Two people in the viewing room and that's more than is in the trench. [Long pause.]

a11_1575632.speaker: Duke
a11_1575632.text: We've got eight in the viewing room, and let's see, about six in the trench right now. And this is the highlight of the day, Buzz's exercise for the surgeon.

a11_1575632.speaker: Duke
a11_1575632.text: 11, you copy? Over.

a11_1575632.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1575632.text: Roger. 11.

a11_1575632.speaker: Duke
a11_1575632.text: Rog, Neil. The highest heartbeat ever seen on a manned space flight, and we just went low bit rate. The surgeon is about to die. [Laughter.]

a11_1575632.speaker: Collins
a11_1575632.text: We're - I measured it up here. It came out to be 247.

a11_1575632.speaker: Duke
a11_1575632.text: Boy, that's super.

a11_1575632.speaker: Collins
a11_1575632.text: The units on that, furlong per fortnight.

a11_1575632.speaker: Duke
a11_1575632.text: Rog. We copy that. EECOM says if you keep that up, you're going to have to change your CO 2 canister.

a11_1575632.speaker: Collins
a11_1575632.text: You were going to make me do that in another 45 minutes anyway.

a11_1575632.speaker: Duke
a11_1575632.text: That's true.

a11_1575632.speaker: Collins
a11_1575632.text: That's the highlight of my day. I'm really looking forward to that. [Long pause.]

a11_1580100.speaker: SC
a11_1580100.text: [Music: Radar Blues from Music Out of the Moon by Harry Revel, Leslie Baxter & Dr. Samuel J. Hoffman, 1947, using a Theremin.]

a11_1580100.speaker: Duke
a11_1580100.text: Thank you, 11. We appreciate you turning that off. [Laughter.]

a11_1580100.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1580100.text: This is Apollo Control, 158 hours, 1 minute Ground Elapsed Time. There's been a certain amount of conversation between Charlie Duke here in Mission Control and the crew of Apollo 11. We'll play back the accumulated tape at this time and then rejoin the conversation when it does resume on a live basis. Let's roll the tape now.

a11_1580324.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1580324.text: Charlie, could you copy our music down there?

a11_1580324.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1580324.text: Did you copy our music down there?

a11_1580324.speaker: Duke
a11_1580324.text: Rog. We sure did. We're wondering who selected - made your selections?

a11_1580324.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1580324.text: That's an old favorite of mine, about - It's an album made about 20 years ago, called Music Out of the Moon.

a11_1580324.speaker: Duke
a11_1580324.text: Roger. It sounded a little scratchy to us, Neil. Either that or your tape was a little slow.

a11_1580324.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1580324.text: It's supposed to sound that way.

a11_1580324.speaker: Collins
a11_1580324.text: ...it sounds a little scratchy to us too, but the czar likes it.

a11_1580324.speaker: Duke
a11_1580324.text: That's what we figured. He and his 40,000 votes.

a11_1580324.speaker: Duke
a11_1580324.text: For your info, we got you - It looks like around 150,000 out now.

a11_1580324.speaker: Collins
a11_1580324.text: It's getting appreciably larger now. It's looking more like the world.

a11_1580324.speaker: Duke
a11_1580324.text: Rog. I'm looking at the right side of the screen this time.

a11_1580324.speaker: Collins
a11_1580324.text: How's everything going on the - Say again, Charlie?

a11_1580324.speaker: Duke
a11_1580324.text: Oh, just - I - I'll never hear the last of that one about that Earth/Moon business during the TV there, and I was just saying that I was looking at the right side of the board here, so you are going towards the Earth. What are - What were you going to say, Mike?

a11_1580324.speaker: Collins
a11_1580324.text: You'll have - You'll have fun at the press conference after this shift then, won't you?

a11_1580324.speaker: Duke
a11_1580324.text: It's 2.30. Everybody will be asleep. I going to sneak off through the back way.

a11_1580324.speaker: Collins
a11_1580324.text: Okay. I was just wondering how everything is going at the home front. All the wives and kids in one piece?

a11_1580324.speaker: Duke
a11_1580324.text: Rog. Sure are. Everything's doing fine. All the gals are having a little party tonight, as far as I know.

a11_1582040.speaker: Duke
a11_1582040.text: Apollo 11, Houston. I was just reading some of the transcripts of earlier today about this earlier PTC that we attempted, and when you keyed in the Verb 24 and did the two Enters, it took off on you. I think we got a story on that, if you'd like to listen to why it had such a high rate, Mike. Over.

a11_1582040.speaker: Duke
a11_1582040.text: Okay. I think it'd be better if you got your checklist out on 9-7, and we could walk you through it, and that way I could probably get the story straight. Over.

a11_1582040.speaker: Duke
a11_1582040.text: Okay, Mike, what happened is, you know, you were sitting there monitoring Verb 16, Noun 20, and at step 7 you went into Verb 24, Noun 01, and keyed in the address and then Information, Information. And on the final Enter of that 35400 Enter, right after that, it - that didn't put you back into the 16, Noun 20. Then when you did the Verb 24 Enter, you were really entering the information in the actual CDUs, and when you got the two entries in in register 1 and 2, it was an instantaneous change in the actual CDUs, and the CMDAC looked at that and saw what it thought it had - My gosh, I got a 600

a11_1582040.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1582040.text: Hey, Charlie, are you saying that for a short period of time, he actually loaded Noun 20 with some value other than what's being read by the CDU?

a11_1582040.speaker: Duke
a11_1582040.text: I think I got that, Buzz. That's affirmative. But when he did that second Verb 24, you were - the Noun was 20, so when he did the 3175 and then a 002 Enter, what he actually did there was load the first two actual CDU locations, and the computer looked at it - the DAP looked at it as an instantaneous change in the actual CDU. Stand by on your comments. We're switching antennas...

a11_1582040.speaker: Duke
a11_1582040.text: 11, Houston. We got you back now on the High Gain. Did you copy all that, Buzz? Over.

a11_1582040.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1582040.text: Yeah, I think so. I - I thought maybe that Noun 20 was one of those that you could never load from the DSKY, and that still may be. Maybe it was loaded just for a short period of time, and then when the counters read the - the gimbal angles, why they changed it back to what they actually are. But in the meantime, the DAP saw this different number. Is that right?

a11_1582040.speaker: Duke
a11_1582040.text: Well, our guidance guy was telling me that you can actually load those ACDUs, the actual CDUs, but we'll - we're checking on that. Over.

a11_1582040.speaker: Duke
a11_1582040.text: 11, Houston. Buzz, the word from the back room is that you can actually load the Noun 20, but you should not.

a11_1582040.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1582040.text: Yeah. I got that. Thank you.

a11_1583330.speaker: Duke
a11_1583330.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We got a recommendation for you on your stowage of the LM E - VVAs. [means LEVAs] Over.

a11_1583330.speaker: Duke
a11_1583330.text: Okay. We'd like - the SPAN guys say it looks - they think that one would go on the helmet that you're going to have in B1, and you could put the other one on Mike's helmet, which will be in the sleep restraint. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1583330.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1583330.text: I doubt if it will fit on the helmet in B1. The other one might - might go in the sleep restraint. We've got them in their helmet bags, and I guess we're going to have to keep the helmets in the helmet bags, and the LEVAs in the LEVA bags.

a11_1583330.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1583330.text: Yeah. I've been thinking maybe they ought to stay sealed up.

a11_1583330.speaker: Collins
a11_1583330.text: It won't hack B1, Charlie, with the cover. I tried it already.

a11_1583330.speaker: Duke
a11_1583330.text: Okay. Fine. We weren't sure of that. It was just a suggestion. We thought we'd - You could check it out. Sounds like you've already done that, so I guess whatever you can come up with, just let us know. Over.

a11_1583330.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1583330.text: Okay. There's no problem. We'll let you know where they end up.

a11_1583330.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1583330.text: This is Apollo Control. We've had no communications with Apollo 11 in the last several minutes. So at this time; 158 hours, 45 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; we will take down the circuit and come back up when and if conversation resumes prior to the time the crew starts their rest period, which tonight is scheduled for 10 hours. 158 hours, 46 minutes Ground Elapsed Time, this is Apollo Control.

a11_1583330.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1583330.text: This is Apollo Control; 159 hours, 49 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 11 crew is giving their final report prior to their starting their 10-hour rest period. We've got a little accumulation of tape, then we'll join live. Let's roll the tape now.

a11_1594900.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1594900.text: Hello, Houston. Apollo 11.

a11_1594900.speaker: Duke
a11_1594900.text: Go ahead, 11. Over.

a11_1594900.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1594900.text: Okay. Crew status report. Radiation: CDR 11020, CMP 10022, LMP 09024. No medication.

a11_1594900.speaker: Duke
a11_1594900.text: Roger. Copy.

a11_1594900.speaker: Duke
a11_1594900.text: And, Neil, we got - we'd like your onboard read-outs of batteries and RCS. Over.

a11_1594900.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1594900.text: Okay, Charlie. Ready to copy?

a11_1594900.speaker: Duke
a11_1594900.text: Rog. Go ahead. Over.

a11_1594900.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1594900.text: Okay. Batt C, Pyro Batt A, and Pyro Batt B are 37.0. RCS A, 51. B, 63. C, 63. D, 59. Go.

a11_1594900.speaker: Duke
a11_1594900.text: Roger. Copy all that, Neil. And we got an Entry PAD if you're ready to copy. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_1594900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1594900.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Ready to copy. Over.

a11_1594900.speaker: Duke
a11_1594900.text: Rog, Buzz. It's an Entry PAD, MPL; starting with roll 05, 35 - correction - 359, 152, 001. GET 194:46:03; 267, plus 11.02, minus 172.03, 06.8. Noun 60; 36194, 6.56, 1189.4, 36275, 195:03:03, 00:27. Noun 69, all four lines are NA. Picking up with D zero; 4.00, 02:09. RET of blackout; 00:17, 03:38, 08:20. Sextant star; 02, 094.5, 14.9. Boresight star is Scorpii Theta, that's Scorpii Theta. Up 315, right 35, lift vector up. And the comments: This Entry PAD assumes no Midcourse 6. And for your information, looking at it right now, based on all the tracking we got, that maneuver would only be a ten

a11_1594900.speaker: Duke
a11_1594900.text: Roger. Very good readback, Buzz, and for your communication setup for tonight's sleep, we'd like Omni to Omni - Stand by.

a11_1594900.speaker: Duke
a11_1594900.text: Apollo 11, Houston. If you didn't copy that, Buzz, it was a good readback on the PAD. We've got a clock update for you that we'll have to you as soon as we can get it out to the site. It's - We're in the process of handing over to Honeysuckle, and it'll be a couple of minutes. Over.

a11_1594900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1594900.text: Okay. You want the computer to Block?

a11_1594900.speaker: Duke
a11_1594900.text: We'll call you. You can stay Block right now. We'll give you a call.

a11_1594900.speaker: Duke
a11_1594900.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Would you please give us P00 and Accept? We've got a clock update for you. [Long pause.]

a11_1594900.speaker: Collins
a11_1594900.text: Go ahead, Charlie. We're P00 and Accept.

a11_1594900.speaker: Duke
a11_1594900.text: Roger.

a11_1594900.speaker: Duke
a11_1594900.text: 11, Houston. We've got the load in. You can go back to Block. Over.

a11_1594900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1594900.text: Roger.

a11_1594900.speaker: Collins
a11_1594900.text: Thank you. [Pause.]

a11_1594900.speaker: Duke
a11_1594900.text: And 11, Houston. One final thing. We'd like you to select your Omni to Omni, Omni A to Bravo, High Gain track to Manual, and beam Wide. Your angles are 270 in yaw, pitch minus 50. Over.

a11_1594900.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1594900.text: Roger. 50 and minus 70.

a11_1594900.speaker: Duke
a11_1594900.text: The angles, Buzz, were yaw 270, pitch minus 50. Over.

a11_1702800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1702800.text: This is Apollo Control at 170 hours, 54 minutes. The Flight Surgeon reported a few minutes ago that telemetry data now indicates all three crewmen are awake after about 10 hours of rest. We expect we will be hearing from them shortly. Apollo 11 at this time is 114,146 nautical miles [211,398 km] from the Earth and the spacecraft velocity is 5,359 feet per second [1,633 m/s]. A press conference with the principal investigators for lunar samples is scheduled to begin in about 4 or 5 minutes and during that press conference we will tape-record any conversations with the crew and play them back fo

a11_1705956.speaker: Garriott
a11_1705956.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Are you up and at them yet? Over.

a11_1705956.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1705956.text: Well, we're up, at least, Owen.

a11_1705956.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1705956.text: Eyeballing my Magellanic Clouds. Over.

a11_1705956.speaker: Garriott
a11_1705956.text: 11, Houston. Got your signals loud and clear, here. How are things this morning? Over. [Pause.]

a11_1705956.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1705956.text: Do you read us, Owen?

a11_1705956.speaker: Garriott
a11_1705956.text: Roger. Loud and clear, 11.

a11_1705956.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1705956.text: Okay. Everything seems to be all right here. So far, we haven't been looking in the cockpit yet. We've been spending our time looking outside the cockpit. [Garble].

a11_1705956.speaker: Garriott
a11_1705956.text: Roger, 11. You're breaking up just a little bit there, Neil. Your signals are loud but are breaking up occasionally. Your spacecraft all looks good here from the ground. We noticed you stirring around the cockpit and thought we'd give you a call. Over.

a11_1705956.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1705956.text: Good morning. [Pause.]

a11_1705956.speaker: Garriott
a11_1705956.text: 11, Houston. We do have a few items for you here, Entry PADs, consumables, and so forth. After you've had a chance to get organized, whenever you're ready to start on a few of these items, why, we'll read them up to you. Over.

a11_1705956.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1705956.text: Okay. Stand by. [Long pause.]

a11_1705956.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1705956.text: Go ahead, Owen. I've got the books out. Ready to copy.

a11_1705956.speaker: Garriott
a11_1705956.text: Okay, Buzz. On your Flight Plan items, a few updates first of all. We've cancelled Midcourse number 6. Just remain - remain in PTC. Give you a little more time this morning. Second item on the Flight Plan is we're ready for a Batt B charge any time you want to put it on the line. And third item, we'd like a waste water dump a little differently this time. We'd like to do it on our marks from the ground. The PTC is a little bit ragged, and we would like to make the water dump at a time which we think will hold it in its proper configuration, so it looks like we'll have a desirable opportunity c

a11_1705956.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1705956.text: Roger. Someone must have stayed up all night figuring this one out.

a11_1705956.speaker: Garriott
a11_1705956.text: 11, Houston. Stand by just a moment here until we get out of the null position on the antenna.

a11_1705956.speaker: Garriott
a11_1705956.text: 11, Houston. We're over on Omni Delta now. I think we can read you better. Did you get all those first three items on your Flight Plan update? Over.

a11_1705956.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1705956.text: I got midcourse correction canceled, Battery B charge and water dump on your call. Over.

a11_1705956.speaker: Garriott
a11_1705956.text: That's right, Buzz.
