And the last item here, we do request that we do a P52, even now, though, we're not doing the midcourse correction, and we'll suggest you get to that after the waste-water dump has been complete. We also have a state vector update for you, if you can give us P00 and Accept. Over.

a11_1705956.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1705956.text: Okay. You have the DSKY now.

a11_1705956.speaker: Garriott
a11_1705956.text: Roger. We'll be sending that up, and I'll give you your consumables update now. It's - for a time of 170 hours. Your RCS total is minus 3.5 percent, Alpha is minus 14.5, Bravo plus 7, Charlie minus 4.5, Delta minus 3; hydrogen total is minus 1, and your oxygen total is plus 24. Over.

a11_1705956.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1705956.text: Roger. Copy those. And onboard readouts, D is 69, C is 73, B is - Let me start over again. Okay. A is 51 and B is 62, C is 63 and D is 59. Over.

a11_1705956.speaker: Garriott
a11_1705956.text: Roger, 11. Copy those, and we've checked them here on the ground, also. One correction to my last transmission. We would like that P52 prior to the waste-water dump, which is coming up in about 30 minutes from now. Will that be possible? Over.

a11_1705956.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1705956.text: Oh, yeah. We'll take care of that.

a11_1705956.speaker: Garriott
a11_1705956.text: Roger. And if you're ready for an Entry PAD, I'll read that up to you now also, 11.

a11_1705956.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1705956.text: Ready to copy.

a11_1705956.speaker: Garriott
a11_1705956.text: Okay. Entry PAD is area MidPac: 359, 153, 001; 194:46:03, 267; plus 11.02, minus 172.03; 06.7; 36194, 6.55; 1187.5, 36275; 195:03:03; 00:28. D L and V L , all four are not applicable. D 0 , 4.00, 02:10; 00:18, 03:38, 08:21. 44, 293.2, 38.0. Boresight star is Scorpio Theta, up 31.4, right 3.4, lift vector up. Comments: Entry data assumes no midcourse maneuvers. Your Earth entry minus 30 minutes horizon check, 194 plus 33 plus 03. Your pitch is 297. This assumes an entry REFSMMAT. Your GDC align stars are Deneb and Vega. Roll, pitch, yaw; 078, 233, 340. Read back. Over.

a11_1711851.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1711851.text: Okay, Houston. The crew status report is 8½, 7, and 8.

a11_1711851.speaker: Garriott
a11_1711851.text: 11, Houston. Roger, Neil. 8½, 7, and 8 for your crew status.

a11_1711851.speaker: Garriott
a11_1711851.text: 11, Houston. Your P52 looked good here on the ground, and we are now estimating that water dump will occur along about 171 plus 40, and we'd like for you to dump to 45 percent. This should let you arrive at Earth Interface with just about a full load of waste water. Over.

a11_1712946.speaker: Garriott
a11_1712946.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We're ready to start your waste water dump at this time. Over.

a11_1713330.speaker: Collins
a11_1713330.text: Houston, Apollo 11. We've dumped to 45 percent, and are stopping now. Do you concur?

a11_1715335.speaker: Garriott
a11_1715335.text: Apollo 11, Houston. I can read up your forecast weather for the recovery area any time you'd like to hear about it. Over.

a11_1715335.speaker: Garriott
a11_1715335.text: 11, Houston. Present forecast shows acceptable conditions in your recovery area - 2,000-foot scattered, high scattered, wind from 070 degrees, 13 knots, visibility 10 miles, and sea state about 4 feet. The forecast yesterday showed a tropical storm, Claudia, some 500 to 1,000 miles east of Hawaii. The - the pictures from Earth satellites taken yesterday afternoon - afternoon showed Claudia dissipating, so this appears to be even less a factor than it was before. Your recovery area is now believed to be just a little ways north of the inter-tropical convergence zone which you can probably see w

a11_1721716.speaker: Garriott
a11_1721716.text: 11, Houston. We'd like to try an operation on the - with the High Gain array here. If you would select Reacquire and your S-Band antenna to High Gain, your positions are pitch plus 40 and yaw 270, and then monitor for acquisition. Over.

a11_1721716.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1721716.text: This is Apollo Control at 172 hours, 20 minutes. During the press conference, we established contact with the crew. Capsule Communicator Owen Garriot put in a call at 171 hours, about 10 minutes after the Surgeon reported biomedical data showed all three crewmen awake. Neil Armstrong responded. We have received a status report from the crew. We also passed up the information - preliminary information that they will use in the re-entry tomorrow and gave them a weather report for the prime recovery area in the Pacific landing zone. We'll play back about 12 minutes of taped conversation we've acc

a11_1722125.speaker: Garriott
a11_1722125.text: 11, Houston. We're just now ready to switch from Omni Delta over to your High Gain Antenna. Can you confirm that you have gone to Reacq? Over.

a11_1733523.speaker: Garriott
a11_1733523.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Over.

a11_1733523.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1733523.text: Go ahead.

a11_1733523.speaker: Garriott
a11_1733523.text: Ah, just wanted to make sure you fellows hadn't gone back to sleep again. And I also have a little bit of late news here if you'd like to find out what's happened in the last 12-14 hours. Over.

a11_1733523.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1733523.text: Okay. Go ahead.

a11_1733523.speaker: Garriott
a11_1733523.text: Okey doke. Hot off the press here, we find Juan Carlos was formally designated yesterday - Tuesday - to become General Franco's successor - as the Chief of State of Spain and eventual King. Juan Carlos will be sworn in today as his successor designate after taking an oath of loyalty to the law and the National Movement, Spain's only legal political organization. He will apparently be called the Prince of Spain.

a11_1733523.speaker: Garriott
a11_1733523.text: House Ways and Means Committee also has agreed yesterday to tax changes affecting oil companies, also banks and utilities, which could add as much as 2 billion dollars per year to the federal revenue. The committee also voted tentatively to change the accounting procedures for telephone, electric, gas, and oil pipeline companies and to reduce tax benefits of mutual savings and loan institutions. So, it looks as if tax reform may be on the way.

a11_1733523.speaker: Garriott
a11_1733523.text: Looking overseas, we find South Korea's first super highway, linking Seoul with the Port of Inchon, has been named the Apollo Highway to commemorate your trip. I think we mentioned last night that President Nixon has already started on his round-the-world trip, and today he is in San Francisco on his first stop which will take him to the U.S.S. Hornet, from which he'll watch the return of your spacecraft. He plans to visit seven nations including Romania during this trip. He, as I think you also knew, had to miss the All Star baseball game yesterday, as it was rained out, but is being played t

a11_1733523.speaker: Garriott
a11_1733523.text: The West Coast residents in Seattle, Washington; Portland, Oregon; Vancouver, British Columbia; and San Francisco all plan to make their areas visible to the three of you by lighting their lights between 9 pm and midnight tonight, according to the Associated Press. We do have clear weather predicted there, so that you may be able to see Christmas lights, porch lights, store lights, and whatever may be turned on.

a11_1733523.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1733523.text: Good show.

a11_1733523.speaker: Garriott
a11_1733523.text: A little closer to home here, back in Memphis, Tennessee, a young lady who is presently tipping the scales at 8 pounds, 2 ounces, was named Module by her parents, Mr. and Mrs. Eddie Lee McGhee. 'It wasn't my idea,' said Mrs. McGhee, 'It was my husband's.' She said she had balked at the name Lunar Module McGhee, because it didn't sound too good, but apparently they have compromised on just Module. Over.

a11_1733523.speaker: SC
a11_1733523.text: [Laughter]...

a11_1733523.speaker: Garriott
a11_1733523.text: Roger. Hear a few chuckles coming from that direction. And we do have a late report on the sports here also. The All Star game currently being played. The present score at the end of the fourth inning has the National League leading the American League by 9 to 3. So the hitters are having a good day as you can tell.

a11_1733523.speaker: Garriott
a11_1733523.text: And rain clouds are over the MSC area at the moment. It began raining here just about 10 minutes ago, and last report, we were having a pretty heavy deluge. So, that's it from the news front for the afternoon here, Apollo 11. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1733523.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1733523.text: Thank you very much, Owen. I think my yard could use some water.

a11_1733523.speaker: Garriott
a11_1733523.text: That's very true. I've forgotten exactly how many days it did go, Buzz, but something like 30 days without rain. And we can appreciate the rain we're getting right now.

a11_1733523.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1733523.text: That was Neil. This is Buzz, here. I wonder if we could find out when the last time my lawn was cut. Over.

a11_1733523.speaker: Garriott
a11_1733523.text: That might be a little more difficult to find out. I'm not sure whether the - whether Mike is ready to admit when he last did the job, but I'll look into that for you.

a11_1733523.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1733523.text: Well, he'll tell you. He's got a new mower.

a11_1733523.speaker: Garriott
a11_1733523.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a11_1733523.speaker: Collins
a11_1733523.text: Hey, ask my chinch bugs how they're doing?

a11_1733523.speaker: Garriott
a11_1733523.text: Well, I'm not sure about yours. I can let you know about my own, and the report isn't very good.

a11_1733523.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1733523.text: Owen Garriott is the Capsule Communicator here in Mission Control at this time.

a11_1733523.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1733523.text: This is Apollo Control at 173 hours, 43 minutes. Apollo 11 now 105,165 nautical miles [194,766 km] from Earth. The velocity continuing to increase gradually; up to 5,652 feet per second [1,723 m/s]. The cabin temperature in the spacecraft has been running around 62 degrees [Fahrenheit, 17°C]. And coming up within the next hour, Apollo 11 will be crossing the midway point in distance - that to occur at 174 hours, 24 minutes and 7 seconds. There will be a briefing at 3 pm Central Daylight Time in the Building 1 Auditorium on the Lunar Receiving Laboratory.

a11_1734745.speaker: Garriott
a11_1734745.text: Roger. Joan wasn't home right now, Buzz, but Janice reports the grass is getting pretty high, and I would estimate that it's going to be close to your knees by the time you get out of quarantine. Over.

a11_1734745.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1734745.text: Okay. I'll have to schedule a little discussion after I get back.

a11_1734745.speaker: Garriott
a11_1734745.text: Rog. And no reports - no report from the chinch bugs there, Mike.

a11_1734745.speaker: Collins
a11_1734745.text: Well, they're sort of taciturn little fellows. They don't say much, they just chomp away.

a11_1734745.speaker: Collins
a11_1734745.text: Which is about what we're doing up here.

a11_1734745.speaker: Unidentified MCC speaker
a11_1734745.text: I'm not used to all this but I'm sitting here right beside... [Long pause.]

a11_1734745.speaker: Collins
a11_1734745.text: Breakfast was magnificent as usual. I had sliced peaches, sausage patties, two cups of coffee, and I forget all what else.

a11_1734745.speaker: Garriott
a11_1734745.text: That does sound pretty good. As a matter of fact, I'm way overdue for a meal myself, here. I could use some of that. [Long pause.]

a11_1734745.speaker: Collins
a11_1734745.text: Why don't you get Milt to give you 5 minutes off and grab a hamburger?

a11_1734745.speaker: Garriott
a11_1734745.text: I suggested that a while ago. He was pointing out about the weight problem here. Got to keep the calories low, so I'd better stand by without it.

a11_1735246.speaker: Collins
a11_1735246.text: Houston, Apollo 11. We - We've been doing a little flight planning for Apollo 12 up here.

a11_1735246.speaker: Collins
a11_1735246.text: We're trying to calculate how much spaghetti and meatballs we can get on board for Al Bean.

a11_1735246.speaker: Garriott
a11_1735246.text: I'm not sure the spacecraft will take that much extra weight. Have you made any estimates?

a11_1735246.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1735246.text: That last comment came from Mike Collins referring to Al Bean who is the Lunar Module Pilot for Apollo 12.

a11_1735246.speaker: Garriott
a11_1735246.text: 11, Houston. The medics at the next console report that the shrew is one animal which can eat six times its own body weight every 24 hours. This may be a satisfactory baseline for your spaghetti calculations on Al Bean. Over.

a11_1735246.speaker: Collins
a11_1735246.text: Okay. Thank you. That's in work.

a11_1735915.speaker: Collins
a11_1735915.text: Houston, Apollo 11. It was slightly colder in here last night than it has been on any previous night. Does EECOM notice any change in his data or any explanation for that?

a11_1735915.speaker: Garriott
a11_1735915.text: Roger. Stand by just a moment. We'll go and check some temperatures. [Pause.]

a11_1735915.speaker: Collins
a11_1735915.text: Up until last night it was - if anything, a little on the warm side at night. Last night it was on the chilly side.

a11_1735915.speaker: Garriott
a11_1735915.text: Roger there. We'll run down the temperatures for the two nights.

a11_1735915.speaker: Collins
a11_1735915.text: Oh, it's no big thing. Just as a matter of interest.

a11_1735915.speaker: Garriott
a11_1735915.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a11_1735915.speaker: Collins
a11_1735915.text: And how'd you like the Command Module RCS temperatures? [Pause.]

a11_1735915.speaker: Garriott
a11_1735915.text: 11, Houston. They all look very good. The lowest temperature was 40 degrees, and we're taking a look at your cabin temperatures now.

a11_1735915.speaker: Collins
a11_1735915.text: We agree on the CM RCS. No heaters are going to be required by a country mile.

a11_1735915.speaker: Garriott
a11_1735915.text: We think that's correct. [Pause.]

a11_1735915.speaker: Collins
a11_1735915.text: We don't like those heaters anyway, working off the direct coils.

a11_1735915.speaker: Garriott
a11_1735915.text: Rog [Long pause.].

a11_1735915.speaker: Collins
a11_1735915.text: Peculiar thing, Owen, on the platform alignment, is that when I really take my time and do a very slow, careful, precise job of marking. I'm getting about the same star angle difference as when I'm doing it in PTC and have to do a hurried rush job with relatively poor tracking. Star angle differences seem insensitive. It almost made me believe there's a very small bias there somewhere in the sextant.

a11_1735915.speaker: Garriott
a11_1735915.text: Roger, 11. Perhaps the 3-degrees-per-second just isn't that much of a bother. Over.

a11_1735915.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1735915.text: Well, he's really trying to explain why he can't get all zeros.

a11_1735915.speaker: Collins
a11_1735915.text: Yeah, that's - I think Buzz is probably right. As a matter of fact, one time I made a mark which I thought was a little bit in error, but I thought, 'Well, heck. I'll go ahead and see how it works out anyway,' and I got five zeros that time. And when I have thought everything was exactly precisely on, I have consistently been getting 0.01. [Pause.]

a11_1735915.speaker: Garriott
a11_1735915.text: Roger. Apparently it pays to hurry. [Pause.]

a11_1735915.speaker: Collins
a11_1735915.text: I usually do.

a11_1735915.speaker: Collins
a11_1735915.text: The visibility through the telescope has been very poor. It's, I would say, even worse than the simulator is right now. It requires long periods of dark adaptation which most times are most inconvenient. So it's really a tremendous asset to keep the platform powered up at all times and to keep it tweaked within the capability of the sextant field of view.

a11_1735915.speaker: Garriott
a11_1735915.text: Understand, Mike.

a11_1735915.speaker: Garriott
a11_1735915.text: 11, Houston. Checking your temperatures, it does look like the spacecraft may have cooled down perhaps 2 or 3 degrees in the last 24 hours, and that sounds to be consistent with your report on the comfort level there. Over.

a11_1735915.speaker: Collins
a11_1735915.text: Okay.

a11_1735915.speaker: Collins
a11_1735915.text: Is that a LM-off phenomenon? [Long pause.]

a11_1735915.speaker: Garriott
a11_1735915.text: 11, Houston. It looks like we'll have to think a little more about that, as to whether it's a LM-off or some effect of being out of lunar orbit, we don't know. So we'll have to puzzle before we can give a better answer.

a11_1735915.speaker: Collins
a11_1735915.text: Okay.

a11_1735915.speaker: Collins
a11_1735915.text: Well, if the systems guys have anything they want chased down, we'll be happy to give you any readings or reports or what have you.

a11_1735915.speaker: Garriott
a11_1735915.text: Roger. We'll think about that and see if there aren't some other tests to be usefully performed there.

a11_1735915.speaker: Collins
a11_1735915.text: Okay.

a11_1741309.speaker: Garriott
a11_1741309.text: 11, Houston. I'll be turning things over to the Green CapCom at this time, and see you on the ground tomorrow. [Pause.]

a11_1741309.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1741309.text: Okay, Owen. I want to thank you and the whole Purple/Maroon group there for a good job helping Apollo 11.

a11_1741309.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1741309.text: Thanks from us to all of you. It was really appreciated.

a11_1741309.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1741309.text: Astronaut Bruce McCandless has just relieved Owen Garriott as Capsule Communicator. At 174 hours, 14 minutes; Apollo 11 is 103,440 nautical miles [191,571 km] from Earth, traveling at a speed of 5,713 feet per second [1,741 m/s].

a11_1742630.speaker: McCandless
a11_1742630.text: 11, this is Houston. With reference to your subjective evaluation that it felt cooler inside the spacecraft last night, we reported earlier that we did indeed see a drop of about 3 degrees over the previous night. Looking back, it appears that the crew of Apollo 10 reported similar feelings during the translunar and trans-Earth coast phases. We're wondering if you could give us any indication of the relative amounts of free or condensed water in the cabin last night and the night before, from which we could infer humidity. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_1742630.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1742630.text: Roger. That might be a little bit difficult to do. We'll take a look at the tunnel now. It does seem as though, between the dirt, we've had a little bit more moisture in the tunnel. Of course, the LM hadn't been vented when we did translunar.

a11_1742630.speaker: McCandless
a11_1742630.text: Roger. We were more curious about the relative amount of moisture between, say, last night and the night before, both of which would have the LM missing. [Pause.]

a11_1742630.speaker: Collins
a11_1742630.text: There's more moisture in the tunnel now than there has been at any previous time. Subjectively we have been unable to determine any change in - any build-up in humidity. There appears to be no moisture any other place in the spacecraft. For example, the windows are not fogging or - and various other cool spots around the spacecraft - all of them appear to be completely dry.

a11_1742630.speaker: McCandless
a11_1742630.text: This is Houston. Roger. Thank you.

a11_1742630.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1742630.text: This is Apollo Control at 174 hours, 35 minutes. Apollo 11 now 102,286 nautical miles [189,434 km] from Earth. We crossed the halfway point in terms of distance at 174 hours and 24 minutes and 7 seconds. The briefing on the Lunar Receiving Laboratory is scheduled to begin at MSC in Building 1. We'll tape-record any conversations with the spacecraft and play those back immediately following the press conference. This is Apollo Control at 174 hours, 36 minutes.

a11_1744207.speaker: Collins
a11_1744207.text: How are all the Greens today, Bruce?

a11_1744207.speaker: McCandless
a11_1744207.text: Oh, the Greens are in good shape. The actual Green Team has been here for several hours. We're dogging the watch down here to position Ron for entry. Over.

a11_1744207.speaker: Collins
a11_1744207.text: Rog. Understand. Did Dave Reed get to explain the lunar sphere at the press conference?

a11_1744207.speaker: McCandless
a11_1744207.text: No, but your comments about Phil Shaffer and the explanations were quoted in the paper last night.

a11_1744207.speaker: McCandless
a11_1744207.text: Do you want to say anything more while you're on the line?

a11_1744405.speaker: Collins
a11_1744405.text: How's old Flight, Bruce? Did he ever let you go get a cup of coffee when we were over on the back side?

a11_1744405.speaker: McCandless
a11_1744405.text: Oh, things have been going pretty smoothly down here. He's really not that hard to get along with.

a11_1744405.speaker: McCandless
a11_1744405.text: We've only got two of them back here right now.

a11_1744405.speaker: Collins
a11_1744405.text: He always used to make me sit at the console through the back-side passes, just for training.

a11_1744405.speaker: McCandless
a11_1744405.text: Well, the word we have here is that that was because whenever you came back, you had to be retrained.

a11_1745108.speaker: Collins
a11_1745108.text: Houston, Apollo 11. A matter of curiosity. On our 70-mm cameras, we figure we exposed around 300 in the LM and around a thousand in the Command Module. And both cameras - or all the 70-mm cameras worked just fine.

a11_1750714.speaker: McCandless
a11_1750714.text: 11, this is Houston. Do you all have 'Change Lima' to your entry operations checklist dated July 23? Over.

a11_1750714.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1750714.text: I'm not sure that we hung - hung around long enough to pick that one up.

a11_1750714.speaker: McCandless
a11_1750714.text: Okay. If you've got the entry operations checklist handy, then I'll pass it up to you. Over.

a11_1750714.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1750714.text: How can you make changes after lift-off?

a11_1750714.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1750714.text: You sure you don't mean June?

a11_1750714.speaker: McCandless
a11_1750714.text: Negative. It just came up today. Over.

a11_1750714.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1750714.text: So, you're the first to get to us. Go ahead.

a11_1750714.speaker: McCandless
a11_1750714.text: Okay. On page 6-1 of the entry-out checklist down toward the bottom after "Main Deploy pushbutton", we have three additional steps we'd like you to accomplish. The intent of this is to reduce the oxygen pressure in your manifold and to eliminate the oxygen bleed flow through the potable and waste-water tanks during descent. Over.

a11_1750714.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1750714.text: Okay. We've got 6-1 out. Go ahead.

a11_1750714.speaker: McCandless
a11_1750714.text: Okay. Down at the bottom, you've got '10,000 feet Main Parachute Deploy, Main Deploy pushbutton, Push within 1 second.' And after that step, we'd like you insert 'Surge Tank O 2 valve, Off. Repress Package valve, Off. And Direct O 2 valve, Open.' Do you copy?

a11_1750714.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1750714.text: Okay. Down at the bottom, after 'Main Deploy pushbutton, Push' - 'Surge Tank O 2 , Off. Repress Package Valve, Off. Direct O 2 , On.' Over.

a11_1750714.speaker: McCandless
a11_1750714.text: Roger. And then down at the very bottom of page 6-2 where you see 'Direct O 2 , Off, Verify,' delete that step completely. Over.

a11_1751534.speaker: McCandless
a11_1751534.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. For your information, the All Star game has just ended with the National League winning 9 to 3 over American. Over.

a11_1751534.speaker: McCandless
a11_1751534.text: And I have a message here for Mike that says, quote, All the chinch bugs are gone, unquote. Over.

a11_1751534.speaker: Collins
a11_1751534.text: Having done their job, I guess.

a11_1751534.speaker: McCandless
a11_1751534.text: Well, along with one tree, it turns out.

a11_1751534.speaker: Collins
a11_1751534.text: Yeah. I heard about that. That was right before the flight.

a11_1751534.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1751534.text: This is Apollo Control at 175 hours, 42 minutes. Apollo 11 is now 98,512 nautical miles [182,444 km] from the Earth. The velocity; 5,892 feet per second [1,796 m/s]. During the preceding press conference, we accumulated about 7 minutes of taped conversation which we'll play back for you now.

a11_1751534.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1751534.text: This is Apollo Control. That brings us up to date with the tape-recorded conversation. We'll continue to stand by for any further communications with the spacecraft. During the previous conversations, you heard Mike Collins toss a couple of good-natured barbs at Flight Director Cliff Charlesworth. Collins was Capsule Communicator on Charlesworth's shift during the Apollo 8 mission. At 175 hours, 51 minutes; Apollo 11 is 98,034 nautical miles [181,559 km] from the Earth.

a11_1762355.speaker: McCandless
a11_1762355.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Are you still up there? Over. [Pause.]

a11_1762355.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1762355.text: Uh, yes, we are. But not quite so far as we were a while ago.

a11_1762355.speaker: McCandless
a11_1762355.text: Roger. We concur. We just wanted to make sure that we still had good comm with you.

a11_1762626.speaker: McCandless
a11_1762626.text: For general information, 11, you are now 95,970 miles [177,736 km] out from the Earth. Over.

a11_1762626.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1762626.text: Right in our own back yard.

a11_1762626.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1762626.text: Right in our own back yard. [Pause.]

a11_1762626.speaker: Collins
a11_1762626.text: Trying to come down hill a little bit now. What's our velocity?

a11_1762626.speaker: McCandless
a11_1762626.text: Your velocity is 5,991 feet per second [1,826 m/s].

a11_1762626.speaker: McCandless
a11_1762626.text: And you are indeed coming downhill.

a11_1762626.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1762626.text: This is Apollo Control at 176 hours, 44 minutes. Apollo 11 now 94,961 nautical miles [175,868 km] from Earth. The velocity has just gone over the 6,000-foot-per-second [1,829 m/s] mark. We're 6,029 feet per second [1,838 m/s]. The next item scheduled on the Flight Plan is a television transmission. That's scheduled to occur at a Ground Elapsed Time of 177 hours, 30 minutes; which would be 6:02 pm Central Daylight Time. Among the clocks counting down or up to and from significant events here in Mission Control, we have one counting down to entry. That clock now shows 18 hours, 18 minutes and 12

a11_1770835.speaker: McCandless
a11_1770835.text: Roger, 11. I've got a Flight Plan update for you, to give you an optimum attitude for the Earth in the number 1 window and the Moon in number 5 window. Over.

a11_1770835.speaker: McCandless
a11_1770835.text: Roger. Your attitude will be roll, 12 degrees; pitch, 270 degrees; yaw, 0 degrees. High Gain Antenna angles: pitch, plus 14; yaw, 263. Over.

a11_1770835.speaker: Collins
a11_1770835.text: Roger. I copy. Roll, 012; pitch, 270; y - yaw is zero. High Gain Antenna; pitch, plus 14 and yaw, 263.

a11_1770835.speaker: McCandless
a11_1770835.text: Roger. And when coming out of PTC, you might be advised that your deadband has been collapsed, so to follow the checklist items. Over.

a11_1770835.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1770835.text: This is Apollo Control; at 177 hours, 11 minutes. Network controller advises that we're starting to get some semblance of TV signal from the spacecraft. We suspect we may be getting some checkout. We'll continue to stand by and be prepared to take whatever's sent.

a11_1771223.speaker: McCandless
a11_1771223.text: 11, this is Houston. We're receiving a black signal from you right now, but we are getting TV. Over.

a11_1771223.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1771223.text: This is Apollo Control. The Network controller now reports that the TV signal is down, apparently having been turned off, and we suspect that what we had was a test of the system by the crew. The television transmission from the spacecraft is scheduled to begin at 177 hours, 30 minutes or about 2 minutes past 6 Central Daylight Time. At the present time, Apollo 11 is 93,218 nautical miles [172,640 km] from the Earth.

a11_1772322.speaker: Comm Tech
a11_1772322.text: I'm gonna go to Net 1 now.

a11_1772322.speaker: McCandless
a11_1772322.text: From signal strength indications, it appears we may be locked up on a side lobe with the High Gain antenna. We'd like you to go into wide beamwidth for about 15 seconds and then back to narrow. Over.

a11_1772322.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1772322.text: This is Apollo Control at 177 hours, 30 minutes. We're standing by at this time to receive television pictures from the Apollo 11 spacecraft. A short while ago we received the test transmission and apparently everything is functioning normally. We were receiving television signal from Goldstone relayed on through to Houston. We'll continue to stand by for the TV.

a11_1773000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1773000.text: You having good S-band signal strength now, Houston?

a11_1773000.speaker: McCandless
a11_1773000.text: That's affirmative, 11.

a11_1773000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1773000.text: Y'all set for TV?

a11_1773000.speaker: McCandless
a11_1773000.text: Roger. We're all set whenever you're ready to send.

a11_1773000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1773000.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a11_1773000.speaker: McCandless
a11_1773000.text: Okay. You're coming through loud and clear now, 11, with your patch.

a11_1773000.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1773000.text: We have black and white signals. We should have the conversion up shortly.

a11_1773000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1773000.text: Good evening. This is the Commander of Apollo 11. A hundred years ago, Jules Verne wrote a book about a voyage to the Moon. His spaceship, Columbia, took off from Florida and landed in the Pacific Ocean after completing a trip to the Moon. It seems appropriate to us to share with you some of the reflections of the crew as the modern-day Columbia completes its rendezvous with the planet Earth and the same Pacific Ocean tomorrow. First, Mike Collins. [Long pause.]

a11_1773000.speaker: McCandless
a11_1773000.text: 11, this is Houston. We have an LOS here.

a11_1773000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1773000.text: We'll be right back with you.

a11_1773000.speaker: McCandless
a11_1773000.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a11_1773000.speaker: McCandless
a11_1773000.text: In the interim, you may be interested in knowing that Jan and the children, and Pat and the youngsters, and Andy Aldrin are down here in the viewing room watching this evening.

a11_1773000.speaker: Collins
a11_1773000.text: Oh, we're glad to hear that. [Long pause.]

a11_1773000.speaker: McCandless
a11_1773000.text: Okay, 11. You're back on, with Mike in the middle of the screen there.

a11_1773000.speaker: Collins
a11_1773000.text: Roger. This trip of ours to the Moon may have looked, to you, simple or easy. I'd like to assure you that has not been the case. The Saturn V rocket which put us into orbit is an incredibly complicated piece of machinery, every piece of which worked flawlessly. This computer up above my head has a 38,000-word vocabulary, each word of which has been very carefully chosen to be of the utmost value to us, the crew. This switch which I have in my hand now, has over 300 counterparts in the Command Module alone, this one single switch design. In addition to that, there are myriads of circuit breaker

a11_1773000.speaker: McCandless
a11_1773000.text: 11, this is Houston. We're getting a good picture of Buzz now, but no voice modulation. And would you open up the f-stop on the TV camera? Try 2 - 2, please [meaning f/2.2].

a11_1773000.speaker: McCandless
a11_1773000.text: That appears to be a lot better now. We're still not receiving Buzz's audio.

a11_1773000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1773000.text: Good evening. I'd like to discuss with you a few of the more symbolic aspects of the flight of our mission, Apollo 11. As we've been discussing the events that have taken place in the past 2 or 3 days here on board our spacecraft, we've come to the conclusion that this has been far more than three men on a voyage to the Moon. More, still, than the efforts of a government and industry team. More, even, than the efforts of one nation. We feel that this stands as a symbol of the insatiable curiosity of all mankind to explore the unknown. Neil's statement the other day upon first setting foot on t

a11_1773000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1773000.text: The responsibility for this flight lies first with - with history and with the giants of science who have preceded this effort. Next to the American people, who have through their will, indicated their desire. Next, to four administrations, and their l - Congresses, for implementing that will. And then, to the agency and industry teams that built our spacecraft, the Saturn, the Columbia, the Eagle, and the little EMU; the space suit and backpack that was our small spacecraft out on the lunar surface. We'd like to give a special thanks to all those Americans who built those spacecraft, who did

a11_1773000.speaker: McCandless
a11_1773000.text: 11, this is Houston. We're getting a zoom view out the window now. [Long pause.]

a11_1773000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1773000.text: Apollo 11, signing off.

a11_1773000.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1773000.text: That brief view of the Earth came from 91,371 nautical miles [169,219 km] out in space after a brief and sincere and moving transmission from the Apollo 11 spacecraft. This is Apollo Control at 177 hours, 45 minutes.

a11_1774748.speaker: Collins
a11_1774748.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Do you want to crank up PTC again? Do you have some reason to hold this attitude, or what's your pleasure?

a11_1774748.speaker: McCandless
a11_1774748.text: You can crank up PTC again, Mike, any time you like. And I might add, I thought that was a mighty fine TV presentation. There's certainly nothing I can add to it from down here.

a11_1775327.speaker: McCandless
a11_1775327.text: Okay, 11. I've got a few small items here - one Flight Plan update and some entry photography information, if you're ready to copy. Over.

a11_1775327.speaker: McCandless
a11_1775327.text: Roger. At 180 hours, 50 minutes GET, we should like to delete your oxygen fuel cell purge.

a11_1775327.speaker: McCandless
a11_1775327.text: And on the entry photography, if you're going to use a fresh magazine of color interior film, we recommend the following exposure settings: f:11 at 1/250th, six frames per second, focus on 7 feet for the fireball; f:2.0, 1/60th of a second, six frames per second, focus on 50 feet when the chutes open. If you're using a magazine, part of which has already been used for interior shots, we recommend f:16 at 1/500th of a second, six frames per second, focus on 7 feet for the fireball; f2.8, 1/60th of a second, six frames per second, focus on 50 feet when the parachutes open. And we would like to k

a11_1775327.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1775327.text: Okay. I think we've got those. We will be using a fresh one and it'll be color interior. Over.

a11_1775327.speaker: McCandless
a11_1775327.text: Roger. When you get - when you get it out, we'd like to have the number of the magazine, or the letter of the magazine relayed down.

a11_1775327.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1775327.text: Okay. And we're thinking that we might want to run some of this at 12 frames a second. I don't think we can get everything from 0.5 - 0.05g down. That'll only give us about 7.8 minutes - frames - double that. I guess maybe just an occasional burst to 12 frames would be what we'd want and the rest of it at six. Over. [Long pause.]

a11_1775327.speaker: McCandless
a11_1775327.text: This is Houston. That plan sounds fine with us, Neil.

a11_1775327.speaker: McCandless
a11_1775327.text: And lastly, we'd like to know if your stowage configuration for entry is going to conform to the nominal. The Retros down here are anxious to get an accurate c.g. computed for you, and in particular, where the LEVAs are being stowed. Over.

a11_1775327.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1775327.text: Okay. We think we're going to put the LEVAs and the helmets in the hatch bag, and we'll let you know any other non-standard stowage locations that we complete this evening.

a11_1780657.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1780657.text: Roger. The magazine we'll be using for entry tomorrow is magazine M. Over.

a11_1780657.speaker: McCandless
a11_1780657.text: Roger. Understand. Magazine M as in Mike.

a11_1781738.speaker: McCandless
a11_1781738.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Your friendly Green Team going off for the night, and going off for the last time. We wish to bid you a good night and Godspeed.

a11_1781738.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1781738.text: Thank you. We appreciate all that fine work done by the - by the Green Team, and we'll be thanking you in person when we get back.

a11_1781738.speaker: McCandless
a11_1781738.text: Roger. We'll see you on the ground.

a11_1781738.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1781738.text: Really enjoyed working with all of you. Thanks very much. Over.

a11_1781738.speaker: McCandless
a11_1781738.text: They're all smiles down here, even the trench.

a11_1781738.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1781738.text: This is Apollo Control. Here in the Mission Operations Control Room of Mission Control Center, the White Team of flight controllers under Flight Director Gene Kranz settling in for the 10-hour shift ahead until 5:00 am. Green Team Flight Director Cliff Charlesworth is now en route to the Houston Apollo News Center and shortly will be there for his Change-of-Shift Press Conference. Estimating about 10 minutes for his arrival. We'll continue to monitor the Apollo 11 air-ground circuit should the communications resume. Standing by; 178 hours, 25 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control

a11_1781738.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1781738.text: This is Apollo Control. Apollo 11 now 88,442 nautical miles [163,795 km] out from Earth, approaching at a velocity of 6,299 feet per second [1,920 m/s]. Change-of-Shift Press Conference with the Green Team Flight Director Cliff Charlesworth due to begin any moment now in the NASA Apollo News Center Auditorium. And at 178 hours, 34 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control.

a11_1784030.speaker: Collins
a11_1784030.text: Roger. How's our thruster firing activity? We're about ready to crank up PTC if you are.

a11_1785651.speaker: McCandless
a11_1785651.text: 11, we'd like you to shift to an Omni antenna configuration at the present time. We're requesting the S-band antenna Omni switch to Bravo, and the S-band antenna Omni switch to Omni. The High Gain Antenna track in Manual. Pitch, minus 50; yaw, 270. Over.

a11_1785651.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1785651.text: Roger. I'll do that right now.

a11_1785651.speaker: McCandless
a11_1785651.text: Roger. And if Mike has a minute, we'd like to do a little bit of trouble-shooting. It seems he's either flat-chested or something because we've lost respiration rate on the Biomed telemetry. That is, his EPN trace down here is flat.

a11_1785651.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1785651.text: He was shaving a little bit ago. He might have just let it slip. Hold on a moment.

a11_1785651.speaker: Collins
a11_1785651.text: All the blasted wires are all connected, is all I know.

a11_1785651.speaker: McCandless
a11_1785651.text: Okay, Mike. We had a request that you disconnect the yellow connector from the signal conditioner and verify that it looks okay, reconnect it and then, if you would, check the two electrodes that are placed one on each side of your lower rib cage. Over.

a11_1785651.speaker: Collins
a11_1785651.text: I'll bet you there's a smile on Charlesworth's face.

a11_1785651.speaker: McCandless
a11_1785651.text: Cliff is not on right now. Gene Kranz just relieved him a few minutes ago.

a11_1790323.speaker: McCandless
a11_1790323.text: Apollo 11, Apollo 11, this is Houston broadcasting in the blind. Request Omni Bravo. Request Omni Bravo. Over.

a11_1790323.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1790323.text: This is Apollo Control; 179 hours, 9 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. During the past half hour, there have been some exchanges between spacecraft communicator Bruce McCandless here in Mission Control and the crew of Apollo 11. One item they're trying to sort out and troubleshoot, some difficulties with the biomedical sensors attached to the chest of Command Module Pilot Mike Collins. Let's play back the accumulated tape, and hopefully by the time it's ended, we will have picked up communications again and we'll re-join the conversation live. Roll tape please.

a11_1791045.speaker: McCandless
a11_1791045.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Communication re-established.

a11_1791045.speaker: McCandless
a11_1791045.text: Apollo 11, this is Houston. Will you confirm you're in Omni Bravo? Over.

a11_1791045.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1791045.text: Okay. That ought to give it to you.

a11_1800745.speaker: McCandless
a11_1800745.text: Hey, 11, this is Houston. You might tell Buzz not to exercise quite so strenuously. Over.

a11_1800745.speaker: McCandless
a11_1800745.text: Okay. That's one - that's one on us. [Laughter. Long pause.]

a11_1800745.speaker: McCandless
a11_1800745.text: 11, Houston. Seriously, that comment was just aimed at your musical selection.

a11_1802122.speaker: McCandless
a11_1802122.text: We'd like to know what your plans are as far as turning in this evening. Our - in the Flight Plan, we show you commencing a rest period at about 182 hours, and what are you planning to do on that? We're going to be watching the weather here, and we expect to have an update on the weather, I guess, in about another half hour or 45 minutes, to pass to you. Over.

a11_1802122.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1802122.text: We're going to probably stick with the Flight Plan pretty much. We are going to - if - check the lights in the northwest corner of the U.S. and southwest corner of Canada. If we can see up that high into the northern hemisphere. Other than that, we'll be on the Flight Plan.

a11_1802122.speaker: McCandless
a11_1802122.text: Roger. For your information, the laser from McDonald Observatory in West Texas will be up from about 181 hours and 30 minutes, on for 1 hour. You should be able to spot the Earth out of the number 1 window every time you pass roll 357 degrees and they, of course, are in West Texas. Over.

a11_1802122.speaker: McCandless
a11_1802122.text: Roger. For the number 5 window. That'll be - every time you pass 230 degrees in roll. Over.

a11_1803656.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1803656.text: Houston, Apollo 11. How much longer do you want to keep charging Battery B? [Long pause.]

a11_1803656.speaker: McCandless
a11_1803656.text: 11, this is Houston. Nominally we're looking for about another hour-and-a-half, but what we'd like to do is continue charging until shortly before you turn in for the night. Over.

a11_1803656.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1803656.text: That'll be fine. Are you going to want to charge A again at all?

a11_1804218.speaker: McCandless
a11_1804218.text: 11, this is Houston. At about 180:45, we'll be handing over from Goldstone to Honeysuckle, and I'm handing over to Charlie. See you when you get back. Over.

a11_1804218.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1804218.text: Okay, Bruce. Good night. Thank you.

a11_1804218.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1804218.text: Thank you very much, Bruce. It's been a pleasure working with you.

a11_1804218.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1804218.text: This is Apollo Control. The weird noise has been reported by network controllers as not being on the downlink from the spacecraft. Now it's stopped. Let's leave the circuit open here in the period prior to the time the crew goes to sleep and monitor the air-ground circuit.

a11_1804218.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1804218.text: This is Apollo Control. We've been standing by now for quite some time for resumption of communications, but apparently no one is saying anything tonight. Apollo 11 now 78,134 nautical miles [144,704] out from Earth, approaching at 6,785 feet per second [2,068 m/s]. And at 181 hours, 17 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control.

a11_1812646.speaker: Collins
a11_1812646.text: Roger, Houston. For RETRO, I have the anticipated location of all the entry stowage, and I suggest you pull out the entry checklist, and we'll go through those maps in the front of it.

a11_1812646.speaker: Lewis
a11_1812646.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Could you stand by just a few minutes? Charlie and Flight are out getting a weather briefing. They'll be back shortly.

a11_1812646.speaker: Lewis
a11_1812646.text: No, this is Chuck Lewis. Charlie Duke is out with Flight getting a weather briefing right now.

a11_1813555.speaker: Duke
a11_1813555.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. Over.

a11_1813555.speaker: Collins
a11_1813555.text: Roger, Houston. Apollo 11. Did you get the word on the entry checklist?

a11_1813555.speaker: Duke
a11_1813555.text: Roger, Mike. We sure did. We're ready to talk about it, if you are. Over.

a11_1813555.speaker: Collins
a11_1813555.text: I think the quickest thing is to go through page by page, the first part of the entry checklist where it has a map. Starting on the page with compartment L2 and L3. Are you with me?

a11_1813555.speaker: Duke
a11_1813555.text: Rog. With you.

a11_1813555.speaker: Collins
a11_1813555.text: Okay. L2 is as shown. L3 is as shown. There is about half the food remaining in L3.

a11_1813555.speaker: Duke
a11_1813555.text: Roger.

a11_1813555.speaker: Collins
a11_1813555.text: Where it says - where it says 'And note', the CMP PGA is located in the L-shaped bag with the other two PGAs. The LM shield was jettisoned with the - Correction, the CMP's helmet shield was jettisoned with the LM, and his helmet and gloves, instead of being in the sleep restraint, are in the hatch bags.

a11_1813555.speaker: Duke
a11_1813555.text: Okay. Let's see now. Your PGA is in the L-shaped bag with the other two PGAs, and your helmet and gloves are in the L-shaped bag instead of the sleep restraint.

a11_1813555.speaker: Collins
a11_1813555.text: The helmet and gloves are in the hatch bag, the great big bag that's underneath the left-hand couch that you put the hatch in.

a11_1813555.speaker: Duke
a11_1813555.text: Rog. I thought I - That's what I copied. Okay. Go ahead.

a11_1813555.speaker: Collins
a11_1813555.text: Okay. The next page is identical except nitpicking point: at R1, we got the entry checklist. Other than that it's identical, and the third page has got some changes.

a11_1813555.speaker: Duke
a11_1813555.text: Go ahead.

a11_1813555.speaker: Collins
a11_1813555.text: In A1 - Are you with me? I'm over there in compartment A1, now.

a11_1813555.speaker: Duke
a11_1813555.text: Go ahead, Mike. Over.

a11_1813555.speaker: Collins
a11_1813555.text: Okay. Compartment A1, the 16-millimeter magazine will be located in window number 4 instead of 5. Tissue dispensers - there's only one of them left. And compartment U3, the 16-millimeter bracket is on window 4, and the PGA bag - add the CMP's PGA, plus add two LCGs. And compartment A8, delete two LCGs, add one PPK, making a total of four; and add 10 pounds of LM miscellaneous equipment. We told you five the other day. We think ten is probably closer. Over.

a11_1813555.speaker: Duke
a11_1813555.text: Copy. [Pause.]

a11_1813555.speaker: Collins
a11_1813555.text: And that's all the changes on that page. Ready for the next page?

a11_1813555.speaker: Duke
a11_1813555.text: Rog. Go ahead, Mike.

a11_1813555.speaker: Collins
a11_1813555.text: On your next page, in compartment B1, we estimate about 15 per cent of that food is remaining. In B2 we took PPK out of there and put trash in it. In B3, the 16-millimeter cable, the 18-millimeter lens, and the right-angle mirror are on window number 4. And that, sir, brings you all up to date.

a11_1813555.speaker: Duke
a11_1813555.text: Roger. How about the LEVAs, Mike? Where did you put those? Over.

a11_1813555.speaker: Collins
a11_1813555.text: They're in the hatch bag.

a11_1813555.speaker: Duke
a11_1813555.text: Roger. Stand by. Our only concern, 11, is with the stuff you got in the hatch bag. That's pretty big bulk between you and A8, and we'd like to talk about moving that over to the sleep restraint. If you'll stand by. I'll verify that. Over.

a11_1813555.speaker: Collins
a11_1813555.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a11_1813555.speaker: Duke
a11_1813555.text: 11, Houston. Our recommendation on the gear you got in the helmet bag - correction, the hatch bag - would be to remove that stuff and put it in the sleep restraint under the right couch. The reason is that the hatch bag straps are only configured for zero g, and it's a pretty difficult job getting it lashed down. With the gear in the sleep restraint, it's a pretty standard lash-down procedure, and you can also use the Beta cord that you have on board. You concur? Over. [Pause.]

a11_1813555.speaker: Collins
a11_1813555.text: Yeah. We'll look at it, Charlie, and let you know.

a11_1813555.speaker: Duke
a11_1813555.text: Roger. And I've got a couple of other things, Mike. We need to terminate Battery B charge at this time, and also, the weather is clobbering in at our targeted landing point due to scattered thunderstorms. We don't want to tangle with one of those, so we're going to move you - your aim point up-range. Correction, it'll be down-range, to target for a 1,500-nautical-mile entry, so we can guarantee uplift control. The new coordinates are 13 degrees, 19 minutes North; 169, 10 minutes West. The weather in that area is super. We got 2,000 scattered, 8,000 scattered with 10 miles visibility and 6-foot

a11_1813555.speaker: Collins
a11_1813555.text: Roger.

a11_1813555.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1813555.text: This is Apollo Control. To recap, briefly, the conversation a few moments ago between Charlie Duke and the crew of Columbia. Because of forecast thunderstorms in the prime recovery area in the mid-Pacific for tomorrow, the Apollo spacecraft's lifting capabilities will be used to stretch the entry path some 215 nautical miles [398 km] further downrange toward Hawaii to a new landing point or aiming point, with the very rough preliminary coordinates of 13 degrees, 19 minutes North by 169 degrees, 10 minutes West. These numbers will be refined through the night, as Retrofire Officer exercises the

a11_1815000.speaker: Duke
a11_1815000.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Some of the general last minute updates here. On the entry, we had told you on the camera to set it at 50 feet. It turns out the biggest number on the camera is 25 feet, so just set it at infinity. Over.

a11_1815742.speaker: Duke
a11_1815742.text: Hello, Apollo 11. Houston. We're ready to put you to bed and say good night, if you give us your crew status report and verify that you changed out the CO 2 canister a moment ago. Over.

a11_1820043.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1820043.text: Okay, Charlie. Crew status report follows. CDR, 11023; CMP, 10025; LMP, 09027. Canister change complete.

a11_1820043.speaker: Duke
a11_1820043.text: Roger. Thank you very much there.

a11_1820043.speaker: Duke
a11_1820043.text: Roger. Thank you. Could you give us an onboard readout, please, sir?

a11_1820043.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1820043.text: Stand by. Okay. Batt C, 37; Pyro Batt A, 37; Batt B, 37. RCS A, 51; B, 63; C, 62; D, 58.

a11_1820347.speaker: Duke
a11_1820347.text: Apollo 11, Houston. It's a good night from the White Team for the last time. We'll be off when you wake up in the morning. It's been a pleasure working with you guys. It was a beautiful show from all three of you. We appreciate it very much, and we'll see you when you get out of the LRL. Over.

a11_1820347.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1820347.text: Okay, Charlie. Thanks to you and all the White Team for a great job down there all the way through. Thank you.

a11_1820347.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1820347.text: Thank you very much, Charlie. Thanks.

a11_1820347.speaker: Duke
a11_1820347.text: Thanks to you guys, too. [Long pause.]

a11_1820347.speaker: Duke
a11_1820347.text: And, 11, Houston. Mike, you get your chance at a landing tomorrow. No go-around.

a11_1820347.speaker: Collins
a11_1820347.text: Rog. You're going to let me land closer to Hawaii too, aren't you?

a11_1820347.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1820347.text: This is Apollo Control. All goodnights having been said, the crew of Apollo 11 is now preparing to get their 10 hours rest and their last night in space. Here in the Control Center, on one of the 10 by 10 Eidophor television projectors - a drawing has been projected on the screen ribbing CapCom Charlie Duke for his slight error yesterday on the television pass where he mistook the Moon for Earth. It has the spacecraft midway between the Moon and Earth and it says, 'Neil, I just spotted a continent on the Moon. Charlie, the camera's on the Earth now.' Apollo 11 now 74,906 nautical miles [138,72

a11_1820759.speaker: Duke
a11_1820759.text: 11, Houston. We got some word just a moment ago that the McDonald Observatory is - said they had picked up the spacecraft in their telescope. Over.

a11_1820759.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1820759.text: Outstanding. We have been looking for their laser but haven't had much luck yet.

a11_1820759.speaker: Duke
a11_1820759.text: Roger. We'll pass it on to them, Neil. Thank you.

a11_1820759.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1820759.text: This is Apollo Control. 182 hours, 10 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. We thought that was all the air-to-ground for tonight prior to the crew going to sleep, but just a few moments ago, there was a brief exchange reporting to the Apollo 11 crew that the McDonald Observatory in far West Texas had the spacecraft in their telescope field of view. Let's roll that tape now and then shut it down again.

a11_1820759.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1820759.text: This is Apollo Control. That completes the very brief exchange of a few moments ago. At 182 hours, 11 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control.

a11_1892800.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1892800.text: Roger. Good morning. What's the status on Mid-Course 7?

a11_1892800.speaker: Evans
a11_1892800.text: Roger. We were going to let you sleep in until about 190 hours. Mid-Course 7 is not required.

a11_1892800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1892800.text: The crew gave us a call at 189 hours, 29 minutes. We advised them of the cancellation of the Mid-Course Correction. Weather in the recovery area: skies will be partly cloudy. Cloud base is at 2,000 feet scattered. Wind, east north east at 18 knots. 6-foot sea. Temperature near 80 degrees [27°C]. This landing area is 215 miles [400 km] to the northeast from the original landing area, moved because of thunder showers in the original area. This new location should allow the recovery ship USS Hornet to arrive in Hawaii 4 to 5 hours earlier than originally planned. We expect it may be possible for

a11_1892800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1892800.text: The crew is probably preparing breakfast now and it's not likely we'll hear a lot from them in the - right away, but we'll continue to stay up live for any conversation.

a11_1892800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1892800.text: Visibility in the recovery area is 10 miles [18.5 km].

a11_1892800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1892800.text: Clock shows we're 5½ hours away from Entry Interface, the point at which Apollo 11 will enter the Earth's atmosphere. That's scheduled to occur at an elapsed time of 195 hours, 3 minutes, 7 seconds. We expect landing at 195 hours, 17 minutes, 49 seconds.

a11_1892800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1892800.text: This is Apollo Control. Apollo 11 is now 38,793 nautical miles [71,845 km] from the Earth. Velocity, 9,947 feet per second [3,032 m/s].

a11_1892800.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1892800.text: This is Apollo Control at 190 hours, 10 minutes. Apollo 11's distance from the Earth, 36,956 nautical miles [68,443 km]. Velocity, 10,195 feet per second [3,107 m/s].

a11_1901907.speaker: Evans
a11_1901907.text: Apollo 11. Good morning from Houston. Over.

a11_1901907.speaker: Evans
a11_1901907.text: Roger. We saw you're up, stirring around, and we thought you're probably eating your breakfast there. Just in general, we'll probably start coming up with the uplink of the state vectors and the target loads and what have you at about 190:50, somewhere in that area, and then get you started to work.

a11_1901907.speaker: Evans
a11_1901907.text: And in the meantime, while you're eating your breakfast there, I've got the Maroon Bugle all standing by here to give you the morning news.

a11_1901907.speaker: Evans
a11_1901907.text: Okay. Apollo 11 remains the prime story with the world awaiting your landing today at about 11:49 am Houston time. In Washington, House tax reformers have fashioned a provision which would make it impossible for wealthy individuals to avoid income tax entirely through tax-free investments or special allowances. Under the proposal tentatively adopted by the House Ways and Means Committee, everyone would pay taxes on at least half of their income.

a11_1901907.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1901907.text: Okay. Okay, Ron. We're ready to go again. Thank you.

a11_1901907.speaker: Evans
a11_1901907.text: Roger. Continuing with the Maroon Bugle. President Nixon surprised your wives with a phone call from San Francisco just before he boarded a plane to fly out to meet you. All of them were very touched by your television broadcast. Jan and Pat watched from Mission Control here. The launch of Intelsat from the Cape was postponed for the fourth time last night. The problem was said to be a malfunctioning nitrogen regulator in the second stage of the Delta. A new attempt will be made to launch it tonight. The research submarine Ben Franklin, which is studying the Gulf Stream, set a record by drifti

a11_1903142.speaker: Evans
a11_1903142.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Roger. We copy. And I have your consumables update, if you're ready to copy.

a11_1903142.speaker: Evans
a11_1903142.text: Roger. GET 189 plus 00: RCS total, minus 1 percent; Alpha, minus 11; Bravo, plus 10; Charlie, minus 1; Delta, minus 1. H 2 total, minus 0.76 pounds; oxygen total, plus 17.6 pounds. Over.

a11_1903142.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1903142.text: Okay. It doesn't look like we're going to be able to get quite back on the Flight Plan.

a11_1903142.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1903142.text: This is Apollo Control at 190 hours, 34 minutes. Apollo 11's distance from the Earth, 34,622 nautical miles [64,120 km]. Velocity, 10,534 feet per second [3,211 m/s].

a11_1904513.speaker: Evans
a11_1904513.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Request P00 and Accept, and we'll send you a REFSMMAT, state vector, and entry target load. Over.

a11_1904513.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1904513.text: You have it.

a11_1904513.speaker: Evans
a11_1904513.text: Roger. It'll be coming up.

a11_1904513.speaker: Evans
a11_1904513.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Can you tell us where the visor assemblies ended up, there?

a11_1904513.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1904513.text: We're going to follow your suggestion and stow them under the right-hand couch.

a11_1904513.speaker: Evans
a11_1904513.text: Roger. Mighty fine. Break. The weather forecast in the landing area right now is 2,000 scattered, high scattered, 10 miles. The wind about 080 at 18 knots. You'll have about 3- to 6-foot waves. Your Delta-H is plus 10 feet. And it looks like you'll be landing about 10 minutes before sunrise. Over.

a11_1904513.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1904513.text: Okay. Sounds good.

a11_1904513.speaker: Evans
a11_1904513.text: Roger.

a11_1904513.speaker: Evans
a11_1904513.text: Apollo 11, Houston. All three loads are in. The computer is yours. Over.

a11_1904513.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1904513.text: Roger.

a11_1904513.speaker: Evans
a11_1904513.text: And Mike, if you're on loop there, to extend the range and the constant-g re-entry, here, I've got a little procedure, if you'd like to listen to it.

a11_1904513.speaker: Collins
a11_1904513.text: Stand by one.

a11_1904513.speaker: Evans
a11_1904513.text: Roger.

a11_1904513.speaker: Collins
a11_1904513.text: I'm right in the middle of my orange juice. Be with you in about 5 minutes.

a11_1904513.speaker: Evans
a11_1904513.text: Sure, no problem, standing by.

a11_1904513.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1904513.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Hey, Ron, I wonder if you could give us a good Navy explanation for this Delta-H term. Over.

a11_1904513.speaker: Evans
a11_1904513.text: Roger. Let me think about it, and I'll come back.

a11_1904513.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1904513.text: You too, huh?

a11_1904513.speaker: Evans
a11_1904513.text: [Laughter] Right.

a11_1904513.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1904513.text: Collins has got one, but I'm not sure I buy it.

a11_1904513.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1904513.text: This is Apollo Control at 190 hours, 56 minutes. Apollo 11's distance from Earth; 32,447 nautical miles [60,092 km]. Velocity; 10,876 feet per second [3,315 m/s].

a11_1905600.speaker: Evans
a11_1905600.text: Roger, 11. We don't have to worry about it any more. The altimeter out there is now standard, 29.92. But basically what it means is that if I give you a plus 10 feet, for instance, that means that you will hit the water with the altimeter reading 10 feet. Over.

a11_1905600.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1905600.text: This is Apollo Control at 191 hours, 15 minutes. Apollo 11 is now 30,469 nautical miles [56,429 km] from Earth, approaching at a velocity of 11,221 feet per second [3,420 m/s].

a11_1905600.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1905600.text: This is Apollo Control at 191 hours, 38 minutes. Apollo 11's distance from Earth now 27,979 nautical miles [51,817 km]. Velocity; 11,689 feet per second [3,563 m/s].

a11_1914331.speaker: Evans
a11_1914331.text: Apollo 11, Houston. I have your Entry PAD. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1914331.speaker: Evans
a11_1914331.text: Roger. Entry PAD: area is the mid-Pacific; roll 000, 152, 001; GET 194:46:06, 267; latitude, plus 13.32, minus 169.17; 06.4; 36194, 6.49; range to go, 1404.5, 36275; 195:03:06, 00:28, D L max, 1.54, 0.84, 22400, 18000; D 0 4.00, 02:13; 00:17, 03:51, 09:02; sextant star, 45, 018.9, 27.7; boresight star, none available; lift vector, Up. Comments: GDC align, Vega and Deneb, roll 078, pitch 223 [means 233 - corrects later], yaw 340. Additional comments: Use non-exit EMS pattern; EI minus 30 horizon check, GET 194:33:06; pitch 298. You'll get P65, but no P66. Additional note: Initial bank angle in

a11_1914331.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1914331.text: Okay, Ron. For MIDPAC: 000, 152, 001; 194:46:06, 267; plus 13.32, minus 169.17; 06.4; 36194, 6.49; 1404.5, 36275; 195:03:06, 00:28, 1.54, 0.84, 2240, 180, 4.00, 02:13; 00:17, 03:51, 09:02; 45, 018.9, 27.7; none available; lift vector, Up; GDC align, Vega and Deneb, roll 078, pitch 223, yaw 340. Use non-exit EMS. EI minus 30 horizon check, 194:33:06, pitch 298. Initial bank angle in P67 may not be full lift, and we will get P65 but no P66.

a11_1914331.speaker: Evans
a11_1914331.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Roger. On your GDC align pitch, it should be 233, 233 in the pitch. Over.

a11_1914331.speaker: Evans
a11_1914331.text: Also your V L and - and Max and Min, I'm sure, are 22,400 and 18,000. Over.

a11_1914331.speaker: Evans
a11_1914331.text: Okay. If you'll dig out your entry checklist there on page E6-1, I'll update your Retro times there for the various altitudes. Over.

a11_1914331.speaker: Evans
a11_1914331.text: Okay. On page E6-1, your RRT is 07:20, your 50k is 08:16; 40k is 08:30; your 24k is 09:02; and your 10k is 09:51. Over.

a11_1914331.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1914331.text: Okay. RRT, 07:20; 50,000, 08:16. That's - 07:20 is - is the time the steam pressure's pegged from RRT; and 40,000, 08:30; 24,000, 09:02; 10,000, 09:51.

a11_1914331.speaker: Evans
a11_1914331.text: 11, Houston. You started out right, and then the numbers you read back were correct, but I didn't get your comment in between there.

a11_1914331.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1914331.text: I assume that - all I want to know is that first time, 07:20, that's the time of steam pressure peg. Right?

a11_1915805.speaker: Collins
a11_1915805.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Ron, I'm ready to copy your message about the constant drag level.

a11_1915805.speaker: Evans
a11_1915805.text: Okay, Mike. Of course, this is in the event the G&N and the EMS quits and you have to fly the constant-g; and what we're trying to do is to extend the constant-g range from 1,100 to 1,500 miles. We've run this procedure in the simulator, and it works fine. Basically, I'll go through it - just go through it, and then if you have any questions, come back. But it's the same lift vector up until Max g, and then lift vector down, and then modulate the lift vector until g-dot goes to zero. Okay, this procedure is essentially the same so far. And then hold g-dot zero until you pass the Retro elapsed

a11_1915805.speaker: Collins
a11_1915805.text: Okay. It sounds straightforward enough. Understand constant-g backup - back-up procedure, lift vector up until Max g and then lift vector down, then modulate until bank angle - until g-dot equals zero. Maintain g-dot equals zero until subcircular, then roll 45 degrees and hold until drogue time. Over.

a11_1915805.speaker: Evans
a11_1915805.text: Okay. That's mighty fine, Mike. That's correct.

a11_1915805.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1915805.text: This is Apollo Control at 192 hours, 2 minutes. This will be first time in Apollo that crews have flown 'lift vector Up' during re-entry. Normally, lift vector is Down. However, we want to extend the range by 215 miles [400 km] so for a short period, about a minute and 24 - 25 seconds during the blackout period, the spacecraft will be flown with lift vector Up. The computer program for that is number 65, Up control. Apollo 11 is now 25,301 nautical miles [46,857 km] from Earth, velocity has increased to 12,263 feet per second [3,738 m/s].

a11_1930157.speaker: Collins
a11_1930157.text: This entry time line is my kind of time line. Nice and slow.

a11_1930157.speaker: Evans
a11_1930157.text: Okay, 11. Houston. Roger. It sure is. EECOM is anxiously awaiting his big moment here for the logic sequence check whenever you're ready.

a11_1930157.speaker: Collins
a11_1930157.text: Okay. We'll be ready for that in just a flash.

a11_1930157.speaker: Evans
a11_1930157.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a11_1930157.speaker: Lovell
a11_1930157.text: Apollo 11, Houston.

a11_1930157.speaker: Collins
a11_1930157.text: Go ahead, Ron.

a11_1930157.speaker: Lovell
a11_1930157.text: This is Jim, Mike. Backup crew is still standing by. I just want to remind you that the most difficult part of your mission is going to be after recovery.

a11_1930157.speaker: Collins
a11_1930157.text: Well, we're looking forward to all parts of it.

a11_1930157.speaker: Lovell
a11_1930157.text: Please don't sneeze. [Pause.]

a11_1930157.speaker: Collins
a11_1930157.text: Yeah, keep the mice healthy. [Pause.]

a11_1930157.speaker: Collins
a11_1930157.text: The Earth is really getting bigger up here and, of course, we see a crescent.

a11_1930157.speaker: Collins
a11_1930157.text: We've been taking pictures and we've still got four exposures to go, and we'll take those and then pack the camera.

a11_1930157.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1930157.text: And the Apollo 11 backup crew has joined CapCom Ron Evans at his console; Jim Lovell, Bill Anders and Fred Haise. Also Donald K. Slayton, Director of Flight Crew Operations, is at that console.

a11_1930157.speaker: Collins
a11_1930157.text: Houston, Apollo 11. We're ready for the logic check whenever you are. We're standing by to arm the logic. We've got the ELS logic on, ELS Auto, and all the circuit breakers in.

a11_1930157.speaker: Evans
a11_1930157.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Roger. You can press on with the SECS logic.

a11_1930157.speaker: Collins
a11_1930157.text: Okay. Logic 1 coming on.

a11_1930157.speaker: Collins
a11_1930157.text: Mark it.

a11_1930157.speaker: Collins
a11_1930157.text: Logic 2 coming on.

a11_1930157.speaker: Collins
a11_1930157.text: Mark it. [Pause.]

a11_1930157.speaker: Evans
a11_1930157.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Logic checks good. You're Go for Pyro Arm.

a11_1930157.speaker: Collins
a11_1930157.text: Thank you, sir.

a11_1930157.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1930157.text: Houston, Apollo 11 has got VHF A Simplex on whenever you want to make a comm check.

a11_1930157.speaker: Evans
a11_1930157.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Roger. You faded out a little bit there, Buzz. I understand you have the VHF Simplex A on now. Is that correct? Over.

a11_1930157.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1930157.text: That's affirmative. VHF Simplex A and we're TR on VHF.

a11_1930157.speaker: Evans
a11_1930157.text: Roger. Mighty fine. We'll watch it as you're coming on in and let you know when the intelligibility is up and we'll make a voice check with you at that time. [Pause.]

a11_1930157.speaker: Collins
a11_1930157.text: Houston, Apollo 11. I've been holding here in SCS control, Minimum Deadband, Rate Low with the limit cycle on, just as a matter of curiosity, if you guys wanted some fuel numbers from that.

a11_1930157.speaker: Evans
a11_1930157.text: 11, Houston. Roger. We copy and we've been figuring it out.

a11_1930157.speaker: Collins
a11_1930157.text: Okay.

a11_1930157.speaker: Collins
a11_1930157.text: It's a pleasure to be able to waste gas.

a11_1930157.speaker: Evans
a11_1930157.text: Roger. That's affirm.

a11_1930157.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1930157.text: This is Apollo Control at 193 hours, 10 minutes. Apollo 11 now 17,158 nautical miles [31,777 km] from Earth. Velocity; 14,633 feet per second [4,460 m/s].

a11_1931611.speaker: Evans
a11_1931611.text: Apollo 11, Houston with a little Recovery Force information. Over.

a11_1931611.speaker: Evans
a11_1931611.text: Roger. The Hornet is on station just far enough off the target point to keep from getting hit. Recovery 1, or the chopper's there; they're on station. And Hawaii Rescue 1 and 2, the C-130s, are within 40 minutes of your target point. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1931611.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1931611.text: This is Apollo Control at 193 hours, 20 minutes. Apollo 11; 15,854 nautical miles [29,362 km] from Earth. Velocity, 15,154 feet per second [4,619 m/s]. We're just - we're 1 hour, 43 minutes away from entry and here are the altitudes at which the entry events are expected to occur: Entry at 75 statute miles [121 km]; beginning blackout at 62 statute miles [100 km]; 05-g, 57 statute miles [92 km]; end blackout, 41 statute miles [66 km]; drogue chute deployment, 23,300 feet [7,100 metres] and main chute deployment, 10,500 feet [3,200 metres].

a11_1940206.speaker: Evans
a11_1940206.text: Roger. We don't want to jettison the hydrogen tank that's stratified, so could you cycle the fans in Tank 2 please? Hydrogen Tank 2.

a11_1940206.speaker: Collins
a11_1940206.text: You better believe. That old Service Module's taken good care of us. We want to take good care of it.

a11_1940206.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1940206.text: Apollo 11 is 1 hour away now from entry into Earth's atmosphere.

a11_1940206.speaker: Evans
a11_1940206.text: 11, Houston. I'll give you a time hack at 58 minutes to go. It's about 15 seconds yet.

a11_1941000.speaker: Evans
a11_1941000.text: Apollo 11, Houston.

a11_1941000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1941000.text: Go ahead, Houston. Apollo 11.

a11_1941000.speaker: Evans
a11_1941000.text: Rog. We have our updated state vector out there for you. Request P00 and Accept. Over. [Pause.]

a11_1941000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1941000.text: Okay. You've got it.

a11_1941000.speaker: Evans
a11_1941000.text: Okay. Here it comes.

a11_1941000.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1941000.text: Spacecraft distance is 8,393 nautical miles [15,544 km]. Velocity; 19,512 feet per second [5,947 m/s]. Rescue and ARIA aircraft are reported on station, and the Hornet's helicopters containing the swimmers are reported airborne. Swim One is helicopter number 53. Three swimmers from that helo are expected to place the collar on the spacecraft, flotation collar. Crew of Swim One consists of Lieutenant Commander Donald G. Pitchmand, pilot.

a11_1941000.speaker: Evans
a11_1941000.text: Apollo 11, Houston.

a11_1941000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1941000.text: Go ahead.

a11_1941000.speaker: Evans
a11_1941000.text: Roger. The computer is yours now. Looks like you're in VHF range, here. So we'll try a VHF check for you. We'll just send the VHF up to you. Stand by.

a11_1941000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1941000.text: Okay.

a11_1941000.speaker: Evans
a11_1941000.text: Apollo 11, Houston. VHF check on Simplex Alpha. Over.

a11_1941000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1941000.text: Roger, Houston. Apollo 11, VHF Simplex Alpha, loud and clear. How me? Over.

a11_1941000.speaker: Evans
a11_1941000.text: Roger, 11. Houston. You're loud. The standard VHF noise, though, makes you realize that S-band is good.

a11_1941000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1941000.text: Roger. Understand. Thank you. [Long pause.]

a11_1941000.speaker: Evans
a11_1941000.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Backup S-band now, and we're standing by for Command Module RCS activation.

a11_1941000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1941000.text: Okay. We're just about there.

a11_1941000.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1941000.text: Swim One's pilot, Commander Pitchmand, is from Orlando, Florida. Co-pilot Lt. William W. Strawn of Plymouth, Michigan; Crewman James R. Johnson, Raleigh, North Carolina. The swimmers aboard Swim One are Lt JG John McLachlan of Spokane, Washington; Petty Officer 2nd Class Terry A. Muehlenbach, Chatsworth, California; and Petty Officer 3rd Class Mitchell L. Bucklew of Sanford, Florida. These 3 swimmers are scheduled to attach the flotation collar and then move away from the Command Module while helicopter number 66, designated Recovery One, moves into the area and deploys one swimmer, Lt. Clance

a11_1941000.speaker: Evans
a11_1941000.text: Apollo 11, Houston, you're Go for Pyro Arm.

a11_1941000.speaker: Collins
a11_1941000.text: Thank you, Houston.

a11_1941000.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1941000.text: Lt. Clancey Hatelberg of Chippewa Falls, Wisconsin, will deploy from Recovery One wearing a biological isolation garment and he will hand to the crew through the hatch their biological isolation garments. At 194 hours, 16 minutes; Apollo 11 is 7,512 nautical miles [13,912 km] from Earth, velocity 20,304 feet per second [6,189 m/s].

a11_1941000.speaker: Evans
a11_1941000.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Your Command Module pressurization looks mighty fine to us.

a11_1941000.speaker: Armstrong
a11_1941000.text: Looks good here, Ron.

a11_1941000.speaker: Evans
a11_1941000.text: And 11, Houston, I've got an update for about four items on your Entry PAD.

a11_1941000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1941000.text: Ready to copy.

a11_1941000.speaker: Evans
a11_1941000.text: Roger. Your Max-g, 06.3; your Noun 60, your Gamma at 400k, 6.48; your range to go on the EMS, 1403.3; and your Retro time for V-circular, 02:14. Over.

a11_1941000.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1941000.text: Roger. Copy Max g, 6.3; R2 at Noun 60, 6.48; range to go EMS, 14033; RET V-circular, 02:14. Over.

a11_1941000.speaker: Evans
a11_1941000.text: Roger. Readback is correct there.

a11_1941000.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1941000.text: The crew of helicopter 66, Recovery One; the pilot Cdr. D. S. Jones of Madison, Wisconsin; Co-pilot Lt JG Bruce A. Johnson, Bremerton, Washington; and the two crewmen who will assist the astronauts into the Helo; Chief Petty Officer Norvel L. Wood of Carmi, Illinois and Chief Petty Officer Stanley G. Robnett of Portales, Mexico - New Mexico.

a11_1941000.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1941000.text: At 194 hours, 22 minutes; distance is 6,509 nautical miles [12,055 km]. Velocity; 21,366 feet per second [6,512 m/s].

a11_1942437.speaker: Collins
a11_1942437.text: Roger. The first horizon check 194:23:06 at a pitch angle of 298 does not quite fall on the 31 7 line. It's just a little high. It's within 5 degrees tolerance.

a11_1942437.speaker: Evans
a11_1942437.text: Apollo 11, Houston. The horizon check there was supposed to be at 33. Over.

a11_1942437.speaker: Collins
a11_1942437.text: Okay. That's fine, sir. Thank you.

a11_1942437.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1942437.text: Helo number 64 is designated Swim Two. If that helicopter is closer than Swim One to the landing point, swimmers will be deployed from Swim Two to attach the collar. Those swimmers are Lt J.G. Wesley T. Chesser of Arlington, Virginia; 3rd Class Petty Officer Michael G. Mallary of Alderwood Manor, Washington, and Seaman John M. Wolfram of Fort Atkinson, Wisconsin. The Helo's crew consists of pilot, Lt. Richard J. Barrett of Squannanoa [Swannanoa], North Carolina; copilot, Lt. George R. Conn, Imperial Beach, California. Crewmen are Petty Officer 2nd Class Curtis E. Hill, Black Rock, Arkansas, an

a11_1942437.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1942437.text: Apollo 11's distance now 5,411 nautical miles [10,021 km]. Velocity; 22,642 feet per second [6,901 m/s].

a11_1942437.speaker: Evans
a11_1942437.text: Apollo 11, Houston. Command Module RCS looks fine to us.

a11_1942437.speaker: Collins
a11_1942437.text: Same here, Ron. Looks very good. Doesn't make as much noise as we thought. Some of them are barely audible.

a11_1942437.speaker: Evans
a11_1942437.text: And 11, Houston. The weather's still holding real fine in the recovery area.

a11_1942437.speaker: Evans
a11_1942437.text: Looks like it's about 1500 scattered, high scattered. And it's still 3- to 6-foot waves.

a11_1942437.speaker: Collins
a11_1942437.text: The air part of it sounds good.

a11_1942437.speaker: Evans
a11_1942437.text: 11, Houston, I'll give you another Mark at 33 minutes. Stand by.

a11_1943237.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1943237.text: Houston, Apollo 11. Do you have any recommended settings to catch the sunset? Over.

a11_1943237.speaker: Evans
a11_1943237.text: Roger. Well, the time is 36:41. And stand by for some settings.

a11_1943237.speaker: Aldrin
a11_1943237.text: Okay. I'll probably only be doing it maybe - part of it at six frames a second, some of it at one. So I can be changing settings as it goes through.

a11_1943237.speaker: Collins
a11_1943237.text: And the horizon check passes. It's right on the money.

a11_1943237.speaker: Evans
a11_1943237.text: Apollo 11, Houston. On the shooting at the Sun, f:16th at 1 over 250.

a11_1943237.speaker: Collins
a11_1943237.text: And the Sun is going down on schedule. It's getting real dark in here.

a11_1943237.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1943237.text: Distance; 3,896 nautical miles [7,215 km]. Velocity; 24,915 feet per second [7,594 m/s].

a11_1943237.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1943237.text: And we're about 10 minutes away from the scheduled separation time now.

a11_1943237.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1943237.text: Apollo 11's distance now is 3,000 nautical miles [5,556 km]. Velocity; 26,685 feet per second [8,134 m/s]. In the next 20 minutes, Apollo 11 will add almost 10,000 feet per second [3,000 m/s] to that figure.

a11_1943237.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1943237.text: Technical difficulties have interrupted the radio-TV news pool feed from the carrier USS Hornet, and also the newswriters' copy feed from that ship.

a11_1943237.speaker: Mission Control
a11_1943237.text: Guidance Officer reports the Command Module computer looks good and the guidance and navigation system is Go aboard the spacecraft.

a11_1944842.speaker: Evans
a11_1944842.text: Apollo 11, Houston. We see you getting ready for Sep. Everything looks mighty fine down here.
